    <title>Hi, I&#39;m Sunny</title>
    <link href="/2026/05/04/im-sunny"/>
    <updated>2026-05-04T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2026/05/04/im-sunny</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;It is not uncommon to meet people in real life who know this blog. Just the
other day I got to talking to someone who had overheard me discussing some
compiler thing with a colleague and asked if they knew &lt;em&gt;mcyoung.xyz&lt;/em&gt;, and when
they said the recent Go articles were pretty cool, I mentioned it was my blog.&lt;p&gt;I also know I have a pretty big audience because I see some of my more popular
articles mentioned in low-level programming discussions, and because I record
anonymized, public analytics at &amp;lt;varz.mcyoung.xyz&gt;.&lt;p&gt;I can pretty fairly call myself a published author and noted compiler writer,
so I find myself needing to write a note on a relevant life update.&lt;p&gt;Starting from today, I would like to be referred to as Sunny. I am queer and
non-binary, and in gradually transitioning to this name in my personal life I
find it feels much more like me than my old one. Sunny has been my fursona&amp;rsquo;s
name for many years so adopting it has felt natural.&lt;p&gt;Unless you know me personally, I ask that you use they/them pronouns. Please do
not use my old name at all.&lt;p&gt;If you follow my work at all, don&amp;rsquo;t worry, I&amp;rsquo;m not changing my handles. I&amp;rsquo;m
keeping M. C. as initials that don&amp;rsquo;t stand for anything, so all of my initialism
usernames stay the same, and so that anyone who has cited me as &amp;ldquo;Young, M.&amp;rdquo; is
still doing something sensible.</content>

  <entry>
    <title>Breaking the Warranty with go:linkname</title>
    <link href="/2026/03/31/shame"/>
    <updated>2026-03-31T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2026/03/31/shame</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s talk about linker symbols.&lt;p&gt;In C, when you write out a function signature, like this, you are informing the
compiler that a symbol of appropriate ABI will exist at link time.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;malloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size_t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;bytes&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;You can prefix this with &lt;code&gt;extern&lt;/code&gt;, but that&amp;rsquo;s technically not necessary and it
irks me a little when people do it. You can also do this with globals, and in
this case &lt;code&gt;extern&lt;/code&gt; is required:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;somewhere_else&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Will exist at link time&amp;rdquo; means that you are promising the compiler that some
other file contains the same signature, but as a &lt;em&gt;definition&lt;/em&gt;, i.e., no &lt;code&gt;extern&lt;/code&gt;
and, in the case of a function, a body.&lt;p&gt;Of course there is no need for the declaration and definition to line up in ABI.
That isn&amp;rsquo;t even checked at link time. And you can reach into whatever symbols
you want in any library so long as they are not marked as &lt;code&gt;static&lt;/code&gt;, because
C has no notion of symbol visibility beyond a single translation unit (in C,
this is a single &lt;code&gt;.c&lt;/code&gt; file).&lt;p&gt;C++ also has this problem; a much scarier version of it, because C++ has complex
symbol-mangling rules that incorporate the (approximate) type of a symbol into
them, necessary because of overload resolution. You can &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;C++&#34;&lt;/code&gt; other
people&amp;rsquo;s symbols in C++, but it&amp;rsquo;s much harder.&lt;p&gt;Rust &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; has &lt;code&gt;extern&lt;/code&gt;. To declare (but not define) a symbol, you use an
&lt;code&gt;extern &#34;Rust&#34;&lt;/code&gt; block. However, declaring symbols with mangled names in Rust
is much, much harder, because Rust symbol names include the versions of crates
that symbols come from in the form of a hash. This is because Rust allows
multiple versions of the same crate to coexist in one linking artifact, and
this hash disambiguates that in a package-manager agnostic fashion.&lt;p&gt;Go has &lt;code&gt;extern&lt;/code&gt;, except it&amp;rsquo;s a funny magic comment because Go gets weird with
it like that (I hate this).&lt;p&gt;In Go, you can declare a symbol like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;//go:linkname foo_stub github.com/victim/pkg.foo
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;foo_stub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This will instruct the linker that &lt;code&gt;foo_stub&lt;/code&gt; is a local alias for the
symbol &lt;code&gt;github.com/victim/pkg.foo&lt;/code&gt; &amp;ndash; yes, Go symbols outside of the standard
library really do look like that to the linker.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;foo_stub&lt;/code&gt; can also have a body, in which case github.com/victim/pkg.foo
must look like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;//go:linkname foo
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This means that this package is expecting some &lt;em&gt;other&lt;/em&gt; package to define one
of its symbols for it.&lt;p&gt;Now, this is a huge problem, because in the former variant, there is no
requirement that the victim package consents to having its symbol table rummaged
in. Go only addressed this in Go 1.23, where now, for standard library packages
only, only symbols explicitly opted into &lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt; can be used like this by
non-standard library packages.&lt;p&gt;The upshot is phew, we solved this problem, why am I writing about it.&lt;p&gt;Well &amp;ndash; because it left behind some lovely official-unofficial APIs.&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;I am going to be very snarky. I am being snarky because: (a) I am friends with
the people who are thanklessly cleaning up this mess and (b) I do &lt;em&gt;gestures
exasperatedly at programming languages&lt;/em&gt; for a living.&lt;p&gt;I am like this about every programming language, as my friends who work on
rustc can tell you.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=the-hall-of-shame&gt;&lt;a href=#the-hall-of-shame&gt;The Hall of Shame&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;When closing the linkname hole, the Go project surveyed existing modules with
50+ dependents that were very naughty and used runtime symbols inappropriately,
and they compiled a list of all such symbols.&lt;p&gt;These symbols have a trivial &lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt; comment allowing them to continue to be
&lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt;d without breaking anyone, along with very stern admonitions and a
list of notable perpetrators. You can find all of these comments by
&lt;a href=&#34;https://cs.opensource.google/search?q=%22Notable%20members%20of%20the%20hall%20of%20shame%20include%22&amp;ss=go%2Fgo&#34;&gt;searching for the admonition&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;In practice, this means these symbols will be supported forever and ever to
prevent wide ecosystem breakage.&lt;p&gt;But writing the &lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt; stubs is very error prone. You have to match the
signature exactly, but not so exactly that you use the names of unexported
types. So you need to know enough about Go&amp;rsquo;s ABI to know what you can change.
You also probably want to mark some things as &lt;code&gt;//go:noescape&lt;/code&gt;. Escape analysis
conservatively assumes that body-less functions always escape their arguments.
This assumption can be lifted with this &lt;em&gt;other&lt;/em&gt; magic comment.&lt;p&gt;Knowing which functions are safe to &lt;code&gt;//go:noescape&lt;/code&gt; is finicky business. That&amp;rsquo;s
where I come in.&lt;p&gt;I wrote a &lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/shame&gt;fun little library&lt;/a&gt; which uses the
admonition to automatically generate bindings for every naughty &lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt; in
the standard library.&lt;p&gt;I did this for a few reasons.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;I have a love-hate relationship with Go. The language itself is gross and
warty but the runtime is very fun. I file &lt;a href=&#34;https://github.com/golang/go/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20author%3Amcy&#34;&gt;weird bugs&lt;/a&gt; against it.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;A flavor of harm reduction. Not documenting the naughty things you could do
leads to people who are &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; compiler nerds into reverse engineering how
language implementation details without knowing why, and wind up hurting
themselves. I would rather there be something well-documented they can
reach for instead.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;A few of the core Go maintainers are friends of mine, and I kind of wonder
if they will be more amused or annoyed that I did this&amp;mldr;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;h2 id=notable-members&gt;&lt;a href=#notable-members&gt;Notable Members&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The top-level package &lt;code&gt;shame&lt;/code&gt; provides nicely-named, documented wrappers to the
most useful of the bindings (in my opinion). Most have to do with low-level
memory operations. There &lt;em&gt;are&lt;/em&gt; scheduler stubs, but I don&amp;rsquo;t provide wrappers
for those because attempting to interact directly with the scheduler is like
sneaking up on a skittish mule from behind.&lt;p&gt;The main non-wrapper thing is &lt;code&gt;*shame.Type&lt;/code&gt;, which is just a wrapper over
&lt;code&gt;*internal/abi.Type&lt;/code&gt;. The latter actually has survived leaking out into the
real world&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, but most of the interesting operations require one.&lt;p&gt;You can easily get one from either an &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt; of that type, or a &lt;code&gt;reflect.Type&lt;/code&gt;,
by either ripping the type pointer out of the &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt; (which is literally an
&lt;code&gt;*abi.Type&lt;/code&gt;), or the data pointer out of the &lt;code&gt;reflect.Type&lt;/code&gt;. &lt;code&gt;*shame.Type&lt;/code&gt;
organizes these operations into a type, to bridge the unchecked but fast
operations of &lt;code&gt;shame&lt;/code&gt; with the safe but slow &lt;code&gt;reflect&lt;/code&gt; package.&lt;h3 id=direct-allocator-calls&gt;&lt;a href=#direct-allocator-calls&gt;Direct Allocator Calls&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;For me, the two most interesting wrapper functions are &lt;code&gt;shame.Alloc&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;shame.Grow&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;shame.Alloc&lt;/code&gt; directly calls &lt;code&gt;runtime.mallocgc&lt;/code&gt;, which allocates from the heap.
It takes a size, a type (which is used to get a GC shape for the allocation)
and whether or not to zero the result. What&amp;rsquo;s interesting is that Go provides
&lt;em&gt;no way to get unzeroed memory&lt;/em&gt;, by design: it is very difficult to use such
memory safely. In fact, &lt;code&gt;mallocgc&lt;/code&gt; will still require that memory which will
contain pointers is zeroed, since otherwise the GC could get very confused.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;TypeFor&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Pointer&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;buf&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Alloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;true&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The other interesting bit, of course, is that you can allocate memory of
arbitrary shape without needing to go through reflection. This is&amp;mldr; less
immediately interesting than being able to dodge the zeroing cost.&lt;p&gt;The latter is the slice resizing primitive that &lt;code&gt;append&lt;/code&gt; can call:
&lt;code&gt;runtime.growslice&lt;/code&gt;. This is Go&amp;rsquo;s version of &lt;code&gt;realloc&lt;/code&gt;, which takes a pointer,
a size, and a desired new size, resizing the underlying storage if necessary
and copying elements into the new buffer.&lt;p&gt;The Go version is much more powerful. It will only copy elements within a
specific prefix of the buffer, and you only tell it how many elements you want
to add; it returns the new capacity, which snaps to the next allocator size
class. &lt;code&gt;append&lt;/code&gt; will show this behavior: &lt;code&gt;make([]T, 0, n)&lt;/code&gt; always has a capacity
of &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;, but &lt;code&gt;append([]T(nil), make([]T, n)...)&lt;/code&gt; may have a larger capacity.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Allocate 56 (rounded up to a size class) bytes of
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// uninitialized memory.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Grow&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Slice&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{},&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;TypeFor&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;byte&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;](),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;56&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Like &lt;code&gt;shame.Alloc&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;shame.Grow&lt;/code&gt; will return uninitialized memory in some cases.
This is because calls to &lt;code&gt;runtime.growslice&lt;/code&gt; generated by the compiler are
followed up by an appropriate call to &lt;code&gt;runtime.memmove&lt;/code&gt; to add the new elements,
so zeroing that region, if it is pointer-free, is wasteful.&lt;p&gt;While &lt;code&gt;shame.Alloc&lt;/code&gt; does not provide large benefits over &lt;code&gt;reflect.New&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;shame.Grow&lt;/code&gt; is much more powerful than &lt;code&gt;reflect.AppendSlice&lt;/code&gt;. This is because
&lt;code&gt;reflect.AppendSlice&lt;/code&gt; does offer an equivalent to the &lt;code&gt;append(xs, make([]T, n)...)&lt;/code&gt;
idiom (i.e., what &lt;code&gt;slices.Grow&lt;/code&gt; does).&lt;p&gt;The compiler recognizes the latter pattern and instead of rewriting it
into &lt;code&gt;runtime.growslice&lt;/code&gt; followed by &lt;code&gt;runtime.memmove&lt;/code&gt;, it follows it up
with a call to &lt;code&gt;runtime.memclrNoHeapPointers&lt;/code&gt; instead (if &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; is pointer-free;
if &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; has pointers, the memory is zeroed automatically by the allocator).&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;shame.Alloc&lt;/code&gt; also helps avoid having to interact with &lt;code&gt;runtime.growslice&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s
weird ABI (the ABI is the way it is for the benefit of register allocation).&lt;h3 id=heap-queries&gt;&lt;a href=#heap-queries&gt;Heap Queries&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is some limited functionality for asking the GC about pointers. One
important feature of Go&amp;rsquo;s GC is that it can handle &lt;em&gt;internal pointers&lt;/em&gt;: given
any pointer the GC knows about, it can calculate the base address for the
corresponding GC allocation, as well as the corresponding GC memory page.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;shame.FindObject&lt;/code&gt; gives access to this feature. You can use it to stick
finalizers on any random pointer, or, given a pointer into a slice allocated
by &lt;code&gt;make&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;append&lt;/code&gt;, the base address of the slice.&lt;p&gt;A related function used to implement &lt;code&gt;-d=checkptr&lt;/code&gt; can be used to determine if
a pointer came from the stack. &lt;code&gt;shame.IsStackPointer&lt;/code&gt; offers this functionality.&lt;h3 id=dynamic-map-operations&gt;&lt;a href=#dynamic-map-operations&gt;Dynamic Map Operations&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;You can already perform dynamic operations on maps using reflection, but they
can trigger unnecessary allocations. But someone &lt;code&gt;linknamed&lt;/code&gt; every single
map shim, so we can use them directly.&lt;p&gt;You can also get access to pointers &lt;em&gt;into&lt;/em&gt; a map, allowing for much faster
RMW operations.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;upsert&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;m&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;map&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;k&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;...&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;MapAssignString&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;TypeOf&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;m&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;shame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;MapData&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;m&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;k&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;append&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;...&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;MapAssign*&lt;/code&gt; family of functions will look up a value, or allocate a fresh
entry for it, and return a pointer to that value for the caller to mutate.
Unfortunately, the API will not tell you if the returned value was freshly
allocated or not.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;MapIndex*&lt;/code&gt; family of functions can be used to obtain pointers to values in
a map, which makes it easy to avoid the cost of copying a large value of a map
and then copying it back in (in normal-people Go, this is achieved by using
&lt;code&gt;map[K]*V&lt;/code&gt; instead).&lt;p&gt;And of course, these functions, along with &lt;code&gt;shame.MapDelete&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;shame.NewMapIter&lt;/code&gt;,
allow for dynamic map operations without the potential escape-to-heap costs of
reflection.&lt;h3 id=data-race-generator&gt;&lt;a href=#data-race-generator&gt;Data Race Generator&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is one other fun API: &lt;code&gt;shame.ChanIndex&lt;/code&gt;. This will extract the &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;th
element from the ring buffer inside of a channel. What does this mean, exactly?&lt;p&gt;Every Go channel is secretly a ring buffer with a mutex in front of it plus a
lockless list for holding waiters. Sending to a channel locks the mutex, pushes
to the list, and unlocks the mutex. Receiving pulls from the list. It&amp;rsquo;s a little
fussier than that because of the need to handle waiters: sending on an empty
channel wakes some goroutine blocked on it, and sending on a full channel blocks
until a goroutine receives.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;shame.ChanIndex&lt;/code&gt; doesn&amp;rsquo;t care about any of that. It just indexes into the
buffer that backs the linked list without looking at the lock or anything else.
This is exactly as useful as you think: it gives you an approximately random
value drawn from the recent sends on the channel, potentially racing with
a receiving goroutine if you decide to write to that pointer.&lt;p&gt;I included this API because I think it&amp;rsquo;s very funny someone &lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt;d this.&lt;h2 id=should-i-use-it&gt;&lt;a href=#should-i-use-it&gt;Should I Use It?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Lol, no. This is about harm reduction. If you were already going to do this,
this makes the thing you were going to do much less dangerous, but it&amp;rsquo;s still
a poor life decision.&lt;p&gt;I actually didn&amp;rsquo;t know the full breadth of exactly what had survived the
&lt;code&gt;linkname&lt;/code&gt; purge of 2024 before I did this, so I&amp;rsquo;m kinda glad I did. It was also
fun tracking down the uses that lead to this, because you might of many of those
libraries &amp;ldquo;oh, I bet they had a really good reason&amp;rdquo;. The answer will often
disappoint you. :P&lt;p&gt;If I were in the Go project&amp;rsquo;s shoes (and you should be glad I&amp;rsquo;m not) I would
have just broken everyone. This kind of reaching into internal APIs needs to
be punished, or else the inexorable march of Hyrum&amp;rsquo;s law will take you to the
dark place C++ has been in for the last decade, where they are incapable of
upgrading basic algorithm implementations because of ABI promises Microsoft
made for them.&lt;p&gt;And I say this as a serial abuser of this kind of thing. Go has been making
a lot of strides in being serious about performance. I&amp;rsquo;ve spent a lot of time
giving the project serious feedback on their very bold SIMD intrinsics effort,
and they take my missed optimization bugs seriously&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;I mean, use my library. I will gladly help you come to terms with your mistakes
after you break something. :)&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Well, you can do things like this, but it really gets into &amp;ldquo;keep both
pieces&amp;rdquo; territory&amp;mldr;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;import&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;reflect&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ptrbytes&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;_&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;reflect&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;ValueOf&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;reflect&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;TypeFor&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]()).&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Elem&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Field&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;).&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Type&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;

tracker making me reluctant to do anything less esoteric than filing

  <entry>
    <title>Optimization Countermeasures</title>
    <link href="/2025/12/15/value-barriers"/>
    <updated>2025-12-15T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/12/15/value-barriers</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Silicon designers are bad at designing secure hardware. &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectre_(security_vulnerability)&gt;Embarrassingly so&lt;/a&gt;, sometimes. This means
that low-level cryptography, as well as code which directly handles key material,
often needs to be written in a particularly delicate style called &amp;ldquo;constant-time&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Constant-time&amp;rdquo; is a bit of a misnomer. It does not mean that the code&amp;rsquo;s time
complexity is &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:1em;vertical-align:-.25em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.02778em&gt;O&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mopen&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mclose&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; (although this is a closely related property).
Constant-time is a threat model for side-channel timing attacks like Spectre,
which ensures that key material is not leaked through the microarchitecture of
CPUs.&lt;p&gt;Although constant-time is a powerful countermeasure against the silicon
designers leaking our keys, the compiler can still screw us. However, there are
magic incantations that can be offered to the compiler to make it behave
correctly in many relevant situations.&lt;p&gt;First: what is constant-time?&lt;h2 id=the-constant-time-threat-model&gt;&lt;a href=#the-constant-time-threat-model&gt;The Constant-Time Threat Model&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The actual threat model is a series of assumptions about the most advanced
attacker we wish to defeat. The assumptions, as applied to a cryptography
software library, are as follows:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The attacker has access to both the source code of the library, the compiled
artifact linking in the the library, the toolchain used to build it, and any
relevant compiler flags (this is true, for example, for an Internet browser).&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The attacker has a complete trace of every program counter value visited by
the program. This is not the same as an instruction trace, which will usually
also record software-visible architectural state at each instruction.
Attackers can often obtain this information by directly timing the software,
since the relevant information is mostly branches-taken. This includes
instructions executed in a privileged mode, such as within the kernel.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The attacker knows the address of every pointer stored or loaded by the
program. That is, each program counter value in the above is annotated with
the values of registers containing pointers relevant to that instruction,
such as the pointer for a load instruction. This data can be obtained through
data cache side-channels such as Spectre.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Programming against this model defeats virtually all known timing side-channel
attacks, although it does not protect against other side-channel attacks, such
as thermal and power analysis.&lt;h3 id=new-footguns&gt;&lt;a href=#new-footguns&gt;New Footguns&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;All cryptography libraries that are safe to use in 2025 implement all of their
critical code in constant-time. This model has broad consequences what kinds of
programs are allowed.&lt;p&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s wrong with this code?&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;int8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;key&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;...&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;k&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;key&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;k&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;k&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;k&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because we are looping over &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;, we immediately leak &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;, because the attacker
can count the number of loop iterations. If &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; is secret, this is a problem.&lt;p&gt;We also leak one eight of the bits in the key: the attacker can see which
loop iterations contain a negation instruction; those iterations correspond
to bytes which had their sign bit set.&lt;p&gt;To protect the value of &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;, we would have to ensure that there is some maximum
value &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt; of &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;, and that &lt;code&gt;key&lt;/code&gt; was allocated to an at-least-&lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt;-byte buffer;
the loop would then be over &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt;, making no reference to &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;. This is a relatively
uncommon situation, since the length of a buffer is almost never a secret in
practice.&lt;p&gt;Protecting the sign bits is simpler: rather than branching to determine if
the value should be negated, we can mask off the sign bit: &lt;code&gt;key[i] &amp;= 0x7f&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h3 id=buffer-comparisons&gt;&lt;a href=#buffer-comparisons&gt;Buffer Comparisons&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Many standard library functions are not constant-time. For example, &lt;code&gt;memcmp&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s
runtime is not constant in the size of its inputs; most implementations break
out early when encountering an unequal value:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;memcmp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;diff&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;diff&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;      &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;diff&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now suppose we have the following code to verify a signature:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;msg&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;...;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;expected&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;compute_signature&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;msg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;body&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;private_key&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;memcmp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;msg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;signature&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;expected&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;==&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Assume msg is authentic.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The attacker can use this as a signing oracle. By providing sending the desired
message to sign with a bad signature, they can determine the first byte of the
signature which is incorrect by timing alone, and brute force that byte. They
can then proceed to the next byte, and so on. The maximum number of queries to
forge a signature is &lt;code&gt;256&lt;/code&gt; times the number of bits, reducing the cost from
&lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:1em;vertical-align:-.25em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.02778em&gt;O&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mopen&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.6644em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal mtight&#34;&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mclose&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; to &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:1em;vertical-align:-.25em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.02778em&gt;O&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mopen&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mclose&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;!&lt;p&gt;To defeat this attack, we need to use constant-time &lt;code&gt;memcmp&lt;/code&gt;. This means that
every byte must be compared, and the comparison must be accumulated without
branching.&lt;p&gt;The typical implementation is something like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;ct_memeq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;acc&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;acc&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;|=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;^&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;acc&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;==&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If at least one byte differs between &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;, their xor will be non-zero,
and so &lt;code&gt;acc&lt;/code&gt; will be nonzero. This function only compares for exact equality,
not lexicographic equality, but the latter is never an operation you want or
need on keys and other sensitive data.&lt;p&gt;There are many variants on this implementation, but the xor one is the most
popular. Subtraction will achieve a similar result (although signed overflow
is UB in C++).&lt;h3 id=constant-time-select&gt;&lt;a href=#constant-time-select&gt;Constant-Time Select&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;A similar trick is used to select one of two values. The ternary operator
cannot be used because it can be compiled into a branch.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:ct_select&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ct_select&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;~&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:ct_select&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If &lt;code&gt;flag&lt;/code&gt; is true, &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt; is the all-ones representation for &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt;, so &lt;code&gt;a &amp; mask&lt;/code&gt;
is &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;b &amp; ~mask&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt;, so their or is &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;. If &lt;code&gt;flag&lt;/code&gt; is false, the
opposite is true.&lt;p&gt;On x86, Clang recognizes this idiom and produces a conditional move instruction,
which does not violate the threat model. However, on architectures without
conditional move, such as RISC-V, Clang still recognizes the pattern&amp;mldr; but
produces a branch.&lt;div class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-x86 highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;_Z9ct_selectIiET_bS0_S0_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mov&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;esi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;test&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;edi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;edi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;cmove&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;edx&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;_Z9ct_selectIiET_bS0_S0_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;bnez&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;LBB0_2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mv&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;LBB0_2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mv&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;You might want to point the finger at the &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt;, but this actually goes much
deeper than that. This type of unwanted optimization happens all the time
in constant-time code, and preventing it is essential to ensure that the
countermeasure works.&lt;p&gt;The &amp;ldquo;easy&amp;rdquo; solution is to just write the assembly directly, which is the case
for performance-critical parts of cryptography implementations, but this is
error-prone and not portable.&lt;p&gt;Thankfully, all modern native compilers provide a hidden feature to block
optimizations inimical to security, and what this post is really about:
the &lt;em&gt;value barrier&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;h2 id=an-incantation&gt;&lt;a href=#an-incantation&gt;An Incantation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The value barrier is a special secret syntax construct that instructs the
compiler to ignore information it could use to prove the correctness of
optimizations.&lt;p&gt;For example, the reason Clang is able to &amp;ldquo;defeat&amp;rdquo; our
&lt;a href=#code:ct_select&gt;&lt;code&gt;ct_select&lt;/code&gt; implementation&lt;/a&gt; is that it knows from &lt;code&gt;-T(flag)&lt;/code&gt;
that &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt; must be either &lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;-1&lt;/code&gt;. If we can hide this fact from Clang,
it will be forced to not emit the branch.&lt;p&gt;One way we can do this is to &amp;ldquo;encrypt&amp;rdquo; &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt; with a value that Clang cannot
see through, such as a global variable:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:xor-barrier&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kr&gt;inline&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;key&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ct_select&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;^=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;key&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;~&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:xor-barrier&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Clang cannot know what the value of &lt;code&gt;key&lt;/code&gt; will be at runtime, because code in
another translation unit might set it. It must therefore assume it knows nothing
about &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt; and the return value could be an arbitrary bit-mix of &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;.

function call is also treated as having side-effects by the compiler, which
impedes desirable optimizations.&lt;p&gt;But a small modification will eliminate this problem: we can simply use an

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;~&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;

register-sized value in-place as a no-op. The &lt;code&gt;&#34;+r&#34;&lt;/code&gt; constraint indicates that
the assembly takes &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt; as an input, and outputs a result onto &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt;, in the
same register.&lt;p&gt;This has the same effect as the xor-with-key solution (prevents optimizations
that depend on the value of &lt;code&gt;mask&lt;/code&gt;) without the load from a global. It&amp;rsquo;s
architecture-independent, because &lt;code&gt;&#34;&#34;&lt;/code&gt; is a valid inline assembly block
regardless of underlying assembly language.&lt;p&gt;The value barrier is often written as its own function (with a massive comment
explaining what it does), to be used in key points in cryptographic algorithms.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:10&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;

but has a profound effect on optimizations.&lt;h2 id=dataflow&gt;&lt;a href=#dataflow&gt;Dataflow&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;A better name for the value barrier is the &amp;ldquo;dataflow barrier&amp;rdquo;, because that more

you&amp;rsquo;ll know that every optimization compiler today puts a heavy emphasis on
dataflow analysis. To figure out how to optimize some operation, we look at its
inputs&amp;rsquo; definitions.&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s look at what LLVM sees when we compile &lt;a href=#code:ct_select&gt;&lt;code&gt;ct_select&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;,
setting &lt;code&gt;T = int&lt;/code&gt; (I have manually lifted everything into registers).&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-llvm highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@_Z9ct_selectIiET_bS0_S0_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;zeroext&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;zext&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%flag&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;to&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c&gt;; int(flag)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;sub&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;nsw&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=c&gt;; mask = 0 - int(flag)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%3&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;and&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=c&gt;; a &amp;amp; mask
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%4&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;xor&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;-1&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=c&gt;; mask ^ -1
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%5&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;and&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%4&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=c&gt;; b &amp;amp; (mask ^ -1)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%6&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;or&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%5&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=c&gt;; (a &amp;amp; mask) | (b &amp;amp; (mask ^ -1))
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%6&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM contains pattern-matching code that matches this code (and various
permutations of it) as a &amp;ldquo;select&amp;rdquo; idiom. LLVM contains an instruction that
selects one of two values based on an &lt;code&gt;i1&lt;/code&gt;, called &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;. It is essentially
the C ternary with SSA register arguments.&lt;p&gt;The pattern-matching code looks for an &lt;code&gt;or&lt;/code&gt; whose arguments are both &lt;code&gt;and&lt;/code&gt;s,
where one argument to the &lt;code&gt;and&lt;/code&gt; is the complement of the other (i.e, xor with &lt;code&gt;-1&lt;/code&gt;).
Call this argument is the &amp;ldquo;mask&amp;rdquo;.
What LLVM has found is a general &amp;ldquo;bit-mixing&amp;rdquo; operations which selects bits from the other
operands to the &lt;code&gt;and&lt;/code&gt;s, depending on which bits of the mask are set.&lt;p&gt;LLVM then wants to prove that the mask is either &lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;-1&lt;/code&gt; (all ones). There
are a number of ways LLVM can discover this, but all of them essentially boil
down to &amp;ldquo;is the mask a &lt;code&gt;sext i1&lt;/code&gt;, i.e., sign-extending a one-bit value&amp;rdquo;. That
does not occur in this code, but a peephole optimization can rewrite
&lt;code&gt;sub nsw i32 0, %1&lt;/code&gt; into &lt;code&gt;sext i1 %0 to i32&lt;/code&gt;, allowing this more complicated
pattern to be detected.&lt;p&gt;LLVM rewrites this into a &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;, which on x86 turns into a &lt;code&gt;cmov&lt;/code&gt;, but on
RISC-V forces a branch.&lt;p&gt;All we need to do is prevent LLVM from looking through to the definition of the
&amp;ldquo;mask&amp;rdquo;. That is precisely what the value barrier accomplishes: it inserts
a new SSA register whose value is, at runtime, equivalent to the mask, but
produced by an instruction that LLVM doesn&amp;rsquo;t have implement dataflow for.
That is the value barrier: an intentional hole left in the compiler&amp;rsquo;s analysis.&lt;p&gt;In theory, LLVM can actually see that the inline assembly block is empty and
optimize it out. However, it does not by design, because cryptography depends on
it remaining an optimization barrier. In fact, LLVM (and GCC) emit special
annotations around inline assembly to stop downstream tools, such as linker
optimizations and post-link optimizers like BOLT, from accidentally optimizing
sensitive sequences. In an assembly dump from LLVM, those regions look like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;_Z9ct_selectIiET_bS0_S0_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mov&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;esi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;neg&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;edi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=cp&gt;#APP
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=cp&gt;#NO_APP
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;xor&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;edx&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;and&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;edi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;xor&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;edx&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;These are just comments; the actual sensitive regions are recorded elsewhere in
the resulting object code.&lt;h3 id=what-does-the-barrier-do&gt;&lt;a href=#what-does-the-barrier-do&gt;What Does the Barrier Do?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The programming model for the value barrier is simple: it produces an arbitrary
value that, at runtime, happens to be bitwise-identical to its input. The
compiler may still make assumptions about the input value, but it cannot connect
them to the output of the barrier through dataflow.&lt;p&gt;In other words, the value barrier is simply a register copy that also severs
the dataflow link from the destination to the source operand.&lt;p&gt;The compiler is still allowed to optimized based on the assumption that this
is some unknown concrete value. For example:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;random&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;value_barrier&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;42&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;x - x&lt;/code&gt; is always zero, so LLVM can optimize away the value barrier and its
input altogether. Critically, the value barrier &lt;em&gt;does not have side effects&lt;/em&gt;,
so if its result is not used, the value barrier will be deleted through dead
code elimination. The following does not work:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ct_select&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;value_barrier&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Unused result warning.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;~&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mask&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because it is side-effect-free, it can also be hoisted out of loops and
conditionals, which is actually a desirable optimization.&lt;h3 id=benchmark-black-box&gt;&lt;a href=#benchmark-black-box&gt;Benchmark Black Box&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is a related function that appears in benchmarking code, which is not
equivalent to the value barrier:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;black_box&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;asm&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;volatile&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;m&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This function guarantees that its input is treated as &amp;ldquo;used&amp;rdquo; by the compiler,
even if it is side-effect free. Rather than blocking dataflow, it blocks
dead code elimination.&lt;p&gt;It works because &lt;code&gt;asm volatile&lt;/code&gt; must be treated as having observable
side-effects that depend on all of its inputs. This means that it cannot be
deleted, hoisted our of loops, or executed speculatively.&lt;p&gt;A benchmark black box is most commonly used to force the result of a function
being benchmarked to not be deleted by the compiler, so that the runtime of
that function can be accurately measured. It &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt; in place of the value barrier,
because the &lt;code&gt;&#34;m&#34;&lt;/code&gt; constraint passes a pointer to the argument into the assembly
block, which it could potentially mutate. However, this is not guaranteed to
work in the same way that the value barrier does: it depends on whether the
surface language (C++ or Rust) considers mutating through that pointer to be
UB.&lt;p&gt;Using the actual value barrier avoids this altogether.&lt;h3 id=unintended-consequences&gt;&lt;a href=#unintended-consequences&gt;Unintended Consequences&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The value barrier works very well at blocking undesirable optimizations, but
it obstructs a few important ones, making its use problematic in
performance-sensitive scenarios.&lt;p&gt;A particularly notable one is automatic vectorization. Consider this function:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;uint64_t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;sum&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;uint64_t&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;~&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;31&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Round n to the nearest multiple of 32.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;u64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
