&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;      &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;body&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;body&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;np&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;bp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;):&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;load&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;load&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;bp&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;c&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;add&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;store&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;store&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;bp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;c&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;load&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;np&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mf&gt;.2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;sub&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;store&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;np&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mf&gt;.2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;goto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;np&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;bp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;exit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;):&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;load&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;goto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:fib-memory&gt;SSA-CFG&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Any time we reference a named variable, we load from its stack slot, and any
time we assign it, we store to that slot. This is very easy to get into from C,
but the code sucks because it&amp;rsquo;s doing lots of unnecessary pointer operations.
How do we get from this to the register-only function I showed earlier?&lt;blockquote id=aside:2 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;We want program order to not matter for the purposes of reordering, but as
we&amp;rsquo;ve written code here, program order &lt;em&gt;does&lt;/em&gt; matter: loads depend on prior
stores but stores don&amp;rsquo;t produce a value that can be used to link the two
operations.&lt;p&gt;We can restore not having program order by introducing operands representing
an &amp;ldquo;address space&amp;rdquo;; loads and stores take an address space as an argument, and
stores return a new address space. An address space, or &lt;code&gt;mem&lt;/code&gt;, represents the
state of some region of memory. Loads and stores are independent when they are
not connected by a &lt;code&gt;mem&lt;/code&gt; argument.&lt;p&gt;This type of enhancement is used by Go&amp;rsquo;s SSA IR, for example. However, it adds
a layer of complexity to the examples, so instead I will hand-wave this away.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=the-dominance-relation&gt;&lt;a href=#the-dominance-relation&gt;The Dominance Relation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now we need to prove some properties about CFGs that are important for the
definition and correctness of our optimization passes.&lt;p&gt;First, some definitions.&lt;blockquote id=def:1 class=def def math&gt;&lt;a href=#def:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;definition&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;strong&gt;predecessors&lt;/strong&gt; (or &amp;ldquo;preds&amp;rdquo;) of a basic block is the set of blocks with
an outgoing edge &lt;strong&gt;to&lt;/strong&gt; that block. A block may be its own predecessors.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Some literature calls the above &amp;ldquo;direct&amp;rdquo; or immediate predecessors. For example,
the preds of in our &lt;a href=#code:fib-memory&gt;example&lt;/a&gt; are &lt;code&gt;@loop.start&lt;/code&gt; are &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt;
(the special name for the function entry-point) &lt;code&gt;@loop.body&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=def:2 class=def def math&gt;&lt;a href=#def:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;definition&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;strong&gt;successors&lt;/strong&gt; (no, not &amp;ldquo;succs&amp;rdquo;) of a basic block is the set of blocks
with an outgoing edge &lt;strong&gt;from&lt;/strong&gt; that block. A block may be its own successors.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;The sucessors of &lt;code&gt;@loop.start&lt;/code&gt; are &lt;code&gt;@exit&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;@loop.body&lt;/code&gt;. The successors are
listed in the loop&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;If a block &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; is a transitive pred of a block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, we say that &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; &lt;em&gt;weakly
dominates&lt;/em&gt; &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, or that it is a &lt;em&gt;weak dominator&lt;/em&gt; of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. For example,
&lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;@loop.start&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;@loop.body&lt;/code&gt; both weakly dominate &lt;code&gt;@exit&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;However, this is not usually an especially useful relationship. Instead, we want
to speak of dominators:&lt;blockquote id=def:3 class=def def math&gt;&lt;a href=#def:3&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;definition&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;A block &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; is a &lt;strong&gt;dominator&lt;/strong&gt; (or &lt;strong&gt;dominates&lt;/strong&gt;) &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; if every pred of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;
is dominated by &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;, or if &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; itself.&lt;p&gt;Equivalently, the dominator set of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is the intersection of the dominator
sets of its preds, plus &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;The dominance relation has some nice order properties that are necessary for
defining the core graph algorithms of SSA.&lt;h3 id=some-graph-theory&gt;&lt;a href=#some-graph-theory&gt;Some Graph Theory&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;We only consider CFGs which are flowgraphs, that is, all blocks are reachable
from the root block &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt;, which has no preds. This is necessary to eliminate
some pathological graphs from our proofs. Importantly, we can always ask for an
acyclic path&lt;sup id=fnref:11&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:11 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;11&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to any block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;An equivalent way to state the dominance relationship is that from every path
from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; contains all of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s dominators.&lt;blockquote id=prop:1 class=prop prop math&gt;&lt;a href=#prop:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;proposition&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; iff every path from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; contains &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=proof:1 class=proof proof&gt;&lt;a href=#proof:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;proof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;First, assume every &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; path contains &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;. If &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;,
we&amp;rsquo;re done. Otherwise we need to prove each predecessor of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is dominated
by &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;; we do this by induction on the length of acyclic paths from
&lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. Consider preds &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt; of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; that are not &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;, and
consider all acyclic paths &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt;; by appending &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; to
them, we have an acyclic path &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.9463em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.7519em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;′&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, which must
contain &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;. Because both the last and second-to-last elements of this are
not &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;, it must be within the shorter path &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; which is shorter than
&lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.9463em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.7519em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;′&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;. Thus, by induction, &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt; and therefore &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;&lt;p&gt;Going the other way, if &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, and consider a path &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; from
&lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. The second-to-last element of &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; is a pred &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt; of
&lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;; if it is &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; we are done. Otherwise, we can consider the path &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
made by deleting &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; at the end. &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt; is dominated by &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.9463em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.7519em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;′&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; is
shorter than &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;, so we can proceed by induction as above.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Onto those nice properties. Dominance allows us to take an arbitrarily
complicated CFG and extract from it a DAG, composed of blocks ordered by
dominance.&lt;blockquote id=thm:1 class=thm thm math&gt;&lt;a href=#thm:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;theorem&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The dominance relation is a partial order.&lt;blockquote id=proof:2 class=proof proof&gt;&lt;a href=#proof:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;proof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Dominance is reflexive and transitive by definition, so we only need to show
blocks can&amp;rsquo;t dominate each other.&lt;p&gt;Suppose distinct &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; dominate each other.Pick an acyclic path&lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;. Because &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; dominates &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;, there is a prefix &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.9463em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.7519em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;′&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
of this path ending in &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. But because &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, some prefix
&lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.9463em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.7519em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;′′&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; of &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.9463em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=msupsub&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-t&gt;&lt;span class=vlist-r&gt;&lt;span class=vlist style=height:.7519em&gt;&lt;span style=top:-3.063em;margin-right:.05em&gt;&lt;span class=pstrut style=height:2.7em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mtight&#34;&gt;′&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; ends in &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;. But now &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.625em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; must contain &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; twice,
contradicting that it is acyclic.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;This allows us to write &lt;code&gt;@a &amp;lt; @b&lt;/code&gt; when &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. There is an even
more refined graph structure that we can build out of dominators, which follows
immediately from the partial order theorem.&lt;blockquote id=cor:1 class=cor cor math&gt;&lt;a href=#cor:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;corollary&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The dominators of a basic block are totally ordered by the dominance relation.&lt;blockquote id=proof:3 class=proof proof&gt;&lt;a href=#proof:3&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;proof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Suppose &lt;code&gt;@a1 &amp;lt; @b&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;@a2 &amp;lt; @b&lt;/code&gt;, but neither dominates the other. Then,
there must exist acyclic paths from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; which contain both, but
in different orders. Take the subpaths of those paths which follow
&lt;code&gt;@entry ... @a1&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;@a1 ... @b&lt;/code&gt;, neither of which contains &lt;code&gt;@a2&lt;/code&gt;.
Concatenating these paths yields a path from &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; that does not
contain &lt;code&gt;@a2&lt;/code&gt;, a contradiction.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;This tells us that the DAG we get from the dominance relation is actually a
tree, rooted at &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt;. The parent of a node in this tree is called its
&lt;em&gt;immediate dominator&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Computing dominators can be done iteratively: the dominator set of a block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;
is the intersection the dominator sets of its preds, plus &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. This algorithm
runs in quadratic time.&lt;p&gt;A better algorithm is the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm[^lta]. It is relatively
simple, but explaining how to implement it is a bit out of scope for this
article. I found a nice treatment of it
&lt;a href=https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~misra/Lengauer+Tarjan.pdf&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s important is we can compute the dominator tree without breaking the bank,
and given any node, we can ask for its immediate dominator. Using immediate
dominators, we can introduce the final, important property of dominators.&lt;blockquote id=def:4 class=def def math&gt;&lt;a href=#def:4&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;definition&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;em&gt;dominance frontier&lt;/em&gt; of a block &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; is the set of all blocks not
dominated by &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; with at least one pred which &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;These are points where control flow merges from &lt;em&gt;distinct&lt;/em&gt; paths: one containing
&lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; and one not. The dominance frontier of &lt;code&gt;@loop.body&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;@loop.start&lt;/code&gt;, whose
preds are &lt;code&gt;@entry&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;@loop.body&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;There are many ways to calculate dominance frontiers, but with a dominance tree
in hand, we can do it like this:&lt;blockquote id=alg:1 class=alg alg math&gt;&lt;a href=#alg:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;algorithm&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;For each block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; with more than one pred, for each of its preds, let &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt;
be that pred. Add &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; to the dominance frontier of &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt; and all of its
dominators, stopping when encountering &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo; immediate dominator.&lt;blockquote id=proof:4 class=proof proof&gt;&lt;a href=#proof:4&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;proof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;We need to prove that every block examined by the algorithm winds up in the
correct frontiers.&lt;p&gt;First, we check that every examined block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is added to the correct
frontier. If &lt;code&gt;@a &amp;lt; @p&lt;/code&gt;, where &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt; is a pred of &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, and a &lt;code&gt;@d&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s
immediate dominator, then if &lt;code&gt;@a &amp;lt; @d&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is not in its frontier, because
&lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; must dominate &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;. Otherwise, &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; must be in &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s frontier, because
&lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; dominates a pred but it cannot dominate &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, because then it would be
dominated by &lt;code&gt;@i&lt;/code&gt;, a contradiction.&lt;p&gt;Second, we check that every frontier is complete. Consider a block &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;. If
an examined block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is in its frontier, then &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; must be among the
dominators of some pred &lt;code&gt;@p&lt;/code&gt;, and it must be dominated by &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s immediate
dominator; otherwise, &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; would dominate &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; (and thus &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; would not be
in its frontier). Thus, &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; gets added to &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s dominator.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;You might notice that all of these algorithms are quadratic. This is actually a
very good time complexity for a compilers-related graph algorithm. Cubic and
quartic algorithms are not especially uncommon, and yes, your optimizing
compiler&amp;rsquo;s time complexity is probably cubic or quartic in the size of the
program!&lt;h2 id=lifting-memory&gt;&lt;a href=#lifting-memory&gt;Lifting Memory&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Ok. Let&amp;rsquo;s construct an optimization. We want to figure out if we can replace a
load from a pointer with the most recent store to that pointer. This will allow
us to fully lift values out of memory by cancelling out store/load pairs.&lt;p&gt;This will make use of yet another implicit graph data structure.&lt;blockquote id=def:5 class=def def math&gt;&lt;a href=#def:5&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;definition&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;strong&gt;dataflow graph&lt;/strong&gt; is the directed graph made up of the internal circuit
graphs of each each basic block, connected along block arguments.&lt;p&gt;To &lt;strong&gt;follow a use-def chain&lt;/strong&gt; is to walk this graph forward from an operation
to discover operations that potentially depend on it, or backwards to find
operations it potentially depends on.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s important to remember that the dataflow graph, like the CFG, does &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt;
have a well defined &amp;ldquo;up&amp;rdquo; direction. Navigating it and the CFG requires the
dominator tree.&lt;p&gt;One other important thing to remember here is that every instruction in a basic
block always executes if the block executes. In much of this analysis, we need
to appeal to &amp;ldquo;program order&amp;rdquo; to select the last load in a block, but we are
always able to do so. This is an important property of basic blocks that makes
them essential for constructing optimizations.&lt;h3 id=forward-dataflow&gt;&lt;a href=#forward-dataflow&gt;Forward Dataflow&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;For a given &lt;code&gt;store %p, %v&lt;/code&gt;, we want to identify all loads that depend on it. We
can follow the use-def chain of &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; to find which blocks contain loads that
potentially depend on the store (call it &lt;code&gt;%s&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;First, we can eliminate loads within the same basic block (call it &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;).
Replace all &lt;code&gt;load %p&lt;/code&gt; instructions after &lt;code&gt;s&lt;/code&gt; (but before any other
&lt;code&gt;store %p, _&lt;/code&gt;s, in program order) with &lt;code&gt;%v&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s def. If &lt;code&gt;s&lt;/code&gt; is not the last store
in this block, we&amp;rsquo;re done.&lt;p&gt;Otherwise, follow the use-def chain of &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; to successors which use &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;, i.e.,
successors whose &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt; case has &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; as at least one argument. Recurse into
those successors, and now replacing the pointer &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; of interest with the
parameters of the successor which were set to &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; (more than one argument may
be &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;If successor &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; loads from one of the registers holding &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;, replace all such
loads before a store to &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;. We also now need to send &lt;code&gt;%v&lt;/code&gt; into &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; somehow.&lt;p&gt;This is where we run into something of a wrinkle. If &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; has exactly one
predecessor, we need to add a new block argument to pass whichever register is
holding &lt;code&gt;%v&lt;/code&gt; (which exists by induction). If &lt;code&gt;%v&lt;/code&gt; is already passed into &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; by
another argument, we can use that one.&lt;p&gt;However, if &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; has multiple predecessors, we need to make sure that every path
from &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; sends &lt;code&gt;%v&lt;/code&gt;, and canonicalizing those will be tricky. Worse
still, if &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; is in &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s domination frontier, a &lt;em&gt;different&lt;/em&gt; store could be
contributing to that load! For this reason, dataflow from stores to loads is not
a great strategy.&lt;p&gt;Instead, we&amp;rsquo;ll look at dataflow from loads backwards to stores (in general,
dataflow from uses to defs tends to be more useful), which we can use to augment
the above forward dataflow analysis to remove the complex issues around
domination frontiers.&lt;h3 id=dependency-analysis&gt;&lt;a href=#dependency-analysis&gt;Dependency Analysis&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s analyze loads instead. For each &lt;code&gt;load %p&lt;/code&gt; in &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;, we want to determine
all stores that could potentially contribute to its value. We can find those
stores as follows:&lt;p&gt;We want to be able to determine which register in a given block corresponds to
the value of &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;, and then find its last store in that block.&lt;p&gt;To do this, we&amp;rsquo;ll flood-fill the CFG backwards in BFS order. This means that
we&amp;rsquo;ll follow preds (through the use-def chain) recursively, visiting each pred
before visiting their preds, and never revisiting a basic block (except we may
need to come back to &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; at the end).&lt;p&gt;Determining the &amp;ldquo;equivalent&amp;rdquo;&lt;sup id=fnref:12&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:12 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;12&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; of &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; in &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; (we&amp;rsquo;ll call it &lt;code&gt;%p.b&lt;/code&gt;)
can be done recursively: while examining &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, follow the def of &lt;code&gt;%p.b&lt;/code&gt;. If
&lt;code&gt;%p.b&lt;/code&gt; is a block parameter, for each pred &lt;code&gt;@c&lt;/code&gt;, set &lt;code&gt;%p.c&lt;/code&gt; to the corresponding
argument in the &lt;code&gt;@b(...)&lt;/code&gt; case in &lt;code&gt;@c&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Using this information, we can collect all stores that the load potentially
depends on. If a predecessor &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; stores to &lt;code&gt;%p.b&lt;/code&gt;, we add the last such store
in &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; (in program order) to our set of stores, and do not recurse to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s
preds (because this store overwrites all past stores). Note that we &lt;em&gt;may&lt;/em&gt;
revisit &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; in this process, and collect a store to &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; from it occurs in the
block. This is necessary in the case of loops.&lt;p&gt;The result is a set &lt;code&gt;stores&lt;/code&gt; of &lt;code&gt;(store %p.s %v.s, @s)&lt;/code&gt; pairs. In the process,
we also collected a set of all blocks visited, &lt;code&gt;subgraph&lt;/code&gt;, which are dominators
of &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; which we need to plumb a &lt;code&gt;%v.b&lt;/code&gt; through. This process is called &lt;em&gt;memory
dependency analysis&lt;/em&gt;, and is a key component of many optimizations.&lt;blockquote id=note:2 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Not all contributing operations are stores. Some may be references to globals
(which we&amp;rsquo;re disregarding), or function arguments or the results of a function
call (which means we probably can&amp;rsquo;t lift this load). For example &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; gets
traced all the way back to a function argument, there is a code path which
loads from a pointer whose stores we can&amp;rsquo;t see.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;It may also trace back to a stack slot that is potentially not stored to. This
means there is a code path that can potentially load uninitialized memory. Like
LLVM, we can assume this is not observable behavior, so we can discount such
dependencies. If all of the dependencies are uninitialized loads, we can
potentially delete not just the load, but operations which depend on it (reverse
dataflow analysis is the origin of so-called &amp;ldquo;time-traveling&amp;rdquo; UB).&lt;h3 id=lifting-loads&gt;&lt;a href=#lifting-loads&gt;Lifting Loads&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that we have the full set of dependency information, we can start lifting
loads. Loads can be safely lifted when all of their dependencies are stores in
the current function, or dependencies we can disregard thanks to UB in the
surface language (such as &lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt; loads or uninitialized loads).&lt;blockquote id=note:3 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:3&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is a lot of fuss in this algorithm about plumbing values through block
arguments. A lot of IRs make a simplifying change, where every block
implicitly receives the registers from its dominators as block arguments.&lt;p&gt;I am keeping the fuss because it makes it clearer what&amp;rsquo;s going on, but in
practice, most of this plumbing, except at dominance frontiers, would be
happening in the background.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Suppose we can safely lift some load. Now we need to plumb the stored values
down to the load. For each block &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; in &lt;code&gt;subgraph&lt;/code&gt; (all other blocks will now
be in &lt;code&gt;subgraph&lt;/code&gt; unless stated otherwise). We will be building two mappings: one
&lt;code&gt;(@s, @b) -&gt; %v.s.b&lt;/code&gt;, which is the register equivalent to &lt;code&gt;%v.s&lt;/code&gt; in that block.
We will also be building a map &lt;code&gt;@b -&gt; %v.b&lt;/code&gt;, which is the value that &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; must
have in that block.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Prepare a work queue, with each &lt;code&gt;@s&lt;/code&gt; in it initially.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Pop a block &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; form the queue. For each successor &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; (in &lt;code&gt;subgraph&lt;/code&gt;):&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;If &lt;code&gt;%v.b&lt;/code&gt; isn&amp;rsquo;t already defined, add it as a block argument. Have &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt;
pass &lt;code&gt;%v.a&lt;/code&gt; to that argument.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;If &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt; hasn&amp;rsquo;t been visited yet, and isn&amp;rsquo;t the block containing the load
we&amp;rsquo;re deleting, add it to the queue.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Once we&amp;rsquo;re done, if &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; is the block that contains the load, we can now replace
all loads to &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; before any stores to &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt; with &lt;code&gt;%v.a&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=tip:1 class=tip tip&gt;&lt;a href=#tip:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;tip&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are cases where this whole process can be skipped, by applying a
&amp;ldquo;peephole&amp;rdquo; optimization. For example, stores followed by loads within the same
basic block can be optimized away locally, leaving the heavy-weight analysis
for cross-block store/load pairs.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h3 id=worked-example&gt;&lt;a href=#worked-example&gt;Worked Example&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s the result of doing dependency analysis on our Fibonacci function. Each

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;exit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;):&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// @entry: S2
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// @loop.body: S5
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// %a = load %ap  // L4
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;goto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;@&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;SSA-CFG&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;After lifting, if we know that a stack slot&amp;rsquo;s pointer does not escape (i.e.,
none of its uses wind up going into a function call&lt;sup id=fnref:13&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:13 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;13&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;) or a write to
a global (or a pointer that escapes), we can delete every store to that pointer.
If we delete every store to a stack slot, we can delete the stack slot
altogether (there should be no loads left for that stack slot at this point).&lt;h3 id=complications&gt;&lt;a href=#complications&gt;Complications&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;This analysis is simple, because it assumes pointers do not alias in general.
Alias analysis is necessary for more accurate dependency analysis. This is
necessary, for example, for lifting loads of fields of structs through subobject
pointers, and dealing with pointer arithmetic in general.&lt;p&gt;However, our dependency analysis &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; robust to passing different pointers as
arguments to the same block from different predecessors. This is the case that
is specifically handled by all of the fussing about with dominance frontiers.
This robustness ultimately comes from SSA&amp;rsquo;s circuital nature.&lt;p&gt;Similarly, this analysis needs to be tweaked to deal with something like
&lt;code&gt;select %cond, %a, %b&lt;/code&gt; (a ternary, essentially). &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;s of pointers need to
be replaced with &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;s of the loaded values, which means we need to do the
lifting transformation &amp;ldquo;all at once&amp;rdquo;: lifting some liftable loads will leave the
IR in an inconsistent state, until all of them have been lifted.&lt;h2 id=cleanup-passes&gt;&lt;a href=#cleanup-passes&gt;Cleanup Passes&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Many optimizations will make a mess of the CFG, so it&amp;rsquo;s useful to have simple
passes that &amp;ldquo;clean up&amp;rdquo; the mess left by transformations. Here&amp;rsquo;s some easy
examples.&lt;h3 id=unused-result-elimination&gt;&lt;a href=#unused-result-elimination&gt;Unused Result Elimination&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;If an operation&amp;rsquo;s result has zero uses, and the operation has no side-effects,
it can be deleted. This allows us to then delete operations that it depended on
that now have no side effects. Doing this is very simple, due to the circuital
nature of SSA: collect all instructions whose outputs have zero uses, and delete
them. Then, examine the defs of their operands; if those operations now have no
uses, delete them, and recurse.&lt;p&gt;This bubbles up all the way to block arguments. Deleting block arguments is a
bit trickier, but we can use a work queue to do it. Put all of the blocks into a
work queue.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Pop a block from the queue.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Run unused result elimination on its operations.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;If it now has parameters with no uses, remove those parameters.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;For each pred, delete the corresponding arguments to this block. Then, Place
those preds into the work queue (since some of their operations may have lost
their last use).&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;If there is still work left, go to 1.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;h3 id=simplifying-the-cfg&gt;&lt;a href=#simplifying-the-cfg&gt;Simplifying the CFG&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are many CFG configurations that are redundant and can be simplified to
reduce the number of basic blocks.&lt;p&gt;For example, unreachable code can help delete blocks. Other optimizations may
cause the &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt; at the end of a function to be empty (because all of its
successors were optimized away). We treat an empty &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt; as being unreachable
(since it has no cases!), so we can delete every operation in the block up to
the last non-pure operation. If we delete every instruction in the block, we can
delete the block entirely, and delete it from its preds&amp;rsquo; &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;s. This is a form
of &lt;em&gt;dead code elimination&lt;/em&gt;, or DCE, which combines with the previous
optimization to aggressively delete redundant code.&lt;p&gt;Some jumps are redundant. For example, if a block has exactly one pred and one
successor, the pred&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt; case for that block can be wired directly to the
successor. Similarly, if two blocks are each other&amp;rsquo;s unique
predecessor/successor, they can be &lt;em&gt;fused&lt;/em&gt;, creating a single block by
connecting the input blocks&amp;rsquo; circuits directly, instead of through a &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;If we have a ternary &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt; operation, we can do more sophisticated fusion. If
a block has two successors, both of which the same unique successor, and those
successors consist only of gotos, we can fuse all four blocks, replacing the CFG
diamond with a &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;. In terms of C, this is this transformation:&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Before.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;cond&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;else&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// After.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;cond&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;?&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nl&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM&amp;rsquo;s CFG simplification pass is very sophisticated and can eliminate complex
forms of control flow.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I am hoping to write more about SSA optimization passes. This is a very rich
subject, and viewing optimizations in isolation is a great way to understand how
a sophisticated optimization pipeline is built out of simple, dumb components.&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s also a practical application of graph theory that shows just how powerful
it can be, and (at least in my opinion), is an intuitive setting for
understanding graph theory, which can feel very abstract otherwise.&lt;p&gt;In the future, I&amp;rsquo;d like to cover CSE/GVN, loop optimizations, and, if I&amp;rsquo;m
feeling brave, getting out of SSA into a finite-register machine (backends are
not my strong suit!).&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Specifically the Swift frontend before lowering into LLVM IR.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Microsoft Visual C++, a non-conforming C++ compiler sold by Microsoft&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;HotSpot is the JVM implementation provided by OpenJDK; C2 is the &amp;ldquo;second
compiler&amp;rdquo;, which has the best performance among HotSpot&amp;rsquo;s Java execution
engines.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;V8 is Chromium&amp;rsquo;s JavaScript runtime.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;SpiderMonkey is Firefox&amp;rsquo;s JavaScript runtime.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;The Android Runtime (ART) is the &amp;ldquo;JVM&amp;rdquo; (scare quotes) on the Android
platform.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;The Glasgow Haskell Compiler (GHC), does &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; use SSA; it (like some other
pure-functional languages) uses a continuation-oriented IR (compare to
Scheme&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;call/cc&lt;/code&gt;).&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:8&gt;&lt;p&gt;Every compiler person firmly believes that &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.8889em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.13889em&gt;P&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.2778em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mrel&gt;&lt;span class=mrel&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord vbox&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=thinbox&gt;&lt;span class=rlap&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.8889em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=inner&gt;&lt;span class=mord&gt;&lt;span class=mrel&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=fix&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mrel&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.2778em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.13889em&gt;NP&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;, because program
optimization is full of NP-hard problems and we would have definitely found
polynomial ideal register allocation by now if it existed.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:8 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:9&gt;&lt;p&gt;Some more recent IRs use a different version of SSA called &amp;ldquo;structured
control flow&amp;rdquo;, or SCF. Wasm is a notable example of an SCF IR. SSA-SCF is
equivalent to SSA-CFG, and polynomial time algorithms exist for losslessly
converting between them (LLVM compiling Wasm, for example, converts its CFG
into SCF using a &amp;ldquo;relooping algorithm&amp;rdquo;).&lt;p&gt;In SCF, operations like switch statements and loops are represented as macro
operations that &lt;em&gt;contain&lt;/em&gt; basic blocks. For example, a &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt; operation
might take a value as input, select a basic block to execute based on that,
and return the value that basic block evaluates to as its output.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05036&gt;RVSDG&lt;/a&gt; is a notable innovation in this
space, because it allows circuit analysis of entire imperative programs.&lt;p&gt;I am convering SSA-CFG instead of SSA-SCF simply because it&amp;rsquo;s more common,
and because it&amp;rsquo;s what LLVM IR is.&lt;p&gt;See also this
&lt;a href=https://llvm.org/devmtg/2024-04/slides/TechnicalTalks/Bock-LiftingCFGs.pdf&gt;MLIR presentation&lt;/a&gt;
for converting between the two.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:10&gt;&lt;p&gt;Tail calling is when a function call is the last operation in a function;
this allows the caller to jump directly to the callee, recycling its own
stack frame for it instead of requiring it to allocate its own.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:10 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:11&gt;&lt;p&gt;Given any path from &lt;code&gt;@a&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@b&lt;/code&gt;, we can make it acyclic by replacing each
subpath from &lt;code&gt;@c&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;@c&lt;/code&gt; with a single &lt;code&gt;@c&lt;/code&gt; node.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:11 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:12&gt;&lt;p&gt;When moving from a basic block to a pred, a register in that block which is
defined as a block parameter corresponds to some register (or immediate) in
each predecessor. That is the &amp;ldquo;equivalent&amp;rdquo; of &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;One possible option for the &amp;ldquo;equivalent&amp;rdquo; is an immediate: for example,
&lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt; or the address of a global. In the case of a global &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;g&lt;/code&gt;, assuming no
data races, we would instead need alias information to tell if stores to
this global within the current function (a) exist and (b) are liftable at
all.&lt;p&gt;If the equivalent is &lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt;, we can proceed in one of two ways depending on
optimization level. If we want loads of &lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt; to trap (as in Go), we need
to mark this load as not being liftable, because it may trap. If we want
loads of &lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt; to be UB, we simply ignore that pred, because we can assume
(for our analysis) that if the pointer is &lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt;, it is never loaded from.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:12 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:13&gt;&lt;p&gt;Returned stack pointers do &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; escape: stack slots&amp;rsquo; lifetimes end at
function exit, so we return a dangling pointer, which we assume are never
loaded. So stores to that pointer before returning it can be discarded.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:13 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Default Methods in Go</title>
    <link href="/2025/08/25/go-default-methods"/>
    <updated>2025-08-25T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/08/25/go-default-methods</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Go&amp;rsquo;s interfaces are very funny. Rather than being explicitly implemented, like
in Java or Rust, they are simply a collection of methods (a &amp;ldquo;method set&amp;rdquo;) that
the concrete type must &lt;em&gt;happen&lt;/em&gt; to have. This is called structural typing, which
is the opposite of nominal typing.&lt;p&gt;Go interfaces are very cute, but this conceptual simplicity leads to a lot of
implementation problems (a theme with Go, honestly). It removes a lot of
intentionality from implementing interfaces, and there is no canonical way to
document that &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; satisfies&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt;, nor can you &lt;em&gt;avoid&lt;/em&gt;
conforming to interfaces, especially if one forces a particular method on you.&lt;p&gt;It also has very quirky results for the language runtime. To cast an interface
value to another interface type (via the type assertion syntax &lt;code&gt;a.(B)&lt;/code&gt;), the
runtime essentially has to use reflection to go through the method set of the
concrete type of &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;. I go into detail on how this is implemented
&lt;a href=/2024/12/12/go-abi#codegen-for-interface-operations&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Because of their structural nature, this &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; means that you can&amp;rsquo;t add new
methods to an interface without breaking existing code, because there is no way
to attach default implementations to interface methods. This results in very
silly APIs because someone screwed up an interface.&lt;h2 id=flagvalue-is-a-mess&gt;&lt;a href=#flagvalue-is-a-mess&gt;flag.Value is a Mess&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;For example, in the standard library&amp;rsquo;s package &lt;code&gt;flag&lt;/code&gt;, the interface
&lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; represents a value which can be parsed as a CLI flag. It looks like
this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Get a string representation of the value.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Parse a value from a string, possibly returning an error.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Set&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;error&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; also has an optional method, which is only specified in the
documentation. If the concrete type happens to provide &lt;code&gt;IsBoolFlag() bool&lt;/code&gt;, it
will be queries for determining if the flag should have bool-like behavior.
Essentially, this means that something like this exists in the flag library:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;isBool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;value&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;IsBoolFlag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;});&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;isBool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;IsBoolFlag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;flag&lt;/code&gt; package already uses reflection, but you can see how it might be a
problem if this interface-to-interface cast happens regularly, even taking into
account Go&amp;rsquo;s caching of cast results.&lt;p&gt;There is also &lt;code&gt;flag.Getter&lt;/code&gt;, which exists because they messed up and didn&amp;rsquo;t
provide a way for a &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; to unwrap into the value it contains. For
example, if a flag is defined with &lt;code&gt;flag.Int&lt;/code&gt;, and then that flag is looked up
with &lt;code&gt;flag.Lookup&lt;/code&gt;, there&amp;rsquo;s no straightforward way to get the int out of the
returned &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Instead, you have to side-cast to &lt;code&gt;flag.Getter&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Getter&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Returns the value of the flag.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;As a result, &lt;code&gt;flag.Lookup(&#34;...&#34;).(flag.Getter)&lt;/code&gt; needs to do a lot more work than
if &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; had just added &lt;code&gt;Get() any&lt;/code&gt;, with a default return value of
&lt;code&gt;nil&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;It turns out that there is a rather elegant workaround for this.&lt;h2 id=struct-embeddings&gt;&lt;a href=#struct-embeddings&gt;Struct Embeddings&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go has this quirky feature called &lt;em&gt;embedding&lt;/em&gt;, where a a field in a struct is
declared without a name:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;B&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;-typed embedded field behaves as if we had declared the field &lt;code&gt;A A&lt;/code&gt;, but
selectors on &lt;code&gt;var b B&lt;/code&gt; will search in &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; if they do not match something on the
&lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt; level. For example, if &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; has a method &lt;code&gt;Bar&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt; does not, &lt;code&gt;b.Bar()&lt;/code&gt;
will resolve to &lt;code&gt;b.A.Bar()&lt;/code&gt;. However, if &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; has a method &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;b.Foo&lt;/code&gt;
resolves to &lt;code&gt;b.Foo&lt;/code&gt;, not &lt;code&gt;b.A.Foo&lt;/code&gt;, because &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt; has a field &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Importantly, any methods from &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; which &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt; does not already have will be added
to &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s method set. So this works:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;B&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;C&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nf&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nf&gt;Bar&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;B&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Bar&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;_&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;C&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;B&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// B satisfies C.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, suppose that we were trying to add &lt;code&gt;Get() any&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt;. Let&amp;rsquo;s
suppose that we had also defined &lt;code&gt;flag.ValueDefaults&lt;/code&gt;, a type that all
satisfiers of &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; must embed. Then, we can write the following:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Set&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;error&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// New method.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;nil&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Then, no code change is required for all clients to pick up the new
implementation of &lt;code&gt;Get()&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h3 id=required-embeds&gt;&lt;a href=#required-embeds&gt;Required Embeds&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, this only works if we had required in the first place that anyone
satisfying &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; embeds &lt;code&gt;flag.ValueDefaults&lt;/code&gt;. How can we force that?&lt;p&gt;A little-known Go feature is that interfaces can have unexported methods. The
way these work, for the purposes of interface conformance, is that exported
methods are matched just by their name, but unexported methods must match both
name and package.&lt;p&gt;So, if we have an interface like &lt;code&gt;interface { foo() }&lt;/code&gt;, then &lt;code&gt;foo&lt;/code&gt; will only
match methods defined in the same package that this interface expression
appears. This is useful for preventing satisfaction of interfaces.&lt;p&gt;However, there is a loophole: embedding inherits the &lt;em&gt;entire&lt;/em&gt; method set,
including unexported methods. Therefore, we can enhance &lt;code&gt;Value&lt;/code&gt; to account for
this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Set&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;error&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// New method.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;value&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Unexported!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;nil&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;value&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, it&amp;rsquo;s impossible for any type defined outside of this package to satisfy
&lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt;, without embedding &lt;code&gt;flag.ValueDefaults&lt;/code&gt; (either directly or through
another embedded &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;h3 id=exported-struct-fields&gt;&lt;a href=#exported-struct-fields&gt;Exported Struct Fields&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, another problem is that you can&amp;rsquo;t control the name of embedded fields. If
the embedded type is &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;, the field&amp;rsquo;s name is &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;. Except, it&amp;rsquo;s not based on
the name of the type itself; it will pick up the name of a type alias. So, if
you want to unexport the defaults struct, you can simply write:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;MyValue&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;valueDefaults&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;valueDefaults&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This also has the side-effect of hiding all of &lt;code&gt;ValueDefaults&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo; methods from
&lt;code&gt;MyValue&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s documentation, despite the fact that exported and fields methods are
still selectable and callable by other packages (including via interfaces). As
far as I can tell, this is simply a bug in &lt;code&gt;godoc&lt;/code&gt;, since this behavior is not
documented.&lt;h3 id=what-about-same-name-methods&gt;&lt;a href=#what-about-same-name-methods&gt;What About Same-Name Methods?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is still a failure mode: if a user type satisfying &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; happened
to define a &lt;code&gt;Get&lt;/code&gt; method with a different interface. In this case, that &lt;code&gt;Get&lt;/code&gt;
takes precedence, and changes to &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; will break users.&lt;p&gt;There are two workarounds:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Tell people not to define methods on their satisfying type, and if they do,
they&amp;rsquo;re screwed. Because satisfying &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; is now explicit, this is not
too difficult to ask for.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Pick a name for new methods that is unlikely to collide with anything.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, this runs into a big issue with structural typing, which is that
it is very difficult to avoid making mistakes when making changes, due to the
lack of intent involved. A similar problem occurs with C++ templates, where the
interfaces defined by concepts are implicit, and can result in violating
contract expectations.&lt;p&gt;Go has historically be relatively cavalier about this kind of issue, so I think
that breaking people based on this is fine.&lt;p&gt;And of course, you cannot retrofit a default struct into a interface; you have
to define it from day one.&lt;h2 id=using-defaults&gt;&lt;a href=#using-defaults&gt;Using Defaults&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that we have defaults, we can also enhance &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; with bool flag

&lt;code&gt;go:itab.*MyIO,io.Seeker&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;m&lt;/code&gt; into the return slots.&lt;li&gt;Return.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The main cost of this conversion is the indirect jump, compared to, at minimum,
hitting a hashmap lookup loop for the cache for &lt;code&gt;r.(io.Seeker)&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Does this performance matter? Not for I/O interfaces, probably, but it &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt;
matter for some uses!&lt;h2 id=shouldnt-this-be-a-language-feature&gt;&lt;a href=#shouldnt-this-be-a-language-feature&gt;Shouldn&amp;rsquo;t This Be a Language Feature?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Yes, it should, but here we are. Although making it a language feature has a few
rather unfortunate quirks that we need to keep in mind.&lt;p&gt;Suppose we can define defaults on interface methods somehow, like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
