&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Then, any type which provides &lt;code&gt;Bar()&lt;/code&gt; automatically satisfies &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;. Suppose
&lt;code&gt;MyFoo&lt;/code&gt; satisfies &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;, but does not provide &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt;. Then we have a problem:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;MyFoo&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Baz&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;       &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Error!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;).&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Baz&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Ok!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, we might consider looking past that, but it becomes a big problem with
reflection. If we passed &lt;code&gt;Foo(x)&lt;/code&gt; into &lt;code&gt;reflect.ValueOf&lt;/code&gt;, the resulting &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt;
conversion would discard the defaulted method, meaning that it would not be
findable by &lt;code&gt;reflect.Value.MethodByName()&lt;/code&gt;. Oops.&lt;p&gt;So we need to somehow add &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;MyFoo&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s method set. Maybe we say that if
&lt;code&gt;MyFoo&lt;/code&gt; is ever converted into &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;, it gets the method. But this doesn&amp;rsquo;t work,
because the compiler might not be able to see through something like
&lt;code&gt;any(MyFoo{...}).(Foo)&lt;/code&gt;. This means that &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; must be applied unconditionally.
But, now we have the problem that if we have another interface
&lt;code&gt;interface { Bar(); Baz(int) }&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;MyFoo&lt;/code&gt; would need to receive incompatible
signatures for &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Again, we&amp;rsquo;re screwed by the non-intentionality of structural typing.&lt;h3 id=missing-methods&gt;&lt;a href=#missing-methods&gt;Missing Methods&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Ok, let&amp;rsquo;s forget about default method implementations, that doesn&amp;rsquo;t seem to be
workable. What if we make some methods optional, like &lt;code&gt;IsBoolFlag()&lt;/code&gt; earlier?
Let&amp;rsquo;s invent some syntax for it.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Bar&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=err&gt;?&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Baz&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Optional method.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Then, suppose that &lt;code&gt;MyFoo&lt;/code&gt; provides &lt;code&gt;Bar&lt;/code&gt; but not &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; (or &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; with the wrong
signature). Then, the entry in the itab for &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; would contain a nil function
pointer, such that &lt;code&gt;x.Baz()&lt;/code&gt; panics! To determine if &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; is safe to call, we
would use the following idiom:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Baz&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;nil&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Baz&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The compiler is already smart enough to elide construction of funcvals for cases
like this, although it does mean that &lt;code&gt;x.Func&lt;/code&gt; in general, for an interface
value &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;, requires an extra &lt;code&gt;cmov&lt;/code&gt; or similar to make sure that &lt;code&gt;x.Func&lt;/code&gt; is nil
when it&amp;rsquo;s a missing method.&lt;p&gt;All of the use cases described above would work Just Fine using this
construction, though! However, we run into the same issue that &lt;code&gt;Foo(x)&lt;/code&gt; appears
to have a larger method set than &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;. It is not clear if &lt;code&gt;Foo(x)&lt;/code&gt; should conform
to &lt;code&gt;interface { Bar(); Baz() }&lt;/code&gt;, where &lt;code&gt;Baz&lt;/code&gt; is required. My intuition would be
no: &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt; is a strictly weaker interface. Perhaps it might be necessary to avoid
the method access syntax for optional methods, but that&amp;rsquo;s a question of
aesthetics.&lt;p&gt;This idea of having nulls in place of function pointers in a vtable is not new,
but to my knowledge is not used especially widely. It would be very useful in
C++, for example, to be able to determine if no implementation was provided for
a non-pure virtual function. However, the nominal nature of C++&amp;rsquo;s virtual
functions does not make this &lt;em&gt;as big&lt;/em&gt; of a need.&lt;h3 id=related-interfaces&gt;&lt;a href=#related-interfaces&gt;Related Interfaces&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Another alternative is to store a related interfaces&amp;rsquo; itabs on in an itab. For
example, suppose that we invent the syntax &lt;code&gt;A&amp;lt;-&lt;/code&gt; within an &lt;code&gt;interface{}&lt;/code&gt; to
indicate that that interface will likely get cast to &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;. For example:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nf&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;B&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nf&gt;Bar&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;-&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Satisfying &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt; does not require satisfying &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;. However, the &lt;code&gt;A&amp;lt;-&lt;/code&gt; must be part
of public API, because a &lt;code&gt;interface{ Bar() }&lt;/code&gt; cannot be used in place of an
&lt;code&gt;interface{ A&amp;lt;- }&lt;/code&gt;&lt;p&gt;Within &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s itab, after all of the methods, there is a pointer to an itab for
&lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;, if the concrete type for this itab also happens to satisfy &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;. Then, a
cast from &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; is just loading a pointer from the itab. If the cast would
fail, the loaded pointer will be &lt;code&gt;nil&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;I had always assumed that Go did an optimization like this for embedding
interfaces, but no! &lt;em&gt;Any&lt;/em&gt; inter-interface conversion, including upcasts, goes
through the whole type assertion machinery! Of course, Go cannot hope to
generate an itab for every possible subset of the method set of an interface
(exponential blow-up), but it&amp;rsquo;s surprising that they don&amp;rsquo;t do this for embedded
interfaces, which are Go&amp;rsquo;s equivalent of superinterfaces (present in basically
every language with interfaces).&lt;p&gt;Using this feature, we can update &lt;code&gt;flag.Value&lt;/code&gt; to look like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Set&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;error&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;BoolValue&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;-&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;Getter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;-&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;BoolValue&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;IsBoolFlag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Getter&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;Value&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, because &lt;code&gt;A&amp;lt;-&lt;/code&gt; changes the ABI of an interface, it does not seem
possible to actually add this to existing interfaces, because the following code
is valid:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:19&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Even though this fix seems really clean, it doesn&amp;rsquo;t work! The only way it could
work is if PGO determines that a particular interface conversion &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt;
happens a lot, and updates the ABI of all interfaces with the method set of &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;,
program-globally, to contain a pointer to a &lt;code&gt;B&lt;/code&gt; itab if available.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go&amp;rsquo;s interfaces are pretty bad; in my opinion, a feature that looks good on a
slide, but which results in a lot of mess due to its granular and intention-less
nature. We can sort of patch over it with embeds, but there&amp;rsquo;s still problems.&lt;p&gt;Due to how method sets work in Go, it&amp;rsquo;s very hard to &amp;ldquo;add&amp;rdquo; methods through an
interface, and honestly at this point, any interface mechanism that makes it
impossible (or expensive) to add new functions is going to be a huge problem.&lt;p&gt;Missing methods seems like the best way out of this problem, but for now, we can
stick to the janky embedded structs.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go uses the term &amp;ldquo;implements&amp;rdquo; to say that a type satisfies an interface. I
am instead intentionally using the term &amp;ldquo;satisfies&amp;rdquo;, because it makes the
structural, passive nature of implementing an interface clearer. This is
also more in-line with interfaces&amp;rsquo; use as generic constraints.&lt;p&gt;Swift uses the term &amp;ldquo;conform&amp;rdquo; instead, which I am avoiding for this reason.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Parsing Protobuf Like Never Before</title>
    <link href="/2025/07/16/hyperpb"/>
    <updated>2025-07-16T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/07/16/hyperpb</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Historically I have worked on many projects related to high-performance
Protobuf, be that on the C++ runtime, on the Rust runtime, or on integrating
&lt;a href=https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/main/upb&gt;UPB&lt;/a&gt;, the fastest
Protobuf runtime, written by my colleague
&lt;a href=https://blog.reverberate.org/2021/04/21/musttail-efficient-interpreters.html&gt;Josh Haberman&lt;/a&gt;.
I &lt;em&gt;generally&lt;/em&gt; don&amp;rsquo;t post directly about my current job, but my most recent
toy-turned-product is something I&amp;rsquo;m very excited to write about:
&lt;a href=https://github.com/bufbuild/hyperpb-go&gt;&lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s how we measure up against other Go Protobuf parsers. This is a subset of
my benchmarks, since the benchmark suite contains many dozens of specimens. This
was recorded on an AMD Zen 4 machine.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/hyperpb/benches.svg alt&gt;&lt;figcaption&gt;&lt;p&gt;Throughput for various configurations
of &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; (colored bars) vs. competing parsers (grey bars).
Each successive &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; includes all previous optimizations, corresponding
to &lt;a href=#zerocopy-strings&gt;zerocopy mode&lt;/a&gt;, &lt;a href=#arena-reuse&gt;arena reuse&lt;/a&gt;, and
&lt;a href=#tdptype&gt;profile-guided optimization&lt;/a&gt;.
Bigger is better.&lt;/figcaption&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Traditionally, Protobuf backends would generate parsers by generating source
code specialized to each type. Naively, this would give the best performance,
because everything would be &amp;ldquo;right-sized&amp;rdquo; to a particular message type.
Unfortunately, now that we know better, there are a bunch of drawbacks:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Every type you care about must be compiled ahead-of-time. Tricky for when you
want to build something generic over schemas your users provide you.&lt;li&gt;Every type contributes to a cost on the instruction cache, meaning that if
your program parses a lot of different types, it will essentially flush your
instruction cache any time you enter a parser. Worse still, if a parse
involves enough types, the parser itself will hit instruction decoding
throughput issues.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;These effects are not directly visible in normal workloads, but other
side-effects are visible: for example, giant switches on field numbers can turn
into chains of branch instructions, meaning that higher-numbered fields will be
quite slow. Even binary-searching on field numbers isn&amp;rsquo;t exactly ideal. However,
we know that every Protobuf codec ever emits fields in index order (i.e.,
declaration order in the &lt;code&gt;.proto&lt;/code&gt; file), which is a data conditioning fact we
don&amp;rsquo;t take advantage of with a switch.&lt;p&gt;UPB solves this problem. It is a small C kernel for parsing Protobuf messages,
which is completely dynamic: a UPB &amp;ldquo;parser&amp;rdquo; is actually a collection of data
tables that are evaluated by a &lt;em&gt;table-driven parser&lt;/em&gt;. In other words, a UPB
parser is actually configuration for an interpreter VM, which executes Protobuf
messages as its bytecode. UPB also contains many arena optimizations to improve
allocation throughput when parsing complex messages.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; is a brand new library, written in the most cursed Go imaginable,
which brings many of the optimizations of UPB to Go, and many new ones, while
being tuned to Go&amp;rsquo;s own weird needs. The result leaves the competition in the
dust in virtually every benchmark, while being completely runtime-dynamic. This
means it&amp;rsquo;s faster than Protobuf Go&amp;rsquo;s own generated code, &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt;
&lt;a href=https://github.com/planetscale/vtprotobuf&gt;&lt;code&gt;vtprotobuf&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; (a popular but
non-conforming&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; parser generator for Go).&lt;p&gt;This post is about some of the internals of &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt;. I have also prepared a
more sales-ey writeup, which you can read on
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/introducing-hyperpb&gt;the Buf blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;h2 id=why-reinvent-upb&gt;&lt;a href=#why-reinvent-upb&gt;Why Reinvent UPB?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;UPB is awesome. It can slot easily into any language that has C FFI, which is
basically every language ever.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, Go&amp;rsquo;s C FFI is really, really bad. It&amp;rsquo;s hard to overstate how bad
cgo is. There isn&amp;rsquo;t a good way to cooperate with C on memory allocation (C can&amp;rsquo;t
really handle Go memory without a lot of problems, due to the GC). Having C
memory get cleaned up by the GC requires finalizers, which are very slow.
Calling into C is very slow, because Go pessimistically assumes that C requires
a large stack, and also calling into C does nasty things to the scheduler.&lt;p&gt;All of these things can be worked around, of course. For a while I considered
compiling UPB to assembly, and rewriting that assembly into Go&amp;rsquo;s awful assembly
syntax&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, and then having Go assemble UPB out of that. This presents a
few issues though, particularly because Go&amp;rsquo;s assembly calling convention is
still in the stone age&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (arguments are passed on the stack), and because
we would still need to do a lot of work to get UPB to match the &lt;code&gt;protoreflect&lt;/code&gt;
API.&lt;p&gt;Go also has a few&amp;mldr; unique qualities that make writing a Protobuf interpreter
an interesting challenge with &lt;em&gt;exciting&lt;/em&gt; optimization opportunities.&lt;p&gt;First, of course, is the register ABI, which on &lt;code&gt;x86_64&lt;/code&gt; gives us a whopping
&lt;em&gt;nine&lt;/em&gt; argument and return registers, meaning that we can simply pass the entire
parser state in registers all the time.&lt;p&gt;Second is that Go does not have much UB to speak of, so we can get away with a
lot of very evil pointer crimes that we could not in C++ or Rust.&lt;p&gt;Third is that Protobuf Go has a robust reflection system that we can target if
we design specifically for it.&lt;p&gt;Also, the Go ecosystem seems much more tolerant of less-than-ideal startup times
(because the language &lt;em&gt;loves&lt;/em&gt; life-before-main due to &lt;code&gt;init()&lt;/code&gt; functions), so
unlike UPB, we can require that the interpreter&amp;rsquo;s program be generated at
runtime, meaning that we can design for online PGO. In other words, we have the
perfect storm to create the first-ever Protobuf JIT compiler (which we also
refer to as &amp;ldquo;online PGO&amp;rdquo; or &amp;ldquo;real-time PGO&amp;rdquo;).&lt;h2 id=hyperpbs-api&gt;&lt;a href=#hyperpbs-api&gt;hyperpb&amp;rsquo;s API&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Right now, &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s API is very simple. There are &lt;code&gt;hyperpb.Compile*&lt;/code&gt;
functions that accept some representation of a message descriptor, and return a
&lt;code&gt;*hyperpb.MessageType&lt;/code&gt;, which implements the &lt;code&gt;protoreflect&lt;/code&gt; type APIs. This can
be used to allocate a new &lt;code&gt;*hyperpb.Message&lt;/code&gt; , which you can shove into
&lt;code&gt;proto.Unmarshal&lt;/code&gt; and do reflection on the result. However, you can&amp;rsquo;t mutate
&lt;code&gt;*hyperpb.Message&lt;/code&gt;s currently, because the main use-cases I am optimizing for
are read-only. All mutations panic instead.&lt;p&gt;The hero use-case, using Buf&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;protovalidate&lt;/code&gt; library, uses reflection to
execute validation predicates. It looks like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Compile a new message type, deserializing an encoded FileDescriptorSet.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;msgType&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;hyperpb&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;CompileForBytes&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;schema&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;my.api.v1.Request&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Allocate a new message of that type.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;msg&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;hyperpb&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;NewMessage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;msgType&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Unmarshal like you would any other message, using proto.Unmarshal.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;proto&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Unmarshal&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;msg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;nil&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Handle parse failure.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Validate the message. Protovalidate uses reflection, so this Just Works.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;protovalidate&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Validate&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;msg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;nil&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Handle validation failure.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;We tell users to make sure to cache the compilation step because compilation can
be arbitrarily slow: it&amp;rsquo;s an optimizing compiler! This is not unlike the same
warning on &lt;code&gt;regexp.Compile&lt;/code&gt;, which makes it easy to teach users how to use this
API correctly.&lt;p&gt;In addition to the main API, there&amp;rsquo;s a bunch of performance tuning knobs for the
compiler, for unmarshaling, and for recording profiles. Types can be recompiled
using a recorded profile to be more optimized for the kinds of messages that
actually come on the wire. &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; PGO&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; affects a number of things
that we&amp;rsquo;ll get into as I dive into the implementation details.&lt;h2 id=the-guts&gt;&lt;a href=#the-guts&gt;The Guts&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Most of the core implementation lives under
&lt;a href=https://github.com/bufbuild/hyperpb-go/tree/main/internal/tdp&gt;&lt;code&gt;internal/tdp&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.
The main components are as follows:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;tdp&lt;/code&gt;, which defines the &amp;ldquo;object code format&amp;rdquo; for the interpreter. This
includes definitions for describing types and fields to the parser.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;tdp/compiler&lt;/code&gt;, which contains all of the code for converting a
&lt;code&gt;protoreflect.MessageDescriptor&lt;/code&gt; into a &lt;code&gt;tdp.Library&lt;/code&gt;, which contains all of
the types relevant to a particular parsing operation.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;tdp/dynamic&lt;/code&gt; defines what dynamic message types look like. The compiler does
a bunch of layout work that gets stored in &lt;code&gt;tdp.Type&lt;/code&gt; values, which a
&lt;code&gt;dynamic.Message&lt;/code&gt; interprets to find the offsets of fields within itself.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;tdp/vm&lt;/code&gt; contains the core interpreter implementation, including the VM state
that is passed in registers everywhere. It also includes hand-optimized
routines for parsing varints and validating UTF-8.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;tdp/thunks&lt;/code&gt; defines &lt;em&gt;archetypes&lt;/em&gt;, which are classes of fields that all use
the same layout and parsers. This corresponds roughly to a &lt;code&gt;(presence, kind)&lt;/code&gt;
pair, but not exactly. There are around 200 different archetypes.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;This article won&amp;rsquo;t be a deep-dive into everything in the parser, and even this
excludes large portions of &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt;. For example, the
&lt;a href=https://mcyoung.xyz/2025/04/21/go-arenas/&gt;&lt;code&gt;internal/arena&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; package is already
described in a different blogpost of mine. I recommend taking a look at that to
learn about how we implement a GC-friendly arena for &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; .&lt;p&gt;Instead, I will give a brief overview of how the object code is organized and
how the parser interprets it. I will also go over a few of the more interesting
optimizations we have.&lt;h3 id=tdptype&gt;&lt;a href=#tdptype&gt;tdp.Type&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Every &lt;code&gt;MessageDescriptor&lt;/code&gt; that is reachable from the root message (either as a
field or as an extension) becomes a &lt;code&gt;tdp.Type&lt;/code&gt; . This contains the dynamic size
of the corresponding message type, a pointer to the type&amp;rsquo;s default parser (there
can be more than one parser for a type) and a variable number of &lt;code&gt;tdp.Field&lt;/code&gt;
values. These specify the offset of each field and provide accessor thunks, for
actually extracting the value of the field.&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;tdp.TypeParser&lt;/code&gt; is what the parser VM interprets alongside encoded Protobuf
data. It contains all of the information needed for decoding a message in
compact form, including &lt;code&gt;tdp.FieldParser&lt;/code&gt;s for each of its fields (and
extensions), as well as a hashtable for looking up a field by tag, which is used
by the VM as a fallback.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;tdp.FieldParser&lt;/code&gt;s each contain:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;The same offset information as a &lt;code&gt;tdp.Field&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;The field&amp;rsquo;s tag, in a special format.&lt;li&gt;A function pointer that gets called to parse the field.&lt;li&gt;The next field(s) to try parsing after this one is parsed.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Each &lt;code&gt;tdp.FieldParser&lt;/code&gt; actually corresponds to a possible tag on a record for
this message. Some fields have multiple different tags: for example, a
&lt;code&gt;repeated int32&lt;/code&gt; can have a &lt;code&gt;VARINT&lt;/code&gt;-type tag for the repeated representation,
and a &lt;code&gt;LEN&lt;/code&gt;-type tag for the packed representation.&lt;p&gt;Each field specifies which fields to try next. This allows the compiler to
perform &lt;em&gt;field scheduling&lt;/em&gt;, by carefully deciding which order to try fields in
based both on their declaration order and a rough estimation of their &amp;ldquo;hotness&amp;rdquo;,
much like branch scheduling happens in a program compiler. This avoids almost
all of the work of looking up the next field in the common case, because we have
already pre-loaded the correct guess.&lt;p&gt;I haven&amp;rsquo;t managed to nail down a good algorithm for this yet, but I am working
on a system for implementing a type of &amp;ldquo;branch prediction&amp;rdquo; for PGO, that tries
to provide better predictions for the next fields to try based on what has been
seen before.&lt;p&gt;The offset information for a field is more than just a memory offset. A
&lt;code&gt;tdp.Offset&lt;/code&gt; includes a bit offset, for fields which request allocation of
individual bits in the message&amp;rsquo;s bitfields. These are used to implement the
hasbits of &lt;code&gt;optional&lt;/code&gt; fields (and the values of &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt; fields). It also includes
a byte offset for larger storage. However, this byte offset can be negative, in
which case it&amp;rsquo;s actually an offset into the &lt;em&gt;cold region&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;In many messages, most fields won&amp;rsquo;t be set, particularly extensions. But we
would like to avoid having to allocate memory for the very rare (i.e., &amp;ldquo;cold&amp;rdquo;)
fields. For this, a special &amp;ldquo;cold region&amp;rdquo; exists in a separate allocation from
the main message, which is referenced via a compressed pointer. If a message
happens to need a cold field set, it takes a slow path to allocate a cold region
only if needed. Whether a field is cold is a dynamic property that can be
affected by PGO.&lt;h3 id=the-parser-vm&gt;&lt;a href=#the-parser-vm&gt;The Parser VM&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The parser is designed to make maximal use of Go&amp;rsquo;s generous ABI without spilling
anything to the stack that isn&amp;rsquo;t absolutely necessary. The parser state consists
of eight 64-bit integers, split across two types: &lt;code&gt;vm.P1&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;vm.P2&lt;/code&gt;.
Unfortunately, these can&amp;rsquo;t be merged due to a
&lt;a href=https://github.com/golang/go/issues/72897&gt;compiler bug&lt;/a&gt;, as documented in
&lt;a href=https://github.com/bufbuild/hyperpb-go/tree/main/internal/tdp/vm/vm.go#L50&gt;&lt;code&gt;vm/vm.go&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Every parser function takes these two structs as its first two arguments, and
returns them as its first two results. This ensures that register allocation
tries its darnedest to keep those eight integers in the first eight argument
registers, even across calls. This leads to the common idiom of&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;p2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;DoSomething&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;p2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Overwriting the parser state like this ensures that future uses of p1 and p2 use
the values that &lt;code&gt;DoSomething&lt;/code&gt; places in registers for us.&lt;p&gt;I spent a lot of time and a lot of profiling catching all of the places where Go
would incorrectly spill parser state to the stack, which would result in stalls.
I found quite a few codegen bugs in the process. Particularly notable (and
shocking!) is &lt;a href=https://github.com/golang/go/issues/73589&gt;#73589&lt;/a&gt;. Go has
somehow made it a decade without a very basic pointer-to-SSA lifting pass (for
comparison, this is a heavy-lifting cleanup pass (&lt;code&gt;mem2reg&lt;/code&gt;) in LLVM).&lt;p&gt;The core loop of the VM goes something like this:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Are we out of bytes to parse? If so, pop a parser stack frame&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. If we
popped the last stack frame, parsing is done; return success.&lt;li&gt;Parse a tag. This does not fully decode the tag, because &lt;code&gt;tdp.FieldParser&lt;/code&gt;s
contain a carefully-formatted, partially-decoded tag to reduce decoding work.&lt;li&gt;Check if the next field we would parse matches the tag.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;If yes, call the function pointer &lt;code&gt;tdp.Field.Parser&lt;/code&gt;; update the current
field to &lt;code&gt;tdp.Field.NextOk&lt;/code&gt;; goto 1.&lt;li&gt;If no, update the current field to &lt;code&gt;tdp.Field.NextErr&lt;/code&gt;; goto 3.&lt;li&gt;If no &amp;ldquo;enough times&amp;rdquo;, fall through.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Slow path: hit &lt;code&gt;tdp.Field.Tags&lt;/code&gt; to find the matching field for that tag.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;If matched, go to 3a.&lt;li&gt;If not, this is an unknown field; put it into the unknown field set; parse
a tag and goto 4.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Naturally, this is implemented as a single function whose control flow consists
exclusively of &lt;code&gt;if&lt;/code&gt;s and &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;s, because getting Go to generate good control
flow otherwise proved too hard.&lt;p&gt;Now, you might be wondering why the hot loop for the parser includes &lt;strong&gt;calling a
virtual function&lt;/strong&gt;. Conventional wisdom holds that virtual calls are slow. After
all, the actual virtual call instruction is quite slow, because it&amp;rsquo;s an indirect
branch, meaning that it can easily stall the CPU. However, it&amp;rsquo;s actually &lt;em&gt;much
faster than the alternatives&lt;/em&gt; in this case, due to a few quirks of our workload
and how modern CPUs are designed:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Modern CPUs are not &lt;em&gt;great&lt;/em&gt; at traversing complex &amp;ldquo;branch mazes&amp;rdquo;. This means
that selecting one of ~100 alternatives using branches, even if they are
well-predicted and you use unrolled binary search, is still likely to result
in frequent mispredictions, and is an obstacle to other JIT optimizations in
the processor&amp;rsquo;s backend.&lt;li&gt;Predicting a single indirect branch with dozens of popular targets &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt;
something modern CPUs are pretty good at. Chips and Cheese have a
&lt;a href=https://chipsandcheese.com/i/138977313/indirect-branch-prediction&gt;great writeup&lt;/a&gt;
on the indirect prediction characteristics of Zen 4 chips.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;In fact, the &amp;ldquo;optimized&amp;rdquo; form of a large switch is a jump table, which is
essentially an array of function pointers. Rather than doing a large number of
comparisons and direct branches, a jump table turns a switch into a load and an
indirect branch.&lt;p&gt;This is great news for us, because it means we can make use of a powerful
assumption about most messages: most messages only feature a handful of field
archetypes. How often is it that you see a message which has more in it than
&lt;code&gt;int32&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;int64&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;string&lt;/code&gt; , and submessages? In effect, this allows us to have
a very large &amp;ldquo;instruction set&amp;rdquo;, consisting of all of the different field
archetypes, but a particular message only pays for what it uses. The fewer
archetypes it uses &lt;em&gt;at runtime&lt;/em&gt;, the better the CPU can predict this indirect
jump.&lt;p&gt;On the other hand, we can just keep adding archetypes over time to specialize
for common parse workloads, which PGO can select for. Adding new archetypes that
are not used by most messages does not incur a performance penalty.&lt;h2 id=other-optimizations&gt;&lt;a href=#other-optimizations&gt;Other Optimizations&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;ve already discussed the hot/cold split, and briefly touched on the message
bitfields used for &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt;s and hasbits. I&amp;rsquo;d like to mention a few other cool
optimizations that help cover all our bases, as far as high-performance parsing
does.&lt;h3 id=zerocopy-strings&gt;&lt;a href=#zerocopy-strings&gt;Zerocopy Strings&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The fastest &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt; implementation is the one you don&amp;rsquo;t call. For this reason,
we try to, whenever possible, avoid copying anything out of the input buffer.
&lt;code&gt;string&lt;/code&gt;s and &lt;code&gt;bytes&lt;/code&gt; are represented as
&lt;a href=https://github.com/bufbuild/hyperpb-go/tree/main/internal/zc/zc.go&gt;&lt;code&gt;zc.Range&lt;/code&gt;s&lt;/a&gt;,
which are a packed pair of offset+length in a &lt;code&gt;uint64&lt;/code&gt;. Protobuf is not able to
handle lengths greater than 2GB properly, so we can assume that this covers all
the data we could ever care about. This means that a &lt;code&gt;bytes&lt;/code&gt; field is 8 bytes,
rather than 24, in our representation.&lt;p&gt;Zerocopy is also used for packed fields. For example, a &lt;code&gt;repeated double&lt;/code&gt; will
typically be encoded as a &lt;code&gt;LEN&lt;/code&gt; record. The number of &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt;s in this record
is equal to its length divided by 8, and the &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt;s are already encoded in
IEEE754 format for us. So we can just retain the whole repeated fields as a
&lt;code&gt;zc.Range&lt;/code&gt; . Of course, we need to be able to handle cases where there are
multiple disjoint records, so the backing
&lt;a href=https://github.com/bufbuild/hyperpb-go/blob/main/internal/tdp/repeated/scalars.go&gt;&lt;code&gt;repeated.Scalars&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
can also function as a 24-byte arena slice. Being able to switch between these
modes gracefully is a delicate and carefully-tested part of the repeated field
thunks.&lt;p&gt;Surprisingly, we also use zerocopy for varint fields, such as &lt;code&gt;repeated int32&lt;/code&gt;.
Varints are variable-length, so we can&amp;rsquo;t just index directly into the packed
buffer to get the &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; th element&amp;mldr; unless all of the elements happen to be the
same size. In the case that every varint is one byte (so, between 0 and 127), we
can zerocopy the packed field. This is a relatively common scenario, too, so it
results in big savings&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. We &lt;em&gt;already&lt;/em&gt; count the number of varints
in the packed field in order to preallocate space for it, so this doesn&amp;rsquo;t add
extra cost. This counting is very efficient because I have manually vectorized
the loop.&lt;h3 id=repeated-preloads&gt;&lt;a href=#repeated-preloads&gt;Repeated Preloads&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;PGO records the median size of each repeated/map field, and that is used to
calculate a &amp;ldquo;preload&amp;rdquo; for each repeated field. Whenever the field is first
allocated, it is pre-allocated using the preload to try to right-size the field
with minimal waste.&lt;p&gt;Using the median ensures that large outliers don&amp;rsquo;t result in huge memory waste;
instead, this guarantees that at least 50% of repeated fields will only need to
allocate from the arena once. Packed fields don&amp;rsquo;t use the preload, since in the
common case only one record appears for packed fields. This mostly benefits
string- and message-typed repeated fields, which can&amp;rsquo;t be packed.&lt;h3 id=map-optimizations&gt;&lt;a href=#map-optimizations&gt;Map Optimizations&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;We don&amp;rsquo;t use Go&amp;rsquo;s built-in map, because it has significant overhead in some
cases: in particular, it has to support Go&amp;rsquo;s mutation-during-iteration
semantics, as well as deletion. Although both are Swisstables&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;
under the hood, my implementation can afford to take a few shortcuts. It also
allows our implementation to use arena-managed memory.
&lt;a href=https://github.com/bufbuild/hyperpb-go/tree/main/internal/swiss/table.go&gt;&lt;code&gt;swiss.Table&lt;/code&gt;s&lt;/a&gt;
are used both for the backing store of &lt;code&gt;map&lt;/code&gt; fields, and for maps inside of
&lt;code&gt;tdp.Type&lt;/code&gt;s.&lt;p&gt;Currently, the hash used is the variant of
&lt;a href=https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc-hash&gt;fxhash used by the Rust compiler&lt;/a&gt;.
This greatly out-performs Go&amp;rsquo;s &lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/hash/maphash&gt;maphash&lt;/a&gt; for
integers, but maphash is better for larger strings. I hope to maybe switch to
maphash at some point for large strings, but it hasn&amp;rsquo;t been a priority.&lt;h3 id=arena-reuse&gt;&lt;a href=#arena-reuse&gt;Arena Reuse&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Hitting the Go allocator is always going to be a little slow, because it&amp;rsquo;s a
general-case allocator. Ideally, we should learn the estimated memory
requirements for a particular workload, and then allocate a single block of that
size for the arena to portion out.&lt;p&gt;The best way to do this is via &lt;em&gt;arena reuse&lt;/em&gt; In the context of a service, each
request has a bounded lifetime on the message that it parses. Once that lifetime
is over (the request is complete), the message is discarded. This gives the
programmer an opportunity to &lt;em&gt;reset&lt;/em&gt; the backing arena, so that it keeps its
largest memory block for re-allocation.&lt;p&gt;You can show that over time, this will cause the arena to never hit the Go
allocator. If the largest block is too small for a message, a block twice as
large will wind up getting allocated. Messages that use the same amount of
memory will keep doubling the largest block, until the largest block is large
enough to fit the whole message. Memory usage will be at worst 2x the size of
this message. Note that, thanks to extensive use of zero-copy optimizations, we
can often avoid allocating memory for large portions of the message.&lt;p&gt;Of course, arena re-use poses a memory safety danger, if the previously
allocated message is kept around after the arena is reset. For this reason, it&amp;rsquo;s
not the default behavior. Using arena resets is a double-digit percentage
improvement, however.&lt;h3 id=oneof-unions&gt;&lt;a href=#oneof-unions&gt;Oneof Unions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go does not properly support unions, because the GC does not keep the necessary
book-keeping to distinguish a memory location that may be an integer &lt;em&gt;or&lt;/em&gt; a
pointer at runtime. Instead, this gets worked around using interfaces, which is
always a pointer to some memory. Go&amp;rsquo;s GC can handle untyped pointers just fine,
so this just works.&lt;p&gt;The generated API for Protobuf Go uses interface values for &lt;code&gt;oneof&lt;/code&gt;s. This API
is&amp;mldr; pretty messy to use, unfortunately, and triggers unnecessary allocations,
(much like &lt;code&gt;optional&lt;/code&gt; fields do in the open API).&lt;p&gt;However, my arena design
(&lt;a href=https://mcyoung.xyz/2025/04/21/go-arenas/&gt;read about it here&lt;/a&gt;) makes it
possible to store arena pointers on the arena as if they are integers, since the
GC does not need to scan through arena memory. Thus, our &lt;code&gt;oneof&lt;/code&gt;s are true
unions, like in C++.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; is really exciting because its growing JIT capabilities offer an
improvement in the state of the art over UPB. It&amp;rsquo;s also been a really fun
challenge working around Go compiler bugs to get the best assembly possible. The
code is already so well-optimized that re-building the benchmarks with the Go
compiler&amp;rsquo;s own PGO mode (based on a profile collected from the benchmarks)
didn&amp;rsquo;t really seem to move the needle!&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m always working on making &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; better (I get paid for it!) and I&amp;rsquo;m
always excited to try new optimizations. If you think of something, file an
issue! I have meticulously commented most things within &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; , so it should
be pretty easy to get an idea of where things are if you want to contribute.&lt;p&gt;I would like to write more posts diving into some of the weeds of the
implementation. I can&amp;rsquo;t promise anything, but there&amp;rsquo;s lots to talk about. For
now&amp;mldr; have fun source-diving!&lt;p&gt;There&amp;rsquo;s a lot of other things we could be doing: for example, we could be using
SIMD to parse varints, we could have smarter parser scheduling, we could be
allocating small submessages inline to improve locality&amp;mldr; there&amp;rsquo;s still so much
we can do!&lt;p&gt;And most importantly, I hope you&amp;rsquo;ve learned something new about performance
optimization!&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;vtprotobuf gets &lt;em&gt;a lot&lt;/em&gt; of things wrong that make it beat us in like two
benchmarks, because it&amp;rsquo;s &lt;em&gt;so&lt;/em&gt; sloppy. For example, vtprotobuf believes that
it&amp;rsquo;s ok to not validate UTF-8 strings. This is &lt;em&gt;non-conforming&lt;/em&gt; behavior. It
also believes that map entries&amp;rsquo; fields are always in order and always
populated, meaning that valid Protobuf messages containing maps can be
parsed &lt;em&gt;incorrectly&lt;/em&gt;. This sloppiness is unacceptable, which is why
&lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; goes to great lengths to implement all of Protobuf correctly.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Never gonna let Rob live that one down. Of all of Rob&amp;rsquo;s careless design
decisions, the assembler is definitely one of the least forgivable ones.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are only really two pieces of code in &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; that could benefit
from hand-written assembly: varint decoding and UTF-8 validation. Both of
these vectorize well, however, &lt;code&gt;ABI0&lt;/code&gt; is so inefficient that no hand-written
implementation will be faster.&lt;p&gt;If I do wind up doing this, it will require a build tag like &lt;code&gt;hyperasm&lt;/code&gt;,
along with something like
&lt;code&gt;-gcflags=buf.build/go/hyperpb/internal/asm/...=-+&lt;/code&gt; to treat the assembly
implementations as part of the Go runtime, allowing the use of
&lt;code&gt;ABIInternal&lt;/code&gt;. But even then, this only speeds up parsing of large (&gt;2 byte)
varints.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is PGO performed by &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; itself; this is unrelated to &lt;code&gt;gc&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s own
PGO mode, which seems to not actually make &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; faster.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;Yes, the parser manages its own stack separate from the goroutine stack.
This ensures that nothing in the parser has to be reentrant. The only time
the stack is pushed to is when we &amp;ldquo;recurse&amp;rdquo; into a submessage.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;Large packed repeated fields are where the biggest wins are for us. Being
able to zero-copy large packed &lt;code&gt;int32&lt;/code&gt; fields full of small values allows us
to eliminate all of the overhead that the other runtimes are paying for; we
also choose different parsing strategies depending on the byte-to-varint
ratio of the record.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/hyperpb/repeated.svg alt&gt;&lt;figcaption&gt;&lt;p&gt;Throughput for various repeated field benchmarks.
This excludes the &lt;code&gt;repeated fixed32&lt;/code&gt; benchmarks, since those achieve
such high throughputs (~20 Gbps) that they make the chart unreadable.&lt;/figcaption&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;These optimizations account for the performance difference between
&lt;code&gt;descriptor/#00&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;descriptor/#01&lt;/code&gt; in the first benchmark chart. The
latter is a &lt;code&gt;FileDescriptorSet&lt;/code&gt; containing &lt;code&gt;SourceCodeInfo&lt;/code&gt;, Protobuf&amp;rsquo;s
janky debuginfo format. It is dominated by &lt;code&gt;repeated int32&lt;/code&gt; fields.&lt;p&gt;NB: This chart is currently missing the Y-axis, I need to have it re-made.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;Map parsing performance has been a bit of a puzzle. &lt;code&gt;vtprotobuf&lt;/code&gt; cheats by
rejecting some valid map entry encodings, such as (in Protoscope)
&lt;code&gt;{1: {&#34;key&#34;}}&lt;/code&gt; (value is implied to be &lt;code&gt;&#34;&#34;&lt;/code&gt;), while mis-parsing others, such
as &lt;code&gt;{2: {&#34;value&#34;} 1: {&#34;key&#34;}}&lt;/code&gt; (fields can go in any order), since they
don&amp;rsquo;t actually validate the field numbers like &lt;code&gt;hyperpb&lt;/code&gt; does.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s where the benchmarks currently stand for maps:&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/hyperpb/maps.svg alt&gt;&lt;figcaption&gt;&lt;p&gt;Throughput for various map parsing benchmarks.&lt;/figcaption&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Maps, I&amp;rsquo;m told, are not very popular in Protobuf, so they&amp;rsquo;re not something I
have tried to optimize as hard as packed repeated fields.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
