    <title>Protobuf Tip #6: The Subtle Dangers of Enum Aliases</title>
    <link href="/2025/05/20/protobuf-tip-6"/>
    <updated>2025-05-20T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/05/20/protobuf-tip-6</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;I&amp;rsquo;ve been very fortunate to dodge a nickname throughout my entire career. I&amp;rsquo;ve
never had one. &amp;ndash; Jimmie Johnson&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: Enum values can have aliases. This feature is poorly designed and
shouldn’t be used. The
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#enum_no_allow_alias&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENUM_NO_ALLOW_ALIAS&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
Buf lint rule prevents you from using them by default.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m editing a series of best practice pieces on Protobuf, a language that I
work on which has lots of evil corner-cases.These are shorter than what I
typically post here, but I think it fits with what you, dear reader, come to
this blog for. These tips are also posted on the
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/totw-5-avoid-import-public-weak&gt;buf.build blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=confusion-and-breakage&gt;&lt;a href=#confusion-and-breakage&gt;Confusion and Breakage&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf permits multiple enum values to have the same number. Such enum values
are said to be &lt;em&gt;aliases&lt;/em&gt; of each other. Protobuf used to allow this by default,
but now you have to set a special option, &lt;code&gt;allow_alias&lt;/code&gt;, for the compiler to not
reject it.&lt;p&gt;This can be used to effectively rename values without breaking existing code:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;myapi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;v1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;MyEnum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;option&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;allow_alias&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;true&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;MY_ENUM_UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;MY_ENUM_BAD&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;deprecated&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kc&gt;true&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;MY_ENUM_MORE_SPECIFIC&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This works perfectly fine, and is fully wire-compatible! And unlike renaming a
field (see &lt;a href=/2025/04/08/protobuf-tip-1&gt;TotW #1&lt;/a&gt;), it won’t
result in source code breakages.&lt;p&gt;But if you use either reflection or JSON, or a runtime like Java that doesn’t
cleanly allow enums with multiple names, you’ll be in for a nasty surprise.&lt;p&gt;For example, if you request an enum value from an enum using reflection, such as
with &lt;code&gt;protoreflect.EnumValueDescriptors.ByNumber()&lt;/code&gt;, the value you’ll get is the
one that appears in the file lexically. In fact, both
&lt;code&gt;myapipb.MyEnum_MY_ENUM_BAD.String()&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;myapipb.MyEnum_MY_ENUM_MORE_SPECIFIC.String()&lt;/code&gt; return the same value, leading
to potential confusion, as the old “bad” value will be used in printed output
like logs.&lt;p&gt;You might think, “oh, I’ll switch the order of the aliases”. But that would be
an &lt;em&gt;actual&lt;/em&gt; wire format break. Not for the binary format, but for JSON. That’s
because JSON preferentially stringifies enum values by using their declared name
(if the value is in range). So, reordering the values means that what once
serialized as &lt;code&gt;{&#34;my_field&#34;: &#34;MY_ENUM_BAD&#34;}&lt;/code&gt; now serializes as
&lt;code&gt;{&#34;my_field&#34;: &#34;MY_ENUM_MORE_SPECIFIC&#34;}&lt;/code&gt; .&lt;p&gt;If an old binary that hasn’t had the new enum value added sees this JSON
document, it won’t parse correctly, and you’ll be in for a bad time.&lt;p&gt;You can argue that this is a language bug, and it kind of is. Protobuf should
include an equivalent of &lt;code&gt;json_name&lt;/code&gt; for enum values, or mandate that JSON
should serialize enum values with multiple names as a number, rather than an
arbitrarily chosen enum name. The feature is intended to allow renaming of enum
values, but unfortunately Protobuf hobbled it enough that it’s pretty dangerous.&lt;h1 id=what-to-do&gt;&lt;a href=#what-to-do&gt;What To Do&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Instead, if you &lt;em&gt;really&lt;/em&gt; need to rename an enum value for usability or
compliance reasons (ideally, not just aesthetics) you’re better off making a new
enum type in a new version of your API. As long as the enum value numbers are
the same, it’ll be binary-compatible, but it will &lt;em&gt;somewhat&lt;/em&gt; reduce the risk of
the above JSON confusion.&lt;p&gt;Buf provides a lint rule against this feature,
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#enum_no_allow_alias&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENUM_NO_ALLOW_ALIAS&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
, and Protobuf requires that you specify a magic option to enable this behavior,
so in practice you don’t need to worry about this. But remember, the
consequences of enum aliases go much further than JSON—they affect anything that
uses reflection. So even if you don’t use JSON, you can still get burned.</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Protobuf Tip #5: Avoid import public/weak</title>
    <link href="/2025/05/13/protobuf-tip-5"/>
    <updated>2025-05-13T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/05/13/protobuf-tip-5</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;My dad had a guitar but it was acoustic, so I smashed a mirror and glued broken
glass to it to make it look more metal. It looked ridiculous! &amp;ndash;Max Cavalera&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: Avoid &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;import weak&lt;/code&gt;. The Buf lint rules
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#import_no_public&gt;&lt;code&gt;IMPORT_NO_PUBLIC&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; and
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#import_no_weak&gt;&lt;code&gt;IMPORT_NO_WEAK&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; enforce
this for you by default.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m editing a series of best practice pieces on Protobuf, a language that I
work on which has lots of evil corner-cases.These are shorter than what I
typically post here, but I think it fits with what you, dear reader, come to
this blog for. These tips are also posted on the &lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/totw-5-avoid-import-public-weak&gt;buf.build blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf &lt;code&gt;import&lt;/code&gt;s allow you to specify two special modes: &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;import weak&lt;/code&gt;. The Buf CLI lints against these by default, but you might be
tempted to try using them anyway, especially because
&lt;a href=https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/df58085901d8fb80c2c021e405923bb2351a6f29/google/spanner/v1/spanner.proto#L19&gt;some GCP APIs use &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.
What are these modes, and why do they exist?&lt;h2 id=import-visibility&gt;&lt;a href=#import-visibility&gt;Import Visibility&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf imports are by file path, a fact that is very strongly baked into the
language and its reflection model.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;import&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;my/other/api.proto&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Importing a file dumps all of its symbols into the current file. For the
purposes of name resolution, it’s as if all if the declarations in that file
have been pasted into the current file. However, this isn’t transitive. If:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;a.proto&lt;/code&gt; imports &lt;code&gt;b.proto&lt;/code&gt; &amp;mldr;&lt;li&gt;and &lt;code&gt;b.proto&lt;/code&gt; imports &lt;code&gt;c.proto&lt;/code&gt; &amp;mldr;&lt;li&gt;and &lt;code&gt;c.proto&lt;/code&gt; defines &lt;code&gt;foo.Bar&lt;/code&gt;&amp;mldr;&lt;li&gt;then, &lt;code&gt;a.proto&lt;/code&gt; must import &lt;code&gt;c.proto&lt;/code&gt; to refer to &lt;code&gt;foo.Bar&lt;/code&gt;, even though
&lt;code&gt;b.proto&lt;/code&gt; imports it.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is similar to how importing a package as &lt;code&gt;.&lt;/code&gt; works in Go. When you write
&lt;code&gt;import . &#34;strings&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, it dumps all of the declarations from the &lt;code&gt;strings&lt;/code&gt;
package into the current file, but not those of any files that &lt;code&gt;&#34;strings&#34;&lt;/code&gt;
imports.&lt;p&gt;Now, what’s nice about Go is that packages can be broken up into files in a way
that is transparent to users; users of a package import &lt;em&gt;the package&lt;/em&gt;, not the
files of that package. Unfortunately, Protobuf is not like that, so the file
structure of a package leaks to its callers.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt; was intended as a mechanism for allowing API writers to break up
files that were getting out of control. You can define a new file &lt;code&gt;new.proto&lt;/code&gt;
for some of the definitions in &lt;code&gt;big.proto&lt;/code&gt;, move them to the new file, and then
add &lt;code&gt;import public &#34;new.proto&#34;;&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;big.proto&lt;/code&gt;. Existing imports of &lt;code&gt;big.proto&lt;/code&gt;
won’t be broken, hooray!&lt;p&gt;Except this feature was designed for C++. In C++, each &lt;code&gt;.proto&lt;/code&gt; file maps to a
&lt;code&gt;.proto.h&lt;/code&gt; header, which you &lt;code&gt;#include&lt;/code&gt; in your application code. In C++,
&lt;code&gt;#include&lt;/code&gt; behaves like &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt;, so marking an import as &lt;code&gt;public&lt;/code&gt; only
changes name resolution in Protobuf—the C++ backend doesn’t have to do anything
to maintain source compatibility when an import is changed to &lt;code&gt;public&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;But other backends, like Go, do not work this way: &lt;code&gt;import&lt;/code&gt; in Go &lt;em&gt;doesn’t&lt;/em&gt; pull
in symbols transitively, so Go would need to explicitly add aliases for all of
the symbols that come in through a public import. That is, if you had:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// foo.proto
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;myapi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;v1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;...&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// bar.proto
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;myotherapi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;v1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;import&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;public&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;foo.proto&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Then the Go backend has to generate a &lt;code&gt;type Foo = foopb.Foo&lt;/code&gt; in &lt;code&gt;bar.pb.go&lt;/code&gt; to
emulate this behavior (in fact, I was surprised to learn Go Protobuf implements
this at all). Go &lt;em&gt;happens&lt;/em&gt; to implement public imports correctly, but not all
backends are as careful, because this feature is obscure.&lt;p&gt;The
&lt;a href=https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/df58085901d8fb80c2c021e405923bb2351a6f29/google/spanner/v1/spanner.proto#L19&gt;&lt;code&gt;spanner.proto&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
example of an &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt; isn’t even used for breaking up an existing file;
instead, it’s used to not make a huge file bigger and avoid making callers have
to add an additional import. This is a &lt;em&gt;bad use&lt;/em&gt; of a &lt;em&gt;bad feature!&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;Using &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt; to effectively “hide” imports makes it harder to
understand what a &lt;code&gt;.proto&lt;/code&gt; file is pulling in. If Protobuf imports were at the
package/symbol level, like Go or Java, this feature would not need to exist.
Unfortunately, Protobuf is closely tailored for C++, and this is one of the
consequences.&lt;p&gt;Instead of using &lt;code&gt;import public&lt;/code&gt; to break up a file, simply plan to break up the
file in the next version of the API.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#import_no_public&gt;&lt;code&gt;IMPORT_NO_PUBLIC&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
Buf lint rule enforces that no one uses this feature by default. It’s tempting,
but the footguns aren&amp;rsquo;t worth it.&lt;h2 id=weak-imports&gt;&lt;a href=#weak-imports&gt;Weak Imports&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Public imports have a good, if flawed, reason to exist. Their implementation
details are the main thing that kneecaps them.&lt;p&gt;Weak imports, however, simply should not exist. They were added to the language
to make it easier for some of Google’s enormous binaries to avoid running out of
linker memory, by making it so that message types could be dropped if they
weren’t accessed. This means that weak imports are “optional”—if the
corresponding descriptors are missing at runtime, the C++ runtime can handle it
gracefully.&lt;p&gt;This leads to all kinds of implementation complexity and subtle behavior
differences across runtimes. Most runtimes implement (or implemented, in the
case of those that removed support) &lt;code&gt;import weak&lt;/code&gt; in a buggy or inconsistent
way. It’s unlikely the feature will ever be truly removed, even though Google
has tried.&lt;p&gt;Don’t use &lt;code&gt;import weak&lt;/code&gt;. It should be treated as completely non-functional. The
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#import_no_weak&gt;&lt;code&gt;IMPORT_NO_WEAK&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; Buf lint
rule takes care of this for you.</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Protobuf Tip #4: Accepting Mistakes We Can&#39;t Fix</title>
    <link href="/2025/04/29/protobuf-tip-4"/>
    <updated>2025-04-29T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/04/29/protobuf-tip-4</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Bad humor is an evasion of reality; good humor is an acceptance of it.
&amp;ndash;Malcolm Muggeridge&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: Protobuf&amp;rsquo;s distributed nature introduces evolution risks that make it
hard to fix some types of mistakes. Sometimes the best thing to do is to just
let it be.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m editing a series of best practice pieces on Protobuf, a language that I
work on which has lots of evil corner-cases.These are shorter than what I
typically post here, but I think it fits with what you, dear reader, come to
this blog for. These tips are also posted on the
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/totw-4-accepting-mistakes&gt;buf.build blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=a-different-mindset&gt;&lt;a href=#a-different-mindset&gt;A Different Mindset&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Often, you&amp;rsquo;ll design and implement a feature for the software you work on, and
despite your best efforts to test it, something terrible happens in production.
We have a playbook for this, though: fix the bug in your program and ship or
deploy the new, fixed version to your users. It might mean working late for big
emergencies, but turnaround for most organizations is a day to a week.&lt;p&gt;Most bugs aren&amp;rsquo;t emergencies, though. Sometimes a function has a confusing name,
or an integer type is just a bit too small for real-world data, or an API
conflates “zero&#34; and “null&#34;. You fix the API, refactor all usages in your API in
one commit, merge, and the fix rolls out gradually.&lt;p&gt;Unless, of course, it&amp;rsquo;s a bug in a communication API, like a serialization
format: your Protobuf types, or your JSON schema, or the not-too-pretty code
that parses fields out of dict built from a YAML file. Here, you can&amp;rsquo;t &lt;em&gt;just&lt;/em&gt;
atomically fix the world. Fixing bugs in your APIs (from here on, “APIs&#34; means
“Protobuf definitions&#34;) requires a different mindset than fixing bugs in
ordinary code.&lt;h2 id=what-are-the-risks&gt;&lt;a href=#what-are-the-risks&gt;What Are the Risks?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf&amp;rsquo;s wire format is designed so that you can safely add new fields to a
type, or values to an enum, without needing to perform an atomic upgrade. But
other changes, like renaming fields or changing their type, are very dangerous.&lt;p&gt;This is because Protobuf types exist on a temporal axis: different versions of
the same type exist simultaneously among programs in the field that are actively
talking to each other. This means that &lt;em&gt;writers from the future&lt;/em&gt; (that is, new
serialization code) must be careful to not confuse the many &lt;em&gt;readers from the
past&lt;/em&gt; (old versions of the deserialization code). Conversely, future readers
must tolerate anything past writers produce.&lt;p&gt;In a modern distributed deployment, the number of versions that exist at once
can be quite large. This is true even in self-hosted clusters, but becomes much
more fraught whenever user-upgradable software is involved. This can include
mobile applications that talk to your servers, or appliance software managed by
a third-party administrator, or even just browser-service communication.&lt;p&gt;The most important principle: you can&amp;rsquo;t easily control when old versions of a
type or service are no longer relevant. As soon as a type escapes out of the
scope of even a single team, upgrading types becomes a departmental effort.&lt;h2 id=learning-to-love-the-bomb&gt;&lt;a href=#learning-to-love-the-bomb&gt;Learning to Love the Bomb&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are many places where Protobuf could have made schema evolution easier,
but didn&amp;rsquo;t. For example, changing &lt;code&gt;int32 foo = 1;&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;sfixed32 foo = 1;&lt;/code&gt; is a
breakage, even though at the wire format level, it is &lt;em&gt;possible&lt;/em&gt; for a parser to
distinguish and accept both forms of &lt;code&gt;foo&lt;/code&gt; correctly. There too many other
examples to list, but it&amp;rsquo;s important to understand that the language is not
always working in our favor.&lt;p&gt;For example, if we notice a &lt;code&gt;int32&lt;/code&gt; value is too small, and should have been
64-bit, you can&amp;rsquo;t upgrade it without readers from the past potentially
truncating it. But we really have to upgrade it! What are our options?&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Issue a new version of the message and all of its dependencies. This is the
main reason why sticking a version number in the package name, as enforced by
Buf&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#package_version_suffix&gt;&lt;code&gt;PACKAGE_VERSION_SUFFIX&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
lint rule, is so important.&lt;li&gt;Do the upgrade anyway and hope nothing breaks. This &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt; work for certain
kinds of upgrades, if the underlying format is compatible, but it can have
&lt;strong&gt;disastrous consequences&lt;/strong&gt; if you don&amp;rsquo;t know what you&amp;rsquo;re doing, especially
if it&amp;rsquo;s a type that&amp;rsquo;s not completely internal to a team&amp;rsquo;s project.
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/breaking/overview/&gt;Buf breaking change detection&lt;/a&gt;
helps you avoid changes with potential for breakage.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course, there is a third option, which is to accept that some things aren&amp;rsquo;t
worth fixing. When the cost of a fix is so high, fixes just aren&amp;rsquo;t worth it,
especially when the language is working against us.&lt;p&gt;This means that even in Buf&amp;rsquo;s own APIs, we sometimes do things in a way that
isn&amp;rsquo;t quite ideal, or is inconsistent with our own best practices. Sometimes,
the ecosystem changes in a way that changes best practice, but we can&amp;rsquo;t upgrade
to it without breaking our users. In the same way, you shouldn&amp;rsquo;t rush to use
new, better language features if they would cause protocol breaks: sometimes,
the right thing is to do nothing, because not breaking your users is more
important.&lt;br&gt;&lt;p&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Protobuf Tip #3: Enum Names Need Prefixes</title>
    <link href="/2025/04/22/protobuf-tip-3"/>
    <updated>2025-04-22T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/04/22/protobuf-tip-3</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Smart people learn from their mistakes. But the real sharp ones learn from the
mistakes of others. &amp;ndash;Brandon Mull&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt;s inherit some unfortunate behaviors from C++. Use the Buf lint
rules
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#enum_value_prefix&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENUM_VALUE_PREFIX&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; and
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#enum_zero_value_suffix&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENUM_ZERO_VALUE_SUFFIX&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
 to avoid this problem (they&amp;rsquo;re part of the &lt;code&gt;DEFAULT&lt;/code&gt; category).&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m editing a series of best practice pieces on Protobuf, a language that I
work on which has lots of evil corner-cases.These are shorter than what I
typically post here, but I think it fits with what you, dear reader, come to
this blog for. These tips are also posted on the
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/totw-3-enum-names-need-prefixes&gt;buf.build blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=c-style-enums&gt;&lt;a href=#c-style-enums&gt;C++-Style Enums&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt;s define data types that represent a small set of valid values.
For example, &lt;code&gt;google.rpc.Code&lt;/code&gt; lists status codes used by various RPC
frameworks, such as GRPC. Under the hood, every &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt; is just an &lt;code&gt;int32&lt;/code&gt;  on
the wire, although codegen backends will generate custom types and constants for
the enum to make it easier to use.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt;s were originally designed to match C++ enums exactly, and
they inadvertently replicate many of those behaviors.&lt;p&gt;If you look at the source for &lt;code&gt;google.rpc.Code&lt;/code&gt;, and compare it to, say,
&lt;code&gt;google.protobuf.FieldDescriptorProto.Type&lt;/code&gt;, you will notice a subtle
difference:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;google&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;rpc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Code&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;OK&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;CANCELLED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;UNKNOWN&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;google&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;protobuf&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;FieldDescriptorProto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// 0 is reserved for errors.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;TYPE_DOUBLE&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;TYPE_FLOAT&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;TYPE_INT64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;FieldDescriptorProto.Type&lt;/code&gt; has values starting with &lt;code&gt;TYPE_&lt;/code&gt;, but &lt;code&gt;Code&lt;/code&gt; &amp;rsquo;s
values don&amp;rsquo;t have a &lt;code&gt;CODE_&lt;/code&gt; prefix.  This is because the fully-qualified names
(FQN) of an enum value &lt;em&gt;don&amp;rsquo;t include the name of the enum.&lt;/em&gt; That is,
&lt;code&gt;TYPE_DOUBLE&lt;/code&gt; actually refers to
&lt;code&gt;google.protobuf.FieldDescriptorProto.TYPE_DOUBLE&lt;/code&gt;. Thus, &lt;code&gt;OK&lt;/code&gt; is not
&lt;code&gt;google.rpc.Code.OK&lt;/code&gt;, but &lt;code&gt;google.rpc.OK&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This is because it matches the behavior of unscoped C++ enums. C++ is the
“reference” implementation, so the language often bends for the sake of the C++
backend.&lt;p&gt;When generating code, &lt;code&gt;protoc&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s C++ backend emits the above as follows:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;namespace&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;google&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rpc&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Code&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;OK&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;CANCELLED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;namespace&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;google&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;protobuf&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;class&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;FieldDescriptorProto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;final&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;public&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;TYPE_DOUBLE&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;TYPE_FLOAT&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;   &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;And in C++, &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt;s don&amp;rsquo;t scope their enumerators: you write &lt;code&gt;google::rpc::OK&lt;/code&gt;,
NOT &lt;code&gt;google::rpc::Code::OK&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;If you know C++, you might be thinking, “why didn&amp;rsquo;t they use &lt;code&gt;enum class&lt;/code&gt;?!”?
Enums were added in &lt;code&gt;proto2&lt;/code&gt;, which was developed around 2007-2008, but Google
didn&amp;rsquo;t start using C++11, which introduced &lt;code&gt;enum class&lt;/code&gt; , until much, much
later.&lt;p&gt;Now, if you&amp;rsquo;re a Go or Java programmer, you&amp;rsquo;re probably wondering why you even
care about C++. Both Go and Java do scope enum values to the enum type (although
Go does it in a somewhat grody way: &lt;code&gt;rpcpb.Code_OK&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, this affects name collision detection in Protobuf. You can&amp;rsquo;t
write the following code:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;myapi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;v1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;RED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;YELLOW&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;GREEN&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Speed&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;SLOW&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;FAST&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because the enum name is not part of the FQN for an enum value, both
&lt;code&gt;UNSPECIFIED&lt;/code&gt;s here have the FQN &lt;code&gt;myapi.v1.UNSPECIFIED&lt;/code&gt;, so Protobuf complains
about duplicate symbols.&lt;p&gt;Thus, the convention we see in &lt;code&gt;FieldDescriptorProto.Type&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nn&gt;myapi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;v1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Stoplight&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;STOPLIGHT_UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;STOPLIGHT_RED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;STOPLIGHT_YELLOW&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;STOPLIGHT_GREEN&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Speed&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;SPEED_UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;SPEED_SLOW&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;SPEED_FAST&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Buf provides a lint rule to enforce this convention:
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#enum_value_prefix&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENUM_VALUE_PREFIX&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.
Even though you might think that an enum name will be unique, because top-level
enums bleed their names into the containing package, the problem spreads across
packages!&lt;h2 id=zero-values&gt;&lt;a href=#zero-values&gt;Zero Values&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;proto3&lt;/code&gt; relies heavily on the concept of &amp;ldquo;zero values&amp;rdquo; &amp;ndash; all non-message fields
that are neither &lt;code&gt;repeated&lt;/code&gt; nor &lt;code&gt;optional&lt;/code&gt; are implicitly zero if they are not
present. Thus, &lt;code&gt;proto3&lt;/code&gt; requires that enums specify a value equal to zero.&lt;p&gt;By convention, this value shouldn&amp;rsquo;t be a specific value of the enum, but rather
a value representing that no value is specified.
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/docs/lint/rules/#enum_zero_value_suffix&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENUM_ZERO_VALUE_SUFFIX&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
enforces this, with a default of &lt;code&gt;_UNSPECIFIED&lt;/code&gt;. Of course, there are situations
where this might not make sense for you, and a suffix like &lt;code&gt;_ZERO&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;_UNKNOWN&lt;/code&gt;
might make more sense.&lt;p&gt;It may be tempting to have a specific &amp;ldquo;good default&amp;rdquo; value for the zero value.
Beware though, because that choice is forever. Picking a generic &amp;ldquo;unknown&amp;rdquo; as
the default reduces the chance you&amp;rsquo;ll burn yourself.&lt;h2 id=why-dont-all-of-googles-protobuf-files-do-this&gt;&lt;a href=#why-dont-all-of-googles-protobuf-files-do-this&gt;Why Don&amp;rsquo;t All of Google&amp;rsquo;s Protobuf Files Do This?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Name prefixes and zero values also teach us an important lesson: because
Protobuf names are forever, it&amp;rsquo;s really hard to fix style mistakes, especially
as we collectively get better at using Protobuf.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;google.rpc.Code&lt;/code&gt; is intended to be source-compatible with very old existing C++
code, so it throws caution to the wind. &lt;code&gt;FieldDescriptorProto.Type&lt;/code&gt; doesn&amp;rsquo;t have
a zero value because in &lt;code&gt;proto2&lt;/code&gt; , which doesn&amp;rsquo;t have zero value footguns in its
wire format, you don&amp;rsquo;t need to worry about that. The lesson isn&amp;rsquo;t just to use
Buf&amp;rsquo;s linter to try to avoid some of the known pitfalls, but also to remember
that even APIs designed by the authors of the language make unfixable mistakes,
so unlike other programming languages, imitating &amp;ldquo;existing practice&amp;rdquo; isn&amp;rsquo;t
always the best strategy.</content>

  <entry>
    <title>Cheating the Reaper in Go</title>
    <link href="/2025/04/21/go-arenas"/>
    <updated>2025-04-21T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/04/21/go-arenas</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Even though I am a C++ programmer at heart, Go fascinates me for none of the
reasons you think. Go has made several interesting design decisions:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;It has virtually no Undefined Behavior&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;It has very simple GC semantics that they&amp;rsquo;re mostly stuck with due to design
decisions in the surface language.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;These things mean that despite Go having a GC, it&amp;rsquo;s possible to do manual memory
management in pure Go and in cooperation with the GC (although without any help
from the &lt;code&gt;runtime&lt;/code&gt; package). To demonstrate this, we will be building an
untyped, garbage-collected arena abstraction in Go which relies on several GC
implementation details.&lt;p&gt;I would never play this kind of game in Rust or C++, because LLVM is extremely
intelligent and able to find all kinds of ways to break you over the course of
frequent compiler upgrades. On the other hand, although Go does not promise any
compatibility across versions for code that imports &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt;, in practice, two
forces work against Go doing this:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go does not attempt to define what is and isn&amp;rsquo;t allowed: &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; lacks any
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_semantics&gt;operational semantics&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go prioritizes not breaking the ecosystem; this allows to assume that
&lt;a href=https://www.hyrumslaw.com/&gt;Hyrum&amp;rsquo;s Law&lt;/a&gt; will protect certain observable
behaviors of the runtime, from which we may infer what can or cannot break
easily.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is in contrast to a high-performance native compiler like LLVM, which has a
carefully defined boundary around all UB, allowing them to arbitrarily break
programs that cross it (mostly) without fear of breaking the ecosystem.&lt;p&gt;So, let&amp;rsquo;s dive in and cheat death.&lt;h2 id=what-are-we-building&gt;&lt;a href=#what-are-we-building&gt;What Are We Building?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Our goal is to build an &lt;em&gt;arena&lt;/em&gt;, which is a data structure for efficient
allocation of memory that has the same lifetime. This reduces pressure on the
general-purpose allocator by only requesting memory in large chunks and then
freeing it all at once.&lt;p&gt;For a comparison in Go, consider the following program:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;import&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;fmt&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1000&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;prev&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;cap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;append&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;cap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;prev&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;      &lt;span class=nx&gt;fmt&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Println&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;cap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;

programming language&amp;rsquo;s dynamic array abstraction makes this optimization.&lt;p&gt;An arena generalizes this concept, but instead of resizing exponentially, it
allocates &lt;em&gt;new&lt;/em&gt; blocks and vends pointers into them. The interface we want to
conform to is as follows:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Allocator&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

layout. Go does not have user-visible uninitialized memory, so we additionally
require that the returned region be zeroed. We also require that &lt;code&gt;align&lt;/code&gt; be a
power of two.&lt;p&gt;We can give this a type-safe interface by writing a generic &lt;code&gt;New&lt;/code&gt; function:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// New allocates a fresh zero value of type T on the given allocator, and
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// returns a pointer to it.

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Alloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Sizeof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;t&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Alignof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;t&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This all feels very fine and dandy to anyone used to hurting themselves with
&lt;code&gt;malloc&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;operator new&lt;/code&gt; in C++, but there is a small problem. What happens
when we allocate pointer-typed memory into this allocator?&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Allocate a pointer in our custom allocator, and then
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// initialize it to a pointer on the Go heap.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;New&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;myAlloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;runtime&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;GC&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;**&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;42&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Use after free!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;Allocator.Alloc&lt;/code&gt; takes a size and an alignment, which is sufficient to describe
the &lt;em&gt;layout&lt;/em&gt; of any type. For example, on 64-bit systems, &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;*int&lt;/code&gt; have
the same layout: 8 bytes of size, and 8 bytes of alignment.&lt;p&gt;However, the Go GC (and all garbage collectors, generally) require one
additional piece of information, which is somewhere between the layout of a
value (how it is placed in memory) and the type of a value (rich information on
its structure). To understand this, we need a brief overview on what a GC does.&lt;h2 id=mark-and-sweep&gt;&lt;a href=#mark-and-sweep&gt;Mark and Sweep&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;For a complete overview on how to build a simple GC, take a look at a toy GC I
designed some time ago: [The Alkyne GC].&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;[The Alkyne GC]: {{ site.baseurl }}2022/06/07/alkyne-gc/&lt;p&gt;A garbage collector&amp;rsquo;s responsibility is to maintain a memory allocator and an
accounting of:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;What memory has been allocated.&lt;li&gt;Whether that memory is still in use.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Memory that is not in use can be reclaimed and marked as unallocated, for
re-use.&lt;p&gt;The most popular way to accomplish this is via a &amp;ldquo;mark and sweep&amp;rdquo; architecture.
The GC will periodically walk the entire object graph of the program from
certain pre-determined &lt;em&gt;roots&lt;/em&gt;; anything it finds is &amp;ldquo;marked&amp;rdquo; as alive. After a
mark is complete, all other memory is &amp;ldquo;swept&amp;rdquo;, which means to mark it is
unallocated for future re-use, or to return it to the OS, in the case of
significant surplus.&lt;p&gt;The roots are typically entities that are actively being manipulated by the
program. In the case of Go, this is anything currently on the stack of some
G&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, or anything in a global (of which there is a compile-time-known set).&lt;p&gt;The marking phase begins with &lt;em&gt;stack scanning&lt;/em&gt;, which looks at the stack of each
G and locates any pointers contained therein. The Go compiler generates metadata
for each function that specifies which stack slots in a function&amp;rsquo;s frame contain
pointers. All of these pointers are live by definition.&lt;p&gt;These pointers are placed into a queue, and each pointer is traced to its
allocation on the heap. If the GC does not know anything about a particular
address, it is discarded as foreign memory that does not need to be marked. If
it does, each pointer in that allocation is pushed onto the queue if it has not
already been marked as alive. The process continues until the queue is empty.&lt;p&gt;The critical step here is to take the address of some allocation, and convert it
into all of the pointer values within. Go has precise garbage collection, which
means that it only treats things declared as pointers in the surface language as
pointers: an integer that happens to look like an address will not result in
sweeping. This results in more efficient memory usage, but trades off some more
complexity in the GC.&lt;p&gt;For example, the types &lt;code&gt;*int&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;map[int]byte&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;string&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;struct {A int; B *int}&lt;/code&gt; all contain at least one pointer, while &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;[1000]byte&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;struct {X bool; F uintptr}&lt;/code&gt; do not. The latter are called
&lt;em&gt;pointer-free&lt;/em&gt; types.&lt;p&gt;Go enhances the layout of a type into a &lt;em&gt;shape&lt;/em&gt; by adding a bitset that
specifies which pointer-aligned, pointer-sized words of the type&amp;rsquo;s memory region
contain a pointer. These are called the &lt;em&gt;pointer bits&lt;/em&gt;. For example, here are
the shapes of a few Go types on a 64-bit system.&lt;table&gt;&lt;thead&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;th&gt;Type&lt;th&gt;Size/Align&lt;th&gt;Pointer Bits&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;tbody&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;byte&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;1/1&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;8/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;rune&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;4/4&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;*int&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;8/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;1&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;8/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;1&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;string&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;16/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;10&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;[]int&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;24/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;100&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;[3]string&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;48/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;101010&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;map[int]byte&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;8/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;1&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;map[int]string&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;8/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;1&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;16/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;01&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;error&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;16/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;01&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;func(int) int&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;8/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;1&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;runtime.hchan&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;td&gt;104/8&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;0010110011110&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/table&gt;&lt;p&gt;In the Go GC, each allocation is tagged with its shape (this is done in a
variety of ways in the GC, either through an explicit header on the allocation,
itself (a &amp;ldquo;malloc header&amp;rdquo;), a runtime type stored in the allocation&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;code&gt;runtime.mspan&lt;/code&gt;, or another mechanism). When scanning a value, it uses this
information to determine where the pointers to scan through are.&lt;p&gt;The most obvious problem with our &lt;code&gt;Allocator.Alloc&lt;/code&gt; type is that it does not
discriminate shapes, so it cannot allocate memory that contains pointers: the GC
will not be able to find the pointers, and will free them prematurely!&lt;p&gt;In our example where we allocated an &lt;code&gt;*int&lt;/code&gt; in our custom allocator, we wind up
with a &lt;code&gt;**int&lt;/code&gt; on the stack. You would think that Go would simply trace through
the first &lt;code&gt;*&lt;/code&gt; to find an &lt;code&gt;*int&lt;/code&gt; and mark it as being alive, but that is not what
happens! Go instead finds a pointer into some chunk that the custom allocator
grabbed from the heap, which is missing the pointer bits of its shape!&lt;p&gt;Why does go not look at the type of the pointer it steps through? Two reasons.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;All pointers in Go are untyped from the runtime&amp;rsquo;s perspective; every &lt;code&gt;*T&lt;/code&gt;
gets erased into an &lt;code&gt;unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt;. This allows much of the Go runtime to
be &amp;ldquo;generic&amp;rdquo; without using actual generics.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Pointee metadata can be aggregated, so that each pointer to an object does
not have to remember its type at runtime.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The end result for us is that we can&amp;rsquo;t put pointers on the arena. This makes our
&lt;code&gt;New&lt;/code&gt; API unsafe, especially since Go does not provide a standard constraint for
marking generic parameters as pointer-free: unsurprisingly, the don&amp;rsquo;t expect
most users to care about such a detail.&lt;p&gt;It &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; possible to deduce the pointer bits of a type using reflection, but
that&amp;rsquo;s very slow, and the whole point of using arenas is to go fast. As we
design our arena, though, it will become clear that there is a safe way to have
pointers on it.&lt;h2 id=designing-the-arena&gt;&lt;a href=#designing-the-arena&gt;Designing The Arena&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that we have a pretty good understanding about what the Go GC is doing, we
can go about designing a fast arena structure.&lt;p&gt;The ideal case is that a call to &lt;code&gt;Alloc&lt;/code&gt; is very fast: just offsetting a pointer
in the common case. One assumption we can make off the bat is that all memory
can be forced to have maximum alignment: most objects are a pointer or larger,
and Go does have a maximum alignment for ordinary user types, so we can just
ignore the &lt;code&gt;align&lt;/code&gt; parameter and always align to say, 8 bytes. This means that
the pointer to the next unallocated chunk will always be well-aligned. Thus, we
might come up with a structure like this one:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Arena&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

the same size. The number of times the &lt;code&gt;for b.Loop()&lt;/code&gt; loop will execute is
unknown, and determined by the benchmarking framework to try to reduce
statistical anomaly. This means that if we instead just benchmark a single
allocation, the result will be &lt;em&gt;very&lt;/em&gt; sensitive to the number of runs.&lt;p&gt;We also use &lt;code&gt;b.SetBytes&lt;/code&gt; to get a throughput measurement on the benchmark. This
is a bit easier to interpret than the gross &lt;code&gt;ns/op&lt;/code&gt;, the benchmark would
otherwise produce. It tells us how much memory each allocator can allocate per
unit time.&lt;p&gt;We want to compare against &lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt;, but just writing &lt;code&gt;_ = new(T)&lt;/code&gt; will get
optimized out, since the resulting pointer does not escape. Writing it to a
global is sufficient to convince Go that it escapes.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s the results, abbreviated to show only the bytes per second. All

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is quite nice, and certainly worth pursuing! The performance increase seems
to scale up with the amount of memory allocated, for a 2x-4x improvement across
different cases.&lt;p&gt;Now we need to contend with the fact that our implementation is completely
broken if we want to have pointers in it.&lt;h3 id=not-dropping-memory-on-the-ground&gt;&lt;a href=#not-dropping-memory-on-the-ground&gt;Not Dropping Memory on the Ground&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;In &lt;code&gt;(*Arena).Alloc&lt;/code&gt;, when we assign a freshly-allocated chunk, we overwrite
&lt;code&gt;a.next&lt;/code&gt;, which means the GC can reclaim it. But this is fine: as long as
pointers into that arena chunk are alive, the GC will not free it, independent
of the arena. So it seems like we don&amp;rsquo;t need to worry about it?&lt;p&gt;However, the whole point of an arena is to allocate lots of memory that has the
same lifetime. This is common for graph data structures, such as an AST or a
compiler IR, which performs a lot of work that allocates a lot and then throws
the result away.&lt;p&gt;We are not allowed to put pointers in the arena, because they would disappear
from the view of the GC and become freed too soon. But, if a pointer wants to go
on an arena, it necessarily outlive the whole arena, since it outlives part of
the arena, and the arena is meant to have the same lifetime.&lt;p&gt;In particular, if we could make it so that holding any pointer returned by
&lt;code&gt;Alloc&lt;/code&gt; prevents the &lt;em&gt;entire arena&lt;/em&gt; from being swept by the GC, the arena can
safely contain pointers into itself! Consider this:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;We have a pointer &lt;code&gt;p **int&lt;/code&gt;. It is allocated on some arena &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The GC sees our pointer (as a type-erased &lt;code&gt;unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt;) and marks its
allocation as live.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Somehow, the GC also marks &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; as alive as a consequence.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Somehow, the GC then marks every chunk &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; has allocated as alive.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Therefore he chunk that &lt;code&gt;*p&lt;/code&gt; points to is also alive, so &lt;code&gt;*p&lt;/code&gt; does not need
to be marked directly, and will not be freed early.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The step (3) is crucial. By forcing the whole arena to be marked, any pointers
stored in the arena into itself will be kept alive automatically, without the GC
needing to know how to scan for them.&lt;p&gt;So, even though &lt;code&gt;*New[*int](a) = new(int)&lt;/code&gt; is still going to result in a
use-after-free, &lt;code&gt;*New[*int](a) = New[int](a)&lt;/code&gt; would not! This small improvement
does not make arenas themselves safe, but a data structure with an internal
arena can be completely safe, so long as the only pointers that go into the
arena are from the arena itself.&lt;p&gt;How can we make this work? The easy part is (4), which we can implement by
adding a &lt;code&gt;[]unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt; to the arena, and sticking every pointer we allocate
into it.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:9&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Arena&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:10&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Seems pretty much the same, which is a good sign.&lt;h3 id=back-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#back-pointers&gt;Back Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that the arena does not discard any allocated memory, we can focus on
condition (3): making it so that if any pointer returned by &lt;code&gt;Alloc&lt;/code&gt; is alive,
then so is the whole arena.&lt;p&gt;Here we can make use of an important property of how Go&amp;rsquo;s GC works: any pointer
into an allocation will keep it alive, as well as &lt;em&gt;anything reachable from that
pointer&lt;/em&gt;. But the chunks we&amp;rsquo;re allocating are &lt;code&gt;[]uintptr&lt;/code&gt;s, which will not be
scanned. If there could &lt;em&gt;somehow&lt;/em&gt; be a single pointer in this slice that was
scanned, we would be able to stick the pointer &lt;code&gt;a *Arena&lt;/code&gt; there, and so when
anything that &lt;code&gt;Alloc&lt;/code&gt; returns is scanned, it would cause &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; to be marked as
alive.&lt;p&gt;So far, we have been allocating &lt;code&gt;[N]uintptr&lt;/code&gt; using &lt;code&gt;make([]T)&lt;/code&gt;, but we would
actually like to allocate &lt;code&gt;struct { A [N]uintptr; P unsafe.Pointer }&lt;/code&gt;, where &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt;
is some dynamic value.&lt;p&gt;In its infintie wisdom, the Go standard library actually gives us a dedicated
mechanism to do this: &lt;code&gt;reflect.StructOf&lt;/code&gt;. This can be used to construct
arbitrary anonymous &lt;code&gt;struct&lt;/code&gt; types at runtime, which we can then allocate on the
heap.&lt;p&gt;So, instead of calling &lt;code&gt;make&lt;/code&gt;, we might call this function:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:11&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Arena&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;allocChunk&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;words&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;uintptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Pointer&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

we call this function. The branch is a bit unfortunate, but it&amp;rsquo;s necessary, as
noted by the comment.&lt;p&gt;In C++, if we have an array of &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt; with &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; elements in it, and &lt;code&gt;int* p&lt;/code&gt; is a

can&amp;rsquo;t be dereferenced; it points &amp;ldquo;one past the end&amp;rdquo; of the array. This is a
useful construction, since, for example, you can use it to eliminate a loop
induction variable:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c++ highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Naive for loop, has an induction variable i.

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;do_something&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go, however, gets very upset if you do this, because it confuses the garbage
collector. The GC can&amp;rsquo;t tell the difference between a one-past-the-end pointer
for allocation A, and for the start of allocation B immediately after it. At
best this causes memory to stay alive for longer, and at worst it triggers
safety interlocks in the GC. The GC will panic if it happens to scan a pointer
for an address that it knows has been freed.&lt;p&gt;But in our code above, every chunk now has an extra element at the very end that
is not used for allocation, so we &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt; have a pointer that &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt;
one-past-the-end of the &lt;code&gt;[N]uintptr&lt;/code&gt; that we are vending memory from.&lt;p&gt;The updated allocation function would look like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Arena&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Alloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;size&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;align&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;uintptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Pointer&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;x86 Assembly (Go Syntax)&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There&amp;rsquo;s a lot going on in this function, but most of it is a mix of Go not being
great at register allocation, and lots of &lt;em&gt;write barriers&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A write barrier is a mechanism for synchronizing ordinary user code with the GC.
Go generates code for one any time a non-pointer-free type is stored. For
example, writing to a &lt;code&gt;**int&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;*string&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;*[]int&lt;/code&gt; requires a write barrier.&lt;p&gt;Write barriers are implemented as follows:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;runtime.writeBarrier&lt;/code&gt; is checked, which determines whether the write barrier
is necessary, which is only when the GC is in the mark phase. Otherwise the
branch is taken to skip the write barrier.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;A call to one of the &lt;code&gt;runtime.gcWriteBarrierN&lt;/code&gt; functions happens. &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt; is the
number of pointers that the GC needs to be informed of.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;This function calls &lt;code&gt;runtime.gcWriteBarrier&lt;/code&gt;, which returns a buffer onto
which pointers the GC needs to now trace through should be written to.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The actual store happens.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;A write barrier is required for a case like the following. Consider the
following code.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;alloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;**&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:19&gt;x86 Assembly (Go Syntax)&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Note that two pointers get written: the pointer returned by &lt;code&gt;new(int)&lt;/code&gt;, and the
old value of &lt;code&gt;*n&lt;/code&gt;. This ensures that regardless of where in this function the GC
happens to be scanning through &lt;code&gt;*n&lt;/code&gt;, it sees both values during the mark phase.&lt;p&gt;Now, this isn&amp;rsquo;t necessary if the relevant pointers are already reachable in some
other way&amp;mldr; which is exactly the case in our arena (thanks to the &lt;code&gt;chunks&lt;/code&gt;
slice). So the write barrier in the fast path is redundant.&lt;p&gt;But, how do we get rid of it? There is &lt;code&gt;//go:nowritebarrier&lt;/code&gt;, but that&amp;rsquo;s not
allowed outside of a list of packages allowlisted in the compiler. It also
doens&amp;rsquo;t disable write barriers; it simply generates a diagnostic if any are
emitted.&lt;p&gt;But remember, write barriers only occur when storing pointer-typed memory&amp;mldr; so
we can just replace &lt;code&gt;next unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt; with &lt;code&gt;next uintptr&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:20&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Arena&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
