it&amp;rsquo;s forced to eagerly clear the huge allocated chunk every time, because it
contains pointers. If you profile this code, a ton of time is spent in
&lt;code&gt;runtime.memclrNoHeapPointers&lt;/code&gt;. Because the chunks of memory we allocate are
always of a specific size, we can use an array of &lt;code&gt;sync.Pool&lt;/code&gt;s to amortize the
cost of allocating and clearing chunks.&lt;p&gt;First, we need an entry in this array of pools, one for each size of memory we
allocate. Then, we need to set a finalizer on the arena to reclaim its memory
once we&amp;rsquo;re done. Finally, we can change the contract of &lt;code&gt;Alloc&lt;/code&gt; to require the
caller to clear the value for us, and change &lt;code&gt;New&lt;/code&gt; take a value as its argument:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:23&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;New&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Allocator&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Alloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Sizeof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Alignof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;

That&amp;rsquo;s a surprise. It does much better for small allocations, but it made
really big allocations worse! It&amp;rsquo;s not immediately clear to me why this is, but
note that &lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt; also got &lt;em&gt;much&lt;/em&gt; faster, which tells me that because the
allocations from the arena are longer-lived, the GC behaves somewhat
differently, causing some of the cost from allocating really large things with
&lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt; to be amortized.&lt;p&gt;Whether this optimization makes sense would require some profiling. An
alternative is to manually manage arena re-use, by adding a very unsafe
&lt;code&gt;Reset()&lt;/code&gt; function that causes the arena to behave as if it was just
constructed, but &lt;em&gt;keeping all of its allocated chunks&lt;/em&gt;. This is analogous to

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:28&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;That&amp;rsquo;s a massive improvement! There&amp;rsquo;s a couple of reasons this is faster. First,
it doesn&amp;rsquo;t require waiting for the GC to collect old arenas to make their memory
get reused. Second, the fast path is &lt;em&gt;very&lt;/em&gt; fast with no synchronization.&lt;p&gt;On the flipside, this is very dangerous: arena re-use needs to be carefully
managed, because you can wind up with unique pointers that aren&amp;rsquo;t.&lt;h3 id=realloc&gt;&lt;a href=#realloc&gt;Realloc&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go does not offer an easy mechanism to &amp;ldquo;reallocate&amp;rdquo; an allocation, as with
&lt;code&gt;realloc()&lt;/code&gt; in C. This is because it has no mechanism for freeing pointers
explicitly, which is necessary for a reallocation abstraction.&lt;p&gt;But we already don&amp;rsquo;t care about safety, so we can offer reallocation on our
arena. Now, the reallocation we can offer is quite primitive: if a chunk happens
to be the most recent one allocated, we can grow it. Otherwise we just allocate
a new chunk and don&amp;rsquo;t free the old one.&lt;p&gt;This makes it possible to implement &amp;ldquo;arena slices&amp;rdquo; that can be constructed by
appending, which will not trigger reallocation on slice growth as long as
nothing else gets put on the arena.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;Realloc&lt;/code&gt; would look something like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:29&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Arena&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Realloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;uintptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;bits&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;uint&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:30&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are other optimizations that we could make here that I haven&amp;rsquo;t discussed.
For example, arenas could be re-used; once an arena is done, it could be &amp;ldquo;reset&amp;rdquo;
and placed into a &lt;code&gt;sync.Pool&lt;/code&gt;. This arena would not need to go into the GC to
request new chunks, re-using the ones previously allocated (and potentially
saving on the cost of zeroing memory over and over again).&lt;p&gt;I did say that this relies very heavily on Go&amp;rsquo;s internal implementation details.
Whats the odds that they get broken in the future? Well, the requirement that
allocations know their shape is forced by the existence of &lt;code&gt;unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt;, and
the requirement that a pointer into any part of an allocation keeps the whole
thing alive essentially comes from slices being both sliceable and mutable; once
a slice escapes to the heap (and thus multiple goroutines) coordinating copies
for shrinking a slice would require much more complexity than the current write
barrier implementation.&lt;p&gt;And in my opinion, it&amp;rsquo;s pretty safe to say that Hyrum&amp;rsquo;s Law has us covered here.
;)&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go &lt;em&gt;does&lt;/em&gt; have some UB. For example, Go assumes that a G&amp;rsquo;s stack is never
read or written to by any other G, except by the GC across a write barrier.&lt;p&gt;That said, what UB does exist is very, very difficult to trip on purpose.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I almost exclusively refer to goroutines as Gs here, since it makes it easy
to refer to Ps and Ms as needed. See
&lt;a href=https://go.dev/src/runtime/HACKING#scheduler-structures&gt;https://go.dev/src/runtime/HACKING#scheduler-structures&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The pointer bits are in big endian order, so the first bit in left-to-right
order corresponds to the first word.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &amp;ldquo;itab&amp;rdquo;, or interface table part of an interface value is not managed by
the GC; it is allocated in persistent memory, so even though it is a
pointer, it is not a pointer the GC needs to care about.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;Internal implementation of the &lt;code&gt;chan T&lt;/code&gt; type, which is implemented as a
&lt;code&gt;*runtime.hchan&lt;/code&gt;. See
&lt;a href=&#34;https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/runtime/chan.go;l=34;drc=a204ed53d907c3b325e3c2bdd6f847a8f97e90d9&#34;&gt;https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/runtime/chan.go;l=34;drc=a204ed53d907c3b325e3c2bdd6f847a8f97e90d9&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;This can be made better by caching the &lt;code&gt;reflect.Type&lt;/code&gt;s, but that is only a
very slight improvement on the order of 1% speedup. Most of the slowdown is
because Go is a bit more eager about zeroing allocations of values that
contain pointers.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:31&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;types&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;reflect&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Type&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;init&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Pre-allocate the whole array. There aren&amp;#39;t that many powers
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// of two. Don&amp;#39;t need to go beyond 1&amp;lt;&amp;lt;61, since that&amp;#39;s about as
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// large of an allocation as Go will service (trying to create
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// a larger array will panic).

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;i&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;types&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;types&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;reflect&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;StructOf&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;([]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;reflect&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;StructField&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

so it&amp;rsquo;s perfectly safe to place arena pointers into arena-allocated memory,
so long as it&amp;rsquo;s across the same arena.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>

  <entry>
    <title>Protobuf Tip #2: Compress Your Protos!</title>
    <link href="/2025/04/15/protobuf-tip-2"/>
    <updated>2025-04-15T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/04/15/protobuf-tip-2</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;As a matter of fact, when compression technology came along, we thought the
future in 1996 was about voice. We got it wrong. It is about voice, video, and
data, and that is what we have today on these cell phones. &amp;ndash;Steve Buyer&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: Compression is everywhere: CDNs, HTTP servers, even in RPC frameworks
like Connect. This pervasiveness means that wire size tradeoffs matter less than
they used to twenty years ago, when Protobuf was designed.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m editing a series of best practice pieces on Protobuf, a language that I
work on which has lots of evil corner-cases.These are shorter than what I
typically post here, but I think it fits with what you, dear reader, come to
this blog for. These tips are also posted on the
&lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/totw-2-compress-protos&gt;buf.build blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=varints-from-1998&gt;&lt;a href=#varints-from-1998&gt;Varints from 1998&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf’s wire format is intended to be relatively small. It makes use of
&lt;em&gt;variable-width integers&lt;/em&gt; so that smaller values take up less space on the wire.
Fixed width integers might be larger on the wire, but often have faster decoding
times.&lt;p&gt;But what if I told you that doesn’t matter?&lt;p&gt;See, most internet traffic is compressed. Bandwidth is precious, and CDN
operators don’t want to waste time sending big blobs full of zeros. There are
many compression algorithms available, but the state of the art for HTTP
requests (which dominates much of global internet traffic) is
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brotli&gt;Brotli&lt;/a&gt;, an algorithm developed at Google
in 2013 and standardized in IETF
&lt;a href=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7932&gt;RFC7932&lt;/a&gt; in 2016. There is a
very good chance that this article was delivered to your web browser as a
Brotli-compressed blob.&lt;h2 id=using-compression&gt;&lt;a href=#using-compression&gt;Using Compression&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;How compression is applied in your case will vary, but both Connect RPC and gRPC
support native compression. For example, Connect has an API for injecting
compression providers:
&lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/connectrpc.com/connect#WithCompression&gt;https://pkg.go.dev/connectrpc.com/connect#WithCompression&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Connect uses &lt;code&gt;gzip&lt;/code&gt; by default, which uses the DEFLATE compression algorithm.
Providing your own compression algorithm (such as Brotli) is pretty simple, as
shown by
&lt;a href=https://github.com/mattrobenolt/connect-brotli/blob/921ee0236bcd2d66827590c6890bb850e56516ad/connect_brotli.go&gt;this third-party package&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Other services may compress for you transparently. Any competent CDN will likely
use Brotli (or &lt;code&gt;gzip&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;zlib&lt;/code&gt;, but probably Brotli) to compress any files it
serves for you. (In fact, JavaScript and HTML minimization can often be rendered
irrelevant by HTTP compression, too.)&lt;p&gt;It’s important to remember that Protobuf predates pervasive compression: if it
didn’t, it would almost certainly not use variable-width integers for anything.
It only uses them because they offer a primitive form of compression in exchange
for being slower to decode. If that tradeoff was eliminated, Protobuf would
almost certainly only use fixed-width integers on the wire.&lt;h2 id=how-good-is-it-really&gt;&lt;a href=#how-good-is-it-really&gt;How Good Is It Really?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let’s do some apples-to-apples comparisons. Consider the following Protobuf
type.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;	&lt;span class=k&gt;repeated&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;varints&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;	&lt;span class=k&gt;repeated&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;sfixed32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;fixeds&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are two fields that contain essentially the same data, which can be
encoded in four different ways: as old-style repeated fields, as packed fields,
and the integers can be encoded as varints or fixed32 values.&lt;p&gt;Using &lt;a href=https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protoscope&gt;Protoscope&lt;/a&gt;, we can create
some data that exercises these four cases:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protoscope highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;# a.pb, repeated varint&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;# ...&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;# b.pb, packed varint&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;# ...&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;# c.pb, repeated fixed32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;# d.pb, packed fixed32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;# ...&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Protoscope&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Each blob contains the integers from 1 to 1000 encoded in different ways. I’ll
compress each one using gzip, zlib, and Brotli, using their default compression
levels, and arrange their sizes, in bytes, in the table below.&lt;table&gt;&lt;thead&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;th&gt;File&lt;th&gt;Uncompressed&lt;th&gt;&lt;code&gt;gzip&lt;/code&gt; (DEFLATE)&lt;th&gt;&lt;code&gt;zlib&lt;/code&gt;&lt;th&gt;Brotli&lt;tbody&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;a.pb&lt;td&gt;2875&lt;td&gt;1899&lt;td&gt;1878&lt;td&gt;1094&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;b.pb&lt;td&gt;1877&lt;td&gt;1534&lt;td&gt;1524&lt;td&gt;885&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;c.pb&lt;td&gt;5005&lt;td&gt;1577&lt;td&gt;1567&lt;td&gt;1140&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;d.pb&lt;td&gt;4007&lt;td&gt;1440&lt;td&gt;1916&lt;td&gt;1140&lt;/table&gt;&lt;p&gt;Compression achieves incredible results: Brotli manages to get all of the files
down to around 1.1 kB, except for the packed varints, which it gets about 250
bytes smaller! Of course, that’s only because most of the values in that
repeated field are small. If the values range from 100000 to 101000, b.pb and
d.pb are 3006 and 4007 bytes respectively (see that d.pb’s size is unchanged!),
but when compressed with brotli, the lead for b.pb starts to disappear: 1039
bytes vs. 1163 bytes. Now it’s only 120 bytes smaller.&lt;h2 id=are-varints-still-better&gt;&lt;a href=#are-varints-still-better&gt;Are Varints Still Better?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Applying compression can often have similar results to replacing everything with
varints, but not exactly: using a varint will likely always be slightly smaller,
at least when using state-of-the-art compression like Brotli. But you can pretty
much always assume you &lt;em&gt;will&lt;/em&gt; be using compression, such as to compress HTTP
headers and other ancillary content in your request. Compression is generic and
highly optimized—it applies to all data, regardless of schema, and is often far
more optimized than application-level codecs like those in a Protobuf library.&lt;p&gt;Not to mention, you should definitely be compressing any large data blobs you’re
storing on disk, too!&lt;p&gt;As a result, you can usually disregard many encoded size concerns when making
tradeoffs in designing a Protobuf type. Fixed integer types will decode faster,
so if decoding speed is important to you, and you’re worried about the size on
the wire, don’t. It’s almost certainly already taken care of at a different
layer of the stack.</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>What the Hell Is a Target Triple?</title>
    <link href="/2025/04/14/target-triples"/>
    <updated>2025-04-14T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/04/14/target-triples</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Cross-compiling&lt;/em&gt; is taking a computer program and compiling it for a machine
that isn&amp;rsquo;t the one hosting the compilation. Although historically compilers
would only compile for the host machine, this is considered an anachronism: all
serious native compilers are now cross-compilers.&lt;p&gt;After all, you don&amp;rsquo;t want to be building your iPhone app on literal iPhone
hardware.&lt;p&gt;Many different compilers have different mechanisms for classifying and
identifying &lt;em&gt;targets&lt;/em&gt;. A target is a platform that the compiler can produce
executable code for. However, due to the runaway popularity of LLVM, virtually
all compilers now use &lt;em&gt;target triples&lt;/em&gt;. You may have already encountered one,
such as the venerable &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux&lt;/code&gt;, or the evil &lt;code&gt;x86_64-pc-windows&lt;/code&gt;.
This system is convoluted and &lt;em&gt;almost&lt;/em&gt; self-consistent.&lt;p&gt;But what is a target triple, and where did they come from?&lt;h2 id=stupid-gcc-conventions&gt;&lt;a href=#stupid-gcc-conventions&gt;Stupid GCC Conventions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;So if you go poking around the
&lt;a href=https://wiki.osdev.org/Target_Triplet&gt;Target Triplet&lt;/a&gt; page on OSDev, you will
learn both true and false things about target triples, because this page is
about GCC, not native compilers in general.&lt;blockquote id=warning:1 class=warning warning&gt;&lt;a href=#warning:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;warning&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Generally, there is no &amp;ldquo;ground truth&amp;rdquo; for what a target triple is. There isn&amp;rsquo;t
some standards body that assigns these names. But as we&amp;rsquo;ll see, LLVM is the
trendsetter.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;If you run the following command you can learn the target triple for your
machine:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-console highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=gp&gt;$&lt;/span&gt; gcc -dumpmachine
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=go&gt;x86_64-linux-gnu
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now if you&amp;rsquo;re at all familiar with any system that makes pervasive use of target
triples, you will know that this is &lt;em&gt;not a target triple&lt;/em&gt;, because this target&amp;rsquo;s
name is &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu&lt;/code&gt;, which is what both &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt; call-&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-console highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=gp&gt;$&lt;/span&gt; clang -dumpmachine
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=go&gt;x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=go&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=gp&gt;$&lt;/span&gt; rustc -vV &lt;span class=p&gt;|&lt;/span&gt; grep host
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=go&gt;host: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Oh no.&lt;p&gt;Well, GCC is missing the the &lt;code&gt;pc&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;unknown&lt;/code&gt; component, and that&amp;rsquo;s
specifically a GCC thing; it allows omitting parts of the triple in such a way
that is unambiguous. And they are a GCC invention, so perhaps it&amp;rsquo;s best to start
by assessing GCC&amp;rsquo;s beliefs.&lt;p&gt;According to GCC, a target triple is a string of the form
&lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;machine&gt;-&amp;lt;vendor&gt;-&amp;lt;os&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. The &amp;ldquo;machine&amp;rdquo; part unambiguously identifies the
architecture of the system. Practically speaking, this is the assembly language
that the compiler will output at the end. The &amp;ldquo;vendor&amp;rdquo; part is essentially
irrelevant, and mostly is of benefit for sorting related operating systems
together. Finally, the &amp;ldquo;os&amp;rdquo; part identifies the operating system that this code
is being compiled for. The main thing this identifies for a compiler is the
executable format: COFF/PE for Windows, Mach-O for Apple&amp;rsquo;s operating systems,
ELF for Linux and friends, and so on (this, however, is an oversimplification).&lt;p&gt;But you may notice that &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu&lt;/code&gt; has an extra, fourth
entry&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, which plays many roles but is most often called the target&amp;rsquo;s
&amp;ldquo;ABI&amp;rdquo;. For &lt;code&gt;linux&lt;/code&gt;, it identifies the target&amp;rsquo;s libc, which has consequences for
code generation of some language features, such as thread locals and unwinding.
It is optional, since many targets only have one ABI.&lt;h3 id=cross-compiling-with-gcc&gt;&lt;a href=#cross-compiling-with-gcc&gt;Cross Compiling with GCC&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;A critical piece of history here is to understand the really stupid way in which
GCC does cross compiling. Traditionally, each GCC binary would be built for
&lt;em&gt;one&lt;/em&gt; target triple. The full name of a GCC binary would include the triple, so
when cross-compiling, you would compile with &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux-gcc&lt;/code&gt;, link
with &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux-ld&lt;/code&gt;, and so on (here, &lt;code&gt;gcc&lt;/code&gt; is not the fourth ABI
component of a triple; it&amp;rsquo;s just one of the tools in the &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux&lt;/code&gt;
toolchain).&lt;p&gt;Nobody with a brain does this&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. LLVM and all cross compilers that
follow it instead put all of the backends in one binary, and use a compiler flag
like &lt;code&gt;--target&lt;/code&gt; to select the backend.&lt;p&gt;But regardless, this is where target triples come from, and why they look the
way they look: they began as prefixes for the names of binaries in &lt;code&gt;autoconf&lt;/code&gt;
scripts.&lt;p&gt;But GCC is ancient technology. In the 21st century, LLVM rules all native
compilers.&lt;h2 id=names-in-the-ancient-language&gt;&lt;a href=#names-in-the-ancient-language&gt;Names in the Ancient Language&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM&amp;rsquo;s target triple list is the one that should be regarded as &amp;ldquo;most official&amp;rdquo;,
for a few reasons:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Inertia. Everyone and their mother uses LLVM as a middleend and backend, so
its naming conventions bubble up into language frontends like &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt; &lt;code&gt;swiftc&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;icc&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;nvcc&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Upstream work by silicon and operating system vendors. LLVM is what people
get hired to work on for the most part, not GCC, so its platform-specific
conventions often reflect the preferences of vendors.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;These are in no small part because Apple, Google, and Nvidia have armies of
compiler engineers contributing to LLVM.&lt;p&gt;The sources for &amp;ldquo;official&amp;rdquo; target triples are many. Generally, I would describe
a target triple as &amp;ldquo;official&amp;rdquo; when:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;A major compiler (so, &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt;) uses it. Rust does a way better job
than LLVM of documenting their targets, so I prefer to give it deference. You
can find Rust&amp;rsquo;s official triples
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/platform-support.html&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;A platform developer (e.g., a hardware manufacturer, OS vendor) distributes a
toolchain with a target triple in the &lt;code&gt;arch-vendor-os&lt;/code&gt; format.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;So, what are the names in class (1)? LLVM does not really go out of its way to
provide such a list. But we gotta start somewhere, so source-diving it is.&lt;p&gt;We can dig into &lt;a href=https://llvm.org/doxygen/Triple_8cpp_source.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;Triple.cpp&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
in LLVM&amp;rsquo;s target triple parser. It lists all of the names LLVM recognizes for
each part of a triple. Looking at &lt;code&gt;Triple::parseArch()&lt;/code&gt;, we have the following
names, including many, many aliases. The first item on the right column is
LLVM&amp;rsquo;s preferred name for the architecture, as indicated by
&lt;code&gt;Triple::getArchTypeName()&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;table&gt;&lt;thead&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;th&gt;Architecture&lt;th&gt;Possible Names&lt;tbody&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86&gt;Intel x86&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;i386&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;i486&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;i586&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;i686&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;i786&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;i886&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;i986&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86&gt;Intel x86&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;x86_64&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;amd64&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;x86_86h&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture_family&gt;ARM&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;arm&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;xscale&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture_family&gt;ARM&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit, big-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;armeb&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;xscaleeb&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture_family&gt;ARM&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;aarch64&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;aarch64e&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;aarch64ec&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;arm64&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture_family&gt;ARM&lt;/a&gt; (big-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;thumbeb&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC&gt;IBM PowerPC&lt;/a&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;powerpc&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;powerpcspe&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;ppc&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;ppc32&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC&gt;IBM PowerPC&lt;/a&gt; (little-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;powerpcle&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;ppcle&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;ppc32le&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC&gt;IBM PowerPC&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit, little-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;powerpc64le&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;ppc64le&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIPS_architecture&gt;MIPS&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;mips64&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mips64eb&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mipsn32&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mipsisa64r6&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mips64r6&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mipsn32r6&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIPS_architecture&gt;MIPS&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit, little-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;mips64el&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mipsn32el&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mipsisa64r6el&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mips64r6el&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;mipsn32r6el&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RISC-V&gt;RISC-V&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;riscv32&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RISC-V&gt;RISC-V&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;riscv64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z/Architecture&gt;IBM z/Architecture&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;s390x&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, &lt;code&gt;systemz&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPARC&gt;SPARC&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;sparc&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPARC&gt;SPARC&lt;/a&gt; (little-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;sparcel&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPARC&gt;SPARC&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;sparcv6&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;sparc64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly&gt;WebAssembly&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;wasm32&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebAssembly&gt;WebAssembly&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;wasm64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loongson&gt;Loongson&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;loongarch32&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loongson&gt;Loongson&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;loongarch64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;-&lt;td&gt;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;ndash;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radeon_HD_2000_series&gt;Radeon R600&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;r600&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_Core_Next&gt;AMD GCN&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;amdgcn&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualcomm_Hexagon&gt;Qualcomm Hexagon&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;hexagon&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_Thread_Execution&gt;Nvidia PTX&lt;/a&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;nvptx&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_Thread_Execution&gt;Nvidia PTX&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;nvptx64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;AMD IL&lt;sup id=fnref:8&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:8 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;8&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;amdil&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;AMD IL (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;amdil64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;Direct-X IL&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;dxil&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterogeneous_System_Architecture&gt;HSAIL&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;hsail&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterogeneous_System_Architecture&gt;HSAIL&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;hsail64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Portable_Intermediate_Representation&gt;Khronos SPIR&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;spirv32&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Portable_Intermediate_Representation&gt;Khronos SPIR-V&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;spirv64&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/renderscript/compute&gt;Android RenderScript&lt;/a&gt; (32-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;renderscript32&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://developer.android.com/guide/topics/renderscript/compute&gt;Android RenderScript&lt;/a&gt; (64-bit)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;renderscript64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikichip.org/wiki/movidius/microarchitectures/shave_v2.0&gt;Movidius SHAVE&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;shave&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;-&lt;td&gt;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;mdash;&amp;ndash;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AVR_microcontrollers&gt;Atmel AVR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;avr&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_68000_series&gt;Motorola 68k&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;m68k&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARC_(processor)&gt;Argonaut ARC&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;arc&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TI_MSP430&gt;Texas Instruments MSP430&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;msp430&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensilica&gt;Tensilica Xtensa&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;xtensa&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://c-sky.github.io/&gt;C-SKY&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;csky&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/cpc/openasip&gt;OpenASIP&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;tce&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/cpc/openasip&gt;OpenASIP&lt;/a&gt; (little-endian)&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;tcele&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://q3k.org/lanai.html&gt;Myracom Lanai&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;lanai&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;XMOS xCore&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;xcore&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;Kalimba&lt;sup id=fnref:9&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:9 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;9&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;kalimba&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;VE&lt;sup id=fnref1:9&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:9 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;9&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;ve&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/table&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here we begin to see that target triples are not a neat system. They are &lt;em&gt;hell&lt;/em&gt;.
Where a list of architecture names contains a &amp;ldquo;&amp;mldr;&amp;rdquo;, it means that LLVM accepts
many more names.&lt;p&gt;The problem is that architectures often have &lt;em&gt;versions&lt;/em&gt; and &lt;em&gt;features&lt;/em&gt;, which
subtly change how the compiler generates code. For example, when compiling for
an &lt;code&gt;x86_64&lt;/code&gt;, we may want to specify that we want AVX512 instructions to be used.
On LLVM, you might do that with &lt;code&gt;-mattr=+avx512&lt;/code&gt;. Every architecture has a
subtly-different way of doing this, because every architecture had a &lt;em&gt;different
GCC&lt;/em&gt;! Each variant of GCC would put different things behind &lt;code&gt;-mXXX&lt;/code&gt; flags (&lt;code&gt;-m&lt;/code&gt;
for &amp;ldquo;machine&amp;rdquo;), meaning that the interface is not actually that uniform. The
meanings of &lt;code&gt;-march&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;-mcpu&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;-mtune&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;-mattr&lt;/code&gt; thus vary wildly for this
reason.&lt;p&gt;Because LLVM is supposed to replace GCC (for the most part), it replicates a lot
of this wacky behavior.&lt;p&gt;So uh, we gotta talk about 32-bit ARM architecture names.&lt;h3 id=armtargetparsercpp&gt;&lt;a href=#armtargetparsercpp&gt;&lt;code&gt;ARMTargetParser.cpp&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is a hellish file in LLVM dedicated to parsing ARM architecture names.
Although members of the ARM family have many configurable features (which you
can discover with &lt;code&gt;llc -march aarch64 -mattr help&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:10&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:10 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;10&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;), the name of the
architecture is somewhat meaningful, and can hav many options, mostly relating
to the many versions of ARM that exist.&lt;p&gt;How bad is it? Well, we can look at all of the various ARM targets that &lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt;
supports with &lt;code&gt;rustc --print target-list&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-console highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=gp&gt;$&lt;/span&gt; rustc --print target-list &lt;span class=p&gt;|&lt;/span&gt; grep -P &lt;span class=s1&gt;&amp;#39;arm|aarch|thumb&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=se&gt;\
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=se&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=go&gt;  | cut -d- -f1 | sort | uniq
