&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Most of these are 32-bit ARM versions, with profile information attached. These
correspond to the names given
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture_family#Cores&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;. Why does
ARM stick version numbers in the architecture name, instead of using &lt;code&gt;-mcpu&lt;/code&gt;
like you would on x86 (e.g. &lt;code&gt;-mcpu alderlake&lt;/code&gt;)? I have no idea, because ARM is
not my strong suit. It&amp;rsquo;s likely because of how early ARM support was added to
GCC.&lt;p&gt;Internally, LLVM calls these &amp;ldquo;subarchitectures&amp;rdquo;, although ARM gets special
handling because there&amp;rsquo;s so many variants. SPIR-V, Direct X, and MIPS all have
subarchitectures, so you might see something like &lt;code&gt;dxilv1.7&lt;/code&gt; if you&amp;rsquo;re having a
bad day.&lt;p&gt;Of course, LLVM&amp;rsquo;s ARM support also sports some naughty subarchitectures not part
of this system, with naughty made up names.&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;arm64e&lt;/code&gt; is an Apple thing, which is an enhancement of &lt;code&gt;aarch64&lt;/code&gt; present on
some Apple hardware, which adds their own flavor of
&lt;a href=https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/preparing-your-app-to-work-with-pointer-authentication&gt;pointer authentication&lt;/a&gt;
and some other features.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;arm64ec&lt;/code&gt; is a completely unrelated Microsoft invention that is essentially
&amp;ldquo;&lt;code&gt;aarch64&lt;/code&gt; but with an &lt;code&gt;x86_64&lt;/code&gt;-ey ABI&amp;rdquo; to make &lt;code&gt;x86_64&lt;/code&gt; emulation on what
would otherwise be &lt;code&gt;aarch64-pc-windows-msvc&lt;/code&gt; target somewhat more amenable.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Why the Windows people invented a whole other ABI instead of making things
clean and simple like Apple did with Rosetta on ARM MacBooks? I have no idea,
but &lt;a href=http://www.emulators.com/docs/abc_arm64ec_explained.htm&gt;http://www.emulators.com/docs/abc_arm64ec_explained.htm&lt;/a&gt; contains various
excuses, none of which I am impressed by. My read is that their compiler org
was just worse at life than Apple&amp;rsquo;s, which is not surprising, since Apple does
compilers better than anyone else in the business.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Actually, since we&amp;rsquo;re on the topic of the names of architectures, I have a few
things I need to straighten out.&lt;h3 id=made-up-names-of-architectures&gt;&lt;a href=#made-up-names-of-architectures&gt;Made Up Names of Architectures&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;x86 and ARM both seem to attract a lot of people making up nicknames for them,
which leads to a lot of confusion in:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;What the &amp;ldquo;real&amp;rdquo; name is.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;What name a particular toolchain wants.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;What name you should use in your own cosmopolitan tooling.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s talk about the incorrect names people like to make up for them. Please
consider the following a relatively normative reference on what people call
these architectures, based on my own experience with many tools.&lt;p&gt;When we say &amp;ldquo;x86&amp;rdquo; unqualified, in 2025, we almost always mean &lt;code&gt;x86_64&lt;/code&gt;, because
32-bit x86 is dead. If you need to talk about 32-bit x86, you should either say
&amp;ldquo;32-bit x86&amp;rdquo;, &amp;ldquo;protected mode&amp;rdquo;&lt;sup id=fnref:11&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:11 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;11&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, or &amp;ldquo;i386&amp;rdquo; (the first Intel
microarchitecture that implemented protected mode)&lt;sup id=fnref:12&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:12 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;12&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. You should not call
it &lt;code&gt;x86_32&lt;/code&gt; or just &lt;code&gt;x86&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;You might also call it IA-32 for Intel Architecture 32, (or &lt;code&gt;ia32&lt;/code&gt;), but nobody
calls it that and you risk confusing people with &lt;code&gt;ia64&lt;/code&gt;, or IA-64, the official
name of Intel&amp;rsquo;s failed general-purpose VLIW architecture,
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itanium&gt;Itanium&lt;/a&gt;, which is in no way compatible
with x86. &lt;code&gt;ia64&lt;/code&gt; was what GCC and LLVM named Itanium triples with. Itanium
support was drowned in a bathtub during the Obama administration, so it&amp;rsquo;s not
really relevant anymore. Rust has never had official Itanium support.&lt;p&gt;32-bit x86 is &lt;em&gt;extremely not&lt;/em&gt; called &amp;ldquo;x32&amp;rdquo;; this is what Linux used to call its
x86 ILP32&lt;sup id=fnref1:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; variant before it was removed (which, following the ARM names,
would have been called &lt;code&gt;x86_6432&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;There are also many ficticious names for 64-bit x86, which you should avoid
unless you want the younger generation to make fun of you. &lt;code&gt;amd64&lt;/code&gt; refers to
AMD&amp;rsquo;s original implementation of long mode in their K8 microarchitecture, first
shipped in their &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athlon_64&gt;Athlon 64&lt;/a&gt; product.
AMD still makes the best x86 chips (I am writing this on a machine socketed with
a Zen2 Threadripper), sure, but calling it &lt;code&gt;amd64&lt;/code&gt; is silly and also looks a lot
like &lt;code&gt;arm64&lt;/code&gt;, and I am honestly kinda annoyed at how much Go code I&amp;rsquo;ve seen with
files named &lt;code&gt;fast_arm64.s&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;fast_amd64.s&lt;/code&gt;. Debian also uses &lt;code&gt;amd64&lt;/code&gt;/&lt;code&gt;arm64&lt;/code&gt;,
which makes browsing packages kind of annoying.&lt;p&gt;On that topic, you should &lt;em&gt;absolutely not&lt;/em&gt; call 64-bit mode &lt;code&gt;k8&lt;/code&gt;, after the AMD
K8. Nobody except for weird computer taxonomists like me know what that is. But
Bazel calls it that, and it&amp;rsquo;s really irritating&lt;sup id=fnref:13&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:13 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;13&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;You should also not call it &lt;code&gt;x64&lt;/code&gt;. Although LLVM does accept &lt;code&gt;amd64&lt;/code&gt; for
historical purposes, no one calls it &lt;code&gt;x64&lt;/code&gt; except for Microsoft. And even though
it is fairly prevalent on Windows, I absolutely give my gamedev friends a hard
time when they write &lt;code&gt;x64&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;On the ARM side, well. Arm&lt;sup id=fnref:14&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:14 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;14&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; has a bad habit of not using
consistent naming for 64-bit ARM, since they used both AArch64 and ARM64 for it.
However, in compiler land, &lt;code&gt;aarch64&lt;/code&gt; appears to be somewhat more popular.&lt;p&gt;You should also probably stick to the LLVM names for the various architectures,
instead of picking your favorite Arm Cortex name (like &lt;code&gt;cortex_m0&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;h2 id=vendors-and-operating-systems&gt;&lt;a href=#vendors-and-operating-systems&gt;Vendors and Operating Systems&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The worst is over. Let&amp;rsquo;s now move onto examinining the rest of the triple: the
platform vendor, and the operating system.&lt;p&gt;The vendor is intended to identify who is responsible for the ABI definition for
that target. Although provides little to no value to the compiler itself, but it
does help to sort related targets together. Sort of.&lt;p&gt;Returning to &lt;code&gt;llvm::Triple&lt;/code&gt;, we can examine &lt;code&gt;Triple::VendorType&lt;/code&gt;. Vendors almost
always correspond to companies which develop operating systems or other
platforms that code runs on, with some exceptions.&lt;p&gt;We can also get the vendors that &lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt; knows about with a handy dandy command:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-console highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=go&gt;rustc --print target-list | grep -P &amp;#39;\w+-\w+-&amp;#39; | cut -d- -f2 | sort | uniq
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Console&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The result is this. This is just a representative list; I have left off a few
that are not going to be especially recognizeable.&lt;table&gt;&lt;thead&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;th&gt;Vendor&lt;th&gt;Name&lt;th&gt;Example Triple&lt;tbody&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;Vendor Unknown&lt;sup id=fnref:15&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:15 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;15&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;unknown&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&amp;ldquo;PC&amp;rdquo;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;pc&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;x86_64-pc-windows-msvc&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMD&gt;Advanced Micro Devices Inc.&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;amd&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;amdgcn-amd-gfx906&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.&gt;Apple Inc.&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;apple&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;aarch64-apple-ios-sim&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel&gt;Intel Corporation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;intel&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;i386-intel-elfiamcu&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM&gt;IBM Corporation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;ibm&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;powerpc64-ibm-aix&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa_(computer_graphics)&gt;Mesa3D Project&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;mesa&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;amdgcn-mesa-mesa3d&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIPS_Technologies&gt;MIPS Technologies LLC&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;mti&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;mips-mti-none-elf&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo&gt;Nintendo&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;nintendo&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;armv6k-nintendo-3ds&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nvidia&gt;Nvidia Corporation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;nvidia&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;nvptx64-nvidia-cuda&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Interactive_Entertainment&gt;Sony Interactive Entertainment&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;scei&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;sie&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;sony&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;x86_64-sie-ps5&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Microsystems&gt;Sun Microsystems&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;sun&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;sparcv9-sun-solaris&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SUSE_S.A.&gt;SUSE S. A.&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;suse&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;aarch64-suse-linux&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hat&gt;Red Hat, Inc&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;redhat&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;x86_64-redhat-linux&lt;/code&gt;&lt;tr&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Windows_Platform&gt;Universal Windows Platform&lt;/a&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;uwp&lt;/code&gt;&lt;td&gt;&lt;code&gt;aarch64-uwp-windows-msvc&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/table&gt;&lt;p&gt;Most vendors are the names of organizations that produce hardware or operating
systems. For example &lt;code&gt;suse&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;redhat&lt;/code&gt; are used for those organizations&amp;rsquo; Linux
distributions, as a funny branding thing. Some vendors are projects, like the
&lt;code&gt;mesa&lt;/code&gt; vendor used with the Mesa3D OpenGL implementation&amp;rsquo;s triples.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;unknown&lt;/code&gt; vendor is used for cases where the vendor is not specified or just
not important. For example, the canonical Linux triple is
&lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux&lt;/code&gt;&amp;mldr; although one could argue it should be
&lt;code&gt;x86_64-torvalds-linux&lt;/code&gt;. It is not uncommon for companies that sell/distribute
Linux distributions to have their own target triples, as do SUSE and sometimes
RedHat. Notably, there are no triples with a &lt;code&gt;google&lt;/code&gt; vendor, even though
&lt;code&gt;aarch64-linux-android&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;aarch64-unknown-fuchsia&lt;/code&gt; should really be called
&lt;code&gt;aarch64-google-linux-android&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;aarch64-google-fuchsia&lt;/code&gt;. The target triple
system begins to show cracks here.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;pc&lt;/code&gt; vendor is a bit weirder, and is mostly used by Windows targets. The
standard Windows target is &lt;code&gt;x86_64-pc-windows-msvc&lt;/code&gt;, but really it should have
been &lt;code&gt;x86_64-microsoft-windows-msvc&lt;/code&gt;. This is likely complicated by the fact
that there is also a &lt;code&gt;x86_64-pc-windows-gnu&lt;/code&gt; triple, which is for
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MinGW&gt;MinGW&lt;/a&gt; code. This platform, despite
running on Windows, is not provided by Microsoft, so it would probably make more
sense to be called &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-windows-gnu&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;But not all Windows targets are &lt;code&gt;pc&lt;/code&gt;! &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Windows_Platform&gt;UWP&lt;/a&gt; apps use a different triple, that
replaces the &lt;code&gt;pc&lt;/code&gt; with &lt;code&gt;uwp&lt;/code&gt;. &lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt; provides targets for Windows 7 backports
that use a &lt;code&gt;win7&lt;/code&gt; &amp;ldquo;vendor&amp;rdquo;.&lt;h3 id=beyond-operating-systems&gt;&lt;a href=#beyond-operating-systems&gt;Beyond Operating Systems&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The third (or sometimes second, ugh) component of a triple is the operating
system, or just &amp;ldquo;system&amp;rdquo;, since it&amp;rsquo;s much more general than that. The main thing
that compilers get from this component relates to generating code to interact
with the operating system (e.g. SEH on Windows) and various details related to
linking, such as object file format and relocations.&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s also used for setting defines like &lt;code&gt;__linux__&lt;/code&gt; in C, which user code can
use to determine what to do based on the target.&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;ve seen &lt;code&gt;linux&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;windows&lt;/code&gt;, but you may have also seen
&lt;code&gt;x86_64-apple-darwin&lt;/code&gt;. &lt;em&gt;Darwin?&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;The operating system formerly known as Mac OS X (now macOS&lt;sup id=fnref:16&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:16 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;16&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;) is a POSIX
operating system. The POSIX substrate that all the Apple-specific things are
built on top of is called Darwin.
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin_(operating_system)&gt;Darwin&lt;/a&gt; is a free
and open source operating system based on Mach, a research kernel whose name
survives in Mach-O, the object file format used by all Apple products.&lt;p&gt;All of the little doodads Apple sells use the actual official names of their
OSes, like &lt;code&gt;aarch64-apple-ios&lt;/code&gt;. For, you know, iOS. On your iPhone. Built with
Xcode on your iMac.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;none&lt;/code&gt; is a common value for this entry, which usually means a free-standing
environment with no operating system. The object file format is usually
specified in the fourth entry of the triple, so you might see something like
&lt;code&gt;riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Sometimes the triple refers not to an operating system, but to a complete
hardware product. This is common with game console triples, which have
&amp;ldquo;operating system&amp;rdquo; names like &lt;code&gt;ps4&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;psvita&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;3ds&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt;. (Both Sony
and Nintendo use LLVM as the basis for their internal toolchains; the Xbox
toolchain is just MSVC).&lt;h2 id=abi-abi&gt;&lt;a href=#abi-abi&gt;ABI! ABI!&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The fourth entry of the triple (and I repeat myself, yes, it&amp;rsquo;s still a triple)
represents the binary interface for the target, when it is ambiguous.&lt;p&gt;For example, Apple targets never have this, because on an Apple platform, you
just shut up and use &lt;code&gt;CoreFoundation.framework&lt;/code&gt; as your libc. Except this isn&amp;rsquo;t
true, because of things like &lt;code&gt;x86_64-apple-ios-sim&lt;/code&gt;, the iOS simulator running
on an x86 host.&lt;p&gt;On the other hand, Windows targets will usually specify &lt;code&gt;-msvc&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;-gnu&lt;/code&gt;, to
indicate whether they are built to match MSVC&amp;rsquo;s ABI or MinGW. Linux targets will
usually specify the libc vendor in this position: &lt;code&gt;-gnu&lt;/code&gt; for glibc, &lt;code&gt;-musl&lt;/code&gt; for
musl, &lt;code&gt;-newlib&lt;/code&gt; for newlib, and so on.&lt;p&gt;This doesn&amp;rsquo;t just influence the calling convention; it also influences how
language features, such as thread locals and dynamic linking, are handled. This
usually requires coordination with the target libc.&lt;p&gt;On ARM free-standing (&lt;code&gt;armxxx-unknown-none&lt;/code&gt;) targets, &lt;code&gt;-eabi&lt;/code&gt; specifies the ARM
EABI, which is a standard embeded ABI for ARM. &lt;code&gt;-eabihf&lt;/code&gt; is similar, but
indicates that no soft float support is necessary (&lt;code&gt;hf&lt;/code&gt; stands for hardfloat).
(Note that Rust does not include a vendor with these architectures, so they&amp;rsquo;re
more like &lt;code&gt;armv7r-none-eabi&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;A lot of jankier targets use the ABI portion to specify the object file, such as
the aforementioned &lt;code&gt;riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h2 id=wasm-targets&gt;&lt;a href=#wasm-targets&gt;WASM Targets&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;One last thing to note are the various WebAssembly targets, which completely
ignore all of the above conventions. Their triples often only have two
components (they are still called triples, hopefully I&amp;rsquo;ve made that clear by
now). Rust is a little bit more on the forefront here than &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt; (and anyways
I don&amp;rsquo;t want to get into Emscripten) so I&amp;rsquo;ll stick to what&amp;rsquo;s going on in
&lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;There&amp;rsquo;s a few variants. &lt;code&gt;wasm32-unknown-unknown&lt;/code&gt; (here using &lt;code&gt;unknown&lt;/code&gt; instead
of &lt;code&gt;none&lt;/code&gt; as the system, oops) is a completely bare WebAssebly runtime where
none of the standard library that needs to interact with the outside world
works. This is essentially for building WebAssembly modules to deploy in a
browser.&lt;p&gt;There are also the WASI targets, which provide a standard ABI for talking to the
host operating system. These are less meant for browsers and more for people who
are using WASI as a security boundary. These have names like &lt;code&gt;wasm32-wasip1&lt;/code&gt;,
which, unusually, lack a vendor! A &amp;ldquo;more correct&amp;rdquo; formulation would have been
&lt;code&gt;wasm32-unknown-wasip1&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h2 id=aside-on-go&gt;&lt;a href=#aside-on-go&gt;Aside on Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go does the correct thing and distributes a cross compiler. This is well and
good.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, they decided to be different and special and do not use the
target triple system for naming their targets. Instead, you set the &lt;code&gt;GOARCH&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;GOOS&lt;/code&gt; environment variables before invoking &lt;code&gt;gc&lt;/code&gt;. This will sometimes be shown
printed with a slash between, such as &lt;code&gt;linux/amd64&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Thankfully, they at least provide documentation for a relevant internal package
&lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/internal/platform&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;, which offers the names of various
&lt;code&gt;GOARCH&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;GOOS&lt;/code&gt; values.&lt;p&gt;They use completely different names from everyone else for a few things, which
is guaranteed to trip you up. They use call the 32- and 64-bit variants of x86
&lt;code&gt;386&lt;/code&gt; (note the lack of leading &lt;code&gt;i&lt;/code&gt;) and &lt;code&gt;amd64&lt;/code&gt;. They call 64-bit ARM &lt;code&gt;arm64&lt;/code&gt;,
instead of &lt;code&gt;aarch64&lt;/code&gt;. They call little-endian MIPSes &lt;code&gt;mipsle&lt;/code&gt; instead of
&lt;code&gt;mipsel&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;They also call 32-bit WebAssembly &lt;code&gt;wasm&lt;/code&gt; instead of &lt;code&gt;wasm32&lt;/code&gt;, which is a bit
silly, and they use &lt;code&gt;js/wasm&lt;/code&gt; as their equivalent of &lt;code&gt;wasm32-unknown-unknown&lt;/code&gt;,
which is &lt;em&gt;very&lt;/em&gt; silly.&lt;p&gt;Android is treated as its own operating system, &lt;code&gt;android&lt;/code&gt;, rather than being
&lt;code&gt;linux&lt;/code&gt; with a particular ABI; their system also can&amp;rsquo;t account for ABI variants
in general, since Go originally wanted to not have to link any system libraries,
something that does not actually work.&lt;p&gt;If you are building a new toolchain, don&amp;rsquo;t be clever by inventing a cute target
triple convention. All you&amp;rsquo;ll do is annoy people who need to work with a lot of
different toolchains by being different and special.&lt;h2 id=inventing-your-own-triples&gt;&lt;a href=#inventing-your-own-triples&gt;Inventing Your Own Triples&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Realistically, you probably shouldn&amp;rsquo;t. But if you must, you should probably
figure out what you want out of the triple.&lt;p&gt;Odds are there isn&amp;rsquo;t anything interesting to put in the vendor field, so you
will avoid people a lot of pain by picking &lt;code&gt;unknown&lt;/code&gt;. Just include a vendor to
avoid pain for people in the future.&lt;p&gt;You should also avoid inventing a new name for an existing architecture. Don&amp;rsquo;t
name your hobby operating system&amp;rsquo;s triple &lt;code&gt;amd64-unknown-whatever&lt;/code&gt;, please. And
you definitely don&amp;rsquo;t want to have an ABI component. One ABI is enough.&lt;p&gt;If you&amp;rsquo;re inventing a triple for a free-standing environment, but want to
specify something about the hardware configuration, you&amp;rsquo;re probably gonna want
to use &lt;code&gt;-none-&amp;lt;abi&gt;&lt;/code&gt; for your system. For some firmware use-cases, though, the
system entry is a better place, such as for the UEFI triples. Although, I have
unforunately seen both &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-uefi&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;x86_64-pc-none-uefi&lt;/code&gt; in the
wild.&lt;p&gt;And most imporantly: this sytem was built up organically. Disabuse yourself now
of the idea that the system is consistent and that target triples are easy to
parse. Trying to parse them will make you very sad.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;And no, a &amp;ldquo;target quadruple&amp;rdquo; is not a thing and if I catch you saying that
I&amp;rsquo;m gonna bonk you with an Intel optimization manual.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m not sure why GCC does this. I suspect that it&amp;rsquo;s because computer hard
drives used to be small and a GCC with every target would have been too
large to cram into every machine. Maybe it has some UNIX philosophy woo
mixed into it.&lt;p&gt;Regardless, it&amp;rsquo;s really annoying and thankfully no one else does this
because cross compiling shouldn&amp;rsquo;t require hunting down a new toolchain for
each platform.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is for Apple&amp;rsquo;s later-gen x86 machines, before they went all-in on ARM
desktop.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;ILP32 means that the &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;long&lt;/code&gt;, and pointer types in C are 32-bit,
despite the architecture being 64-bit. This allows writing programs that are
small enough top jive in a 32-bit address space, while taking advantage of
fast 64-bit operations. It is a bit of a frankentarget. Also existed once as
a process mode on &lt;code&gt;x86_64-unknown-linux&lt;/code&gt; by the name of &lt;code&gt;x32&lt;/code&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref1:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;Not to be confused with POWER, an older IBM CPU.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;This name is Linux&amp;rsquo;s name for IBM&amp;rsquo;s z/Architecture. See
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux_on_IBM_Z#Hardware&gt;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux_on_IBM_Z#Hardware&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;Not a real chip; refers to Nvidia&amp;rsquo;s PTX IR, which is what CUDA compiles to.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:8&gt;&lt;p&gt;Similar to PTX; an IR used by AMD for graphics. See
&lt;a href=https://openwall.info/wiki/john/development/AMD-IL&gt;https://openwall.info/wiki/john/development/AMD-IL&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:8 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:9&gt;&lt;p&gt;No idea what this is, and Google won&amp;rsquo;t help me.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref1:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:10&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;llc&lt;/code&gt; is the LLVM compiler, which takes LLVM IR as its input. Its interface
is much more regular than &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s because it&amp;rsquo;s not intended to be a
substitute for GCC the way &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt; is.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:10 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:11&gt;&lt;p&gt;Very kernel-hacker-brained name. It references the three processor modes of
an x86 machine: real mode, protected mode, long mode, which correspond to
16-, 32-, and 64-bit modes. There is also a secret fourth mode called
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unreal_mode&gt;unreal mode&lt;/a&gt;, which is just what
happens when you come down to real mode from protected mode after setting up
a protected mode GDT.&lt;p&gt;If you need to refer to real mode, call it &amp;ldquo;real mode&amp;rdquo;. Don&amp;rsquo;t try to be
clever by calling it &amp;ldquo;8086&amp;rdquo; because you are almost certainly going to be
using features that were not in the original Intel 8086.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:11 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:12&gt;&lt;p&gt;I actually don&amp;rsquo;t like this name, but it&amp;rsquo;s the one LLVM uses so I don&amp;rsquo;t
really get to complain.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:12 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:13&gt;&lt;p&gt;Bazel also calls 32-bit x86 &lt;code&gt;piii&lt;/code&gt;, which stands for, you guessed it,
&amp;ldquo;Pentium III&amp;rdquo;. Extremely unserious.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:13 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:14&gt;&lt;p&gt;The intelectual property around ARM, the architecture famility, is owned by
the British company Arm Holdings. Yes, the spelling difference is
significant.&lt;p&gt;Relatedly, ARM is not an acronym, and is sometimes styled in all-lowercase
as arm. The distant predecesor of Arm Holdings is Acorn Computers. Their
first compute, the Acorn Archimedes, contained a chip whose target triple
name today might have been &lt;code&gt;armv1&lt;/code&gt;. Here, ARM was an acronym, for Acorn RISC
Machine. Wikipedia alleges without citation that the name was at once point
changed to Advanced RISC Machine at the behest of Apple, but I am unable to
find more details.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:14 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:15&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;You are not cool enough for your company to be on the list.&amp;rdquo;&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:15 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:16&gt;&lt;p&gt;Which I pronounce as one word, &amp;ldquo;macos&amp;rdquo;, to drive people crazy.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:16 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Protobuf Tip #1: Field Names Are Forever</title>
    <link href="/2025/04/08/protobuf-tip-1"/>
    <updated>2025-04-08T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/04/08/protobuf-tip-1</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;I wake up every morning and grab the morning paper. Then I look at the obituary
page. If my name is not on it, I get up. &amp;ndash;Ben Franklin&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: Don’t rename fields. Even though there are a slim number of cases where
you can get away with it, it’s rarely worth doing, and is a potential source of
bugs.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m editing a series of best practice pieces on Protobuf, a language that I
work on which has lots of evil corner-cases.These are shorter than what I
typically post here, but I think it fits with what you, dear reader, come to
this blog for. These tips are also posted on the &lt;a href=https://buf.build/blog/totw-1-field-names&gt;buf.build blog&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=names-and-tags&gt;&lt;a href=#names-and-tags&gt;Names and Tags&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Protobuf message fields have &lt;em&gt;field tags&lt;/em&gt; that are used in the binary wire
format to discriminate fields. This means that the wire format serialization
does not actually depend on the &lt;em&gt;names&lt;/em&gt; of the fields. For example, the
following messages will use the exact same serialization format.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;bar&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Foo2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;bar2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;In fact, the designers of Protobuf intended for it to be feasible to rename an
in-use field. However, they were not successful: it can still be a breaking
change.&lt;h2 id=schema-consumers-need-to-update&gt;&lt;a href=#schema-consumers-need-to-update&gt;Schema Consumers Need to Update&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;If your schema is public, the generated code will change. For example, renaming
a field from &lt;code&gt;first_name&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;given_name&lt;/code&gt; will cause the corresponding Go
accessor to change from &lt;code&gt;FirstName&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;GivenName&lt;/code&gt;, potentially breaking
downstream consumers.&lt;p&gt;Renaming a field to a “better” name is almost never a worthwhile change, simply
because of this breakage.&lt;h2 id=json-serialization-breaks&gt;&lt;a href=#json-serialization-breaks&gt;JSON Serialization Breaks&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Wire format serialization doesn’t look at names, but JSON does! This means that
&lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;Foo2&lt;/code&gt; above serialize as &lt;code&gt;{&#34;bar&#34;:&#34;content&#34;}&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;{&#34;bar2&#34;:&#34;content&#34;}&lt;/code&gt;
respectively, making them non-interchangeable.&lt;p&gt;This can be partially mitigated by using the &lt;code&gt;[json_name = &#34;...&#34;]&lt;/code&gt; option on a
field. However, this doesn’t actually work, because many Protobuf runtimes’ JSON
codecs will accept both the name set in &lt;code&gt;json_name&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; the specified field
name. So &lt;code&gt;string given_name = 1 [json_name = &#34;firstName&#34;];&lt;/code&gt; will allow
deserializing from a key named &lt;code&gt;given_name&lt;/code&gt;, but not &lt;code&gt;first_name&lt;/code&gt; like it used
to. This is still a breaking protocol change!&lt;p&gt;This is a place where Protobuf could have done better—if &lt;code&gt;json_name&lt;/code&gt; had been a
&lt;code&gt;repeated string&lt;/code&gt;, this wire format breakage would have been avoidable. However,
for reasons given below, renames are still a bad idea.&lt;h2 id=reflection&gt;&lt;a href=#reflection&gt;Reflection!&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Even if you could avoid source and JSON breakages, the names are always visible
to reflection. Although it’s &lt;em&gt;very&lt;/em&gt; hard to guard against reflection breakages
in general (since it can even see the order fields are declared in), this is one
part of reflection that can be especially insidious—for example, if callers
choose to sort fields by name, or if some middleware is using the name of a
field to identify its frequency, or logging/redaction needs.&lt;p&gt;Don’t change the name, because reflection means you can’t know what’ll go wrong!&lt;h2 id=but-i-really-have-to&gt;&lt;a href=#but-i-really-have-to&gt;But I Really Have To!&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are valid reasons for wanting to rename a field, such as expanding its
scope. For example, &lt;code&gt;first_name&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;given_name&lt;/code&gt; are not the same concept: in
the Sinosphere, as well as in Hungary, the first name in a person’s full name is
their family name, not their given name.&lt;p&gt;Or maybe a field that previously referred to a monetary amount, say &lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt;,
is being updated to not specify the currency:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Before&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;sint64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;cost_usd&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;message&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;After&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Currency&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;CURRENCY_UNSPECIFIED&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;CURRENCY_USD&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;CURRENCY_EUR&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;CURRENCY_JPY&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;CURRENCY_USD_1000TH&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// 0.1 cents.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;sint64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;cost&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;Currency&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;currency&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;In cases like this, &lt;strong&gt;renaming the field is a terrible idea&lt;/strong&gt;. Setting aside
source code or JSON breakage, the new field has completely different semantics.
If an old consumer, expecting a price in USD, receives a new wire format message
serialized from &lt;code&gt;{&#34;cost&#34;:990,&#34;currency&#34;:&#34;CURRENCY_USD_1000TH&#34;}&lt;/code&gt;, it will
incorrectly interpret the price as 990USD, rather than 0.99USD. That’s a
disastrous bug!&lt;p&gt;Instead, the right plan is to add &lt;code&gt;cost&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;currency&lt;/code&gt; side-by-side &lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt;.
Then, readers should first check for &lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt; when reading &lt;code&gt;cost&lt;/code&gt;, and take
that to imply that &lt;code&gt;currency&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;CURRENCY_USD&lt;/code&gt; (it’s also worth generating an
error if &lt;code&gt;cost&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt; are both present).&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt; can then be marked as &lt;code&gt;[deprecated = true]&lt;/code&gt; . It is possible to even
delete &lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt; in some cases, such as when you control all readers and
writers — but if you don’t, the risk is very high. Plus, you kind of need to be
able to re-interpret &lt;code&gt;cost_usd&lt;/code&gt; as the value of &lt;code&gt;cost&lt;/code&gt; in perpetuity.&lt;p&gt;If you do wind up deleting them, make sure to reserve the field’s number and
name, to avoid accidental re-use.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-protobuf highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;reserved&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;reserved&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;cost_usd&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Protobuf&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;But try not to. Renaming fields is nothing but tears and pain.</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>The Art of Formatting Code</title>
    <link href="/2025/03/11/formatters"/>
    <updated>2025-03-11T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2025/03/11/formatters</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Every modern programming language needs a &lt;em&gt;formatter&lt;/em&gt; to make your code look
pretty and consistent. Formatters are source-transformation tools that parse
source code and re-print the resulting AST in some canonical form that
normalizes whitespace and optional syntactic constructs. They remove the tedium
of matching indentation and brace placement to match a style guide.&lt;p&gt;Go is particularly well-known for providing a formatter as part of its toolchain
from day one. It is not a &lt;em&gt;good&lt;/em&gt; formatter, though, because it cannot enforce a
maximum column width. Later formatters of the 2010s, such as rustfmt and
clang-format, do provide this feature, which ensure that individual lines of
code don&amp;rsquo;t get too long.&lt;p&gt;The reason Go doesn&amp;rsquo;t do this is because the naive approach to formatting code
makes it intractable to do so. There are many approaches to implementing this,
which can make it seem like a very complicated layout constraint solving
problem.&lt;p&gt;So what&amp;rsquo;s so tricky about formatting code? Aren&amp;rsquo;t you just printing out an AST?&lt;h2 id=just-an-ast&gt;&lt;a href=#just-an-ast&gt;&amp;ldquo;Just&amp;rdquo; an AST&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;An AST&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (abstract syntax tree) is a graph representation of a
program&amp;rsquo;s syntax. Let&amp;rsquo;s consider something like JSON, whose naively-defined AST
type might look something like this.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Null&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Number&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;f64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Array&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Object&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;HashMap&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The AST for the document &lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;: null, &#34;bar&#34;: 42}&lt;/code&gt; might look something like
this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_doc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;Object&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;([&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;foo&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;to_string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;Null&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;bar&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;to_string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;Number&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;42&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;].&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;into&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This AST has some pretty major problems. A formatter must &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; change the
syntactic structure of the program (beyond removing things like redundant
braces). Formatting must also be deterministic.&lt;p&gt;First off, &lt;code&gt;Json::Object&lt;/code&gt; is a &lt;code&gt;HashMap&lt;/code&gt;, which is unordered. So it will
immediately discard the order of the keys. &lt;code&gt;Json::String&lt;/code&gt; does not retain the
escapes from the original string, so &lt;code&gt;&#34;\n&#34;&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;&#34;\u000a&#34;&lt;/code&gt; are
indistinguishable. &lt;code&gt;Json::Number&lt;/code&gt; will destroy information: JSON numbers can
specify values outside of the &lt;code&gt;f64&lt;/code&gt; representable range, but converting to &lt;code&gt;f64&lt;/code&gt;
will quantize to the nearest float.&lt;p&gt;Now, JSON doesn&amp;rsquo;t have comments, but if it did, our AST has no way to record it!
So it would destroy all comment information! Plus, if someone has a document
that separates keys into stanzas&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, as shown below, this information is
lost too.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-json highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;this&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;is my first stanza&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;second&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;line&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;here&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;is my second stanza&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;fourth&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;line&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;JSON&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Truth is, the AST for virtually all competent toolchains are much more
complicated than this. Here&amp;rsquo;s some important properties an AST needs to have to
be useful.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Retain &lt;em&gt;span&lt;/em&gt; information. Every node in the graph remembers what piece of
the file it was parsed from.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Retain whitespace information. &amp;ldquo;Whitespace&amp;rdquo; typically includes both
whitespace characters, and comments.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Retain ordering information. The children of each node need to be stored in
ordered containers.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first point is achieved in a number of ways, but boils down to somehow
associating to each token a pair of integers&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, identifying the start
and end offsets of the token in the input file.&lt;p&gt;Given the span information for each token, we can then define the span for each
node to be the &lt;em&gt;join&lt;/em&gt; of its tokens&amp;rsquo; spans, namely the start is the min of its
constituent tokens&amp;rsquo; starts and its end is the max of the ends. This can be
easily calculated recursively.&lt;p&gt;Once we have spans, it&amp;rsquo;s easy to recover the whitespace between any two adjacent
syntactic constructs by calculating the text between them. This approach is more
robust than, say, associating each comment with a specific token, because it
makes it easier to discriminate stanzas for formatting.&lt;p&gt;Being able to retrieve the comments between any two syntax nodes is crucial.
Suppose the user writes the following Rust code:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kc&gt;false&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// HACK: disable this check.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;some_complicated_check&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If we&amp;rsquo;re formatting the binary expression containing the &lt;code&gt;&amp;&amp;&lt;/code&gt;, and we can&amp;rsquo;t
query for comments between the LHS and the operator, or the operator and the
RHS, the &lt;code&gt;// HACK&lt;/code&gt; comment will get deleted on format, which is pretty bad!&lt;p&gt;An AST that retains this level of information is sometimes called a &amp;ldquo;concrete
syntax tree&amp;rdquo;. I do not consider this a useful distinction, because any useful
AST must retain span and whitespace information, and it&amp;rsquo;s kind of pointless to
implement the same AST more than once. To me, an AST without spans is
incomplete.&lt;h3 id=updating-our-json-ast&gt;&lt;a href=#updating-our-json-ast&gt;Updating Our JSON AST&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;With all this in mind, the bare minimum for a &amp;ldquo;good&amp;rdquo; AST is gonna be something
like this.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Array&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Object&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Vec, not HashMap.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are various layout optimizations we can do: for example, the vast majority
of strings exist literally in the original file, so there&amp;rsquo;s no need to copy them
into a &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt;; it&amp;rsquo;s only necessary if the string contains escapes. My
&lt;code&gt;byteyarn&lt;/code&gt; crate, which I wrote about &lt;a href=/2023/08/09/yarns&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;,
is meant to make handling this case easy. So we might rewrite this to be
lifetime-bound to the original file.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;src&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;span&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Number&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;f64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Object&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Yarn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;src&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Vec, not HashMap.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;But wait, there&amp;rsquo;s some things that don&amp;rsquo;t have spans here. We need to include
spans for the braces of &lt;code&gt;Array&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;Object&lt;/code&gt;, their commas, and the colons on
object keys. &lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, this doesn&amp;rsquo;t handle the similar case of a small but non-empty
list. &lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;: [1, 2]}&lt;/code&gt; formats as&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-nofmt highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Nofmt&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Really, we&amp;rsquo;d like to keep &lt;code&gt;&#34;foo&#34;: [1, 2]&lt;/code&gt; on one line. And now we enter the
realm of column wrapping.&lt;h2 id=how-wide-is-a-codepoint&gt;&lt;a href=#how-wide-is-a-codepoint&gt;How Wide Is a Codepoint?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The whole point of a formatter is to work with &lt;em&gt;monospaced text&lt;/em&gt;, which is text
formatted using a monospaced or &lt;em&gt;fixed-width&lt;/em&gt; typeface, which means each
character is the same width, leading to the measure of the width of lines in
&lt;em&gt;columns&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;So how many columns does the string &lt;code&gt;cat&lt;/code&gt; take up? Three, pretty easy. But we
obviously don&amp;rsquo;t want to count bytes, this isn&amp;rsquo;t 1971. If we did, &lt;code&gt;кішка&lt;/code&gt;, when
UTF-8 encoded, it would be 10, rather than 5 columns wide. So we seem to want to
count Unicode characters instead?&lt;p&gt;Oh, but what &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; a Unicode character? Well, we could say that you&amp;rsquo;re counting
Unicode scalar values (what Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;char&lt;/code&gt; and Go&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;rune&lt;/code&gt;) types represent. Or
you could count grapheme clusters (like Swift&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;Character&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;But that would give wrong answers. CJK languages&amp;rsquo; characters, such as &lt;code&gt;猫&lt;/code&gt;,
usually want to be rendered as &lt;em&gt;two&lt;/em&gt; columns, even in monospaced contexts. So,
you might go to Unicode and discover
&lt;a href=https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr11/&gt;UAX#11&lt;/a&gt;, and attempt to use it for
assigning column widths. But it turns out that the precise rules that monospaced
fonts use are not written down in a single place in Unicode. You would also
discover that some scripts, such as Arabic, have complex ligature rules that
mean that the width of a single character depends on the characters around it.&lt;p&gt;This is a place where you should hunt for a library.
&lt;a href=https://docs.rs/unicode-width/latest/unicode_width/#rules-for-determining-width&gt;&lt;code&gt;unicode_width&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
is the one for Rust. Given that Unicode segmentation is a closely associated
operation to width, segmentation libraries are a good place to look for a width
calculation routine.&lt;p&gt;But most such libraries will still give wrong answers, because of tabs. The tab
character &lt;code&gt;U+0009 CHARACTER TABULATION&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s width depends on the width of all
characters before it, because a tab is as wide as needed to reach the next
&lt;em&gt;tabstop&lt;/em&gt;, which is a column position an integer multiple of the &lt;em&gt;tab width&lt;/em&gt;
(usually 2, 4, or, on most terminals, 8).&lt;p&gt;With a tab width of 4, &lt;code&gt;&#34;\t&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;&#34;a\t&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;&#34;abc\t&#34;&lt;/code&gt; are all four columns wide.
Depending on the context, you will either want to treat tabs as behaving as
going to the next tabstop (and thus being variable width), or having a fixed
width. The former is necessary for assigning correct column numbers in
diagnostics, but we&amp;rsquo;ll find that the latter is a better match for what we&amp;rsquo;re
doing.&lt;p&gt;The reason for being able to calculate the width of a string is to enable line
wrapping. At some point in the 2010s, people started writing a lot of code on
laptops, where it is not easy to have two editors side by side on the small
screen. This removes the motivation to wrap all lines at 80 columns&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;,
which in turn results in lines that tend to get arbitrarily long.&lt;p&gt;Line wrapping helps ensure that no matter how wide everyone&amp;rsquo;s editors are, the
code &lt;em&gt;I&lt;/em&gt; have to read fits on my very narrow editors.&lt;h2 id=accidentally-quadratic&gt;&lt;a href=#accidentally-quadratic&gt;Accidentally Quadratic&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;A lot of folks&amp;rsquo; first formatter recursively formats a node by formatting its
children to determine if they fit on one line or not, and based on that, and
their length if they are single-line, determine if their parent should break.&lt;p&gt;This is a naive approach, which has several disadvantages. First, it&amp;rsquo;s very easy
to accidentally backtrack, trying to only break smaller and smaller
subexpressions until things fit on one line, which can lead to quadratic
complexity. The logic for whether a node can break is bespoke per node and that
makes it easy to make mistakes.&lt;p&gt;Consider formatting &lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;: [1, 2]}&lt;/code&gt;. In our AST, this will look something like
this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;},&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;span&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;Span&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;start&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;end&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=mi&gt;15&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;},&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;To format the whole document, we need to know the width of each field in the
object to decide whether the object fits on one line. To do that, we need to
calculate the width of each value, and add to it the width of the key, and the
width of the &lt;code&gt;: &lt;/code&gt;separating them.&lt;p&gt;How can this be accidentally quadratic? If we simply say &amp;ldquo;format this node&amp;rdquo; to
obtain its width, that will recursively format all of the children it contains
without introducing line breaks, performing work that is linear in how many
transitive children that node contains. Having done this, we can now decide if
we need to introduce line breaks or not, which increases the indentation at
which the children are rendered. This means that the children cannot know ahead
of time how much of the line is left for them, so we need to recurse into
formatting them again, now knowing the indentation at which the direct children
are rendered.&lt;p&gt;Thus, each node performs work equal to the number of nodes beneath it. This has
resulted in many slow formatters.&lt;p&gt;Now, you could be more clever and have each node be capable of returning its
width based on querying its children&amp;rsquo;s width directly, but that means you need
to do complicated arithmetic for each node that needs to be synchronized with
the code that actually formats it. Easy to make mistakes.&lt;p&gt;The solution is to invent some kind of model for your document that specifies
how lines should be broken if necessary, and which tracks layout information so
that it can be computed in one pass, and then used in a second pass to figure
out whether to actually break lines or not.&lt;p&gt;This is actually how HTML works. The markup describes constraints on the layout
of the content, and then a layout engine, over several passes, calculates sizes,
solves constraints, and finally produces a raster image representing that HTML
document. Following the lead of HTML, we can design&amp;mldr;&lt;h2 id=a-dom-for-your-code&gt;&lt;a href=#a-dom-for-your-code&gt;A DOM for Your Code&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The HTML DOM is a markup document: a tree of tags where each tag has a type,
such as &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;p&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;a&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;hr&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;strong&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, properties, such as &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;a href=...&gt;&lt;/code&gt;,
and content consisting of nested tags (and bare text, which every HTML engine
just handles as a special kind of tag), such as &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;p&gt;Hello &amp;lt;em&gt;World&amp;lt;/em&gt;!&amp;lt;/p&gt;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;We obviously want to have a tag for text that should be rendered literally. We
also want a tag for line breaks that is distinct from the text tag, so that they
can be merged during rendering. It might be good to treat text tags consisting
of just whitespace, such as whitespace, specially: two newlines &lt;code&gt;\n\n&lt;/code&gt; are a
blank line, but we might want to merge consecutive blank lines. Similarly, we
might want to merge consecutive spaces to simplify generating the DOM.&lt;p&gt;Consider formatting a language like C++, where a function can have many
modifiers on it that can show up in any order, such as &lt;code&gt;inline&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;virtual&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;constexpr&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;explicit&lt;/code&gt;. We might want to canonicalize the order of these
modifiers. We don&amp;rsquo;t want to accidentally wind up printing
&lt;code&gt;inline constexpr Foo()&lt;/code&gt; because we printed an empty string for &lt;code&gt;virtual&lt;/code&gt;.
Having special merging for spaces means that all entities are always one space
apart if necessary. This is a small convenience in the DOM that multiplies to
significant simplification when lowering from AST to DOM.&lt;p&gt;Another useful tag is something like &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;indent by=&#34; &#34;&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, which increases the
indentation level by some string (or perhaps simply a number of spaces; the
string just makes supporting tabs easier) for the tags inside of it. This allows
control of indentation in a carefully-scoped manner.&lt;p&gt;Finally, we need some way to group tags that are candidates for &amp;ldquo;breaking&amp;rdquo;: if
the width of all of the tags inside of a &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;group&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is greater than the maximum
width that group can have (determined by indentation and any elements on the
same line as that group), we can set that group to &amp;ldquo;broken&amp;rdquo;, and&amp;mldr; well, what
should breaking do?&lt;p&gt;We want breaking to not just cause certain newlines (at strategic locations) to
appear, but we also want it to cause an indentation increase, and in languages
with trailing commas like Rust and Go, we want (or in the case of Go, &lt;em&gt;need&lt;/em&gt;) to
insert a trailing comma only when broken into multiple lines. We can achieve
this by allowing any tag to be &lt;em&gt;conditioned&lt;/em&gt; on whether the enclosing group is
broken or not.&lt;p&gt;Taken all together, we can render the AST for our &lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;: [1, 2]}&lt;/code&gt; document
into this DOM, according to the tags we&amp;rsquo;ve described above.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-XML highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;lt;group&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
