&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;Xml&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Notice a few things: All of the newlines are set to appear only &lt;code&gt;if=broken&lt;/code&gt;. The
space between the two commas only appears if the enclosing group is &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt;
broken, that is &lt;code&gt;if=flat&lt;/code&gt;. The groups encompass everything that can move due to
a break, which includes the outer braces. This is necessary because if that
brace is not part of the group, and it is the only character past the line width
limit, it will not cause the group to break.&lt;h3 id=laying-out-your-dom&gt;&lt;a href=#laying-out-your-dom&gt;Laying Out Your DOM&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first pass is easy: it measures how wide every node is. But we don&amp;rsquo;t know
whether any groups will break, so how can we measure that without calculating
breaks, which depend on indentation, and the width of their children, and&amp;mldr;&lt;p&gt;This is one tricky thing about multi-pass graph algorithms (or graph algorithms
in general): it can be easy to become overwhelmed trying to factor the
dependencies at each node so that they are not cyclic. I struggled with this
algorithm, until I realized that the only width we care about is the width &lt;em&gt;if
no groups are ever broken&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Consider the following logic: if a group needs to break, all of its parents must
obviously break, because the group will now contain a newline, so its parents
must break no matter what. Therefore, we only consider the width of a node when
deciding if a group must break intrinsically, i.e., because all of its children
decided not to break. This can happen for a document like the following, where
each inner node is quite large, but not large enough to hit the limit.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-_ highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;6&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;7&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;9&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;10&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;11&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;12&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;13&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;14&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;15&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;17&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;18&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;19&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;20&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;21&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;22&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;23&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;_&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because we prefer to break outer groups rather than inner groups, we can measure
the &amp;ldquo;widest a single line could be&amp;rdquo; in one pass, bottom-up: each node&amp;rsquo;s width is
the sum of the width of its children, or its literal contents for &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;text&gt;&lt;/code&gt;
elements. However, we must exclude all text nodes that are &lt;code&gt;if=broken&lt;/code&gt;, because
they obviously do not contribute to the single-line length. We can also ignore
indentation because indentation never happens in a single line.&lt;p&gt;However, this doesn&amp;rsquo;t give the full answer for whether a given group should
break, because that depends on indentation and what nodes came before on the
same line.&lt;p&gt;This means we need to perform a second pass: having laid everything out assuming
no group is broken, we must lay things out as they would appear when we render
them, taking into account breaking. But now that we know the maximum width of
each group if left unbroken, we can make breaking decisions.&lt;p&gt;As we walk the DOM, we keep track of the current column and indentation value.
For each group, we decide to break it if either:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Its width, plus the current column value, exceeds the maximum column width.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;It contains any newlines, something that can be determined in the first pass.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first case is why we can&amp;rsquo;t actually treat tabs as if they advance to a
tabstop. We cannot know the column at which a node will be placed at the time
that we measure its width, so we need to assume the worst case.&lt;p&gt;Whenever we hit a newline, we update the current width to the width induced by
indentation, simulating a newline plus indent. We also need to evaluate the
condition, if present, on each tag now, since by the time we inspect a non-group
tag, we have already made a decision as to whether to break or not.&lt;h3 id=render-it&gt;&lt;a href=#render-it&gt;Render It!&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that everything is determined, rendering is super easy: just walk the DOM
and print out all the text nodes that either have no condition or whose
condition matches the innermost group they&amp;rsquo;re inside of.&lt;p&gt;And, of course, this is where we need to be careful with indentation: you don&amp;rsquo;t
want to have lines that end in whitespace, so you should make sure to not print
out any spaces until text is written after a newline. This is also a good
opportunity to merge adjacent only-newlines text blocks. The merge algorithm I
like is to make sure that when &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;m&lt;/code&gt; newline blocks are adjacent, print
&lt;code&gt;max(n, m)&lt;/code&gt; newlines. This ensures that a DOM node containing &lt;code&gt;\n\n\n&lt;/code&gt; is
respected, while deleting a bunch of &lt;code&gt;\n&lt;/code&gt;s in a row that would result in many
blank lines.&lt;p&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s awesome about this approach is that the layout algorithm is highly
generic: you can re-use it for whatever compiler frontend you like, without
needing to fuss with layout yourself. There is a very direct conversion from AST
to DOM, and the result is very declarative.&lt;h3 id=more-complicated-yaml&gt;&lt;a href=#more-complicated-yaml&gt;More Complicated: YAML&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;YAML is a superset of JSON that SREs use to write sentient configuration files.
It has a funny list syntax that we might want to use for multi-line lists, but
we might want to keep JSON-style lists for short ones.&lt;p&gt;A document of nested lists might look something like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-yaml highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;- &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;6&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;7&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;9&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;10&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;11&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;12&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;lt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=na&gt;s=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;}&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=na&gt;if=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;flat&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;/&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;Xml&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here, we&amp;rsquo;ve made the &lt;code&gt;[]&lt;/code&gt; and the comma only appear in flat mode, while in
broken mode, we have a &lt;code&gt;- &lt;/code&gt;prefix for each item. The inserted newlines have
also changed somewhat, and the indentation blocks have moved: now only the value
is indented, since YAML allows the &lt;code&gt;-&lt;/code&gt;s of list items to be at the same
indentation level as the parent value for lists nested in objects. (This is a
case where some layout logic is language-specific, but now the output is
worrying about declarative markup rather than physical measurements.)&lt;p&gt;There are other enhancements you might want to make to the DOM I don&amp;rsquo;t describe
here. For example, comments want to be word-wrapped, but you might not know what
the width is until layout happens. Having a separate tag for word-wrapped blocks
would help here.&lt;p&gt;Similarly, a mechanism for &amp;ldquo;partial breaks&amp;rdquo;, such as for the document below,
could be implemented by having a type of line break tag that breaks if the text
that follows overflows the column, which can be easily implemented by tracking
the position of the last such break tag.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-_ highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;foo&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;very&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;long&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;list&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;          &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;of&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=s2&gt;&amp;#34;strings&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;_&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h2 id=using-this-yourself&gt;&lt;a href=#using-this-yourself&gt;Using This Yourself&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I think that a really good formatter is essential for any programming language,
and I think that a high-quality library that does most of the heavy-lifting is
important to make it easier to demand good formatters.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/strings/tree/main/allman&gt;So I wrote a Rust library.&lt;/a&gt; I
haven&amp;rsquo;t released it on crates.io because I don&amp;rsquo;t think it&amp;rsquo;s quite at the state I
want, but it turns out that the layout algorithm is very simple, so porting this
to other languages should be EZ.&lt;p&gt;Now you have no excuse. :D&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Everyone pronounces this acronym &amp;ldquo;ay ess tee&amp;rdquo;, but I have a friend who
really like to say &lt;em&gt;ast&lt;/em&gt;, rhyming with &lt;em&gt;mast&lt;/em&gt;, so I&amp;rsquo;m making a callout post
my twitter dot com.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;In computing, a group of lines not separated by blank lines is called a
stanza, in analogy to the stanzas of a poem, which are typeset with no blank
lines between the lines of the stanza.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;You could also just store a string, containing the original text, but
storing offsets is necessary for &lt;em&gt;diagnostics&lt;/em&gt;, which is the jargon term for
a compiler error. Compiler errors are recorded using an AST node as context,
and to report the line at which the error occurred, we need to be able to
map the node back to its offset in the file.&lt;p&gt;Once we have the offset, we can calculate the line in &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:1em;vertical-align:-.25em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.02778em&gt;O&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mopen&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mop&gt;lo&lt;span style=margin-right:.01389em&gt;g&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.1667em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mclose&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; time
using binary search. Having pre-computed an array of the offset of each &lt;code&gt;\n&lt;/code&gt;
byte in the input file, binary search will tell us the index and offset of
the &lt;code&gt;\n&lt;/code&gt; before the token; this index is the zero-indexed line number, and
the string from that &lt;code&gt;\n&lt;/code&gt; to the offset can be used to calculate the column.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;use&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;unicode_width&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;UnicodeWidthStr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// Returns the index of each newline. Can be pre-computed and re-used
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// multiple times.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;newlines&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;file&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// Returns the line and column of the given offset, given the line
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// tarts of the file.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;location&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;file&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;newlines&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;offset&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;match&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;newlines&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;binary_search&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;offset&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Ok means that offset refers to a newline, so this means
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// we want to return the width of the line that it ends as
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// the column.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;//
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Err means that this is after the nth newline, except Err(0),
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// which means it is before the first one.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Ok&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;file&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;offset&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;].&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;width&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Ok&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;file&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;newlines&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;offset&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;].&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;width&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;file&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;newlines&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;offset&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;].&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;width&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

    <title>Go&#39;s Weird Little Iterators</title>
    <link href="/2024/12/16/rangefuncs"/>
    <updated>2024-12-16T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2024/12/16/rangefuncs</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;A second post on Go silliness (Sunny, aren&amp;rsquo;t you a C++ programmer?): in 1.23,
Go &lt;em&gt;finally&lt;/em&gt; added custom iterators. Now, back when I was at Google and involved
in the Go compiler as &amp;ldquo;the annoying Rust guy who gets lunch with us&amp;rdquo;, there were
proposals suggesting adding something like this, implemented as either an
interface or a func:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Iter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is not what Go did. No, Go did something really weird. And the
implementation is &lt;em&gt;incredible&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;h2 id=whats-an-iterator&gt;&lt;a href=#whats-an-iterator&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s an Iterator?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;An &lt;em&gt;iterator&lt;/em&gt;, in the context of programming language design, is a special type
of value that can be used to walk through a sequence of values, without
necessarily materializing the sequence as whatever the language&amp;rsquo;s array type is.&lt;p&gt;But, a proper iterator must fit with the language&amp;rsquo;s looping construct. An
&lt;em&gt;iterable type&lt;/em&gt; is one which can be used in a for-each loop, such as C++&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;code&gt;for (T x : y)&lt;/code&gt; or Python&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;for x in y&lt;/code&gt; (modern languages usually only have a
for-each loop as their only &lt;code&gt;for&lt;/code&gt; loop, because C-style for loops are not in
anymore).&lt;h3 id=c-iterator-pairs&gt;&lt;a href=#c-iterator-pairs&gt;C++ Iterator Pairs&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Every language defines a &lt;em&gt;desugaring&lt;/em&gt; that defines how custom iteration works in
term of the more primitive loops. For example, in C++, when we write
&lt;code&gt;for (T x : y) { ... }&lt;/code&gt; (called a
&lt;a href=https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/range-for&gt;&lt;em&gt;range-based for loop&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt;,
added in C++11), desugars as follows&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;__range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;__begin&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;begin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;__range&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ADL
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;__end&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;end&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;__range&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ADL
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;__begin&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;__end&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;__begin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;__begin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;break&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;continue&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;return&lt;/code&gt; inside of the loop body require no special
handling: they Just Work, because this is just a plain ol for loop.&lt;p&gt;This begin and end weirdness is because, if the iterator backs an actual array,
begin and end can just be pointers to the first element and one-past-the-end and
this will Just Work. Before C++11, the convention for C++ iterators was to
construct types that imitated pointers; you would usually write loops over
non-array types like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;things&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;begin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;things&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;end&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;whatever&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;C++ simply codified common (if gross) practice. It is very tedious to implement
C++ iterators, though. You need to provide a dummy end iterator, you need to
provide some kind of comparison operator, and iterators that don&amp;rsquo;t return a
reference out of &lt;code&gt;operator*()&lt;/code&gt; are&amp;mldr; weird.&lt;p&gt;Begin and end can be different types (which is how C++20 ranges pretend to be
iterable), but being able to query done-ness separately from the next value
makes implementation annoying: it means that an iterator that has not begun
iteration (i.e., &lt;code&gt;++&lt;/code&gt; has not been executed yet, because it occurs in the loop&amp;rsquo;s

which usually means an extra bool to keep track of whether iteration has started
or not.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s what writing an iterator (that is also an iterable usable in a range
for-loop) over the non-zero elements of a &lt;code&gt;std::span&amp;lt;const int&gt;&lt;/code&gt; might look

you don&amp;rsquo;t plan on consuming the entire iterator. Alternatively, you can
partially iterate over an iterator by taking a mutable reference to it. This is
useful for iterators that can yield their remainder.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:11&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_slice&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;chunks_exact&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;chunk&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;in&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;do_thing&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;chunk&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;do_thing&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;remainder&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;break&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;continue&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;return&lt;/code&gt; work in the obvious way.&lt;p&gt;The interface solves the problems C++ and Java had very cleanly: &lt;code&gt;next&lt;/code&gt; both
computes the next item and whether the iterator has more elements. Rust even
allows iterators to resume yielding &lt;code&gt;Some&lt;/code&gt; after yielding &lt;code&gt;None&lt;/code&gt;, although few
algorithms will make use of this.&lt;p&gt;Implementing the non-zero iterator we&amp;rsquo;ve been writing so far is quite simple:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;std&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;from_fn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;move&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;||&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;while&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;==&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Some&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;item&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;item&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;});&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;However, this can be written far more simply&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; using iterator
combinators:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;..&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;it&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ints&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;copied&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;filter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;It requires a little bit of effort to implement some iterators, but most of the
common cases are easy to put together with composition.&lt;p&gt;Python iterators are basically the same thing, but there&amp;rsquo;s no interface to
implement (because Python doesn&amp;rsquo;t believe in type safety). Lua iterators are
similar. The Rust pattern of a function that returns the next item (or a special
end-of-sequence value) is relatively popular because of this simplicity and
composability, and because they can model a lot of iteration strategies.&lt;h2 id=so-what-did-go-do&gt;&lt;a href=#so-what-did-go-do&gt;So, What Did Go Do?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Well. Go has a range for syntax like many other languages. The syntax looks like
this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; can be a list of places, and the &lt;code&gt;:=&lt;/code&gt; can be plain assignment, &lt;code&gt;=&lt;/code&gt;. You
can also write &lt;code&gt;for range y { ... }&lt;/code&gt; if the iteration values aren&amp;rsquo;t needed.&lt;p&gt;The behavior of this construct, like many others in Go, depends explicitly on
the type after &lt;code&gt;range&lt;/code&gt;. Each range iteration can yield zero or more values; the&lt;p&gt;These are:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;For &lt;code&gt;[]T&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;[n]T&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;*[n]T&lt;/code&gt;, each step yields an index of the slice and
the value at that offset, in order.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;For &lt;code&gt;map[K]V&lt;/code&gt;, each step yields a key and a value, in a random order.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;For &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;- chan T&lt;/code&gt;, it desugars into&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;break&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Starting in Go 1.22, ranging on an integer type would desugar into&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;All of these desugars are essentially still just loops, so &lt;code&gt;break&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;continue&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;return&lt;/code&gt; all work as expected.&lt;p&gt;But, how do custom types, like weird map types, implement iteration? The
usual&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; implementation is
&lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/sync#Map.Range&gt;&lt;code&gt;sync.Map.Range&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;, which looks like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Map&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Range&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;yield&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;key&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;value&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This function will call &lt;code&gt;yield&lt;/code&gt; for each element in the map. If the function
returns &lt;code&gt;false&lt;/code&gt;, iteration will stop. This pattern is not uncommon, but
sometimes libraries omit the &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt; return (like
&lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/container/ring@go1.23.4#Ring.Do&gt;&lt;code&gt;container/ring.Ring.Do&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;).
Some, like &lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/path/filepath#WalkFunc&gt;&lt;code&gt;filepath.WalkDir&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;, have
a more complex interface involving errors.&lt;p&gt;This is the template for what became &lt;em&gt;rangefuncs&lt;/em&gt;, a mechanism for using the
for-range syntax with certain function values.&lt;h2 id=rangefuncs&gt;&lt;a href=#rangefuncs&gt;Rangefuncs&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The word &amp;ldquo;rangefunc&amp;rdquo; does not appear in Go&amp;rsquo;s specification. It is a term used to
refer to them in some documentation, within the compiler, and in the runtime.&lt;p&gt;A rangefunc is any function with one of the following signatures:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;func(yield func() bool)&lt;/code&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;func(yield func(V) bool)&lt;/code&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;func(yield func(K, V) bool)&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;They work like &lt;code&gt;sync.Map.Range&lt;/code&gt; does: the function calls &lt;code&gt;yield&lt;/code&gt; (hereafter
simply called &amp;ldquo;the yield&amp;rdquo;) for each element, and stops early if yield returns
false. The &lt;code&gt;iter&lt;/code&gt; package contains types for the second and third of these:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Seq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;yield&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:19&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;So. These things are actually pretty nuts. They break my brain somewhat, because
this is the opposite of how iterators usually work. Go calls what I&amp;rsquo;ve described
all the other languages do a &amp;ldquo;pull iterator&amp;rdquo;, whereas rangefuncs are &amp;ldquo;push
iterators&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;They have a few obvious limitations. For one, you can&amp;rsquo;t do smart sizing like
with Rust or C++ iterators&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. Another is that you can&amp;rsquo;t easily
&amp;ldquo;pause&amp;rdquo; iteration.&lt;p&gt;But they do have one advantage, which I think is the real reason Go went to so
much trouble to implement them (and yes, I will dig into how insane that part
is). Using push iterators by default means that users &amp;ldquo;only&amp;rdquo; need to write an
ordinary for loop packaged into a function. Given that Go makes major
performance sacrifices in order to be easy to learn&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, trying to make it
so that an iterator packages the actual looping construct it represents makes
quite a bit of sense.&lt;p&gt;Rangefuncs are actually really cool in some respects, because they enable
unusual patterns. For example, you can use a rangefunc to provide RAII blocks.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:20&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Open&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;fs&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;fs&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;FS&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;path&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Seq2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;fs&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;File&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;error&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

non-local returns?!&lt;h2 id=go-now-has-non-local-returns&gt;&lt;a href=#go-now-has-non-local-returns&gt;Go Now Has Non-Local Returns&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The desugaring for rangefuncs is very complicated. This is because &lt;code&gt;break&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;continue&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;return&lt;/code&gt; all work in a rangefunc! How does this work?
Let&amp;rsquo;s Godbolt it.&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s start with something really basic: a loop body that just calls a function.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:22&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nf&gt;sink&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;

syntax, and removed some extraneous ABI things, including a writer barrier where

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// execute a range-over-function loop in which the loop body
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// may execute a defer statement. That defer needs to add to
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// the chain for the current function, not the func literal synthesized
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// to represent the loop body. To do that, the original function
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// calls deferrangefunc to obtain an opaque token representing
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// the current frame, and then the loop body uses deferprocat
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// instead of deferproc to add to that frame&amp;#39;s defer lists.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;//
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// The token is an &amp;#39;any&amp;#39; with underlying type *atomic.Pointer[_defer].
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// It is the atomically-updated head of a linked list of _defer structs
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// representing deferred calls. At the same time, we create a _defer
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// struct on the main g._defer list with d.head set to this head pointer.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;//
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// The g._defer list is now a linked list of deferred calls,
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// but an atomic list hanging off:
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;//
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// (increasingly terrifying discussion of concurrent data structures)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:31&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This raises one more thing that works in range funcs, seamlessly: &lt;code&gt;defer&lt;/code&gt;. Yes,
despite the yield executing multiple call stacks away, possibly on a different
goroutine&amp;mldr; &lt;code&gt;defer&lt;/code&gt; still gets attached to the calling function.&lt;h2 id=go-now-has-non-local-defer&gt;&lt;a href=#go-now-has-non-local-defer&gt;Go Now Has Non-Local Defer&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The way defer works is that each G (the goroutine struct, &lt;code&gt;runtime.g&lt;/code&gt;) holds a
linked list of defer records, of type &lt;code&gt;_defer&lt;/code&gt;. Each call to &lt;code&gt;defer&lt;/code&gt; sticks one
of these onto this list. On function return, Go calls &lt;code&gt;runtime.deferreturn()&lt;/code&gt;,
which essentially executes and pops defers off of the list until it finds one
whose stack pointer is not the current function&amp;rsquo;s stack pointer (so, it must
belong to another function).&lt;p&gt;Rangefuncs throw a wrench in that mix: if &lt;code&gt;myFunc.range-n&lt;/code&gt; defers, that defer
has to be attached to &lt;code&gt;myFunc&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s defer records somehow. So the list must have a
way of inserting in the middle.&lt;p&gt;This is what this comment is about: when &lt;code&gt;defer&lt;/code&gt; occurs in the loop body, that
defer gets attached to a defer record for that function, using a token that the
yield captures; this is later canonicalized when walking the defer list on the
way out of &lt;code&gt;myFunc&lt;/code&gt;. Because the yield can escape onto another goroutine, this
part of the &lt;code&gt;defer&lt;/code&gt; chain has to be atomic.&lt;p&gt;Incredibly, this approach is extremely robust. For example, if we spawn the
yield as a goroutine, and carefully synchronize between that and the outer
function, we can force the runtime to hard-crash when &lt;code&gt;defer&lt;/code&gt;ing to a function
that has returned.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:32&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;

Pretty sick! It
accomplishes this by poisoning the token the yield func uses to defer.&lt;p&gt;I have tried various other attempts at causing memory unsafety with rangefuncs,
but Go actually does a really good job of avoiding this. The only thing I&amp;rsquo;ve
managed to do that&amp;rsquo;s especially interesting is to tear the return slot on a
function without named returns, but that&amp;rsquo;s no worse than tearing any other value
(which is still really bad, because you can tear interface values, but it&amp;rsquo;s not
&lt;em&gt;worse&lt;/em&gt;).&lt;h2 id=pull-iterators-and-coroutines&gt;&lt;a href=#pull-iterators-and-coroutines&gt;Pull Iterators and Coroutines&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course we&amp;rsquo;re not done. Go provides a mechanism for converting push iterators

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:33&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Essentially, you can request values with &lt;code&gt;next()&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;stop()&lt;/code&gt; can be used if
you finish early. But also, this spawns a whole goroutine and uses channels to
communicate and synchronize, which feels very unnecessary.&lt;p&gt;The implementation doesn&amp;rsquo;t use goroutines. It uses coroutines.&lt;h3 id=giving-up-on-goroutines&gt;&lt;a href=#giving-up-on-goroutines&gt;Giving Up on Goroutines&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Spawning a goroutine is expensive. Doing so expends scheduler and memory
resources. It&amp;rsquo;s overkill for a helper like this (ironic, because the original
premise of Go was that goroutines would be cheap enough to allocate
willy-nilly).&lt;p&gt;Go instead implements this using &amp;ldquo;coroutines&amp;rdquo;, a mechanism for concurrency
without parallelism. This is intended to make context switching very cheap,
because it does not need to go through the scheduler: instead, it uses
cooperative multitasking.&lt;p&gt;The coroutine interface is something like the following. My &amp;ldquo;userland&amp;rdquo;
implementation will not be very efficient, because it relies on the scheduler to
transfer control. The goroutines may run on different CPUs, so synchronization
is necessary for communication, even if they are not running concurrently.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:34&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;coro&lt;/span&gt;
