&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;next&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;stop&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:35&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If you look at the implementation in
&lt;a href=https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.23.4:src/iter/iter.go&gt;&lt;code&gt;iter.go&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;,
it&amp;rsquo;s basically this, but with a lot of error checking and race detection, to
prevent misuse, such as if &lt;code&gt;next&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;stop&lt;/code&gt; escape to other goroutines.&lt;p&gt;Now, the main thing that runtime support brings here is that &lt;code&gt;Resume()&lt;/code&gt; is
immediate: it does not go to the scheduler, which might not decide to
immediately run the goroutine that last called &lt;code&gt;Resume()&lt;/code&gt; for a variety of
reasons (for example, to ensure wakeup fairness). Coroutines sidestep fairness,
by making &lt;code&gt;Resume()&lt;/code&gt; little more than a jump to the last &lt;code&gt;Resume()&lt;/code&gt; (with
registers fixed up accordingly).&lt;p&gt;This is not going to be &lt;em&gt;that&lt;/em&gt; cheap: a goroutine still needs to be allocated,
and switching needs to poke and prod the underlying Gs a little bit. But it&amp;rsquo;s a
cool optimization, and I hope coroutines eventually make their way into more
things in Go, hopefully as a language or &lt;code&gt;sync&lt;/code&gt; primitive.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Congratulations, you have survived over 3000 words of me going on about
iterators. Go&amp;rsquo;s push iterators are a unique approach to a common language design
problem (even if it took a decade for them to materialize).&lt;p&gt;I encountered rangefuncs for the first time earlier this year and have found
them absolutely fascinating, both from a &amp;ldquo;oh my god they actually did that&amp;rdquo;
perspective and from a &amp;ldquo;how do we express iteration&amp;rdquo; perspective. I don&amp;rsquo;t think
the result was perfect by any means, and it is unsuitable for languages that
need the performance you can only get from pull iterators. I think they would be
a great match for a language like Python or Java, though.&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;d like to thank David Chase, an old colleague, for tolerating my excited
contrived questions about the guts of this feature.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Ugh, ok. This is the C++20 desugaring, and there are cases where we do not
just call &lt;code&gt;std::begin()&lt;/code&gt;. In particular, array references and class type
references with &lt;code&gt;.begin()&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;.end()&lt;/code&gt; do not call &lt;code&gt;std::begin()&lt;/code&gt; and are
open-coded. This means that you can&amp;rsquo;t use ADL to override these types&#39;
iterator.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;But please don&amp;rsquo;t use proto3. I&amp;rsquo;m telling you that as the guy who maintained
the compiler. Just don&amp;rsquo;t.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;In compiler jargon, a loop is broken up into three parts: the &lt;em&gt;header&lt;/em&gt;,
which is where the loop is entered, the &lt;em&gt;body&lt;/em&gt;, which is one step of
iteration, and the &lt;em&gt;latch&lt;/em&gt;, which is the part that jumps back to the start
of the body. This is where incrementation in a C-style for loop happens.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;And with better performance. Rust&amp;rsquo;s iterators can provide a size hint to
help size containers before a call to &lt;code&gt;collect()&lt;/code&gt;, via the
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.FromIterator.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;FromIterator&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
trait.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;Some people observed that you can use a channel as a custom iterator, by
having a parallel goroutine run a for loop to feed the channel. &lt;em&gt;Do not do
this.&lt;/em&gt; It is slow: it has to transit each element through the heap, forcing
anything it points to escape. It takes up an extra M and a P in the
scheduler, and requires potentially allocating a stack for a G. It&amp;rsquo;s
probably faster to just build a slice and return that, especially for small
iterations.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;For this reason, I wish that Go had instead defined something along these
lines.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:36&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Seq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;Iterate&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;yield&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:36&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is functionally identical to what they did, but it would have permitted
future extensions such as the following interface:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:37&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;SizedSeq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;Seq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nf&gt;SizeHint&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;lower&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;upper&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:37&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This would mean that &lt;code&gt;slices.Collect&lt;/code&gt; could be enhanced into something like
this.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:38&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;slices&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Collect&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;E&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;seq&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Seq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;E&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;])&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;E&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;out&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;E&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;sized&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;seq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;iter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;SizedSeq&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;E&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;lower&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;_&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;sized&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;SizeHint&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;out&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;make&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;([]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;E&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;lower&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;seq&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;out&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;append&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;out&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:38&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;I don&amp;rsquo;t think there&amp;rsquo;s an easy way to patch this up, at this point.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;Disclaimer: I am not going to dig into Go&amp;rsquo;s rationale for rangefuncs.
Knowing how the sausage is made, most big Go proposals are a mix of
understandable reasoning and less reasonable veiled post-hoc justification
to compensate for either Google planning/approvals weirdness or because the
design was some principal engineer&amp;rsquo;s pony. This isn&amp;rsquo;t even a Go thing, it&amp;rsquo;s
a Google culture problem. I say this as the architect of
&lt;a href=https://protobuf.dev/editions/overview&gt;Protobuf Editions&lt;/a&gt;, the biggest
change to Protobuf since Rob&amp;rsquo;s misguided proto3&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; experiment. &lt;em&gt;I&lt;/em&gt;
have written this kind of language proposal, on purpose, because bad culture
mandated it.&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;The purpose of a system is what it does.&lt;/em&gt; It is easier to understand a
system by observing its response to stimuli, rather than what it says on the
tin. So let&amp;rsquo;s use that lens.&lt;p&gt;Go wants to be easy to learn. It intended to replace C++ at Google (lol,
lmao), which, of course, failed disastrously, because performance of the
things already written in C++ is tied to revenue. They have successfully
pivoted to being an easy-to-learn language that makes it easy to onboard
programmers regardless of what they already use, as opposed to onboarding
them to C++.&lt;p&gt;This does not mean that Go is user-friendly. In fact, user-friendliness is
clearly not a core value. Rob and his greybeard crowd didn&amp;rsquo;t seem to care
about the human aspect of interacting with a toolchain, so Go tooling rarely
provides good diagnostics, nor did the language, until the last few years,
try to reduce toil. After all, if it is tedious to use but simple, that does
make it easy to onboard new programmers.&lt;p&gt;Rust is the opposite: it is very difficult to learn with a famously steep
learning curve; however, it is very accessible, because the implementors
have sanded down every corner and sharp edge using diagnostics, error
messages, and tooling. C++ is neither of these things. It is very difficult
to learn, and most compilers are pretty unhelpful (if they diagnose anything
at all).&lt;p&gt;I think that Go has at least realized the language can be a pain to use in
some situations, which is fueled in part by legitimate UX research. This is
why Go has generics and other recent advanced language features, like being
able to use the &lt;code&gt;for&lt;/code&gt; syntax with integers or with custom iterators.&lt;p&gt;I think that rangefuncs are easy to learn in the way Go needs them to be. If
you expect more users to want to write rangefuncs than users want to write
complicated &lt;em&gt;uses&lt;/em&gt; of rangefuncs, I think push iterators are the easiest to
learn how to use.&lt;p&gt;I think this is a much more important reason for all the trouble that
rangefuncs generate for the compiler and runtime than, say, compatibility
with existing code; I have not seen many cases in the wild or in the
standard library that conform to the rangefunc signatures.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Things You Never Wanted To Know About Go Interfaces</title>
    <link href="/2024/12/12/go-abi"/>
    <updated>2024-12-12T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2024/12/12/go-abi</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Lately I&amp;rsquo;ve been finding myself writing a bit of Go, and I&amp;rsquo;ve picked up various
fun &amp;ldquo;layout secrets&amp;rdquo; that help inform how I write code to minimize hidden
allocations, and generally be kind to the optimizer. This article is a series of
notes on the topic.&lt;p&gt;This post is about Go implementation details, so they can probably break you at
any time if you rely on it. On the other hand, Hyrum&amp;rsquo;s law is a bitch, so taking
your chances may not be that bad. After all, they&amp;rsquo;re probably never going to be
able to properly clean up the mess people made with &lt;code&gt;//go:linkname&lt;/code&gt; with runtime
symbols&amp;mldr;&lt;p&gt;As with many of my other posts, I&amp;rsquo;ll assume a basic familiarity with being able
to read assembly. I&amp;rsquo;m using x86 for this post, but it&amp;rsquo;s worth looking at my
&lt;a href=/2021/11/29/assembly-1&gt;RISC-V post&lt;/a&gt; for a refresher.&lt;h2 id=gc-shapes&gt;&lt;a href=#gc-shapes&gt;GC Shapes&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The most basic Go-specific concept when it comes to type layouts is the &lt;em&gt;shape&lt;/em&gt;
of a type. This is an implementation detail of Go&amp;rsquo;s garbage collector that leaks
through the &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; package.&lt;p&gt;Like in most native programming languages, every Go type has a size (the number
of bytes that type takes up in memory) and an alignment (a power of two that
every pointer to that type must be divisible by). Go, like most other languages,
requires that size be divisible by the alignment: that is, the size is equal to
the stride of an array of that type.&lt;p&gt;The size an alignment of a type can be queried by the intrinsics
&lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/unsafe#Sizeof&gt;&lt;code&gt;unsafe.Sizeof&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; and &lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/unsafe#Alignof&gt;&lt;code&gt;unsafe.Alignof&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. These are very unwieldy in generic
code, so I like to define a couple of helpers&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Size&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Sizeof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Align&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Alignof&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Together, these two quantities are called the &lt;em&gt;layout&lt;/em&gt; of a type (a term common
to many native languages). However, the &lt;em&gt;shape&lt;/em&gt; of a type also records what
pieces thereof contain &lt;em&gt;pointers&lt;/em&gt;. This is because memory visible to the GC
(such as globals, heap memory, or stack roots) is typed, and the GC needs to
know which parts of those types are pointers that it needs to trace through.&lt;p&gt;Because all pointers have the same size and alignment (4 or 8 bytes depending on
the system) the pointer words of a type can be represented as a bitset, one bit
for every 4 or 8 bytes in the type. This, in fact, is the representation used by
the GC&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;In particular, this means that whether a field is to be interpreted as an
&lt;code&gt;unsafe.Pointer&lt;/code&gt; or as a &lt;code&gt;uintptr&lt;/code&gt; is a static property of the type. As we will
see when we discuss interfaces, this restriction prevents a few layout
optimizations.&lt;h2 id=slices-and-strings&gt;&lt;a href=#slices-and-strings&gt;Slices and Strings&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go is very public about the layout of slices and strings. A slice is&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;slice&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;cap&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;cap&lt;/code&gt; are extracted by their eponymous builtins, and &lt;code&gt;data&lt;/code&gt; can be
obtained using &lt;code&gt;unsafe.SliceData&lt;/code&gt; (or &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;s[0]&lt;/code&gt; if the slice is nonempty, but that
costs a bounds-check).&lt;p&gt;A string has the same layout as a &lt;code&gt;[]byte&lt;/code&gt;, except for a capacity:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;data&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;byte&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nx&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Despite essentially being slices, Go treats strings subtly differently. Strings
are &lt;code&gt;comparable&lt;/code&gt;, so they can be used as map keys. They are also immutable,
which enables a handful of optimizations. Immutability is also why they are
&lt;code&gt;comparable&lt;/code&gt;: Go made the mistake of not keeping &lt;code&gt;const&lt;/code&gt; from C, but they really
want map keys to be &lt;code&gt;const&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;There is nothing stopping us from aliasing strings to data pointed to by a
slice: after all, &lt;code&gt;strings.Builder&lt;/code&gt; does it to avoid a copy in &lt;code&gt;String()&lt;/code&gt;. We
can implement this easily enough with some &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;StringAlias&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;data&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;byte&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;string&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;String&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;SliceData&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Doing this is perfectly safe, so long as data is not mutated while the returned
string is accessible. This allows virtually any slice type to be used as a key
in a map, with some caveats.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Types which contain alignment padding cannot be used, because Go does not
promise that it zeros memory returned by &lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Types which contain pointers will cause those pointers to become unreachable
if the only reference is the aliased string; this is because the pointed to
data&amp;rsquo;s shape contains no pointer words.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Incomparable types and interfaces will be compared by address (that is, maps,
channels and funcs).&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;h3 id=dynamic-arrays-with-reflection&gt;&lt;a href=#dynamic-arrays-with-reflection&gt;Dynamic Arrays with Reflection&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, this isn&amp;rsquo;t the only to accomplish this: you can create dynamically-sized
array types using reflection, like so:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;Slice2Array&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;s&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The switch determines precisely how the interface data pointer is computed. It
turns out that (almost all) array types return true for &lt;code&gt;t.IfaceIndr()&lt;/code&gt;, so the
first case is selected, which triggers a copy (that being the call to
&lt;code&gt;unsafe_New()&lt;/code&gt; followed by a &lt;code&gt;typedmemmove&lt;/code&gt;). This copy is to ensure that the
value of the resulting interface cannot be mutated.&lt;p&gt;Now, if only we knew the layout of Go&amp;rsquo;s interfaces, we might be able to get
somewhere here&amp;mldr;&lt;h2 id=the-layout-of-gos-interfaces&gt;&lt;a href=#the-layout-of-gos-interfaces&gt;The Layout of Go&amp;rsquo;s Interfaces&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Oh, yes, that&amp;rsquo;s what this article is about. So, if we look at the &lt;code&gt;runtime2.go&lt;/code&gt;
file in the runtime (yes, that&amp;rsquo;s what it&amp;rsquo;s called), nestled among the giant
scheduler types for Gs, Ps, and Ms, we&amp;rsquo;ll find a couple of structs that really
elucidate what&amp;rsquo;s going on:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;runtime&lt;/span&gt;

inter&lt;em&gt;face&lt;/em&gt;).&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;eface&lt;/code&gt; having its own layout is an optimization. Because &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt; exists to be
downcast from dynamically, storing the type directly cuts out a pointer load
when doing a type switch on an &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt; specifically. If we look at what an &lt;code&gt;itab&lt;/code&gt;
is (which is &amp;ldquo;just&amp;rdquo; an

&lt;code&gt;rcx&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;rdi&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;rsi&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;r8&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;r9&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;r10&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;r11&lt;/code&gt; (with &lt;code&gt;rdx&lt;/code&gt; reserved for

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This function seems to be doing a lot more than it actually is. Part of it is
that its prologue has to do a call to &lt;code&gt;runtime.morestack_noctxt()&lt;/code&gt;, which is
simply a call to &lt;code&gt;runtime.morestack&lt;/code&gt; that clobbers &lt;code&gt;rdx&lt;/code&gt;, the closure capture
parameter. The meat of it comes when it loads &lt;code&gt;[rax + 24]&lt;/code&gt;, the first element of
&lt;code&gt;ITab.Fun&lt;/code&gt;. It then moves the data pointer in &lt;code&gt;rbx&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt;, the argument into
&lt;code&gt;rbx&lt;/code&gt;, and issues the call.&lt;p&gt;What about upcasts? An upcast to a concrete type is quite simple: simply compare
the type in the interface (either directly or in the &lt;code&gt;*ITab&lt;/code&gt;) to a particular
statically-known one. Downcasting to an interface (sometimes called a
&lt;em&gt;sidecast&lt;/em&gt;) is much more complicated, because it essentially requires a little
bit of reflection.&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=c1&gt;// type of source value (a *runtime._type)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;Typ&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;uintptr&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=c1&gt;// itab to use for result (a *runtime.itab)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;	&lt;span class=c1&gt;// nil if CanFail is set and conversion would fail.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;Itab&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;uintptr&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first thing this function does is check if &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt; contains 0, i.e., if this
is a nil &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt;, and panics if that&amp;rsquo;s the case (that&amp;rsquo;s a call to
&lt;code&gt;runtime.panicnildottype&lt;/code&gt;). It then loads &lt;code&gt;foo..typeAssert0&lt;/code&gt;, a synthetic global
variable containing an &lt;code&gt;abi.TypeAssert&lt;/code&gt; value. It loads the &lt;code&gt;Cache&lt;/code&gt; field, as
well as the &lt;code&gt;Hash&lt;/code&gt; field of the &lt;code&gt;abi.Type&lt;/code&gt; attached to the &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt;. It masks off
the low bits using &lt;code&gt;typeAssert0.Cache.Mask&lt;/code&gt;, and uses that to start probing the
very simple open-addressed hash table located in &lt;code&gt;typeAssert0.Cache.Entries&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;If it finds a &lt;code&gt;TypeAssertCacheEntry&lt;/code&gt; with the type we&amp;rsquo;re looking for (compared
by address), we&amp;rsquo;ve found it. We load that entry&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;Itab&lt;/code&gt; value into &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt; to
change the value from being an &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt; to being a &lt;code&gt;MyIface&lt;/code&gt;, and we&amp;rsquo;re done.&lt;p&gt;If it finds a &lt;code&gt;TypeAssertCacheEntry&lt;/code&gt; with a nil &lt;code&gt;Typ&lt;/code&gt; pointer, we&amp;rsquo;re forced to
hit the slow path, implemented at &lt;code&gt;runtime.typeAssert()&lt;/code&gt;. This dynamically
builds an itab by searching the method set of the type inside the &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This then calls the reflection code in &lt;code&gt;runtime.getitab()&lt;/code&gt;, which is what
actually performs the messy search through the method set, comparing the names
and signatures of methods with those in the interface, to produce an itab at
runtime.&lt;p&gt;Then, it shoves this the resulting itab into the global itab cache, which is
protected by a global lock! There are lots of scary atomics in this code. There
are many places where this can potentially panic, bubbling up a type assertion
failure to the user.&lt;p&gt;When &lt;code&gt;runtime.getitab()&lt;/code&gt; returns, &lt;code&gt;runtime.typeAssert()&lt;/code&gt; will
&lt;em&gt;maybe&lt;/em&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; update the type assertion cache, and return the new itab.
This allows the code in our function to return directly, without needing to take
another trip into the &lt;code&gt;hashProbe&lt;/code&gt; loop.&lt;p&gt;In theory, PGO could be used to pre-fill the cache, but I couldn&amp;rsquo;t find any code
in the compiler that indicates that this is something they do. In the meantime,
you can optimize a hot type assert ahead of time by asserting to a known common
type:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;DoSomething&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;r&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;io&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Reader&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;rs&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;io&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ReadSeeker&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;f&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;r&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;os&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;File&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Check for a known implementation first. This only costs
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// a pointer comparison with the *abi.Type in the itab.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;rs&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;f&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;else&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;f&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;r&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;io&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;ReadSeeker&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;ok&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Do an interface type assertion. This would eventually
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// learn os.File, but the branch above skips that &amp;#34;warmup&amp;#34;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// time. It also lets the hardware branch predictor allocate
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// a prediction slot just for os.File.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=nx&gt;rs&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;f&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;else&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Type switches, incidentally, use a very similar caching mechanism for switches
that include interface types among the cases.&lt;h3 id=what-was-that-about-indirect-interfaces&gt;&lt;a href=#what-was-that-about-indirect-interfaces&gt;What Was That About Indirect Interfaces?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Back when we were hacking arrays into existence with reflection, there was some
trouble in &lt;code&gt;reflect.Value.Interface()&lt;/code&gt;, where it would do a seemingly
unnecessary copy.&lt;p&gt;This is because an interface&amp;rsquo;s data pointer must be a pointer. If you cram, say,
an &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt; into an &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt;, Go will spill it to the heap. This is often called
&lt;em&gt;boxing&lt;/em&gt;, but the Go runtime refers to it as an &amp;ldquo;indirect interface&amp;rdquo;.&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Int2Any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-x86 highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;Int2Any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;push&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;rbp&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mov&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;rbp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rsp&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;add&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;rsp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;call&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;runtime&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;convT64&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;move&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;rbx&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;lea&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;type&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;add&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;rsp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;pop&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;rbp&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Like many other managed languages, Go will skip boxing very small values by
instead returning pointers into some global array.&lt;p&gt;Now, this boxing could be avoided: after all, an &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt; is no larger than a
pointer, so we could cram it into the data pointer field directly. However, the
GC &lt;em&gt;really&lt;/em&gt; doesn&amp;rsquo;t like that: the GC assumes it can trace through any pointer.
Now, the GC &lt;em&gt;could&lt;/em&gt; treat interfaces differently, and look at the type/itab
pointer to determine if the data value pointer or a scalar. However, this would
add significant complexity to both the representation of shapes, and to the
tracing code in the GC, resulting in more branches and slower tracing.&lt;p&gt;However, if the type being wrapped in an interface happens to be a pointer, it
can just use that pointer value directly.&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;Int2Any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;any&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:19&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:20&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-x86 highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;Int2Any&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;move&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;rbx&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;lea&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;type&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:20&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Any type that has the same shape as a pointer will be indirect. This includes
maps, channels, and funcs. It also includes one element arrays of such types,
such as &lt;code&gt;[1]*int&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;[1]chan error&lt;/code&gt;, and single-field structs of such types.
Curiously, this does not include structs which contain a zero-sized field before
the pointer-sized field, even though those have the same shape as a pointer.&lt;p&gt;This means it&amp;rsquo;s generally not safe to play games with forging an interface out
of a pointer to some type: whether that type is indirect in an interface is a
subtle implementation detail of the compiler.&lt;p&gt;And of course, it&amp;rsquo;s important to remember that if you want to return a value by
interface, you had best hope it can get inlined, so the compiler can promote the
heap allocation to the stack.&lt;h2 id=function-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#function-pointers&gt;Function Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The last thing to look at are Go&amp;rsquo;s function pointers. For the longest time, I
assumed they had the same layout as an interface: a pointer to closure data, and
a hardware function pointer.&lt;p&gt;It turns out the layout is weirder: let&amp;rsquo;s revisit the &lt;code&gt;runtime.funcval&lt;/code&gt; we found
in &lt;code&gt;runtime2.go&lt;/code&gt; earlier.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:21&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;runtime&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;funcval&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;uintptr&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=c1&gt;// variable-size, fn-specific data here
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:21&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This unusual layout is best understood by looking at the generated assembly.&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:22&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
