&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:27&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because we pass the closure arguments in an extra register not used by regular
functions, we don&amp;rsquo;t need to create a thunk for this case.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, we do need to create a thunk for methods, even methods with a
pointer receiver. This is because of the following incompatible constraints:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The receiver pointer for a method must point exactly to the value the method
is called on. It can&amp;rsquo;t be a fixed offset before, because that would create
an out-of-bounds pointer, which the GC does not tolerate.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The closure pointer must point to the start of the funcval, &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; its
captures, because adjusting the pointer to point to the captures would cause
it to point one-past-the-end of a value, which the GC &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; does not
tolerate!&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Thus, &lt;em&gt;even&lt;/em&gt; if methods accepted a pointer receiver via &lt;code&gt;rdx&lt;/code&gt;, closures and
methods disagree about where that pointer should be passed.&lt;p&gt;Of course, there are adjustments we can make to fix this problem. For example,
we could require that all &lt;code&gt;funcval&lt;/code&gt; values have at least one capture. No-capture
&lt;code&gt;funcvals&lt;/code&gt; would have a synthetic &lt;code&gt;_ byte&lt;/code&gt; field. This is not unlike how a
non-empty struct whose final field is empty will be padded with an extra
&lt;code&gt;_ byte&lt;/code&gt; field: this is specifically to avoid a pointer to that field being a
past-the-end pointer. The cost is that every non-capturing closure costs twice
as much binary size.&lt;p&gt;Another fix is to make the GC blind to the pointer in &lt;code&gt;rdx&lt;/code&gt;. This will never be
the only pointer by which a value is reachable, so it would be safe to replace
&lt;code&gt;mov rdx, rax&lt;/code&gt; with a &lt;code&gt;lea rdx, [rax + 8]&lt;/code&gt;. The GC would never know!&lt;p&gt;Until then, beware that writing &lt;code&gt;return foo.Method&lt;/code&gt; secretly allocates 16 bytes
or so. (Aside: I used to sit next to the Go team at Google, and I remember
having a conversation with Austin Clements about this. Apparently I
misremembered, because until recently I thought Go already implemented this
optimization!)&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;If you made it this far this is probably you right now:&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/stickers/dizzy.png alt=&#34;Sunny, dizzy with register names.&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;This isn&amp;rsquo;t intended to be as polished as most of my articles, but there&amp;rsquo;s been
enough things I&amp;rsquo;ve come across that I wanted to write this all up for my own
reference.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;Sizeof&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;Alignof&lt;/code&gt; are intrinsics, so the compiler will turn them into
constants. However, they are only constants if the type being measured is
not generic, so wrapping them in a function like this doesn&amp;rsquo;t actually hurt
in generic code.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Except for very large types that would have more words than can be recorded
by an array of size
&lt;a href=&#34;https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.23.4:src/internal/abi/type.go;l=803;bpv=0&#34;&gt;&lt;code&gt;abi.MaxPtrmaskBytes&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.
For larger types, we use GC programs! A GC program is an LZ-compressed
bitset serving the same purpose as the pointer bitset most smaller types
use. See
&lt;a href=https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.23.4:src/cmd/internal/gcprog/gcprog.go&gt;gcprog.go&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;In fact, &lt;code&gt;reflection&lt;/code&gt; knows how to create programs on the fly for most
types! See
&lt;a href=&#34;https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.23.4:src/reflect/type.go;l=2658&#34;&gt;reflect/type.go&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;I will be writing assembly examples in Intel-syntax x86. Go&amp;rsquo;s assembly
syntax is horrible and an impediment to the point I&amp;rsquo;m making.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Maybe? Well, the cache will only get updated about 0.1% of the time. This is
to amortize the costs of growing the cache. I assume they benchmarked this,
and found that the cost of growing the cache makes it only worthwhile when
that assertion is getting hammered.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Nobody Gets Fired for Picking JSON, but Maybe They Should?</title>
    <link href="/2024/12/10/json-sucks"/>
    <updated>2024-12-10T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2024/12/10/json-sucks</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;JSON is extremely popular but deeply flawed. This article discusses the
details of JSON’s design, how it’s used (and misused), and how seemingly helpful
“human readability” features cause headaches instead. Crucially, you rarely find
JSON-based tools (except dedicated tools like &lt;code&gt;jq&lt;/code&gt;) that can safely handle
arbitrary JSON documents without a schema—common corner cases can lead to data
corruption!&lt;h2 id=what-is-json&gt;&lt;a href=#what-is-json&gt;What is JSON?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;JSON is famously simple. In fact, you can
&lt;a href=https://www.flickr.com/photos/equanimity/3763158824/in/photostream/&gt;fit the entire grammar on the back of a business card&lt;/a&gt;.
It’s so omnipresent in REST APIs that you might assume you already know JSON
quite well. It has decimal numbers, quoted strings, arrays with square brackets,
and key-value maps (called “objects”) with curly braces. A JSON document
consists of any of these constructs: &lt;code&gt;null&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;42&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;:&#34;bar&#34;}&lt;/code&gt; are all
valid JSON documents.&lt;p&gt;However, the formal definition of JSON is quite complicated. JSON is defined by
the IETF document &lt;a href=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8259&gt;RFC8259&lt;/a&gt; (if
you don’t know what the IETF is, it’s the standards body for Internet
protocols). However, it&amp;rsquo;s &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; normatively defined by
&lt;a href=https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-404/&gt;ECMA-404&lt;/a&gt;,
which is from ECMA, the standards body that defines JavaScript&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;JavaScript? Yes, JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is closely linked with
JavaScript and is, in fact, (almost) a subset of it. While JSON&amp;rsquo;s JavaScript
ancestry is the main source of its quirks, several other poor design decisions
add additional unforced errors.&lt;p&gt;However, the biggest problem with JSON isn’t any specific design decision but
rather the incredible diversity of parser behavior and non-conformance across
and within language ecosystems. RFC8259 goes out of its way to call this out:&lt;blockquote id=ref:1 class=ref ref math&gt;&lt;a href=#ref:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;reference&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Note, however, that ECMA-404 allows several practices that this specification
recommends avoiding in the interests of maximal interoperability.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;The RFC makes many observations regarding interoperability elsewhere in the
document. Probably the most glaring—and terrifying—is how numbers work.&lt;h2 id=everything-is-implementation-defined&gt;&lt;a href=#everything-is-implementation-defined&gt;Everything is Implementation-Defined&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;JSON numbers are encoded in decimal, with an optional minus sign, a fractional
part after a decimal point, and a scientific notation exponent. This is similar
to how many programming languages define their own numeric literals.&lt;p&gt;Presumably, JSON numbers are meant to be floats, right?&lt;p&gt;Wrong.&lt;p&gt;RFC8259 reveals that the answer is, unfortunately, “whatever you want.&#34;&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and
precision of numbers accepted. Since software that implements IEEE 754
binary64 (double precision) numbers is generally available and widely used,
good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more
precision or range than these provide, in the sense that implementations will
approximate JSON numbers within the expected precision.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;binary64&lt;/code&gt; is the &amp;ldquo;standards-ese&amp;rdquo; name for the type usually known as &lt;code&gt;double&lt;/code&gt; or
&lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt;. Floats have great dynamic range but often can’t represent exact
values. For example, &lt;code&gt;1.1&lt;/code&gt; isn&amp;rsquo;t representable as a float because all floats are
fractions of the form &lt;code&gt;n / 2^m&lt;/code&gt; for integers &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;m&lt;/code&gt;, but &lt;code&gt;1.1 = 11/10&lt;/code&gt;,
which has a factor of 5 in its denominator. The closest &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt; value is&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language- highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;2476979795053773 / 2^51 = 1.100000000000000088817841970012523233890533447265625
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course, you might think to declare “all JSON values map to their closest
&lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt; value”. Unfortunately, this value might not be unique. For example,
the value &lt;code&gt;900000000000.00006103515625&lt;/code&gt; isn&amp;rsquo;t representable as a &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt;, and
it&amp;rsquo;s precisely between two exact &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt; values. Depending on the rounding
mode, this rounds to either or &lt;code&gt;900000000000&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;900000000000.0001220703125&lt;/code&gt; .&lt;p&gt;IEEE 754 recommends “round ties to even” as the default rounding mode, so for
almost all software, the result is &lt;code&gt;900000000000&lt;/code&gt;. But remember, floating-point
state is a global variable implemented in hardware, and might just happen to be
clobbered by some dependency that calls &lt;code&gt;fesetround()&lt;/code&gt; or a similar system
function.&lt;h2 id=data-loss-data-loss&gt;&lt;a href=#data-loss-data-loss&gt;Data Loss! Data Loss!&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;You’re probably thinking, “I don’t care about such fussy precision stuff. None
of my numbers have any fractional parts—and there is where you would be wrong.
The &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; part of &lt;code&gt;n / 2^m&lt;/code&gt; only has 53 bits available, but &lt;code&gt;int64&lt;/code&gt; values fall
outside of that range. This means that for very large 64-bit integers, such as
randomly generated IDs, a JSON parser that converts integers into floats results
in &lt;em&gt;data loss.&lt;/em&gt; Go’s &lt;code&gt;encoding/json&lt;/code&gt; package does this, for example.&lt;p&gt;How often does this actually happen for randomly-generated numbers? We can do a
little Monte Carlo simulation to find out.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;package&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kn&gt;import&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;fmt&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;math&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;math/big&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;math/rand&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;trials&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;5_000_000&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;func&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;misses&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;big&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;Float&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;trials&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;		&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;int64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;rand&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Uint64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;())&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;		&lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;int64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;float64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Round-trip through binary64.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;		&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;			&lt;span class=nx&gt;misses&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;			&lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Add&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;big&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;NewFloat&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;math&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Abs&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;float64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;		&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Quo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;big&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;NewFloat&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;trials&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;))&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;fmt&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Printf&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;misses: %d/%d, avg: %f&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;misses&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;trials&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;err&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Output:
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// misses: 4970572/5000000, avg: 170.638499
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;It turns out that almost all randomly distributed &lt;code&gt;int64&lt;/code&gt; values are affected by
round-trip data loss. Roughly, the only numbers that are safe are those with at
most 16 digits (although not exactly: 9,999,999,999,999,999, for example, gets
rounded up to a nice round 10 quadrillion).&lt;p&gt;How does this affect you? Suppose you have a JSON document somewhere that
includes a user ID and a transcript of their private messages with another user.
Data loss due to rounding would result in the wrong user ID being associated
with the private messages, which could result in leaking PII or incorrect
management of privacy consent (such as GDPR requirements).&lt;p&gt;This isn’t just about &lt;em&gt;your&lt;/em&gt; user IDs, mind you. Plenty of other vendors’ IDs
are nice big integers, which the JSON grammar can technically accommodate and
which random tools will mangle. Some examples:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;License keys: for example, Adobe uses 24 digits for
&lt;a href=https://helpx.adobe.com/x-productkb/global/invalid-revoked-serial-numbers.html&gt;their serial numbers&lt;/a&gt;,
which may be tempting to store as an integer.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Barcode IDs like the unique serial numbers of medical devices,
&lt;a href=https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/unique-device-identification-system-udi-system/udi-basics&gt;which are tightly regulated&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Visa and Mastercard credit card numbers &lt;em&gt;happen&lt;/em&gt; to fit in the “safe” range
for &lt;code&gt;binary64&lt;/code&gt; , which may lull you into a false sense of security, since
they’re so common. But not all credit cards have 16 digit numbers:
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_card_number#Structure&gt;some now support 19&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;These are pretty bad compliance consequences purely due to a data serialization
format.&lt;p&gt;This problem is avoidable with care. After all, Go can parse JSON into any
arbitrary type using reflection. For example, if we replace the inner loop of
the Monte Carlo simulation with something like the following:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-go highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;range&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;trials&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;int64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;rand&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Uint64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;())&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=kd&gt;var&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;N&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;json&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Unmarshal&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;([]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;byte&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;fmt&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nf&gt;Sprintf&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;`{&amp;#34;N&amp;#34;:%d}`&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;v&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nx&gt;N&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;	&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nx&gt;y&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;		&lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;	&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Go&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;We suddenly see that &lt;code&gt;x == y&lt;/code&gt; in every trial. This is because with type
information, Go’s JSON library knows exactly what the target precision is. If we
were parsing to an &lt;code&gt;any&lt;/code&gt; instead of to a &lt;code&gt;struct { N int64 }&lt;/code&gt;, we’d be in deep
trouble: the outer object would be parsed into a &lt;code&gt;map[string]any&lt;/code&gt;, and the &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt;
field would become a &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This means that your system probably can’t safely handle JSON documents with
unknown fields. Tools like &lt;code&gt;jq&lt;/code&gt; must be extremely careful about number handling
to avoid data loss. This is an easy mistake for third-party tools to make.&lt;p&gt;But again, &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt; isn&amp;rsquo;t the standard—there is no standard. Some
implementations might only have 32-bit floats available, making the problem
worse. Some implementations might try to be clever, using a &lt;code&gt;float64&lt;/code&gt; for
fractional values and an &lt;code&gt;int64&lt;/code&gt; for integer values; however, this still imposes
arbitrary limits on the parsed values, potentially resulting in data loss.&lt;p&gt;Some implementations such as Python use bignums, so they appear not to have this
problem. However, this can lead to a false sense of security where issues are
not caught until it’s too late: some database now contains ostensibly valid but
non-interoperable JSON.&lt;p&gt;Protobuf is forced to deal with this in a pretty non-portable way. To avoid data
loss, large 64-bit integers are serialized as quoted strings when serializing to
JSON. So, instead of writing &lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;:6574404881820635023}&lt;/code&gt;, it emits
&lt;code&gt;{&#34;foo&#34;:&#34;6574404881820635023&#34;}&lt;/code&gt;. This solves the data loss issue but does not
work with other JSON libraries such as Go’s, producing errors like this one:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language- highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field .N of type int64
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=non-finite-values&gt;&lt;a href=#non-finite-values&gt;Non-Finite Values&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The special floating point values &lt;code&gt;Infinity&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;-Infinity&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;NaN&lt;/code&gt; are not
representable: it’s the wild west as to what happens when you try to serialize
the equivalent of &lt;code&gt;{x:1.0/0.0}&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Go refuses to serialize, citing &lt;code&gt;json: unsupported value: +Inf&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Protobuf serializes it as &lt;code&gt;{&#34;x&#34;:&#34;inf&#34;}&lt;/code&gt; (or should—it’s unclear which
implementations get it right).&lt;li&gt;JavaScript won’t even bother trying: &lt;code&gt;JSON.stringify({x:Infinity})&lt;/code&gt; prints
&lt;code&gt;{&#34;x&#34;:null}.&lt;/code&gt;&lt;li&gt;Python is arguably the worst offender: &lt;code&gt;json.dumps({&#34;x&#34;:float(&#34;inf&#34;)})&lt;/code&gt; prints
&lt;code&gt;{&#34;x&#34;:Infinity}&lt;/code&gt;, which isn’t even valid JSON per RFC8259.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;NaN is arguably an even worse offender, because the NaN payload (yes,
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f32.html#nan-bit-patterns&gt;NaNs have a special payload&lt;/a&gt;)
is discarded when converting to &lt;code&gt;&#34;nan&#34;&lt;/code&gt; or however your library represents it.&lt;p&gt;Does this affect you? Well, if you’re doing anything with floats, you’re one
division-by-zero or overflow away from triggering serialization errors. At best,
it’s “benign” data corruption (JavaScript). At worst, when the data is partially
user-controlled, it might result in crashes or unparseable output, which is the
making of a DoS vector.&lt;p&gt;In comparison, Protobuf serialization can’t fail except due to non-UTF-8
&lt;code&gt;string&lt;/code&gt; fields or cyclic message references, both of which are comparatively
unlikely to a NaN popping up in a calculation.&lt;p&gt;The upshot is that all the parsers end up parsing a bunch of crazy things for
the special floating-point values over time because of
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robustness_principle&gt;Postel’s law&lt;/a&gt;. RFC8259
makes no effort to provide suggestions for dealing with such real-world
situations beyond “tough luck, not interoperable.”&lt;h2 id=text-encodings-and-invalid-unicode&gt;&lt;a href=#text-encodings-and-invalid-unicode&gt;Text Encodings and Invalid Unicode&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;JSON strings are relatively tame, with some marked (but good) divergence from
JavaScript. Specifically, JavaScript, being a language of a certain age (along
with Java), uses UTF-16 as its Unicode text encoding. Most of the world has
realized this is a bad idea (it doubles the size of ASCII text, which makes up
almost all of Internet traffic), so JSON uses UTF-8 instead. RFC8259 actually
specifies that the whole document MUST be encoded in UTF-8.&lt;p&gt;But when we go to read about Unicode characters in §8.2, we are disappointed: it
merely says that it’s &lt;em&gt;really great&lt;/em&gt; when all quoted strings consist entirely of
Unicode characters, which means that unpaired surrogates are allowed. In effect,
the spec merely requires that JSON strings be
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8#Surrogates&gt;WTF-8&lt;/a&gt;: UTF-8 that permits
unpaired surrogates.&lt;p&gt;What’s an unpaired surrogate? It’s any encoded Unicode 32-bit value in the range
&lt;code&gt;U+D800&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;U+DFFF&lt;/code&gt; , which form a gap in the Unicode codepoint range. UTF-8’s
variable-length integer encoding can encode them, but their presence in a
bytestream makes it invalid UTF-8. WTF-8 is UTF-8 but permitting the appearance
of these values.&lt;p&gt;So, who actually supports parsing (or serializing) these? Consider the document
&lt;code&gt;{&#34;x&#34;:&#34;\udead&#34;}&lt;/code&gt;, which contains an unpaired surrogate, &lt;code&gt;U+DEAD&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Go gladly deserializes AND serializes it (Go’s strings are arbitrary byte
strings, not UTF-8). However, Go serializes a non-UTF-8 string such as
&lt;code&gt;&#34;\xff&#34;&lt;/code&gt; as &lt;code&gt;&#34;\ufffd&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, having replaced the invalid byte with a &lt;code&gt;U+FFFD&lt;/code&gt;
replacement character (this thing: �).&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Most Java parsers seem to follow the same behavior as Go, but there are many
different parsers available, and we’ve already learned that different JSON
parsers may behave differently.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;JavaScript and Python similarly gladly parse unpaired surrogates, but they
also serialize them back without converting them into &lt;code&gt;U+FFFD&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Different Protobuf runtimes may not handle this identically, but the reference
C++ implementation (whose JSON codec I wrote!) refuses to parse unpaired surrogates.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are other surprising pitfalls around strings: are &lt;code&gt;&#34;x&#34;&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;“\x78&#34;&lt;/code&gt; the
same string? RFC8259 feels the need to call out that they are, for the purposes
of checking that object keys are equal. The fact that they feel the need to call
it out indicates that this is also a source of potential problems.&lt;h2 id=byte-strings&gt;&lt;a href=#byte-strings&gt;Byte Strings&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;What if I don’t want to send text? A common type of byte blob to send is a
cryptographic hash that identifies a document in a content-addressed blobstore,
or perhaps a digital signature (an encrypted hash). JSON has no native way of
representing byte strings.&lt;p&gt;You could send a quoted string full of ASCII and &lt;code&gt;\xNN&lt;/code&gt; escapes (for bytes which
are not in the ASCII range), but this is wasteful in terms of bandwidth, and has
serious interoperability problems (as noted above, Go actively destroys data in
this case). You could also encode it as an array of JSON numbers, which is much
worse for bandwidth and serialization speed.&lt;p&gt;What everyone winds up doing, one way or another, is to rely on base64 encoding.
Protobuf, for example, encodes &lt;code&gt;bytes&lt;/code&gt; fields into base64 strings in JSON. This
has the unfortunate side-effect of defeating JSON’s human-readable property: if
the blob contains mostly ASCII, a human reader can’t tell.&lt;p&gt;Because this isn&amp;rsquo;t part of JSON, virtually no JSON codec does this decoding for
you, particularly because in a schema-less context, there’s nothing to
distinguish a byte blob encoded with base64 from an actual textual string that
&lt;em&gt;happens&lt;/em&gt; to contain valid base64, such as an alphanumeric username.&lt;p&gt;Compared to other problems, this is more like a paper cut, but it’s unnecessary
and adds complexity and interop problems.
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base64#Variants_summary_table&gt;By the way, did you know there are multiple incompatible Base64 alphabets?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;h1 id=streaming-doesnt-work&gt;&lt;a href=#streaming-doesnt-work&gt;Streaming Doesn&amp;rsquo;t Work&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;A less obvious problem with JSON is that it can’t be streamed. Almost all JSON
documents are objects or arrays and are therefore &lt;em&gt;incomplete&lt;/em&gt; until they reach
the closing &lt;code&gt;}&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;]&lt;/code&gt;, respectively. This means you can’t send a stream of JSON
documents that form a part of a larger document without some additional protocol
for combining them in post-processing.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://jsonlines.org/&gt;JSONL&lt;/a&gt; is the world’s silliest spec that &amp;ldquo;solves&amp;rdquo; this
problem in the simplest way possible: a JSONL document is a sequence of JSON
documents separated by newlines. JSONL &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; streamable, but because it&amp;rsquo;s done in
the simplest way possible, it only supports streaming a giant array. You can&amp;rsquo;t,
for example, stream an object field-by-field or stream an array within that
object.&lt;p&gt;Protobuf doesn’t have this problem: in a nutshell, the Protobuf wire format is
as if we removed the braces and brackets from the top-level array or object of a
document, and made it so that values with the same key get merged. In the wire
format, the equivalent of the JSONL document&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-json highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;foo&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;x&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;},&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;bar&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;6&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;foo&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;y&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;},&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;bar&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;7&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;JSON&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;is automatically “merged” into the single document&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-json highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;foo&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;x&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;y&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;},&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nt&gt;&amp;#34;bar&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;6&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;JSON&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This forms the basis of the “message merge” operation, which is intimately
connected to how the wire format was designed. We’ll dive into this fundamental
operation in a future article.&lt;h1 id=canonicalization-leads-to-data-loss&gt;&lt;a href=#canonicalization-leads-to-data-loss&gt;Canonicalization Leads to Data Loss&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Thanks to &lt;a href=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519&gt;RFC7519&lt;/a&gt; and
&lt;a href=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515&gt;RFC7515&lt;/a&gt;, which define JSON Web
Tokens (JWT) and JSON Web Signatures (JWS), digitally signing JSON documents is
a very common operation. However, digital signatures can only sign specific byte
blobs and are sensitive to things that JSON isn&amp;rsquo;t, such as whitespace and key
ordering.&lt;p&gt;This results in specifications like
&lt;a href=https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8785&gt;RFC8785&lt;/a&gt; for &lt;em&gt;canonicalization&lt;/em&gt;
of JSON documents. This introduces a new avenue by which existing JSON
documents, which accidentally happen to contain non-interoperable (or, thanks to
non-conforming implementations such as Python’s) invalid JSON that must be
manipulated and reformatted by third-party tools. RFC8785 itself references
ECMA-262 (the JavaScript standard) for how to serialize numbers, meaning that
it’s &lt;em&gt;required&lt;/em&gt; to induce data loss for 64-bit numerical values!&lt;h1 id=is-json-fixable&gt;&lt;a href=#is-json-fixable&gt;Is JSON Fixable?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Plainly? No. JSON can’t be fixed because of how extremely popular it is. Common
mistakes are baked into the format. Are comments allowed? Trailing commas?
Number formats? Nobody knows!&lt;p&gt;What tools are touching your JSON? Are they aware of all of the rakes they can
step on? Do they emit invalid JSON (like Python does)? How do you even begin to
audit that?&lt;p&gt;Thankfully, you don’t have to use JSON. There are alternatives—BSON, UBJSON,
MessagePack, and CBOR are just a few binary formats that try to replicate JSON’s
data model. Unfortunately, many of them have their own problems.&lt;p&gt;Protobuf, however, has none of these problems, because it was &lt;em&gt;designed&lt;/em&gt; to
fulfill needs JSON couldn&amp;rsquo;t meet. Using a strongly-typed schema system, like
Protobuf, makes all of these problems go away.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course, some wise guy will probably want to cite &amp;lt;json.org&gt;. I should
underscore: &amp;lt;json.org&gt; is &lt;strong&gt;NOT&lt;/strong&gt; a standard. It is &lt;strong&gt;NOT&lt;/strong&gt; normative.
the documents produced by the IETF and by ECMA, which are international
standards organizations that represent the industry &lt;strong&gt;ARE&lt;/strong&gt; normative. When
a browser implementer wants to implement JSON to the letter, they go to
ECMA, not to some dude&amp;rsquo;s 90&amp;rsquo;s ass website.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>The Rust Calling Convention We Deserve</title>
    <link href="/2024/04/17/calling-convention"/>
    <updated>2024-04-17T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2024/04/17/calling-convention</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I will often say that the so-called &amp;ldquo;C ABI&amp;rdquo; is a very bad one, and a relatively
unimaginative one when it comes to passing complicated types effectively. A lot
of people ask me &amp;ldquo;ok, what would you use instead&amp;rdquo;, and I just point them to the
&lt;a href=https://go.googlesource.com/go/+/refs/heads/dev.regabi/src/cmd/compile/internal-abi.md&gt;Go register ABI&lt;/a&gt;,
but it seems most people have trouble filling in the gaps of what I mean. This
article explains what I mean in detail.&lt;p&gt;I have discussed
&lt;a href=/2021/11/29/assembly-1#the-calling-convention&gt;calling conventions&lt;/a&gt;
in the past, but as a reminder: the &lt;em&gt;calling convention&lt;/em&gt; is the part of the ABI
that concerns itself with how to pass arguments to and from a function, and how
to actually call a function. This includes which registers arguments go in,
which registers values are returned out of, what function prologues/epilogues
look like, how unwinding works, etc.&lt;p&gt;This particular post is primarily about x86, but I intend to be reasonably
generic (so that what I&amp;rsquo;ve written applies just as well to ARM, RISC-V, etc). I
will assume a general familiarity with x86 assembly, LLVM IR, and Rust (but not
rustc&amp;rsquo;s internals).&lt;h2 id=the-problem&gt;&lt;a href=#the-problem&gt;The Problem&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Today, like many other natively compiled languages, Rust defines an
unspecified0- calling convention that lets it call functions however it likes.
In practice, Rust lowers to LLVM&amp;rsquo;s built-in C calling convention, which LLVM&amp;rsquo;s
prologue/epilogue codegen generates calls for.&lt;p&gt;Rust is fairly conservative: it tries to generate LLVM function signatures that
Clang could have plausibly generated. This has two significant benefits:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Good probability debuggers won&amp;rsquo;t choke on it. This is not a concern on Linux,
though, because DWARF is very general and does not bake-in the Linux C ABI.
We will concern ourselves only with ELF-based systems and assume that
debuggability is a nonissue.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;It is less likely to tickle LLVM bugs due to using ABI codegen that Clang
does not exercise. I think that if Rust tickles LLVM bugs, we should actually
fix them (a very small number of rustc contributors do in fact do this).&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;However, we are too conservative. We get terrible codegen for simple functions:&lt;div class=code-multicol markdown=1&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;extract&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;arr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;])&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;arr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-x86 highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;extract&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mov&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;eax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;dword&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rdi&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;arr&lt;/code&gt; is 12 bytes wide, so you&amp;rsquo;d think it would be passed in registers, but no!
It is passed by pointer! Rust is actually &lt;em&gt;more&lt;/em&gt; conservative than what the
Linux C ABI mandates, because it actually passes the &lt;code&gt;[i32; 3]&lt;/code&gt; in registers
when &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;C&#34;&lt;/code&gt; is requested.&lt;div class=code-multicol markdown=1&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;C&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;extract&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;arr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;])&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;arr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-x86 highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;extract&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mov&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rdi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;shr&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;32&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The array is passed in &lt;code&gt;rdi&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;rsi&lt;/code&gt;, with the &lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt;s packed into registers.
The function moves &lt;code&gt;rdi&lt;/code&gt; into &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt;, the output register, and shifts the upper
half down.&lt;p&gt;Not only does clang produce patently &lt;em&gt;bad&lt;/em&gt; code for passing things by value, but
it also knows how to do it better, if you request a standard calling convention!
We could be generating &lt;em&gt;way&lt;/em&gt; better code than Clang, but we don&amp;rsquo;t!&lt;p&gt;Hereforth, I will describe how to do it.&lt;h3 id=-zcallconv&gt;&lt;a href=#-zcallconv&gt;&lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s suppose that we keep the current calling convention for
&lt;code&gt;extern &#34;Rust&#34;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, but we add a flag &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv&lt;/code&gt; that sets
the calling convention for &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;Rust&#34;&lt;/code&gt; when compiling a crate. The supported
values will be &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=legacy&lt;/code&gt; for the current one, and &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=fast&lt;/code&gt;
for the one we&amp;rsquo;re going to design. We could even let &lt;code&gt;-O&lt;/code&gt; set &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=fast&lt;/code&gt;
automatically.&lt;p&gt;Why keep the old calling convention? Although I did sweep debugability under the
rug, one nice property &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=fast&lt;/code&gt; will not have is that it does not place
arguments in the C ABI order, which means that a reader replying on the &amp;ldquo;Diana&amp;rsquo;s
silk dress cost $89&amp;rdquo; mnemonic on x86 will get fairly confused.&lt;p&gt;I am also assuming we may not even support &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=fast&lt;/code&gt; for some targets,
like WASM, where there is no concept of &amp;ldquo;registers&amp;rdquo; and &amp;ldquo;spilling&amp;rdquo;. It may not
even make sense to enable it for for debug builds, because it will produce much
worse code with optimizations turned off.&lt;p&gt;There is also a mild wrinkle with function pointers, and &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;Rust&#34; {}&lt;/code&gt;
blocks. Because this flag is per-crate, even though functions can advertise
which version of &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;Rust&#34;&lt;/code&gt; they use, function pointers have no such
luxury. However, calling through a function pointer is slow and rare, so we can
simply force them to use &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=legacy&lt;/code&gt;. We can generate a shim to
translate calling conventions as needed.&lt;p&gt;Similarly, we can, in principle, call any Rust function like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;secret_call&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;Rust&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;my_func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;However, this mechanism can only be used to call unmangled symbols. Thus, we can
simply force &lt;code&gt;#[no_mangle]&lt;/code&gt; symbols to use the legacy calling convention.&lt;h2 id=bending-llvm-to-our-will&gt;&lt;a href=#bending-llvm-to-our-will&gt;Bending LLVM to Our Will&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;In an ideal world, LLVM would provide a way for us to specify the calling
convention directly. E.g., this argument goes in that register, this return goes
in that one, etc. Unfortunately, adding a calling convention to LLVM requires
writing a bunch of C++.&lt;p&gt;However, we can get away with specifying our own calling convention by following
the following procedure.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;First, determine, for a given target triple, the maximum number of values
that can be passed &amp;ldquo;by register&amp;rdquo;. I will explain how to do this below.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Decide how to pass the return value. It will either fit in the output
registers, or it will need to be returned &amp;ldquo;by reference&amp;rdquo;, in which case we
pass an extra &lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt; argument to the function (tagged with the &lt;code&gt;sret&lt;/code&gt;
attribute) and the actual return value of the function is that pointer.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Decide which arguments that have been passed by value need to be demoted to
being passed by reference. This will be a heuristic, but generally will be
approximately &amp;ldquo;arguments larger than the by-register space&amp;rdquo;. For example, on
x86, this comes out to 176 bytes.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Decide which arguments get passed by register, so as to maximize register
space usage. This problem is NP-hard (it&amp;rsquo;s the knapsack problem) so it will
require a heuristic. All other arguments are passed on the stack.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Generate the function signature in LLVM IR. This will be all of the arguments
that are passed by register encoded as various non-aggregates, such as &lt;code&gt;i64&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;double&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;2 x i64&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. What valid choices are for said
non-aggregates depends on the target, but the above are what you will
generally get on a 64-bit architecture. Arguments passed on the stack will
follow the &amp;ldquo;register inputs&amp;rdquo;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Generate a function prologue. This is code to decode each Rust-level argument
from the register inputs, so that there are &lt;code&gt;%ssa&lt;/code&gt; values corresponding to
those that would be present when using &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=legacy&lt;/code&gt;. This allows us to
generate the same code for the body of the function regardless of calling
convention. Redundant decoding code will be eliminated by DCE passes.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Generate a function exit block. This is a block that contains a single &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;
instruction for the return type as it would be for &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=legacy&lt;/code&gt;. This
block will encode it into the requisite output format and then &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt; as
appropriate. All exit paths through the function should &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; to this block
instead of &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt;-ing.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;If a non-polymorphic, non-inline function may have its address taken (as a
function pointer), either because it is exported out of the crate or the
crate takes a function pointer to it, generate a shim that uses
&lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=legacy&lt;/code&gt; and immediately tail-calls the real implementation. This
is necessary to preserve function pointer equality.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The main upshot here is that we need to cook up heuristics for figuring out what
goes in registers (since we allow reordering arguments to get better
throughput). This is equivalent to the knapsack problem; knapsack heuristics are
beyond the scope of this article. This should happen early enough that this
information can be stuffed into &lt;code&gt;rmeta&lt;/code&gt; to avoid needing to recompute it. We may
want to use different, faster heuristics depending on &lt;code&gt;-Copt-level&lt;/code&gt;. Note that
correctness requires that we forbid linking code generated by multiple different
Rust compilers, which is already the case, since Rust breaks ABI from release to
release.&lt;h3 id=what-is-llvm-willing-to-do&gt;&lt;a href=#what-is-llvm-willing-to-do&gt;What Is LLVM Willing to Do?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Assuming we do that, how do we actually get LLVM to pass things in the way we
want it to? We need to determine what the largest &amp;ldquo;by register&amp;rdquo; passing LLVM
will permit is. The following LLVM program is useful for determining this on a
particular version of LLVM:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputI&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;6&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputF&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;double&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputV&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;8&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%OutputI&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;3&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%OutputV&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;4&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@inputs&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;({&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputI&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputF&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputV&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;})&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;alloca&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;4096&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;store&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;volatile&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputI&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputF&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%InputV&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%p&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;When you pass an aggregate by-value to an LLVM function, LLVM will attempt to
&amp;ldquo;explode&amp;rdquo; that aggregate into as many registers as possible. There are distinct
register classes on different systems. For example, on both x86 and ARM, floats
and vectors share the same register class (kind of&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;).&lt;p&gt;The above values are for x86&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. LLVM will pass six integers and
eight SSE vectors by register, and return half as many (3 and 4) by register.
Increasing any of the values generates extra loads and stores that indicate LLVM
gave up and passed arguments on the stack.&lt;p&gt;The values for &lt;code&gt;aarch64-unknown-linux&lt;/code&gt; are 8 integers and 8 vectors for both
inputs and outputs, respectively.&lt;p&gt;This is the maximum number of registers we get to play with for each class.
Anything extra gets passed on the stack.&lt;p&gt;I recommend that &lt;em&gt;every function&lt;/em&gt; have the same number of by-register arguments.

bytes!&amp;rdquo; And you&amp;rsquo;d be right, if not for the magic of LLVM&amp;rsquo;s very well-specified
&lt;code&gt;poison&lt;/code&gt; semantics.&lt;p&gt;We can get away with not doing extra work if every argument we do not use is
passed &lt;code&gt;poison&lt;/code&gt;. Because &lt;code&gt;poison&lt;/code&gt; is equal to &amp;ldquo;the most convenient possible

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:9&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;It is perfectly legal to pass poison to a function, if it does not interact with
the poisoned argument in any proscribed way. And as we see, &lt;code&gt;load_rcx()&lt;/code&gt;
receives its pointer argument in &lt;code&gt;rcx&lt;/code&gt;, whereas &lt;code&gt;make_the_call()&lt;/code&gt; takes no
penalty in setting up the call: loading poison into the other thirteen registers
compiles down to nothing&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, so it only needs to load the pointer
returned by malloc into &lt;code&gt;rcx&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This gives us almost total control over argument passing; unfortunately, it is
not total. In an ideal world, the same registers are used for input and output,
to allow easier pipelining of calls without introducing extra register traffic.
This is true on ARM and RISC-V, but not x86. However, because register ordering
is merely a suggestion for us, we can choose to allocate the return registers in
whatever order we want. For example, we can pretend the order registers should
be allocated in is &lt;code&gt;rdx&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;rcx&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;rdi&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;rsi&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;r8&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;r9&lt;/code&gt; for inputs, and &lt;code&gt;rdx&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;rcx&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt; for outputs.&lt;div class=code-multicol markdown=1&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:10&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%Out&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;3&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;4&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;&amp;gt;]}&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;square&lt;/code&gt; generates extremely simple code: the input and output register is

effectively do &lt;code&gt;@square(@square(%0))&lt;/code&gt;, there is no setup between the functions.
This is similar to code seen on aarch64, which uses the same register sequence
for input and output. We can see that the &amp;ldquo;naive&amp;rdquo; version of this IR produces
the exact same code on aarch64 for this reason.&lt;div class=code-multicol markdown=1&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mul&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;make_the_call&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;str&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x30&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;#&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;bl&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ldr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x30&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;#&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Tail call.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;ARM Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=rust-structs-and-unions&gt;&lt;a href=#rust-structs-and-unions&gt;Rust Structs and Unions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that we&amp;rsquo;ve established total control on how registers are assigned, we can
turn towards maximizing use of these registers in Rust.&lt;p&gt;For simplicity, we can assume that rustc has already processed the users&amp;rsquo;s types
into basic aggregates and unions; no enums here! We then have to make some
decisions about which portions of the arguments to allocate to registers.&lt;p&gt;First, return values. This is relatively straightforward, since there is only
one value to pass. The amount of data we need to return is &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; the size of the
struct. For example, &lt;code&gt;[(u64, u32); 2]&lt;/code&gt; measures 32 bytes wide. However, eight of
those bytes are padding! We do not need to preserve padding when returning by
value, so we can flatten the struct into &lt;code&gt;(u64, u32, u64, u32)&lt;/code&gt; and sort by size
into &lt;code&gt;(u64, u64, u32, u32)&lt;/code&gt;. This has no padding and is 24 bytes wide, which
fits into the three return registers LLVM gives us on x86. We define the
&lt;em&gt;effective size&lt;/em&gt; of a type to be the number of non-&lt;code&gt;undef&lt;/code&gt; bits it occupies. For
&lt;code&gt;[(u64, u32); 2]&lt;/code&gt;, this is 192 bits, since it excludes the padding. For &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt;,
this is one. For &lt;code&gt;char&lt;/code&gt; this is technically 21, but it&amp;rsquo;s simpler to treat &lt;code&gt;char&lt;/code&gt;
as an alias for &lt;code&gt;u32&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The reason for counting bits this way is that it permits significant compaction.
For example, returning a struct full of bools can simply bit-pack the bools into
a single register.&lt;p&gt;So, a return value is converted to a by-ref return if its effective size is
smaller than the output register space (on x86, this is three integer registers
and four SSE registers, so we get 88 bytes total, or 704 bits).&lt;p&gt;Argument registers are much harder, because we hit the
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knapsack_problem&gt;knapsack problem&lt;/a&gt;, which is
NP-hard. The following relatively naive heuristic is where I would start, but it
can be made infinitely smarter over time.&lt;p&gt;First, demote to by-ref any argument whose effective size is larget than the
total by-register input space (on x86, 176 bytes or 1408 bits). This means we
get a pointer argument instead. This is beneficial to do first, since a single
pointer might pack better than the huge struct.&lt;p&gt;Enums should be replaced by the appropriate discriminant-union pair. For
example, &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;i32&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is, internally, &lt;code&gt;(union { i32, () }, i1)&lt;/code&gt;, while
&lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;Option&amp;lt;i32&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;(union { i32, (), () }, i2)&lt;/code&gt;. Using a small
non-power-of-two integer improves our ability to pack things, since enum
discriminants are often quite tiny.&lt;p&gt;Next, we need to handle unions. Because mucking about with unions&amp;rsquo; uninitialized
bits behind our backs is allowed, we need to either pass it as an array of &lt;code&gt;u8&lt;/code&gt;,
unless it only has a single non-empty variant, in which case it is replaced with
that variant&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Now, we can proceed to flatten everything. All of the converted arguments are
flattened into their most primitive components: pointers, integers, floats, and
bools. Every field should be no larger than the smallest argument register; this
may require splitting large types such as &lt;code&gt;u128&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;f64&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This big list of primitives is next sorted by effective size, from smallest to
largest. We take the largest prefix of this that will fit in the available
register space; everything else goes on the stack.&lt;p&gt;If part of a Rust-level input is sent to the stack in this way, and that part is
larger than a small multiple of the pointer size (e.g., 2x), it is demoted to
being passed by pointer-on-the-stack, to minimize memory traffic. Everything
else is passed directly on the stack in the order those inputs were before the
sort. This helps keep regions that need to be copied relatively contiguous, to
minimize calls to &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The things we choose to pass in registers are allocated to registers in reverse
size order, so e.g. first 64-bit things, then 32-bit things, etc. This is the
same layout algorithm that &lt;code&gt;repr(Rust)&lt;/code&gt; structs use to move all the padding into
the tail. Once we get to the &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt;s, those are bit-packed, 64 to a register.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s a relatively complicated example.
