&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c&gt;; Codegen as usual.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c&gt;; ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Above, &lt;code&gt;!dbg&lt;/code&gt; metadata for the argument values should be attached to the
instruction that actually materializes it. This ensures that gdb does something
halfway intelligent when you ask it to print argument values.&lt;p&gt;On the other hand, in current rustc, it gives LLVM eight pointer-sized
parameters, so it winds up spending all six integer registers, plus two values
passed on the stack. Not great!&lt;p&gt;This is not a complete description of what a completely over-engineered calling
convention could entail: in some cases we might know that we have additional
registers available (such as AVX registers on x86). There are cases where we
might want to split a struct across registers and the stack.&lt;p&gt;This also isn&amp;rsquo;t even getting into what returns &lt;em&gt;could&lt;/em&gt; look like. &lt;code&gt;Result&lt;/code&gt;s are
often passed through several layers of functions via &lt;code&gt;?&lt;/code&gt;, which can result in a
lot of redundant register moves. Often, a &lt;code&gt;Result&lt;/code&gt; is large enough that it
doesn&amp;rsquo;t fit in registers, so each call in the &lt;code&gt;?&lt;/code&gt; stack has to inspect an ok bit
by loading it from memory. Instead, a &lt;code&gt;Result&lt;/code&gt; return might be implemented as an
out-parameter pointer for the error, with the ok variant&amp;rsquo;s payload, and the is
ok bit, returned as an &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. There are some fussy details with &lt;code&gt;Into&lt;/code&gt;
calls via &lt;code&gt;?&lt;/code&gt;, but the idea is implementable.&lt;h3 id=optimization-dependent-abi&gt;&lt;a href=#optimization-dependent-abi&gt;Optimization-Dependent ABI&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, because we&amp;rsquo;re Rust, we&amp;rsquo;ve also got a trick up our sleeve that C doesn&amp;rsquo;t
(but Go does)! When we&amp;rsquo;re generating the ABI that all callers will see (for
&lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv=fast&lt;/code&gt;), we can look at the function body. This means that a crate
can advertise the &lt;em&gt;precise&lt;/em&gt; ABI (in terms of register-passing) of its functions.&lt;p&gt;This opens the door to a more extreme optimization-based ABIs. We can start by
simply throwing out unused arguments: if the function never does anything with a
parameter, don&amp;rsquo;t bother spending registers on it.&lt;p&gt;Another example: suppose that we know that an &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; argument is not retained (a
question the borrow checker can answer at this point in the compiler) and is
never converted to a raw pointer (or written to memory a raw pointer is taken
of, etc). We also know that &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; is fairly small, and &lt;code&gt;T: Freeze&lt;/code&gt;. Then, we can
replace the reference with the pointee directly, passed by value.&lt;p&gt;The most obvious candidates for this is APIs like &lt;code&gt;HashMap::get()&lt;/code&gt;. If the key
is something like an &lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt;, we need to spill that integer to the stack and pass
a pointer to it! This results in unnecessary, avoidable memory traffic.&lt;p&gt;Profile-guided ABI is a step further. We might know that some arguments are
hotter than others, which might cause them to be prioritized in the register
allocation order.&lt;p&gt;You could even imagine a case where a function takes a very large struct by
reference, but three &lt;code&gt;i64&lt;/code&gt; fields are very hot, so the caller can &lt;em&gt;preload&lt;/em&gt;
those fields, passing them both by register &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; via the pointer to the large
struct. The callee does not see additional cost: it had to issue those loads
anyway. However, the caller probably has those values in registers already,
which avoids some memory traffic.&lt;p&gt;Instrumentation profiles may even indicate that it makes sense to duplicate
whole functions, which are identical except for their ABIs. Maybe they take
different arguments by register to avoid costly spills.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a bit more advanced (and ranty) than my usual writing, but this is an
aspect of Rust that I find really frustrating. We could be doing &lt;em&gt;so much
better&lt;/em&gt; than C++ ever can (because of their ABI constraints). None of this is
new ideas; this is &lt;em&gt;literally&lt;/em&gt; how Go does it!&lt;p&gt;So why don&amp;rsquo;t we? Part of the reason is that ABI codegen is complex, and as I
described above, LLVM gives us very few useful knobs. It&amp;rsquo;s not a friendly part
of rustc, and doing things wrong can have nasty consequences for usability. The
other part is a lack of expertise. As of writing, only a handful of people
contributing to rustc have the necessary grasp of LLVM&amp;rsquo;s semantics (and mood
swings) to emit the Right Code such that we get good codegen and don&amp;rsquo;t crash
LLVM.&lt;p&gt;Another reason is compilation time. The more complicated the function
signatures, the more prologue/epilogue code we have to generate that LLVM has to
chew on. But &lt;code&gt;-Zcallconv&lt;/code&gt; is intended to only be used with optimizations turned
on, so I don&amp;rsquo;t think this is a meaningful complaint. Nor do I think the
project&amp;rsquo;s Goodhartization of compilation time as a metric is healthy&amp;mldr; but I do
not think this is ultimately a relevant drawback.&lt;p&gt;I, unfortunately, do not have the spare time to dive into fixing rustc&amp;rsquo;s ABI
code, but I do know LLVM really well, and I know that this is a place where Rust
has a low bus factor. For that reason, I am happy to provide the Rust compiler
team expert knowledge on getting LLVM to do the right thing in service of making
optimized code faster.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Or just switch it to the codepath for &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;C&#34;&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;fastcall&#34;&lt;/code&gt;
since those are clearly better. We will always need to know how to generate
code for the non-&lt;code&gt;extern &#34;Rust&#34;&lt;/code&gt; calling conventions.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s Complicated. Passing a &lt;code&gt;double&lt;/code&gt; burns a whole &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;2 x i64&gt;&lt;/code&gt; slot. This
seems bad, but it can be beneficial since keeping a &lt;code&gt;double&lt;/code&gt; in vector
registers reduces register traffic, since usually, fp instructions use the
vector registers (or the fp registers shadow the vector registers, like on
ARM).&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;On the one hand, you might say this &amp;ldquo;extended calling convention&amp;rdquo; isn&amp;rsquo;t an
explicitly supported part of LLVM&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;ccc&lt;/code&gt; calling convention. On the other
hand, &lt;a href=hyrumslaw.com&gt;Hyrum&amp;rsquo;s Law&lt;/a&gt; cuts both ways: Rust is big enough of an
LLVM user that LLVM cannot simply miscompile all Rust programs at this
point, and the IR I propose Rust emits is extremely reasonable.&lt;p&gt;If Rust causes LLVM to misbehave, that&amp;rsquo;s an LLVM bug, and we should fix
LLVM bugs, not work around them.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Only on &lt;code&gt;-O1&lt;/code&gt; or higher, bizarrely. At &lt;code&gt;-O0&lt;/code&gt;, LLVM decides that all of the
&lt;code&gt;poison&lt;/code&gt;s must have the same value, so it copies a bunch of registers around
needlessly. This seems like a bug?&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are other cases where we might want to replace a union with one of its
variants: for example, there&amp;rsquo;s a lot of cases where &lt;code&gt;Result&amp;lt;&amp;amp;T, Error&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is
secretly a &lt;code&gt;union { ptr, u32 }&lt;/code&gt;, in which case it should be replaced with a
single &lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Designing a SIMD Algorithm from Scratch</title>
    <link href="/2023/11/27/simd-base64"/>
    <updated>2023-11-27T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2023/11/27/simd-base64</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Another explainer on a fun, esoteric topic: optimizing code with SIMD (single
instruction multiple data, also sometimes called &lt;em&gt;vectorization&lt;/em&gt;). Designing a
good, fast, portable SIMD algorithm is not a simple matter and requires thinking
a little bit like a circuit designer.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s the mandatory performance benchmark graph to catch your eye.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/graph.png alt=&#34;perf perf perf&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;SIMD&amp;rdquo; often gets thrown around as a buzzword by performance and HPC (high
performance computing) nerds, but I don&amp;rsquo;t think it&amp;rsquo;s a topic that has very
friendly introductions out there, for a lot of reasons.&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s not something you will really want to care about unless you think
performance is cool.&lt;li&gt;APIs for programming with SIMD in most programming languages are &lt;em&gt;garbage&lt;/em&gt;
(I&amp;rsquo;ll get into why).&lt;li&gt;SIMD algorithms are hard to think about if you&amp;rsquo;re very
procedural-programming-brained. A functional programming mindset can help a
lot.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;This post is mostly about &lt;a href=https://docs.rs/vb64/latest/vb64/&gt;&lt;code&gt;vb64&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; (which
stands for &lt;em&gt;v&lt;/em&gt;ector &lt;em&gt;b&lt;/em&gt;ase&lt;em&gt;64&lt;/em&gt;), a base64 codec I wrote to see for myself if
Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;std::simd&lt;/code&gt; library is any good, but it&amp;rsquo;s also an excuse to talk about
SIMD in general.&lt;p&gt;What &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; SIMD, anyways? Let&amp;rsquo;s dive in.&lt;p&gt;If you want to skip straight to the writeup on &lt;code&gt;vb64&lt;/code&gt;, click
&lt;a href=#parsing-with-simd&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;h2 id=problems-with-physics&gt;&lt;a href=#problems-with-physics&gt;Problems with Physics&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, computers exist in the real world&lt;sup&gt;[citation-needed]&lt;/sup&gt;,
and are bound by the laws of nature. SIMD has relatively little to do with
theoretical CS considerations, and everything to do with &lt;em&gt;physics&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;In the infancy of modern computing, you could simply improve performance of
existing programs by buying new computers. This is often incorrectly attributed
to Moore&amp;rsquo;s law (the number of transistors on IC designs doubles every two
years). Moore&amp;rsquo;s law still appears to hold as of 2023, but some time in the last
15 years the &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling&gt;Dennard scaling&lt;/a&gt;
effect broke down. This means that denser transistors eventually means increased
power dissipation density. In simpler terms, we don&amp;rsquo;t know how to continue to
increase the clock frequency of computers without literally &lt;em&gt;liquefying&lt;/em&gt; them.&lt;p&gt;So, since the early aughts, the hot new thing has been bigger core counts. Make
your program more multi-threaded and it will run faster on bigger CPUs. This
comes with synchronization overhead, since now the cores need to cooperate. All
control flow, be it jumps, virtual calls, or synchronization will result in
&amp;ldquo;stall&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;The main causes of stall are &lt;em&gt;branches&lt;/em&gt;, instructions that indicate code can
take one of two possible paths (like an &lt;code&gt;if&lt;/code&gt; statement), and &lt;em&gt;memory
operations&lt;/em&gt;. Branches include all control flow: &lt;code&gt;if&lt;/code&gt; statements, loops, function
calls, function returns, even &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt; statements in C. Memory operations are
loads and stores, especially ones that are cache-unfriendly.&lt;h3 id=procedural-code-is-slow&gt;&lt;a href=#procedural-code-is-slow&gt;Procedural Code Is Slow&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Modern compute cores do not execute code line-by-line, because that would be
very inefficient. Suppose I have this program:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;b&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;^&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=fm&gt;println!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;{a}, {b}&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There&amp;rsquo;s no reason for the CPU to wait to finish computing &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; before it begins
computing &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;; it does not depend on &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;, and while the add is being executed,
the xor circuits are idle. Computers say &amp;ldquo;program order be damned&amp;rdquo; and issue the
add for &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and the xor for &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt; simultaneously. This is called
&lt;em&gt;instruction-level parallelism&lt;/em&gt;, and dependencies that get in the way of it are
often called &lt;em&gt;data hazards&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Of course, the Zen 2 in the machine I&amp;rsquo;m writing this with does not have one
measly adder per core. It has dozens and dozens! The opportunities for
parallelism are massive, as long as the compiler in your CPU&amp;rsquo;s execution
pipeline can clear any data hazards in the way.&lt;p&gt;The better the core can do this, the more it can saturate all of the &amp;ldquo;functional
units&amp;rdquo; for things like arithmetic, and the more numbers it can crunch per unit
time, approaching maximum utilization of the hardware. Whenever the compiler
can&amp;rsquo;t do this, the execution pipeline stalls and your code is slower.&lt;p&gt;Branches stall because they need to wait for the branch condition to be computed
before fetching the next instruction (speculative execution is a somewhat iffy
workaround for this). Memory operations stall because the data needs to
physically arrive at the CPU, and the speed of light is finite in this universe.&lt;p&gt;Trying to reduce stall by improving opportunities for single-core parallelism is
not a new idea. Consider the not-so-humble GPU, whose purpose in life is to
render images. Images are vectors of pixels (i.e., color values), and rendering
operations tend to be highly local. For example, a convolution kernel for a
Gaussian blur will be two or even three orders of magnitude smaller than the
final image, lending itself to locality.&lt;p&gt;Thus, GPUs are built for divide-and-conquer: they provide primitives for doing
batched operations, and extremely limited control flow.&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;SIMD&amp;rdquo; is synonymous with &amp;ldquo;batching&amp;rdquo;. It stands for &amp;ldquo;single instruction,
multiple data&amp;rdquo;: a single instruction dispatches parallel operations on multiple
&lt;em&gt;lanes&lt;/em&gt; of data. GPUs are the original SIMD machines.&lt;h2 id=lane-wise&gt;&lt;a href=#lane-wise&gt;Lane-Wise&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;SIMD&amp;rdquo; and &amp;ldquo;vector&amp;rdquo; are often used interchangeably. The fundamental unit a SIMD
instruction (or &amp;ldquo;vector instruction&amp;rdquo;) operates on is a vector: a fixed-size
array of numbers that you primarily operate on component-wise These components
are called &lt;em&gt;lanes&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;SIMD vectors are usually quite small, since they need to fit into registers. For
example, on my machine, the largest vectors are 256 bits wide. This is enough
for 32 bytes (a &lt;code&gt;u8x32&lt;/code&gt;), 4 double-precision floats (an &lt;code&gt;f64x8&lt;/code&gt;), or all kinds
of things in between.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/vectors.png alt=&#34;some 256-bit vectors&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Although this doesn&amp;rsquo;t seem like much, remember that offloading the overhead of
keeping the pipeline saturated by a factor of 4x can translate to that big of a
speedup in latency.&lt;h3 id=one-bit-lanes&gt;&lt;a href=#one-bit-lanes&gt;One-Bit Lanes&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The simplest vector operations are bitwise: and, or, xor. Ordinary integers can
be thought of as vectors themselves, with respect to the bitwise operations.
That&amp;rsquo;s literally what &amp;ldquo;bitwise&amp;rdquo; means: lanes-wise with lanes that are one bit
wide. An &lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt; is, in this regard, an &lt;code&gt;i1x32&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;In fact, as a warmup, let&amp;rsquo;s look at the problem of counting the number of 1 bits
in an integer. This operation is called &amp;ldquo;population count&amp;rdquo;, or &lt;code&gt;popcnt&lt;/code&gt;. If we
view an &lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt; as an &lt;code&gt;i1x32&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;popcnt&lt;/code&gt; is just a fold or reduce operation:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;popcnt&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bits&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;in&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bits&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;iter_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;enumerate&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bits&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;into_iter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;fold&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;total&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;total&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button godbolt&#34; href=&#34;https://godbolt.&#34;&gt;godbolt&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;In other words, we interpret the integer as an array of bits and then add the
bits together to a 32-bit accumulator. Note that the accumulator needs to be
higher precision to avoid overflow: accumulating into an &lt;code&gt;i1&lt;/code&gt; (as with the
&lt;code&gt;Iterator::reduce()&lt;/code&gt; method) will only tell us whether the number of 1 bits is
even or odd.&lt;p&gt;Of course, this produces&amp;mldr; comically bad code, frankly. We can do much better
if we notice that we can &lt;em&gt;vectorize&lt;/em&gt; the addition: first we add all of the
adjacent pairs of bits together, then the pairs of pairs, and so on. This means
the number of adds is logarithmic in the number of bits in the integer.&lt;p&gt;Visually, what we do is we &amp;ldquo;unzip&amp;rdquo; each vector, shift one to line up the lanes,
add them, and then repeat with lanes twice as big.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/popcnt.png alt=&#34;first two popcnt merge steps&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is what that looks like in code.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;popcnt&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// View x as a i1x32, and split it into two vectors
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// that contain the even and odd bits, respectively.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;even&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x55555555&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// 0x5 == 0b0101.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;odds&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0xaaaaaaaa&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// 0xa == 0b1010.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Shift odds down to align the bits, and then add them together.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// We interpret x now as a i2x16. When adding, each two-bit
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// lane cannot overflow, because the value in each lane is

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Repeat again but now splitting even and odd bit-pairs.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;even&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x33333333&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// 0x3 == 0b0011.

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Because the value of `x` is at most 32, although we interpret this as a
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// i32x1 add, we could get away with just one e.g. i16 add.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;even&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;odds&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Done. All bits have been added.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button godbolt&#34; href=&#34;https://godbolt.&#34;&gt;godbolt&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This still won&amp;rsquo;t optimize down to a &lt;code&gt;popcnt&lt;/code&gt; instruction, of course. The search
scope for such a simplification is in the regime of superoptimizers. However,
the generated code is small and fast, which is why this is the ideal
implementation of &lt;code&gt;popcnt&lt;/code&gt; for systems without such an instruction.&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s &lt;em&gt;especially&lt;/em&gt; nice because it is implementable for e.g. &lt;code&gt;u64&lt;/code&gt; with only one
more reduction step (remember: it&amp;rsquo;s &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:1em;vertical-align:-.25em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.02778em&gt;O&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mopen&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mop&gt;lo&lt;span style=margin-right:.01389em&gt;g&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.1667em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mclose&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;!), and does not at any point
require a full &lt;code&gt;u64&lt;/code&gt; addition.&lt;p&gt;Even though this is &amp;ldquo;just&amp;rdquo; using scalars, divide-and-conquer approaches like
this are the bread and butter of the SIMD programmer.&lt;h3 id=scaling-up-operations-on-real-vectors&gt;&lt;a href=#scaling-up-operations-on-real-vectors&gt;Scaling Up: Operations on Real Vectors&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Proper SIMD vectors provide more sophisticated semantics than scalars do,
particularly because there is more need to provide replacements for things like
control flow. Remember, control flow is slow!&lt;p&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s actually available is highly dependent on the architecture you&amp;rsquo;re
compiling to (more on this later), but the way vector instruction sets are
usually structured is something like this.&lt;p&gt;We have &lt;em&gt;vector registers&lt;/em&gt; that are kind of like really big general-purpose
registers. For example, on x86, most &amp;ldquo;high performance&amp;rdquo; cores (like my Zen 2)
implement AVX2, which provides 256 bit &lt;code&gt;ymm&lt;/code&gt; vectors. The registers themselves
do not have a &amp;ldquo;lane count&amp;rdquo;; that is specified by the instructions. For example,
the &amp;ldquo;vector byte add instruction&amp;rdquo; interprets the register as being divided into
eight-byte lanes and adds them. The corresponding x86 instruction is &lt;code&gt;vpaddb&lt;/code&gt;,
which interprets a &lt;code&gt;ymm&lt;/code&gt; as an &lt;code&gt;i8x32&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The operations you usually get are:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Bitwise operations. These don&amp;rsquo;t need to specify a lane width because it&amp;rsquo;s
always implicitly &lt;code&gt;1&lt;/code&gt;: they&amp;rsquo;re &lt;em&gt;bit&lt;/em&gt;wise.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Lane-wise arithmetic. This is addition, subtraction, multiplication, division
(both int and float), and shifts&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (int only).
Lane-wise min and max are also common. These require specifying a lane width.
Typically the smallest number of lanes is two or four.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Lane-wise compare. Given &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;, we can create a new &lt;em&gt;mask vector&lt;/em&gt; &lt;code&gt;m&lt;/code&gt;
such that &lt;code&gt;m[i] = a[i] &amp;lt; b[i]&lt;/code&gt; (or any other comparison operation). A mask
vector&amp;rsquo;s lanes contain boolean values with an unusual bit-pattern: all-zeros
(for false) or all-ones (for true)&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Masks can be used to select between two vectors: for example, given &lt;code&gt;m&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;y&lt;/code&gt;, you can form a fourth vector &lt;code&gt;z&lt;/code&gt; such that
&lt;code&gt;z[i] = m[i] ? a[i] : b[i]&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Shuffles (sometimes called swizzles). Given &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;, create a third
vector &lt;code&gt;s&lt;/code&gt; such that &lt;code&gt;s[i] = a[x[i]]&lt;/code&gt;. &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; is used as a lookup table, and &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;
as a set of indices. Out of bounds produces a special value, usually zero.
This emulates parallelized array access without needing to actually touch RAM
(RAM is extremely slow).&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Often there is a &amp;ldquo;shuffle2&amp;rdquo; or &amp;ldquo;riffle&amp;rdquo; operation that allows taking
elements from one of two vectors. Given &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;, we now define
&lt;code&gt;s&lt;/code&gt; as being &lt;code&gt;s[i] = (a ++ b)[x[i]]&lt;/code&gt;, where &lt;code&gt;a ++ b&lt;/code&gt; is a double-width
concatenation. How this is actually implemented depends on architecture,
and it&amp;rsquo;s easy to build out of single shuffles regardless.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;(1) and (2) are ordinary number crunching. Nothing deeply special about them.&lt;p&gt;The comparison and select operations in (3) are intended to help SIMD code stay
&amp;ldquo;branchless&amp;rdquo;. Branchless code is written such that it performs the same
operations regardless of its inputs, and relies on the properties of those
operations to produce correct results. For example, this might mean taking
advantage of identities like &lt;code&gt;x * 0 = 0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;a ^ b ^ a = b&lt;/code&gt; to discard
&amp;ldquo;garbage&amp;rdquo; results.&lt;p&gt;The shuffles described in (4) are much more powerful than meets the eye.&lt;p&gt;For example, &amp;ldquo;broadcast&amp;rdquo; (sometimes called &amp;ldquo;splat&amp;rdquo;) makes a vector whose lanes
are all the same scalar, like Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;[42; N]&lt;/code&gt; array literal. A broadcast can be
expressed as a shuffle: create a vector with the desired value in the first
lane, and then shuffle it with an index vector of &lt;code&gt;[0, 0, ...]&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/broadcast.png alt=&#34;diagram of a broadcast&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Interleave&amp;rdquo; (also called &amp;ldquo;zip&amp;rdquo; or &amp;ldquo;pack&amp;rdquo;) takes two vectors &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt; and
creates two new vectors &lt;code&gt;c&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;d&lt;/code&gt; whose lanes are alternating lanes from &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;
and &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;. If the lane count is &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;, then &lt;code&gt;c = [a[0], b[0], a[1], b[1], ...]&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;d = [a[n/2], b[n/2], a[n/2 + 1], b[n/2 + 1], ...]&lt;/code&gt;. This can also be
implemented as a shuffle2, with shuffle indices of &lt;code&gt;[0, n, 1, n + 1, ...]&lt;/code&gt;.
&amp;ldquo;Deinterleave&amp;rdquo; (or &amp;ldquo;unzip&amp;rdquo;, or &amp;ldquo;unpack&amp;rdquo;) is the opposite operation: it
interprets a pair of vectors as two halves of a larger vector of pairs, and
produces two new vectors consisting of the halves of each pair.&lt;p&gt;Interleave can also be interpreted as taking a &lt;code&gt;[T; N]&lt;/code&gt;, transmuting it to a
&lt;code&gt;[[T; N/2]; 2]&lt;/code&gt;, performing a matrix transpose to turn it into a
&lt;code&gt;[[T; 2]; N/2]&lt;/code&gt;, and then transmuting that back to &lt;code&gt;[T; N]&lt;/code&gt; again. Deinterleave
is the same but it transmutes to &lt;code&gt;[[T; 2]; N/2]&lt;/code&gt; first.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/interleave.png alt=&#34;diagram of a interleave&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Rotate&amp;rdquo; takes a vector &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; with &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; lanes and produces a new vector &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt; such
that &lt;code&gt;b[i] = a[(i + j) % n]&lt;/code&gt;, for some chosen integer &lt;code&gt;j&lt;/code&gt;. This is yet another
shuffle, with indices &lt;code&gt;[j, j + 1, ..., n - 1, 0, 1, ... j - 1]&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/rotate.png alt=&#34;diagram of a rotate&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Shuffles are worth trying to wrap your mind around. SIMD programming is all
about reinterpreting larger-than-an-integer-sized blocks of data as smaller
blocks of varying sizes, and shuffling is important for getting data into the
right &amp;ldquo;place&amp;rdquo;.&lt;h3 id=intrinsics-and-instruction-selection&gt;&lt;a href=#intrinsics-and-instruction-selection&gt;Intrinsics and Instruction Selection&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Earlier, I mentioned that what you get varies by architecture. This section is
basically a giant footnote.&lt;p&gt;So, there&amp;rsquo;s two big factors that go into this.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;We&amp;rsquo;ve learned over time which operations tend to be most useful to
programmers. x86 might have something that ARM doesn&amp;rsquo;t because it &amp;ldquo;seemed
like a good idea at the time&amp;rdquo; but turned out to be kinda niche.&lt;li&gt;Instruction set extensions are often market differentiators, even within the
same vendor. Intel has AVX-512, which provides even more sophisticated
instructions, but it&amp;rsquo;s only available on high-end server chips, because it
makes manufacturing more expensive.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Toolchains generalize different extensions as &amp;ldquo;target features&amp;rdquo;. Features can be
detected at runtime through architecture-specific magic. On Linux, the &lt;code&gt;lscpu&lt;/code&gt;
command will list what features the CPU advertises that it recognizes, which
correlate with the names of features that e.g. LLVM understands. What features
are enabled for a particular function affects how LLVM compiles it. For example,
LLVM will only emit &lt;code&gt;ymm&lt;/code&gt;-using code when compiling with &lt;code&gt;+avx2&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;So how do you write portable SIMD code? On the surface, the answer is mostly
&amp;ldquo;you don&amp;rsquo;t&amp;rdquo;, but it&amp;rsquo;s more complicated than that, and for that we need to
understand how the later parts of a compiler works.&lt;p&gt;When a user requests an add by writing &lt;code&gt;a + b&lt;/code&gt;, how should I decide which
instruction to use for it? This seems like a trick question&amp;mldr; &lt;em&gt;just&lt;/em&gt; an &lt;code&gt;add&lt;/code&gt;
right? On x86, even this isn&amp;rsquo;t so easy, since you have a choice between the
actual &lt;code&gt;add&lt;/code&gt; instruction, or a &lt;code&gt;lea&lt;/code&gt; instruction (which, among other things,
preserves the &lt;code&gt;rflags&lt;/code&gt; register). This question becomes more complicated for
more sophisticated operations. This general problem is called &lt;em&gt;instruction
selection&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Because which &amp;ldquo;target features&amp;rdquo; are enabled affects which instructions are
available, they affect instruction selection. When I went over operations
&amp;ldquo;typically available&amp;rdquo;, this means that compilers will usually be able to select
good choices of instructions for them on most architectures.&lt;p&gt;Compiling with something like &lt;code&gt;-march=native&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;-Ctarget-cpu=native&lt;/code&gt; gets you
&amp;ldquo;the best&amp;rdquo; code possible for the machine you&amp;rsquo;re building on, but it might not be
portable&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; to different processors. Gentoo was quite famous for building
packages from source on user machines to take advantage of this (not to mention
that they loved using &lt;code&gt;-O3&lt;/code&gt;, which mostly exists to slow down build times with
little benefit).&lt;p&gt;There is also runtime feature detection, where a program decides which version
of a function to call at runtime by asking the CPU what it supports. Code
deployed on heterogenous devices (like cryptography libraries) often make use of
this. Doing this correctly is very hard and something I don&amp;rsquo;t particularly want
to dig deeply into here.&lt;p&gt;The situation is made worse by the fact that in C++, you usually write SIMD code
using &amp;ldquo;intrinsics&amp;rdquo;, which are special functions with inscrutable names like
&lt;code&gt;_mm256_cvtps_epu32&lt;/code&gt; that represent a low-level operation in a specific
instruction set (this is a float to int cast from AVX2). Intrinsics are defined
by hardware vendors, but don&amp;rsquo;t necessarily map down to single instructions; the
compiler can still optimize these instructions by merging, deduplication, and
through instruction selection.&lt;p&gt;As a result you wind up writing the same code multiple times for different
instruction sets, with only minor maintainability benefits over writing
assembly.&lt;p&gt;The alternative is a portable SIMD library, which does some instruction
selection behind the scenes at the library level but tries to rely on the
compiler for most of the heavy-duty work. For a long time I was skeptical that
this approach would actually produce good, competitive code, which brings us to
the actual point of this article: using Rust&amp;rsquo;s portable SIMD library to
implement a somewhat fussy algorithm, and measuring performance.&lt;h2 id=parsing-with-simd&gt;&lt;a href=#parsing-with-simd&gt;Parsing with SIMD&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s design a SIMD implementation for a well-known algorithm. Although it
doesn&amp;rsquo;t look like it at first, the power of shuffles makes it possible to parse
text with SIMD. And this parsing can be very, very fast.&lt;p&gt;In this case, we&amp;rsquo;re going to implement base64 decoding. To review, base64 is an
encoding scheme for arbitrary binary data into ASCII. We interpret a byte slice
as a bit vector, and divide it into six-bit chunks called &lt;em&gt;sextets&lt;/em&gt;. Then, each
sextet from 0 to 63 is mapped to an ASCII character:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;25&lt;/code&gt; go to &lt;code&gt;&#39;A&#39;&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;&#39;Z&#39;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;26&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;51&lt;/code&gt; go to &lt;code&gt;&#39;a&#39;&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;&#39;z&#39;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;52&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;61&lt;/code&gt; go to &lt;code&gt;&#39;0&#39;&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;&#39;9&#39;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;62&lt;/code&gt; goes to &lt;code&gt;+&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;63&lt;/code&gt; goes to &lt;code&gt;/&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;There &lt;em&gt;are&lt;/em&gt; other variants of base64, but the bulk of the complexity is the same
for each variant.&lt;p&gt;There are a few basic pitfalls to keep in mind.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Base64 is a &amp;ldquo;big endian&amp;rdquo; format: specifically, the bits in each byte are big
endian. Because a sextet can span only parts of a byte, this distinction is
important.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;We need to beware of cases where the input length is not divisible by 4;
ostensibly messages should be padded with &lt;code&gt;=&lt;/code&gt; to a multiple of 4, but it&amp;rsquo;s
easy to just handle messages that aren&amp;rsquo;t padded correctly.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;The length of a decoded message is given by this function:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;decoded_len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;input&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;input&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;/&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;match&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;input&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;So, what&amp;rsquo;s the process of turning this into a SIMD version? We want to follow
one directive with inexorable, robotic dedication.&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Eliminate all branches.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is not completely feasible, since the input is of variable length. But we
can try. There are several branches in this code:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;The &lt;code&gt;for chunk in&lt;/code&gt; line. This one is is the length check: it checks if there
is any data left to process.&lt;li&gt;The &lt;code&gt;for &amp;amp;byte in&lt;/code&gt; line. This is the hottest loop: it branches once per input
byte.&lt;li&gt;The &lt;code&gt;match byte&lt;/code&gt; line is several branches, to determine which of the five
&amp;ldquo;valid&amp;rdquo; match arms we land in.&lt;li&gt;The &lt;code&gt;return Err&lt;/code&gt; line. Returning in a hot loop is extra control flow, which
is not ideal.&lt;li&gt;The call to &lt;code&gt;decoded_len&lt;/code&gt; contains a &lt;code&gt;match&lt;/code&gt;, which generates branches.&lt;li&gt;The call to &lt;code&gt;Vec::extend_from_slice&lt;/code&gt;. This contains not just branches, but
potential calls into the allocator. Extremely slow.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;(5) is the easiest to deal with. The &lt;code&gt;match&lt;/code&gt; is mapping the values &lt;code&gt;0, 1, 2, 3&lt;/code&gt;
to &lt;code&gt;0, 1, 1, 2&lt;/code&gt;. Call this function &lt;code&gt;f&lt;/code&gt;. Then, the sequence given by &lt;code&gt;x - f(x)&lt;/code&gt;
is &lt;code&gt;0, 0, 1, 1&lt;/code&gt;. This just happens to equal &lt;code&gt;x / 2&lt;/code&gt; (or &lt;code&gt;x &gt;&gt; 1&lt;/code&gt;), so we can
write a completely branchless version of &lt;code&gt;decoded_len&lt;/code&gt; like so.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;decoded_len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;input&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;That&amp;rsquo;s one branch eliminated&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. ✅&lt;p&gt;The others will not prove so easy. Let&amp;rsquo;s turn our attention to the innermost
loop next, branches (2), (3), and (4).&lt;h3 id=the-hottest-loop&gt;&lt;a href=#the-hottest-loop&gt;The Hottest Loop&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The superpower of SIMD is that because you operate on so much data at a time,
you can unroll the loop so hard it becomes branchless.&lt;p&gt;The insight is this: we want to load at most four bytes, do something to them,
and then spit out at most three decoded bytes. While doing this operation, we
may encounter a syntax error so we need to report that somehow.&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s some facts we can take advantage of.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;We don&amp;rsquo;t need to figure out how many bytes are in the &amp;ldquo;output&amp;rdquo; of the hot
loop: our handy branchless &lt;code&gt;decoded_len()&lt;/code&gt; does that for us.&lt;li&gt;Invalid base64 is extremely rare. We want that syntax error to cost as little
as possible. If the user still cares about which byte was the problem, they
can scan the input for it after the fact.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; is zero in base64. If we&amp;rsquo;re parsing a truncated chunk, padding it with
&lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt; won&amp;rsquo;t change the value&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;This suggests an interface for the body of the &amp;ldquo;hottest loop&amp;rdquo;. We can factor it
out as a separate function, and simplify since we can assume our input is always
four bytes now.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;decode_hot&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ascii&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;])&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;([&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;3&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:10&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This solution is quite elegant, and will produce very competitive code, but it&amp;rsquo;s
not actually ideal. We need to do a lot of comparisons here: eight in total. We
also keep lots of values alive at the same time, which might lead to unwanted
register pressure.&lt;h3 id=simd-hash-table&gt;&lt;a href=#simd-hash-table&gt;SIMD Hash Table&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s look at the byte representations of the ranges. &lt;code&gt;A-Z&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;a-z&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;0-9&lt;/code&gt;
are, as byte ranges, &lt;code&gt;0x41..0x5b&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;0x61..0x7b&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;0x30..0x3a&lt;/code&gt;. Notice they
all have different high nybbles! What&amp;rsquo;s more, &lt;code&gt;+&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;/&lt;/code&gt; are &lt;code&gt;0x2b&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;0x2f&lt;/code&gt;,
so the function &lt;code&gt;byte &gt;&gt; 4&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;em&gt;almost&lt;/em&gt; enough to distinguish all the ranges. If
we subtract one if &lt;code&gt;byte == b&#39;/&#39;&lt;/code&gt;, we have a &lt;em&gt;perfect hash&lt;/em&gt; for the ranges.&lt;p&gt;In other words, the value &lt;code&gt;(byte &gt;&gt; 4) - (byte == &#39;/&#39;)&lt;/code&gt; maps the ranges as
follows:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;A-Z&lt;/code&gt; goes to 4 or 5.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;a-z&lt;/code&gt; goes to 6 or 7.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;0-9&lt;/code&gt; goes to 3.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;+&lt;/code&gt; goes to 2.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;/&lt;/code&gt; goes to 1.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is small enough that we could cram a lookup table of values for building
the &lt;code&gt;offsets&lt;/code&gt; vector into another SIMD vector, and use a shuffle operation to do
the lookup.&lt;p&gt;This is not my original idea; I came across a
&lt;a href=https://github.com/WojciechMula/base64simd/issues/3&gt;GitHub issue&lt;/a&gt; where an
anonymous user points out this perfect hash.&lt;p&gt;Our new ascii-to-sextet code looks like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:11&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Compute the perfect hash for each lane.

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;to_int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// to_int() is equivalent to masked_splat(-1, 0).

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// indices that the perfect hash produces.

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;cast&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;swizzle_dyn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;hashes&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is a small wrinkle here:
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/simd/struct.Simd.html#method.swizzle_dyn&gt;&lt;code&gt;Simd::swizzle_dyn()&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
requires that the index array be the same length as the lookup table. This is
annoying because right now &lt;code&gt;ascii&lt;/code&gt; is a &lt;code&gt;Simd&amp;lt;u8, 4&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, but that will not be the
case later on, so I will simply sweep this under the rug.&lt;p&gt;Note that we no longer get validation as a side-effect of computing the sextets
vector. The same GitHub issue also provides an exact bloom-filter for checking
that a particular byte is valid; you can see my implementation
&lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/vb64/blob/894f833e933860e070dabcfcc189430c45fecbd7/src/simd.rs#L93&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.
I&amp;rsquo;m not sure how the OP constructed the bloom filter, but the search space is
small enough that you could have written a little script to brute force it.&lt;h3 id=riffling-the-sextets&gt;&lt;a href=#riffling-the-sextets&gt;Riffling the Sextets&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now comes a much tricker operation: we need to somehow pack all four sextets
into three bytes. One way to try to wrap our head around what the packing code
in &lt;code&gt;decode_hot()&lt;/code&gt; is doing is to pass in the all-ones sextet in one of the four
bytes, and see where those ones end up in the return value.&lt;p&gt;This is not unlike how they use radioactive dyes in biology to track the moment

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button godbolt&#34; href=&#34;https://godbolt.&#34;&gt;godbolt&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Bingo. Playing around with the inputs lets us verify which pieces of the bytes
wind up where. For example, by passing &lt;code&gt;0b110000&lt;/code&gt; as &lt;code&gt;input[1]&lt;/code&gt;, we see that the
two high bits of &lt;code&gt;input[1]&lt;/code&gt; correspond to the low bits of &lt;code&gt;output[0]&lt;/code&gt;. I&amp;rsquo;ve
written the code so that the bits in each byte are printed in little-endian
order, so bits on the left are the low bits.&lt;p&gt;Putting this all together, we can draw a schematic of what this operation does
to a general &lt;code&gt;Simd&amp;lt;u8, 4&gt;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/riffle.png alt=&#34;the riffling operation&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, there&amp;rsquo;s no single instruction that will do this for us. Shuffles can be
used to move bytes around, but we&amp;rsquo;re dealing with &lt;em&gt;pieces&lt;/em&gt; of bytes here. We
also can&amp;rsquo;t really do a shift, since we need bits that are overshifted to move
into adjacent lanes.&lt;p&gt;The trick is to just make the lanes bigger.&lt;p&gt;Among the operations available for SIMD vectors are lane-wise casts, which allow
us to zero-extend, sign-extend, or truncate each lane. So what we can do is cast
&lt;code&gt;sextets&lt;/code&gt; to a vector of &lt;code&gt;u16&lt;/code&gt;, do the shift there and then&amp;mldr; somehow put the
parts back together?&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s see how far shifting gets us. How much do we need to shift things by?
First, notice that the order of the bits within each chunk that doesn&amp;rsquo;t cross a
byte boundary doesn&amp;rsquo;t change. For example, the four low bits of &lt;code&gt;input[1]&lt;/code&gt; are
in the same order when they become the high bits of &lt;code&gt;output[1]&lt;/code&gt;, and the two
high bits of &lt;code&gt;input[1]&lt;/code&gt; are also in the same order when they become the low bits
of &lt;code&gt;output[0]&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This means we can determine how far to shift by comparing the bit position of
the lowest bit of a byte of &lt;code&gt;input&lt;/code&gt; with the bit position of the corresponding
bit in &lt;code&gt;output&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;input[0]&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s low bit is the third bit of &lt;code&gt;output[0]&lt;/code&gt;, so we need to shift
&lt;code&gt;input[0]&lt;/code&gt; by 2. &lt;code&gt;input[1]&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s lowest bit is the fifth bit of &lt;code&gt;output[1]&lt;/code&gt;, so we
need to shift by 4. Analogously, the shifts for &lt;code&gt;input[2]&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;input[3]&lt;/code&gt; turn
out to be 6 and 0. as being analogous to a &lt;code&gt;[[u8; 2]; 4]&lt;/code&gt;. For example, &lt;code&gt;shifted[0][0]&lt;/code&gt; contains

schematic. The smaller blue segment is given by &lt;code&gt;shifted[1][1]&lt;/code&gt;, i.e., the high
byte of the second &lt;code&gt;u16&lt;/code&gt;. It&amp;rsquo;s already in the right place within that byte, so
we want &lt;code&gt;output[0] = shifted[0][0] | shifted[1][1]&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This suggests a more general strategy: we want to take two vectors, the low
bytes and the high bytes of each &lt;code&gt;u16&lt;/code&gt; in &lt;code&gt;shifted&lt;/code&gt;, respectively, and somehow

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;We have to change virtually nothing, which is pretty awesome! But unfortunately,
this code is subtly incorrect. Remember how in the &lt;code&gt;N = 4&lt;/code&gt; case, the result of
&lt;code&gt;output&lt;/code&gt; had a garbage value that we ignore in its highest lane? Well, now that
garbage data is interleaved into output: every fourth lane contains garbage.&lt;p&gt;We can use a shuffle to delete these lanes, thankfully. Specifically, we want
&lt;code&gt;shuffled[i] = output[i + i / 3]&lt;/code&gt;, which skips every forth index. So,
&lt;code&gt;shuffled[3] = output[4]&lt;/code&gt;, skipping over the garbage value in &lt;code&gt;output[3]&lt;/code&gt;. If
&lt;code&gt;i + i / 3&lt;/code&gt; overflows &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt;, that&amp;rsquo;s ok, because that&amp;rsquo;s the high quarter of the
final output vector, which is ignored anyways. &lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;What branches are left? There&amp;rsquo;s still the branch from &lt;code&gt;for chunks in ...&lt;/code&gt;. It&amp;rsquo;s
not ideal because it can&amp;rsquo;t do an exact pointer comparison, and needs to do a
&lt;code&gt;&gt;=&lt;/code&gt; comparison on a length instead.&lt;p&gt;We call &lt;code&gt;[T]::copy_from_slice&lt;/code&gt;, which is super slow because it needs to make a
variable-length &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt; call, which can&amp;rsquo;t be inlined. Function calls are
branches! The bounds checks are also a problem.&lt;p&gt;We branch on &lt;code&gt;ok&lt;/code&gt; every loop iteration, still. Not returning early in
&lt;code&gt;decode_hot&lt;/code&gt; doesn&amp;rsquo;t win us anything (yet).&lt;p&gt;We potentially call the allocator in &lt;code&gt;extend_from_slice&lt;/code&gt;, and perform another
non-inline-able &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt; call.&lt;h3 id=preallocating-with-slop&gt;&lt;a href=#preallocating-with-slop&gt;Preallocating with Slop&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The last of these is the easiest to address: we can reserve space in &lt;code&gt;out&lt;/code&gt;,
since we know exactly how much data we need to write thanks to &lt;code&gt;decoded_len&lt;/code&gt;.
Better yet, we can reserve some &amp;ldquo;slop&amp;rdquo;: i.e., scratch space past where the end
of the message would be, so we can perform full SIMD stores, instead of the
variable-length memcpy.&lt;p&gt;This way, in each iteration, we write the full SIMD vector, including any
garbage bytes in the upper quarter. Then, the next write is offset &lt;code&gt;3/4 * N&lt;/code&gt;
bytes over, so it overwrites the garbage bytes with decoded message bytes. The
garbage bytes from the final right get &amp;ldquo;deleted&amp;rdquo; by not being included in the
final &lt;code&gt;Vec::set_len()&lt;/code&gt; that &amp;ldquo;commits&amp;rdquo; the memory we wrote to.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;decode&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;N&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;out&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nc&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;Result&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Error&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

loop. The loop has already been partly unrolled: it does &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt; iterations with

missing data (padding with &lt;code&gt;A&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;We can take this a step further by doing an &amp;ldquo;unroll and jam&amp;rdquo; optimization. This

benchmarks are in order. I wrote a benchmark that decodes messages of every
length from 0 to something like 200 or 500 bytes, and compared it against the
baseline base64 implementation on crates.io.&lt;p&gt;I compiled with &lt;code&gt;-Zbuild-std&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;-Ctarget-cpu=native&lt;/code&gt; to try to get the best
results. Based on some tuning, &lt;code&gt;N = 32&lt;/code&gt; was the best length, since it used one
YMM register for each iteration of the hot loop.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/simd-b64/graph-old.png alt=&#34;a performance graph; our code is really good compared to the baseline, but variance is high&#34;&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;So, we have the baseline beat. But what&amp;rsquo;s up with that crazy heartbeat waveform?
You can tell it has something to do with the &amp;ldquo;remainder&amp;rdquo; part of the loop, since
it correlates strongly with &lt;code&gt;data.len() % 32&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;I stared at the assembly for a while. I don&amp;rsquo;t remember what was there, but I
think that &lt;code&gt;copy_from_slice&lt;/code&gt; had been inlined and unrolled into a loop
that loaded each byte at a time. What&amp;rsquo;s the least number of
unaligned loads you need to do to load 15 bytes from memory? It&amp;rsquo;s two! You can
load a &lt;code&gt;u64&lt;/code&gt; from &lt;code&gt;p&lt;/code&gt;, and then another one from &lt;code&gt;p + 7&lt;/code&gt;; these loads (call them
&lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;) overlap by one byte, but we can or them together to merge that
byte, so our loaded value is &lt;code&gt;a as u128 | (b as u128 &amp;lt;&amp;lt; 56)&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A similar trick works if the data to load is between a &lt;code&gt;u32&lt;/code&gt; and a &lt;code&gt;u64&lt;/code&gt;.
Finally, to load 1, 2, or 3 bytes, we can load &lt;code&gt;p&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;p + len/2&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;p + len-1&lt;/code&gt;;
depending on whether &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; is 1, 2, or 3, this will potentially load the same
byte multiple times; however, this reduces the number of branches necessary,
since we don&amp;rsquo;t need to distinguish the 1, 2, or 3 lines.&lt;p&gt;This is the kind of code that&amp;rsquo;s probably easier to read than to explain.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:24&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
