These matrices &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.05764em&gt;S&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; and
&lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.00773em&gt;R&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; represent a &lt;em&gt;change of basis&lt;/em&gt;, and indicate that the linear maps
&lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.8778em;vertical-align:-.1944em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mpunct&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.1667em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.05017em&gt;B&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.2778em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mrel&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.2778em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.22222em&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.2778em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mrel&gt;→&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mspace style=margin-right:.2778em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.13889em&gt;W&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; these matrices come from do &amp;ldquo;the same thing&amp;rdquo; to elements
of &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34; style=margin-right:.22222em&gt;V&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Over an algebraically closed field like &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6889em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathbb&#34;&gt;C&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; (i.e. all polynomials have
solutions), there is an even stronger way to capture the information content
of a linear map via
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form&gt;&lt;em&gt;Jordan canonicalization&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt;,
which takes any square matrix &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt; and produces an almost-diagonal square
matrix that only depends on the eigenvalues of &lt;span class=katex&gt;&lt;span class=katex-html aria-hidden=true&gt;&lt;span class=base&gt;&lt;span class=strut style=height:.6833em&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=&#34;mord mathnormal&#34;&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;, which is the same for
similar matrices, and thus basis-independent.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here, as always, matrix dimensions are given in RC (row-column) order. You
can think of this as being &amp;ldquo;input dimension&amp;rdquo; to &amp;ldquo;output dimension&amp;rdquo;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>I Wrote A String Type
</title>
    <link href="/2023/08/09/yarns"/>
    <updated>2023-08-09T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2023/08/09/yarns</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I write compilers for fun. I can&amp;rsquo;t help it. Consequently, I also write a lot of
parsers. In systems programming, it&amp;rsquo;s usually a good idea to try to share memory
rather than reuse it, so as such my AST types tend to look like this.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Expr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;src&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Ident&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;src&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Whenever we parse an identifier, rather than copy its name into a fresh
&lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt;, we borrow from the input source string. This avoids an extra
allocation, an extra copy, and saves a word in the representation. Compilers can
be memory-hungry, so it helps to pick a lean representation.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, it&amp;rsquo;s not so easy for quoted strings. Most strings, like
&lt;code&gt;&#34;all my jelly babies&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, are &amp;ldquo;literally&amp;rdquo; in the original source, like an
identifier. But strings with escapes aren&amp;rsquo;t: &lt;code&gt;\n&lt;/code&gt; is encoded in the source code
with the bytes &lt;code&gt;[0x5c, 0x6e]&lt;/code&gt;, but the actual &amp;ldquo;decoded&amp;rdquo; value of a string
literal replaces each escape with a single &lt;code&gt;0x0a&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The usual solution is a &lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/borrow/enum.Cow.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. In the more common, escape-less verison,
we can use &lt;code&gt;Cow::Borrowed&lt;/code&gt;, which avoids the extra allocation and copy, and in
the escaped version, we decode the escapes into a &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt; and wrap it in a
&lt;code&gt;Cow::Owned&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;For example, suppose that we&amp;rsquo;re writing a parser for a language that has quoted
strings with escapes. The string &lt;code&gt;&#34;all my jelly babies&#34;&lt;/code&gt; can be represented as a
byte string that borrows the input source code, so we&amp;rsquo;d use the &lt;code&gt;Cow::Borrowed&lt;/code&gt;
variant. This is most strings in any language: escapes tend to be rare.&lt;p&gt;For example, if we have the string &lt;code&gt;&#34;not UTF-8 \xff&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, the actual byte string
value is different from that in the source code.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-text highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;// Bytes in the source.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;hex:   6e 6f 74 20 55 54 46 2d 38 20 5c 78 66 66
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;ascii: n  o  t     U  T  F  -  8     \  x  f  f
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;// Bytes represented by the string.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;hex:   6e 6f 74 20 55 54 46 2d 38 20 ff
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;ascii: n  o  t     U  T  F  -  8
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Escapes are relatively rare, so most strings processed by the parser do not need
to pay for an allocation.&lt;p&gt;However, we still pay for that extra word, since &lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is 24 bytes (unless
otherwise specified, all byte counts assume a 64-bit system), which is eight
more than our &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;str&lt;/code&gt;. Even worse, this is bigger than the string data itself,
which is 11 bytes.&lt;p&gt;If most of your strings are small (which is not uncommon in an AST parser), you
will wind up paying for significant overhead.&lt;p&gt;Over the years I&amp;rsquo;ve implemented various optimized string types to deal with this
use-case, in various contexts. I finally got around to putting all of the tricks
I know into a library, which I call
&lt;a href=https://docs.rs/byteyarn/latest/byteyarn/&gt;&lt;code&gt;byteyarn&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. It advertises the
following nice properties.&lt;blockquote id=ref:1 class=ref ref math&gt;&lt;a href=#ref:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;reference&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;Yarn&lt;/code&gt; is a highly optimized string type that provides a number of useful
properties over &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Always two pointers wide, so it is always passed into and out of functions
in registers.&lt;li&gt;Small string optimization (SSO) up to 15 bytes on 64-bit architectures.&lt;li&gt;Can be either an owned buffer or a borrowed buffer (like &lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;li&gt;Can be upcast to &lt;code&gt;&#39;static&lt;/code&gt; lifetime if it was constructed from a
known-static string.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;d like to share how these properties are achieved through careful layout
optimization.&lt;h2 id=assumptions&gt;&lt;a href=#assumptions&gt;Assumptions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;re going to start by stating assumptions about how our strings will be used:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Most strings are not mutated most of the time.&lt;li&gt;Most strings are small.&lt;li&gt;Most strings are substrings.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;h3 id=most-strings-are-immutable&gt;&lt;a href=#most-strings-are-immutable&gt;Most Strings are Immutable&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt; is modeled after C++&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;std::string&lt;/code&gt;, which is a growable buffer that
implements amortized linear-time append. This means that if we are appending &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt;
bytes to the buffer, we only pay for &lt;code&gt;n&lt;/code&gt; bytes of &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This is a useful but often unnecessary property. For example, Go strings are
immutable, and when building up a large string, you are expected to use
&lt;code&gt;strings.Builder&lt;/code&gt;, which is implemented as essentially a Rust &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt;. Java
also as a similar story for strings, which allows for highly compact
representations of &lt;code&gt;java.lang.String&lt;/code&gt;s.&lt;p&gt;In Rust, this kind of immutable string is represented by a &lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, which is
eight bytes smaller than &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt;. Converting from &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is
just a call to &lt;code&gt;realloc()&lt;/code&gt; to resize the underlying allocation (which is often
cheap&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;) from being &lt;code&gt;capacity&lt;/code&gt; bytes long to &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; bytes long.&lt;p&gt;Thus, this assumption means we only need to store a pointer and a length, which
puts our memory footprint floor at 16 bytes.&lt;h3 id=most-strings-are-substrings&gt;&lt;a href=#most-strings-are-substrings&gt;Most Strings are Substrings&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Suppose again that we&amp;rsquo;re parsing some textual format. Many structural elements
will be verbatim references into the textual input. Not only string literals
without escapes, but also identifiers.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt; cannot hold borrowed data, because it will always instruct the
allocator to free its pointer when it goes out of scope. &lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, as we saw
above, allows us to handle maybe-owned data uniformly, but has a minimum 24 byte
overhead. This can&amp;rsquo;t be made any smaller, because a &lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt; can contain a
24-byte &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt; value.&lt;p&gt;But, we don&amp;rsquo;t want to store a capacity. Can we avoid the extra word of overhead
in &lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;?&lt;h3 id=most-strings-are-small&gt;&lt;a href=#most-strings-are-small&gt;Most Strings are Small&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Consider a string that is not a substring but which is small. For example, when
parsing a string literal like &lt;code&gt;&#34;Hello, world!\n&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, the trailing &lt;code&gt;\n&lt;/code&gt; (bytes
&lt;code&gt;0x5c 0x6e&lt;/code&gt;) must be replaced with a newline byte (&lt;code&gt;0x0a&lt;/code&gt;). This means we must
handle a tiny heap allocation, 14 bytes long, that is smaller than a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;str&lt;/code&gt;
referring to it.&lt;p&gt;This is worse for single character&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; strings. The overhead for a
&lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is large.&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;The &lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt; struct itself has a pointer field (eight bytes), and a length
field (also eight bytes). Spelled out to show all the stored bits, the length
is &lt;code&gt;0x0000_0000_0000_0001&lt;/code&gt;. That&amp;rsquo;s a lot of zeroes!&lt;li&gt;The pointer itself points to a heap allocation, which will not be a single
byte! Allocators are not in the business of handing out such small pieces of
memory. Instead, the allocation is likely costing us another eight bytes!&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;So, the string &lt;code&gt;&#34;a&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, whose data is just a &lt;em&gt;single byte&lt;/em&gt;, instead takes up 24
bytes of memory.&lt;p&gt;It turns out that for really small strings we can avoid the allocation
altogether, &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; make effective use of all those zeroes in the &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; field.&lt;h2 id=stealing-bits&gt;&lt;a href=#stealing-bits&gt;Stealing Bits&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s say we want to stick to a budget of 16 bytes for our &lt;code&gt;Yarn&lt;/code&gt; type. Is there
any extra space left for data in a &lt;code&gt;(*mut u8, usize)&lt;/code&gt; pair?&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;*cracks Fermi estimation knuckles*&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;usize&lt;/code&gt; is 64 bits, which means that the length of an &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;str&lt;/code&gt; can be anywhere
from zero to 18446744073709551615, or around 18 exabytes. For reference,
&amp;ldquo;hundreds of exabytes&amp;rdquo; is a reasonable ballpark guess for how much RAM exists in
2023 (consider: 4 billion smartphones with 4GB each). More practically, the
largest quantity of RAM you can fit in a server blade is measured in terabytes
(much more than your measly eight DIMs on your gaming rig).&lt;p&gt;If we instead use one less bit, 63 bits, this halves the maximum representable
memory to nine exabytes. If we take another, it&amp;rsquo;s now four exabytes. Much more
memory than you will ever &lt;em&gt;ever&lt;/em&gt; want to stick in a string.
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_of_Wikipedia#Size_of_the_English_Wikipedia_database&gt;Wikpedia asserts&lt;/a&gt;
that Wikimedia Commons contains around 428 terabytes of media (the articles&#39;
text with history is a measly 10 TB).&lt;p&gt;Ah, but you say you&amp;rsquo;re programming for a 32-bit machine (today, this likely
means either a low-end mobile phone, an embedded micro controller, or WASM).&lt;p&gt;On a 32-bit machine it&amp;rsquo;s a little bit harrier: Now &lt;code&gt;usize&lt;/code&gt; is 32 bits, for a
maximum string size of 4 gigabytes (if you remember the 32-bit era, this limit
may sound familiar). &amp;ldquo;Gigabytes&amp;rdquo; is an amount of memory that you can actually
imagine having in a string.&lt;p&gt;Even then, 1 GB of memory (if we steal two bits) on a 32-bit machine is a lot of
data. You can only have four strings that big in a single address space, and
every 32-bit allocator in the universe will refuse to serve an allocation of
that size. If your strings are comparable in size to the whole address space,
you should build your own string type.&lt;p&gt;The upshot is that every &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;str&lt;/code&gt; contains two bits we can reasonably assume are
not used. &lt;em&gt;Free real-estate.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;h3 id=a-hand-written-niche-optimization&gt;&lt;a href=#a-hand-written-niche-optimization&gt;A Hand-Written Niche Optimization&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Rust has the concept of &lt;em&gt;niches&lt;/em&gt;, or invalid bit-patterns of a particular type,
which it uses for automatic layout optimization of &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt;s. For example,
references cannot be null, so the pointer bit-pattern of &lt;code&gt;0x0000_0000_0000_0000&lt;/code&gt;
is never used; this bit-pattern is called a &amp;ldquo;niche&amp;rdquo;. Consider:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;First&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Second&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;An &lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt; of this form will not need any &amp;ldquo;extra&amp;rdquo; space to store the value that
discriminates between the two variants: if a &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s bits are all zero, it&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;code&gt;Foo::Second&lt;/code&gt;; otherwise it&amp;rsquo;s a &lt;code&gt;Foo::First&lt;/code&gt; and the payload is formed from
&lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s bit-pattern. This, incidentally, is what makes &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;&amp;amp;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; a valid
representation for a &amp;ldquo;nullable pinter&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;There are more general forms of this: &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt; is represented as a single byte, of
which two bit are valid; the other 254 potential bit-patterns are niches. In
Recent versions of Rust, &lt;code&gt;RawFd&lt;/code&gt; has a niche for the all-ones bit-pattern, since
POSIX file descriptors are always non-negative &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt;s.&lt;p&gt;By stealing two bits off of the length, we have given ourselves four niches,
which essentially means we&amp;rsquo;ll have a hand-written version of something like this
&lt;code&gt;enum&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Yarn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The remaining two niches can be put to use for optimizing small strings.&lt;h2 id=small-string-optimization&gt;&lt;a href=#small-string-optimization&gt;Small String Optimization&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;C++&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;std::string&lt;/code&gt; also makes the &amp;ldquo;most strings are small&amp;rdquo; assumption. In the
&lt;code&gt;libc++&lt;/code&gt; implementation of the standard library, &lt;code&gt;std::string&lt;/code&gt;s of up to 23
bytes never hit the heap!&lt;p&gt;C++ implementations do this by using most of the pointer, length, and capacity
fields as a storage buffer for small strings, the so-called &amp;ldquo;small string
optimization&amp;rdquo; (SSO). In &lt;code&gt;libc++&lt;/code&gt;, in SSO mode, a &lt;code&gt;std::string&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s length fits in
one byte, so the other 23 bytes can be used as storage. The capacity isn&amp;rsquo;t
stored at all: an SSO string always has a capacity of 23.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;RawYarn&lt;/code&gt; still has another two niches, so let&amp;rsquo;s dedicate one to a &amp;ldquo;small&amp;rdquo;
representation. In small mode, the kind will be 2, and only the 16th byte will
be the length.&lt;p&gt;This is why we used the two &lt;em&gt;high&lt;/em&gt; bits of &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; for our scratch space: no
matter what mode it&amp;rsquo;s in, we can easily extract these bits&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. Some of
the existing &lt;code&gt;RawYarn&lt;/code&gt; methods need to be updated, though.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[repr(C)]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

a static lifetime, and we pass &lt;code&gt;STATIC&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;RawYarn::from_raw_parts()&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Because of how we&amp;rsquo;ve written all of the prior code, this does not require any
special support in &lt;code&gt;Yarn::immortalize()&lt;/code&gt; or in the low-level &lt;code&gt;RawYarn&lt;/code&gt; code.&lt;p&gt;The actual &lt;code&gt;byteyarn&lt;/code&gt; library provides a &lt;code&gt;yarn!()&lt;/code&gt; macro that has the same
syntax as &lt;code&gt;format!()&lt;/code&gt;. This is the primary way in which yarns are created. It is
has been carefully written so that &lt;code&gt;yarn!(&#34;this is a literal&#34;)&lt;/code&gt; always produces
a &lt;code&gt;STATIC&lt;/code&gt; string, rather than a heap-allocated string.&lt;h2 id=an-extra-niche-as-a-treat&gt;&lt;a href=#an-extra-niche-as-a-treat&gt;An extra niche, as a treat?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, because of how we&amp;rsquo;ve written it, &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;Yarn&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is 24 bytes, a
whole word larger than a &lt;code&gt;Yarn&lt;/code&gt;. However, there&amp;rsquo;s still a little gap where we
can fit the &lt;code&gt;None&lt;/code&gt; variant. It turns out that because of how we&amp;rsquo;ve chosen the
discriminants, &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; is zero if and only if it is an empty &lt;code&gt;BORROWED&lt;/code&gt; string.
But this is not the only zero: if the high byte is &lt;code&gt;0x80&lt;/code&gt;, this is an empty
&lt;code&gt;SMALL&lt;/code&gt; string. If we simply require that no other empty string is ever
constructed (by marking &lt;code&gt;RawYarn::from_raw_parts()&lt;/code&gt; as unsafe and specifying it
should not be passed a length of zero), we can guarantee that &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;em&gt;never&lt;/em&gt;
zero.&lt;p&gt;Thus, we can update &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; to be a &lt;code&gt;NonZeroUsize&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[repr(C)]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a type especially known to the Rust compiler to have a niche bit-pattern
of all zeros, which allows &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;Yarn&gt;&lt;/code&gt; to be 16 bytes too. This also has the
convenient property that the all zeros bit-pattern for &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;Yarn&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;None&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;a href=https://docs.rs/byteyarn/latest/byteyarn/&gt;&lt;code&gt;byteyarn&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; blurb describes what
we&amp;rsquo;ve built:&lt;blockquote id=ref:2 class=ref ref math&gt;&lt;a href=#ref:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;reference&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;Yarn&lt;/code&gt; is a highly optimized string type that provides a number of useful
properties over &lt;code&gt;String&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Always two pointers wide, so it is always passed into and out of functions
in registers.&lt;li&gt;Small string optimization (SSO) up to 15 bytes on 64-bit architectures.&lt;li&gt;Can be either an owned buffer or a borrowed buffer (like &lt;code&gt;Cow&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;li&gt;Can be upcast to &lt;code&gt;&#39;static&lt;/code&gt; lifetime if it was constructed from a
known-static string.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are, of course, some trade-offs. Not only do we need the assumptions we
made originally to hold, but we also need to relatively care more about memory
than cycle-count performance, since basic operations like reading the length of
the string require more math (but no extra branching).&lt;p&gt;The actual implementation of &lt;code&gt;Yarn&lt;/code&gt; is a bit more complicated, partly to keep
all of the low-level book-keeping in one place, and partly to offer an ergonomic
API that makes &lt;code&gt;Yarn&lt;/code&gt; into a mostly-drop-in replacement for &lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;str&gt;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;I hope this peek under the hood has given you a new appreciation for what can be
achieved by clever layout-hacking.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Allocators rarely serve you memory with precisely the size you asked for.
Instead, they will have some notion of a &amp;ldquo;size class&amp;rdquo; that allows them to
use more efficient allocation techniques,
&lt;a href=/2022/06/07/alkyne-gc&gt;which I have written about&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;As a result, if the size change in a &lt;code&gt;realloc()&lt;/code&gt; would not change the size
class, it becomes a no-op, especially if the allocator can take advantage of
the current-size information Rust provides it.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here and henceforth &amp;ldquo;character&amp;rdquo; means &amp;ldquo;32-bit Unicode scalar&amp;rdquo;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now, you might also point out that Rust and C do not allow an allocation
whose size is larger than the pointer offset type (&lt;code&gt;isize&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;ptrdiff_t&lt;/code&gt;,
respectively). In practice this means that the high bit is &lt;em&gt;always&lt;/em&gt; zero
according to the language&amp;rsquo;s own rules.&lt;p&gt;This is true, but we need to steal two bits, and I wanted to demonstrate
that this is an extremely reasonable desire. 64-bit integers are so
comically large.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Interestingly, LLVM will compile &lt;code&gt;(x &amp;lt;&amp;lt; 2) &gt;&gt; 2&lt;/code&gt; to&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-x86 highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;movabs&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x3fffffffffffffff&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;and&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rdi&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If we want to play the byte-for-byte game, this costs 14 bytes when encoded
in the Intel variable-length encoding. You would think that two shifts would
result in marginally smaller code, but no, since the input comes in in &lt;code&gt;rdi&lt;/code&gt;
and needs to wind up in &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;On RISC-V, though, it seems to decide that two shifts is in fact cheaper,
and will even optimize &lt;code&gt;x &amp; 0x3fff_ffff_ffff_ffff&lt;/code&gt; back into two shifts.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;This only works on little endian. Thankfully all computers are little
endian.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;Technically, a &lt;code&gt;&amp;&#39;static str&lt;/code&gt; may also point to leaked memory. For our
purposes, there is no essential difference.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>A Gentle Introduction to LLVM IR
</title>
    <link href="/2023/08/01/llvm-ir"/>
    <updated>2023-08-01T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2023/08/01/llvm-ir</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;The other day, I saw
&lt;a href=&#34;https://twitter.com/burntsushi5/status/1684204136571478021?s=20&#34;&gt;this tweet&lt;/a&gt;.
In it, Andrew Gallant argues that reaching for LLVM IR, instead of assembly, is
a useful tool for someone working on performance. Unfortunately, learning
material on LLVM is usually aimed at compiler engineers, not generalist working
programmers.&lt;p&gt;Now, &lt;em&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m&lt;/em&gt; a compiler engineer, so my answer is &lt;em&gt;of course&lt;/em&gt; you should know your
optimizer&amp;rsquo;s IR. But I do think there&amp;rsquo;s a legitimate reason to be able to read
it, in the same way that being able to read assembly to understand what your
processor is doing is a powerful tool. I wrote an
&lt;a href={{site.baseurl}}/2021/11/29/assembly-1&gt;introduction to assembly&lt;/a&gt; over a year
ago (still have to finish the followups&amp;mldr; 💀), which I recommend reading first.&lt;p&gt;Learning LLVM IR is similar, but it helps you understand what your &lt;em&gt;compiler&lt;/em&gt; is
doing to create highly optimized code. LLVM IR is very popular, and as such
well-documented and reasonably well-specified, to the point that we can just
treat it as a slightly weird programming language.&lt;p&gt;In this article, I want to dig into what LLVM IR &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; and how to read it.&lt;h2 id=whats-llvm-ir&gt;&lt;a href=#whats-llvm-ir&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s LLVM IR?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;LLVM&amp;rdquo; is an umbrella name for a number of software components that can be used
to build compilers. If you write performance-critical code, you&amp;rsquo;ve probably
heard of it.&lt;p&gt;Its flagship product is Clang, a high-end C/C++/Objective-C compiler. Clang
follows the orthodox compiler architecture: a frontend that parses source code
into an AST and lowers it into an &lt;em&gt;intermediate representation&lt;/em&gt;, an &amp;ldquo;IR&amp;rdquo;; an
optimizer (or &amp;ldquo;middle-end&amp;rdquo;) that transforms IR into better IR, and a backend
that converts IR into machine code for a particular platform.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-hide highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;                               optimizer (opt)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;                                    ___
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;                                   |   v
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;          .c file  --&amp;gt;  AST  --&amp;gt;  LLVM IR  --&amp;gt;  assembly
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;                    ^         ^             ^
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;                 parser    lowering    backend (llc)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;         \____________________/  \_____________________/
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;             Clang Frontend                LLVM
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM often also refers to just the optimizer and backend parts of Clang; this is
can be thought of as a compiler for the &amp;ldquo;LLVM language&amp;rdquo; or &amp;ldquo;LLVM assembly&amp;rdquo;.
Clang, and other language frontends like Rust, essentially compile to LLVM IR,
which LLVM then compiles to machine code.&lt;p&gt;LLVM IR is well documented and&amp;mldr; &lt;em&gt;somewhat&lt;/em&gt; stable, which makes it a very good
compilation target, since language implementers can re-use the thousands of
engineer hours poured into LLVM already. The source of truth for &amp;ldquo;what is LLVM
IR?&amp;rdquo; is the &lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html&gt;LangRef&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;LLVM IR is also binary format (sometimes called &amp;ldquo;bitcode&amp;rdquo;), although we will be
working exclusively with its text format (which uses the &lt;code&gt;.ll&lt;/code&gt; extension).&lt;p&gt;LLVM-targeting compilers will have debugging flags to make them emit IR instead
of their final output. For Clang, this is e.g. &lt;code&gt;clang++ -S -emit-llvm foo.cc&lt;/code&gt;,
while for Rust this is &lt;code&gt;rustc --emit=llvm-ir foo.rs&lt;/code&gt;. Godbolt will also respect
these options and correctly display LLVM IR output.&lt;h2 id=back-to-basic-blocks&gt;&lt;a href=#back-to-basic-blocks&gt;Back to Basic Blocks&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM IR can be quite intimidating to read, since it contains much more ancillary
information than an assembly dump. Consider this function:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button godbolt&#34; href=&#34;https://godbolt.org/clientstate/eyJzZXNzaW9ucyI6W3siY29tcGlsZXJzIjpbeyJpZCI6ImJldGEiLCJvcHRpb25zIjoiLS1lbWl0PWxsdm0taXIifV0sImlkIjoxLCJsYW5ndWFnZSI6InJ1c3QiLCJzb3VyY2UiOiJwdWIgZm4gc3F1YXJlKHg6IGkzMikgLVx1MDAzZSBpMzIge1xuICB4ICogeFxufVxuIn1dfQ==&#34;&gt;godbolt&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If you click on the &amp;ldquo;Godbolt&amp;rdquo; widget, it will take you to a Godbolt that lowers
it to LLVM IR. Most of that code is just metadata, but it&amp;rsquo;s really intimidating!&lt;p&gt;Starting from compiler output will have a steep difficulty curve, because we
have to face the full complexity of LLVM IR. For Rust, this will likely mean
encountering exception-handling, which is how panics are implemented, and
function attributes that forward Rust&amp;rsquo;s guarantees (e.g. non-null pointers) to
LLVM.&lt;p&gt;Instead, we&amp;rsquo;ll start by introducing the basic syntax of LLVM IR, and &lt;em&gt;then&lt;/em&gt;
we&amp;rsquo;ll tackle reading compiler output.&lt;h3 id=a-trivial-function&gt;&lt;a href=#a-trivial-function&gt;A Trivial Function&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The meat of LLVM IR is function definitions, introduced with a &lt;code&gt;define&lt;/code&gt;. There
is also &lt;code&gt;declare&lt;/code&gt;, which has exactly the same purpose as a function without a
body in C: it brings an external symbol into scope.&lt;p&gt;For example, the following function takes no arguments and returns immediately:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@do_nothing&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The return type of the function (&lt;code&gt;void&lt;/code&gt;) immediately follows the &lt;code&gt;define&lt;/code&gt;
keyword; the name of the function starts with an &lt;code&gt;@&lt;/code&gt;, which introduces us to the
concept of &lt;em&gt;sigils&lt;/em&gt;: every user-defined symbol starts with a sigil, indicating
what kind of symbol it is. &lt;code&gt;@&lt;/code&gt; is used for global and functions: things you can
take the address of (when used as a value, they are always &lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt;-typed).&lt;p&gt;The body of a function resembles assembly: a list of labels and instructions.
Unlike ordinary assembly, however, there are significant restrictions on the
structure of these instructions.&lt;p&gt;In this case, there is only one instruction: a &lt;code&gt;void&lt;/code&gt;-typed return. Unlike most
assembly languages, LLVM IR is strongly typed, and requires explicit type
annotations almost everywhere.&lt;p&gt;Here is another trivial function.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@do_not_call&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;unreachable&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This function will trigger undefined behavior upon being called: the
&lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt; instruction represents a codepath that the compiler can assume is
never executed; this is unlike e.g. the unimplemented &lt;code&gt;ud2&lt;/code&gt; instruction in x86,
which is guaranteed to issue a fault.&lt;p&gt;This is an important distinction between LLVM IR and an assembly language: some
operations are explicitly left undefined to leave room for potential
optimizations. For example, LLVM can reason that, because &lt;code&gt;@do_not_call&lt;/code&gt;
immediately triggers undefined behavior, all calls to &lt;code&gt;@do_not_call&lt;/code&gt; are also
unreachable (and propagate unreachability from there).&lt;h3 id=purely-scalar-code&gt;&lt;a href=#purely-scalar-code&gt;Purely Scalar Code&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s start with basic functions that only operate on integers. Consider the
following function, that squares a 32-bit integer:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;mul&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now our function takes arguments and has multiple instructions.&lt;p&gt;The argument is specified as &lt;code&gt;i32 %x&lt;/code&gt;. Names a &lt;code&gt;%&lt;/code&gt; sigil are sort of like local
variables, but with some restrictions that make them more optimization-friendly;
as we&amp;rsquo;ll see later, they&amp;rsquo;re not really &amp;ldquo;variable&amp;rdquo; at all. LLVM sometimes calls
them &lt;em&gt;registers&lt;/em&gt;; in a sense, LLVM IR is assembly for an abstract machine with
an infinite number of registers. I&amp;rsquo;ll be calling &lt;code&gt;%&lt;/code&gt;-prefixed names &amp;ldquo;registers&amp;rdquo;
throughout this article.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt; is a primitive integer types. All integer types in LLVM are of the form
&lt;code&gt;iN&lt;/code&gt;, for any &lt;code&gt;N&lt;/code&gt; (even non-multiples of eight). There are no signed or unsigned
types; instead, instructions that care about signedness will specify which
semantic they use.&lt;p&gt;The first instruction is a &lt;code&gt;mul i32&lt;/code&gt;, which multiples the two &lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt; operands
together, and returns a value; we assign this to the new register
&lt;code&gt;%1&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. The next instruction returns this value.&lt;p&gt;The other arithmetic operations have the names you expect: &lt;code&gt;add&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;sub&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;and&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;or&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;xor&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;shl&lt;/code&gt; (shift left). There are two division and remainder
instructions, signed (&lt;code&gt;sdiv&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;srem&lt;/code&gt;) and unsigned (&lt;code&gt;udiv&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;urem&lt;/code&gt;). There two
shift right instructions, again signed (&lt;code&gt;ashr&lt;/code&gt;) and unsigned (&lt;code&gt;lshr&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;blockquote id=tip:1 class=tip tip&gt;&lt;a href=#tip:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;tip&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Exercise for the reader: why are &lt;code&gt;/&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;%&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; the only operations with
signed and unsigned versions?&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;We can also convert from one integer type to another using &lt;code&gt;trunc&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;zext&lt;/code&gt;, and
&lt;code&gt;sext&lt;/code&gt;, which truncate, zero-extend, and sign-extend, respectively (&lt;code&gt;sext&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;zext&lt;/code&gt; are another signed/unsigned pair). For example, if we wanted the &lt;code&gt;square&lt;/code&gt;
function to never overflow, we could write&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;sext&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;to&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;mul&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here, we cast &lt;code&gt;%x&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;i64&lt;/code&gt; by sign-extension (since we&amp;rsquo;ve decided we&amp;rsquo;re
squaring signed integers) and then square the result. &lt;code&gt;trunc&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;zext&lt;/code&gt; both
have the same syntax as &lt;code&gt;sext&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h3 id=ill-be-back&gt;&lt;a href=#ill-be-back&gt;&amp;ldquo;I&amp;rsquo;ll Be Back&amp;rdquo;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course, interesting functions have &lt;em&gt;control flow&lt;/em&gt;. Suppose we want a safe
division function: division by zero is UB, so we need to handle it explicitly.
Perhaps something like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;safe_div&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;u64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;d&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;u64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;u64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;==&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u64&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;MAX&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;/&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;We could try doing this using &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;, LLVM&amp;rsquo;s &amp;ldquo;ternary&amp;rdquo; operation.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@safe_div&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;icmp&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;eq&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;udiv&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%d&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%3&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;select&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;-1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%3&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;However, this has a problem: division by zero is UB&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt; is not
short-circuiting: its semantics are closer to that of &lt;code&gt;cmov&lt;/code&gt; in x86.&lt;p&gt;To compile this correctly, need to use the &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; instruction, which represents a
general branch operation&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. In C terms, a
&lt;code&gt;br i1 %cond, label %a, label %b&lt;/code&gt; is equivalent to
&lt;code&gt;if (cond) goto a; else goto b;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This is how we might write that:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:9&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@safe_div&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;icmp&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;eq&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;br&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%iszero&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%nonzero&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;iszero:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;-1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;nonzero:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;udiv&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%d&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;%2&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:9&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now our function has labels, which are used by the &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; instruction as jump
targets.&lt;p&gt;In the first block, we do the &lt;code&gt;d == 0&lt;/code&gt; check, implemented by an &lt;code&gt;icmp eq&lt;/code&gt;
instruction. This returns an &lt;code&gt;i1&lt;/code&gt; (the type LLVM uses for booleans). We then
pass the result into a &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; instruction, which jumps to the first label if it&amp;rsquo;s
zero, otherwise to the second if it isn&amp;rsquo;t.&lt;p&gt;The second block is the early-return; it returns the &amp;ldquo;sentinel&amp;rdquo; value; the third
block is self-explanatory.&lt;p&gt;Each of these blocks is a &amp;ldquo;basic block&amp;rdquo;: a sequence of non-control flow
operations, plus an instruction that moves control flow away from the block.
These blocks form the control flow graph (CFG) of the function.&lt;p&gt;There are a few other &amp;ldquo;block terminator&amp;rdquo; instructions. The one-argument form of
&lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; takes a single label, and is a simple unconditional &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;. There&amp;rsquo;s also
&lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt;, which is similar to a C &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:10&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;switch&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%value&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%default&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%if_zero&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%if_one&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c&gt;; etc
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:10&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The type of the &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt; must be an integer type. Although you could represent
this operation with a chain of &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt;s, a separate &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt; instruction makes it
easier for LLVM to generate jump tables.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;, which we saw before, is a special terminator that does not
trigger control flow per se, but which can terminate a block because reaching it
is undefined behavior; it is equivalent to e.g. &lt;code&gt;std::unreachable()&lt;/code&gt; in C++.&lt;blockquote id=aside:1 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt; instruction provides a good example of why LLVM uses a basic
block CFG: a naive dead code elimination (DCE) optimization pass can be
implemented as follows:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Fill a set with every block that ends in &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;For every block, if its terminator references a block in the unreachable
set, delete that label from the terminator. For example, if we have
&lt;code&gt;br i1 %c, label %a, label %b&lt;/code&gt;, and the unreachable set contains &lt;code&gt;%a&lt;/code&gt;, we
can replace this with a &lt;code&gt;br label %b&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;If every outgoing edge from a block is deleted in (2), replace the
terminator with &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Delete all blocks in the unreachable set.&lt;li&gt;Repeat from (1) as many times as desired.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Intuitively, &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;s bubble &lt;em&gt;upwards&lt;/em&gt; in the CFG, dissolving parts of
the CFG among them. Other passes can generate &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;s to represent UB:
interplay between this and DCE results in the &amp;ldquo;the compiler &lt;em&gt;will&lt;/em&gt; delete your
code&amp;rdquo; outcome from UB.&lt;p&gt;The actual DCE pass is much more complicated, since function calls make it
harder to decide if a block is &amp;ldquo;pure&amp;rdquo; and thus transparently deletable.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;But, what if we want to implement something more complicated, like &lt;code&gt;a / b + 1&lt;/code&gt;?
This expression needs the intermediate result, so we can&amp;rsquo;t use two return
statements as before.&lt;p&gt;Working around this is not so straightforward: if we try to assign the same
register in different blocks, the IR verifier will complain. This brings us to
the concept of static single assignment.&lt;h3 id=phony-phony&gt;&lt;a href=#phony-phony&gt;Phony! Phony!&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM IR is a &lt;em&gt;static single assignment form&lt;/em&gt; (SSA) IR. LLVM was actually started
at the turn of the century to create a modern SSA optimizer as an academic
project. These days, SSA is extremely fashionable for optimizing imperative
code.&lt;p&gt;SSA form means that every register is assigned by at most one instruction per
function. Different executions of the same block in the same function may
produce different values for particular registers, but we cannot &lt;em&gt;mutate&lt;/em&gt;
already-assigned registers.&lt;p&gt;In other words:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Every register is guaranteed to be initialized by a single expression.&lt;li&gt;Every register depends only on the values of registers assigned before its
definition.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;This has many useful properties for writing optimizations: for example, within a
basic block, every use of a particular register &lt;code&gt;%x&lt;/code&gt; always refers to the same
value, which makes optimizations like
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_numbering&gt;global value numbering&lt;/a&gt; and
constant-folding much simpler to write, since the state of a register throughout
a block doesn&amp;rsquo;t need to be tracked separately.&lt;p&gt;In SSA, we reinterpret mutation as many &lt;em&gt;versions&lt;/em&gt; of a single variable. Thus,
we might lower &lt;code&gt;x += y&lt;/code&gt; as&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:11&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%x.1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;add&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x.0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%y.0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here, we&amp;rsquo;ve used a &lt;code&gt;var.n&lt;/code&gt; convention to indicate which version of a variable a
specific register represents (LLVM does not enforce any naming conventions).&lt;p&gt;However, when loops enter the mix, it&amp;rsquo;s not clear how to manage versions. The
number of registers in a function is static, but the number of loop iterations
is dynamic.&lt;p&gt;Concretely, how do we implement this function?&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;pow&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;r&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;But there&amp;rsquo;s a problem! What are the original definitions of &lt;code&gt;%r&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%i&lt;/code&gt;? The
IR verifier will complain that these registers depend directly on themselves,
which violates SSA form. What&amp;rsquo;s the &amp;ldquo;right&amp;rdquo; way to implement this function?&lt;p&gt;One option is to ask LLVM! We&amp;rsquo;ll implement the function poorly, and let the
optimizer clean it up for us.&lt;p&gt;First, let&amp;rsquo;s write the function using memory operations, like &lt;code&gt;load&lt;/code&gt;s and
&lt;code&gt;store&lt;/code&gt;s, to implement mutation. We can use the &lt;code&gt;alloca&lt;/code&gt; instruction to create
statically-sized stack slots; these instructions return a &lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt;[^clang-codegen].&lt;blockquote id=aside:2 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Incidentally, this is how Clang and Rust both generate LLVM IR: stack
variables are turned into &lt;code&gt;alloca&lt;/code&gt;s and manipulated through loads and stores;
temporaries are mostly turned into &lt;code&gt;%regs&lt;/code&gt;s, but the compiler will sometimes
emit extra allocas to avoid thinking too hard about needing to create &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;
instructions.&lt;p&gt;This is pretty convenient, because it avoids needing to think very hard about
SSA form outside of LLVM, and LLVM can trivially eliminate unnecessary
allocas. The code I wrote for the codegen of &lt;code&gt;@pow&lt;/code&gt; is very similar to what
Rust would send to LLVM (although because we used an iterator, there&amp;rsquo;s a lot
of extra junk Rust emits that LLVM has to work to eliminate).&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@pow&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
