&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;loop_start:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%i.0&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;phi&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%i.new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r.0&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;phi&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%r.new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%done&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;icmp&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;eq&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%i.0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%y&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;br&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%done&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%exit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%loop&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;loop:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r.new&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;mul&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r.0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%i.new&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;add&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%i.0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;br&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;label&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%loop_start&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;exit:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r.0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;alloca&lt;/code&gt;s are gone, but now we&amp;rsquo;re faced with a new instruction: &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;. &amp;ldquo;φ
node&amp;rdquo; is jargon from the original SSA paper; the greek letter φ means &amp;ldquo;phoney&amp;rdquo;.
These instructions select a value from a list based on which basic block we
jumped to the block from.&lt;p&gt;For example, &lt;code&gt;phi i32 [0, %start], [%i.new, %loop]&lt;/code&gt; says &amp;ldquo;this value should be 0
if we came from the &lt;code&gt;start&lt;/code&gt; block; otherwise &lt;code&gt;%i.new&lt;/code&gt; if it came from &lt;code&gt;%loop&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;Unlike all other instructions, &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt; can refer to values that are not defined in
all blocks that dominate the current block. This lets us have a dynamic number
of versions of a variable! Here&amp;rsquo;s what that looks like in a dynamic execution
context.&lt;blockquote id=tip:2 class=tip tip&gt;&lt;a href=#tip:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;tip&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;A block &lt;code&gt;%a&lt;/code&gt; is said to dominate a block &lt;code&gt;%b&lt;/code&gt; if each of its predecessors is
either &lt;code&gt;%a&lt;/code&gt; or a block dominated by &lt;code&gt;%a&lt;/code&gt;. In other words, every path from the
first block to &lt;code&gt;%b&lt;/code&gt; passes through &lt;code&gt;%a&lt;/code&gt;. In general instructions can only
refer to values defined in previous instructions in the current block or
values from blocks that dominate it.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;%start&lt;/code&gt; directly jumps into &lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt;. The first block cannot be a jump
target, since it cannot have &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt; nodes because its predecessors include
function&amp;rsquo;s callsite.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;In &lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt;, since we&amp;rsquo;ve entered from &lt;code&gt;%start&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;%i.0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%r.0&lt;/code&gt; are
selected to be the first versions of the (platonic) &lt;code&gt;i&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;r&lt;/code&gt; variables,
i.e., their initial values; we jump to &lt;code&gt;%loop&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Then, &lt;code&gt;%loop&lt;/code&gt; is dominated by &lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt; so we can use &lt;code&gt;%i.0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%r.0&lt;/code&gt;
there directly; these are the &lt;code&gt;*=&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;+=&lt;/code&gt; operations. Then we jump back to
&lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Back in &lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt;, the &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;s now select &lt;code&gt;%i.new&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%r.new&lt;/code&gt;, so now
&lt;code&gt;%i.0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%r.0&lt;/code&gt; are the &lt;em&gt;second&lt;/em&gt; versions of &lt;code&gt;i&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;r&lt;/code&gt;. By induction, the
nth execution of &lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt; has the nth versions of &lt;code&gt;i&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;r&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;When we finally get sent to &lt;code&gt;%exit&lt;/code&gt;, we can use &lt;code&gt;%r.0&lt;/code&gt; (since &lt;code&gt;%loop_start&lt;/code&gt;
dominates &lt;code&gt;%r.0&lt;/code&gt;), which will be the &lt;code&gt;%y&lt;/code&gt;th version of &lt;code&gt;r&lt;/code&gt;; this is our
return value.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a good place to stop and think about what we&amp;rsquo;ve done so far. SSA,
domination, and &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;s can be hard to wrap your head around, and are not
absolutely necessary for reading most IR. However, it is absolutely worth trying
to understand, because it captures essential facts about how compilers like to
reason about code&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;With &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt;, we can build arbitrarily complicated control flow within a
function&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;h2 id=types-and-aggregates&gt;&lt;a href=#types-and-aggregates&gt;Types and Aggregates&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now that we have basic scalar functions, let&amp;rsquo;s review LLVM&amp;rsquo;s type system.&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;ve seen &lt;code&gt;i32&lt;/code&gt; and its friends; these are arbitrary-bit-with integers. &lt;code&gt;i1&lt;/code&gt; is
special because it is used as the boolean type. LLVM optimizations have been
known to generate integer types with non-power-of-two sizes.&lt;p&gt;LLVM also has &lt;code&gt;float&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;double&lt;/code&gt;, and some exotic float types like &lt;code&gt;bfloat&lt;/code&gt;;
these use their own arithmetic instructions with different options. I&amp;rsquo;ll pass on
them in this explainer; see &lt;code&gt;fadd&lt;/code&gt; and friends in the
&lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html&gt;LangRef&lt;/a&gt; for more.&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;ve also seen &lt;code&gt;void&lt;/code&gt;, which is only used as a return value, and &lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt;, which
is an untyped&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; pointer.&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;ve also seen the &lt;code&gt;label&lt;/code&gt; pseudo-type, which represents a block label. It does
not appear directly at runtime and has limited uses; the &lt;code&gt;token&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;metadata&lt;/code&gt;
types are similar.&lt;p&gt;Arrays are spelled &lt;code&gt;[n x T]&lt;/code&gt;; the number must be an integer and the type must
have a definite size. E.g., &lt;code&gt;[1024 x i8]&lt;/code&gt;. Zero-sized arrays are supported.&lt;p&gt;Structs are spelled &lt;code&gt;{T1, T2, ...}&lt;/code&gt;. E.g., &lt;code&gt;{i64, ptr}&lt;/code&gt; is a Rust slice. Struct
fields do not have names and are indexed, instead. The form &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;{...}&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is a
&lt;em&gt;packed&lt;/em&gt; struct, which removes inter-field padding. E.g. &lt;code&gt;#[repr(packed)]&lt;/code&gt;
compiles down to this.&lt;p&gt;Vectors are like arrays but spelled &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;n x T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. These are used to represent types
used in SIMD operations. For example, adding two &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;4 x i32&gt;&lt;/code&gt; would lower to an
AVX2 vector add on x86. I will not touch on SIMD stuff beyond this, although at
higher optimization levels LLVM will merge scalar operations into vector
operations, so you may come across them.&lt;p&gt;Type aliases can be created at file scope with the syntax&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%Slice&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This means that &lt;code&gt;%T&lt;/code&gt; can be either a type or a register/label inside of a
function, depending on syntactic position.&lt;h3 id=operations-on-aggregates&gt;&lt;a href=#operations-on-aggregates&gt;Operations on Aggregates&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;insertvalue&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;extractvalue&lt;/code&gt; can be used with struct or array types to
statically access a field. For example,&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%MyStruct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=m&gt;5&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;; In Rust-like syntax, this is `let v = s.1.0[4];`
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;extractvalue&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%MyStruct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%s&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;insertvalue&lt;/code&gt; is the reverse: it produces a copy of the aggregate with a
specific field changed. It &lt;em&gt;does not&lt;/em&gt; mutate in-place, because SSA forbids that.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;; In Rust-like syntax, this is
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;;   let s2 = { let mut s = s; s2.1.1 = 42; s };
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%s2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;insertvalue&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%MyStruct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%s&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;42&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are similar operations called &lt;code&gt;insertelement&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;extractelement&lt;/code&gt; work on
vectors, but have slightly different syntax and semantics.&lt;p&gt;Finally, there&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;getelementptr&lt;/code&gt;, the &amp;ldquo;pointer arithmetic instruction&amp;rdquo;, often
abbreviated to GEP. A GEP can be used to calculate an offset pointer into a
struct. For example,&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;define&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@get_inner_in_array&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%idx&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nv&gt;%q&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;getelementptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%MyStruct&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%idx&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=m&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%q&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:19&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This function takes in a pointer, ostensibly pointing to an array of
&lt;code&gt;%MyStruct&lt;/code&gt;s, and an index. This returns a pointer to the &lt;code&gt;i64&lt;/code&gt; field of the
&lt;code&gt;%idx&lt;/code&gt;th element of &lt;code&gt;%p&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A few important differences between GEP and &lt;code&gt;extractvalue&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;It takes an untyped pointer instead of a value of a particular struct/array
type.&lt;li&gt;There is an extra parameter that specifies an index; from the perspective of
GEP, every pointer is a pointer to an array of unspecified bound. When
operating on a pointer that does not (at runtime) point to an array, an index
operand of &lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt; is still required. (Alternatively, you can view a pointer to
&lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; as being a pointer to a one-element array.)&lt;li&gt;The index parameters need explicit types.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM provides a helpful&lt;sup id=fnref:8&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:8 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;8&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; FAQ on the GEP instruction:
&lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/GetElementPtr.html&gt;https://llvm.org/docs/GetElementPtr.html&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;h2 id=other-operations&gt;&lt;a href=#other-operations&gt;Other Operations&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Some other operations are very relevant for reading IR, but don&amp;rsquo;t fit into any
specific category. As always, the &lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html&gt;LangRef&lt;/a&gt;
provides a full description of what all of these instructions do.&lt;h3 id=function-calls&gt;&lt;a href=#function-calls&gt;Function Calls&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt;, which calls any &lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt; as a function. For example:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:20&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;; Arguments are passed in parentheses.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%r&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;call&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@my_func&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:20&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Note that this could have been a &lt;code&gt;%reg&lt;/code&gt; instead of a &lt;code&gt;@global&lt;/code&gt;, which indicates
a function pointer call.&lt;p&gt;Sometimes you will see &lt;code&gt;invoke&lt;/code&gt;, which is used to implement &amp;ldquo;call a function
inside of a C++ &lt;code&gt;try {}&lt;/code&gt; block&amp;rdquo;. This is rare in Rust, but can occur in some C++
code.&lt;p&gt;Function calls are often noisy areas of IR, because they will be very heavily
annotated.&lt;h3 id=synchronization&gt;&lt;a href=#synchronization&gt;Synchronization&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;load&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;store&lt;/code&gt; instructions we&amp;rsquo;ve already seen can be annotated as
&lt;code&gt;atomic&lt;/code&gt;, which is used to implement e.g. &lt;code&gt;AtomicU32::load&lt;/code&gt; in Rust; this
requires that an atomic ordering be specified, too. E.g.,&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:21&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%v&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;load&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;atomic&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%p&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;acquire&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:21&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;fence&lt;/code&gt; operation is a general memory fence operation corresponding to e.g.
Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;std::sync::atomic::fence&lt;/code&gt; function.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;cmpxchg&lt;/code&gt; provides the CAS (compare-and-swap) primitive. It returns a &lt;code&gt;{T, i1}&lt;/code&gt;
containing the old value and whether the CAS succeeded. &lt;code&gt;cmpxchg weak&lt;/code&gt;
implements the spuriously-failing &amp;ldquo;weak CAS&amp;rdquo; primitive.&lt;p&gt;Finally, &lt;code&gt;atomicrmw&lt;/code&gt; performs a read-modify-write (e.g., &lt;code&gt;*p = op(*p, val)&lt;/code&gt;)
atomically. This is used to implement things like &lt;code&gt;AtomicU32::fetch_add&lt;/code&gt; and
friends.&lt;p&gt;All of these operations, except for &lt;code&gt;fence&lt;/code&gt;, can also be marked as &lt;code&gt;volatile&lt;/code&gt;.
In LLVM IR, much like in Rust but unlike in C/C++, individual loads and stores
are volatile (i.e., have compiler-invisible side-effects). &lt;code&gt;volatile&lt;/code&gt; &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt; be
combined with atomic operations (e.g. &lt;code&gt;load atomic volatile&lt;/code&gt;), although most
languages don&amp;rsquo;t provide access to these (except older C++ versions).&lt;h3 id=reinterpret-shenanigans&gt;&lt;a href=#reinterpret-shenanigans&gt;Reinterpret Shenanigans&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;bitcast&lt;/code&gt; is what &lt;code&gt;mem::transmute&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;reinterpret_cast&lt;/code&gt; in Rust and C++,
respectively, ultimately compile into. It can convert any non-aggregate type
(integers, vectors) to any other type of the same bit width. For example, it can
be used to get at the bits of a floating-point value:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:22&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nv&gt;%bits&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;bitcast&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;double&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%fp&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;to&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:22&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;It also used to be what was used to cast pointer types (e.g. &lt;code&gt;i32*&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;i8*&lt;/code&gt;).
Pointers are now all untyped (&lt;code&gt;ptr&lt;/code&gt;) so this use is no longer present.&lt;p&gt;However, &lt;code&gt;bitcast&lt;/code&gt; cannot cast between pointer and integer data. For this we
must use the &lt;code&gt;inttoptr&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;ptrtoint&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:9&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:9 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;9&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; instructions. These have the same
syntax, but interact with the sketchy semantics of pointer-to-integer conversion
and pointer provenance. This part of LLVM&amp;rsquo;s semantics is a bit of an ongoing
trashfire; see
&lt;a href=https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2020/12/14/provenance.html&gt;Ralf Jung&amp;rsquo;s post&lt;/a&gt; for an
introduction to this problem.&lt;h3 id=intrinsics&gt;&lt;a href=#intrinsics&gt;Intrinsics&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is also a vast collection of LLVM intrinsics, which are specified in the
&lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html&gt;LangRef&lt;/a&gt;. For example, if we need a
particular built-in memcpy, we can bring it into scope with a &lt;code&gt;declare&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:23&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;; ptr %dst, ptr %src, i64 %len, i1 %volatile
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;declare&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;@llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i64&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:23&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;All of the LLVM intrinsics are functions that start with &lt;code&gt;llvm.&lt;/code&gt;; diving into
all of them is far beyond what we can do here.&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m also leaving out discussion of floating point, SIMD, and exception handling,
each of which would require their own articles!&lt;h2 id=undefined-behavior&gt;&lt;a href=#undefined-behavior&gt;Undefined Behavior&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM exists to generate optimized code, and optimizations require that we
declare certain machine states &amp;ldquo;impossible&amp;rdquo;, so that we can detect when we can
simplify what the programmer has said. This is &amp;ldquo;undefined behavior&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;For example, we&amp;rsquo;ve already encountered &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;, which LLVM assumes cannot
be executed. Division by zero and accessing memory out of bounds is also
undefined.&lt;p&gt;Most LLVM UB factors through the concept of &amp;ldquo;poisoned values&amp;rdquo;. A poison value
can be thought of as &amp;ldquo;taking on every value at once&amp;rdquo;, whichever is convenient
for the current optimization pass with no respect to any other passes. This also
means that if optimizations &lt;em&gt;don&amp;rsquo;t&lt;/em&gt; detect a use of poison, it is ok from LLVM&amp;rsquo;s
perspective to give you a garbage value. This is most visible at &lt;code&gt;-O0&lt;/code&gt;, which
performs minimal optimization.&lt;p&gt;Using a poison value as a pointer in a &lt;code&gt;load&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;store&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt; must be UB,
because LLVM can choose it to be a null pointer. It also can&amp;rsquo;t be the
denominator of a &lt;code&gt;udiv&lt;/code&gt; or similar, because LLVM can choose it to be zero, which
is UB. Passing poison into a &lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; or a &lt;code&gt;switch&lt;/code&gt; is also defined to be UB.&lt;p&gt;LLVM can perform dataflow analysis to try to determine what operations a
poisonous value that was used in a UB way came from, and thus assume those
operations cannot produce poison. Because all operations (other than &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt;
and &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;) with a poison input produce poison, backwards reasoning allows LLVM
to propagate UB forward. This is where so-called &amp;ldquo;time traveling UB&amp;rdquo; comes from.&lt;p&gt;Many operations generate poison. For example, in C, signed overflow is UB, so
addition lowers to an &lt;code&gt;add nsw&lt;/code&gt; (&lt;code&gt;nsw&lt;/code&gt; stands for no signed wrap). Instead of
wrapping on overflow, the instruction produces poison. There is also an unsigned
version of the annotation, &lt;code&gt;nuw&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Many other operations have &amp;ldquo;less defined&amp;rdquo; versions, which are either generated
by optimizations, or inserted directly by the compiler that invokes LLVM when
the language rules allow it (see C above). More examples include:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;udiv&lt;/code&gt; and friends have an &lt;code&gt;exact&lt;/code&gt; annotation, which requires that the
division have a zero remainder, else poison.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;getelementptr&lt;/code&gt; has an &lt;code&gt;inbounds&lt;/code&gt; annotation, which produces poison if the
access is actually out of bounds. This changes it from a pure arithmetic
operation to one more closely matching C&amp;rsquo;s pointer arithmetic restrictions.
GEP without &lt;code&gt;inbounds&lt;/code&gt; corresponds to Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;*mut T&gt;::wrapping_offset()&lt;/code&gt;
function.&lt;li&gt;Floating point operations marked with &lt;code&gt;nnan&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;ninf&lt;/code&gt; will produce poison
instead of a NaN or an infinite value, respectively (or when a NaN or infinity
is an argument).&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;Creating poison is &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; UB; only using it is. This is weaker than the way UB
works in most languages; in C, overflow is instantly UB, but in LLVM overflow
that is never &amp;ldquo;witnessed&amp;rdquo; is simply ignored. This is a simpler operational
semantics for reasoning about the validity of optimizations: UB must often be
viewed as a side-effect, because the compiler will generate code that puts the
program into a broken state. For example, division by zero will cause a fault in
many architectures. This means UB-causing operations cannot always be reordered
soundly. Replacing &amp;ldquo;causes UB&amp;rdquo; with &amp;ldquo;produces poison&amp;rdquo; ensures the vast majority
of operations are pure and freely reorderable.&lt;h2 id=reading-some-codegen&gt;&lt;a href=#reading-some-codegen&gt;Reading Some Codegen&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s go back to our original Rust example!&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:24&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;attributes&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;#0&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;nonlazybind&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;uwtable&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;attributes&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;#1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;nocallback&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;no&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;free&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;nosyn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;c&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;nounwind&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;speculatable&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;willreturn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;memory&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;none&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;attributes&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;#2&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;nocallback&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;no&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;free&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;nosyn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;c&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;nounwind&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;willreturn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=err&gt;memory&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;none&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;attributes&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=vg&gt;#3&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;cold&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;noinline&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;noreturn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;nonlazybind&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;uwtable&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:25&gt;LLVM IR&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The main function is &lt;code&gt;@_ZN7example6square17hb32bcde4463f37c3E&lt;/code&gt;, which is the
mangled name of &lt;code&gt;example::square&lt;/code&gt;. Because this code was compiled in debug mode,
overflow panics, so we need to generate code for that. The first operation is a
&lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt; to the LLVM intrinsic for &amp;ldquo;multiply and tell us if it overflowed&amp;rdquo;. This
returns the equivalent of a &lt;code&gt;(i32, bool)&lt;/code&gt;; we extract both value out of it with
&lt;code&gt;extractvalue&lt;/code&gt;. We then pass the bool through &lt;code&gt;@llvm.expect&lt;/code&gt;, which is used to
tell the optimizer to treat the panicking branch as &amp;ldquo;cold&amp;rdquo;. The success branch
goes to a return, which returns the product; otherwise, we go to a function that
calls &lt;code&gt;core::panicking::panic()&lt;/code&gt; to panic the current thread. This function
never returns, so we can terminate the block with an &lt;code&gt;unreachable&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The rest of the file consists of:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;declare&lt;/code&gt;s for the llvm intrinsics we used.&lt;li&gt;A &lt;code&gt;declare&lt;/code&gt; for &lt;code&gt;core::panicking::panic&lt;/code&gt;. Any external function we call needs
to be &lt;code&gt;declare&lt;/code&gt;d. This also gives us a place to hang attributes for the
function off of.&lt;li&gt;Global constants for a &lt;code&gt;core::panic::Location&lt;/code&gt; and a panic message.&lt;li&gt;Attributes for the functions above.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a good place to mention attributes: LLVM has all kinds of attributes
that can be placed on functions (and function calls) to record
optimization-relevant information. For example, &lt;code&gt;@llvm.expect.i1&lt;/code&gt; is annotated
as &lt;code&gt;willreturn&lt;/code&gt;, which means this function will eventually return; this means
that, for example, any UB that comes after the function is guaranteed to occur
after finite time, so LLVM can conclude that the code is unreachable despite the
call to &lt;code&gt;@llvm.expect.i1&lt;/code&gt;. The full set of attributes is vast, but the
&lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html&gt;LangRef&lt;/a&gt; documents all of them!&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;LLVM IR is huge, bigger than any individual ISA, because it is intended to
capture &lt;em&gt;every&lt;/em&gt; interesting operation. It also has a rich annotation language,
so passes can record information for future passes to make use of. Its
operational semantics attempt to leave enough space for optimizations to occur,
while ensuring that multiple sound optimizations in sequence are not unsound
(this last part is a work in progress).&lt;p&gt;Being able to read assembly reveals what will happen, exactly, when code is
executed, but reading IR, before and after optimization, shows how the compiler
is &lt;em&gt;thinking&lt;/em&gt; about your code. Using &lt;code&gt;opt&lt;/code&gt; to run individual optimization passes
can also help further this understanding (in fact, &amp;ldquo;bisecting on passes&amp;rdquo; is a
powerful debugging technique in compiler development).&lt;p&gt;I got into compilers by reading LLVM IR. Hopefully this article inspires you to
learn more, too!&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Registers within a function may have a numeric name. They must be defined in
order: you must define &lt;code&gt;%0&lt;/code&gt; (either as a register or a label), then &lt;code&gt;%1&lt;/code&gt;,
then &lt;code&gt;%2&lt;/code&gt;, etc. These are often used to represent &amp;ldquo;temporary results&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;If a function does not specify names for its parameters, they will be given
the names &lt;code&gt;%0&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;%1&lt;/code&gt;, etc implicitly, which affect what the first explicit
numeric register name you can use is. Similarly, if the function does not
start with a label, it will be implicitly be given the next numeric name.&lt;p&gt;This can result in significant confusion, because if we have
&lt;code&gt;define void @foo(i32, i32) { ... }&lt;/code&gt;, the arguments will be &lt;code&gt;%0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%1&lt;/code&gt;,
but if we tried to write &lt;code&gt;%2 = add i32 %0, %1&lt;/code&gt;, we would get an extremely
confusing parser error, because &lt;code&gt;%2&lt;/code&gt; is already taken as the name of the
first block.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;For some reason, the optimizer can&amp;rsquo;t figure out that the &lt;code&gt;select&lt;/code&gt; is
redundant? Alive2 (an SMT-solver correctness checker for optimizations)
&lt;a href=https://alive2.llvm.org/ce/z/7nLDRe&gt;seems to agree&lt;/a&gt; this is a valid
optimization.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/64240&gt;So I&amp;rsquo;ve filed a bug.&lt;/a&gt; :D&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;If you read my assembly article, you&amp;rsquo;ll recall that there are many branch
instructions. On RV, we have &lt;code&gt;beq&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;bne&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;bgt&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;bge&lt;/code&gt;. Later on in the
compilation process, after the optimizer runs, LLVM will perform
&lt;em&gt;instruction selection&lt;/em&gt; (isel) to choose the best machine instruction(s) to
implement a particular LLVM instruction (or sequence), which is highly
context-dependent: for example, we want to fuse an &lt;code&gt;icmp eq&lt;/code&gt; followed by a
&lt;code&gt;br&lt;/code&gt; on the result into a &lt;code&gt;beq&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Isel is far outside my wheelhouse, and doing it efficiently and profitably
is an active area of academic research.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Not exactly the same: language frontends like Clang and Rust will perform
their own optimizations. For example, I have an
&lt;a href=https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/59484&gt;open bug&lt;/a&gt; for LLVM being
unable to convert &lt;code&gt;&amp;&amp;&lt;/code&gt; into &lt;code&gt;&amp;&lt;/code&gt; in some cases; this was never noticed,
because Clang performs this optimization while lowering from C/C++ to LLVM,
but Rust does not do the equivalent optimization.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;A more intuitive model is used in more modern IRs, like MLIR. In MLIR, you
cannot use variables defined in other blocks; instead, each block takes a
set of &lt;em&gt;arguments&lt;/em&gt;, just like a function call. This is equivalent to &lt;code&gt;phi&lt;/code&gt;
instructions, except that now instead of selecting which value we want in
the target, each predecessor specifies what it wants to send to the target.&lt;p&gt;If we instead treat each block as having &amp;ldquo;arguments&amp;rdquo;, we can rewrite it in
the following fantasy syntax where register names are scoped to their block.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:26&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ll highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c&gt;;; Not actual LLVM IR! ;;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;br&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i1&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%done&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%exit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=err&gt;loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%i&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nv&gt;%r&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;$ dot -Tsvg .parse_hex.dot -o parse_hex.svg

various CFG cleanups).&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=/assets/images/cfg-svg/parse_hex_unopt.svg alt&gt;&lt;figcaption&gt;&lt;p&gt;A worse one.&lt;/figcaption&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Exercise: try to trace through what each basic block is doing. You will want
to open the SVGs in a separate tab to do that. I recommend following the
optimized version, since it is much less noisy.&lt;p&gt;Comparing optimized vs. unoptimized is a good way to see how much the
compiler does to simplify the stuff the language frontend gives it. At -O0?
All allocas. At -O2? No allocas!&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;Once upon a time we had typed pointers, like &lt;code&gt;i32*&lt;/code&gt;. These turned out to
generate more problems than they solved, requiring frequent casts in IR in
exchange for mediocre type safety. See
&lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/OpaquePointers.html&gt;https://llvm.org/docs/OpaquePointers.html&lt;/a&gt; for a more complete history.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:8&gt;&lt;p&gt;Sarcasm.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:8 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:9&gt;&lt;p&gt;I quietly judge LLVM for having instructions named &lt;code&gt;inttoptr&lt;/code&gt; when &lt;code&gt;int2ptr&lt;/code&gt;
just reads so much nicer.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>

    <title>Single Abstract Method Traits</title>
    <link href="/2023/05/11/sam-closures"/>
    <updated>2023-05-11T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2023/05/11/sam-closures</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Rust and C++ both have very similar operational semantics for their &amp;ldquo;anonymous
function&amp;rdquo; expressions (they call them &amp;ldquo;closures&amp;rdquo; and &amp;ldquo;lambdas&amp;rdquo; respectively; I
will use these interchangably). Here&amp;rsquo;s what those expressions look like.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;square&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;[](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The type of &lt;code&gt;square&lt;/code&gt; in both versions is an anonymous type that holds the
captures for that closure. In C++, this type provides an &lt;code&gt;operator()&lt;/code&gt; member
that can be used to call it, wheras in Rust, it implements &lt;code&gt;FnOnce&lt;/code&gt; (and
possibly &lt;code&gt;FnMut&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;Fn&lt;/code&gt;, depending on the captures), which represent a
&amp;ldquo;callable&amp;rdquo; object.&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;For the purposes of this article, I am going to regard &amp;ldquo;function item values&amp;rdquo;
as being identical to closures that explicitly specify their inputs and
outputs for all intents and purposes. This is not completely accurate, because
when I write &lt;code&gt;let x = drop;&lt;/code&gt;, the resulting object is generic, but whenever I
say &amp;ldquo;a closure&amp;rdquo; in Rust, I am also including these closure-like types too.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is one thing C++ closures can express which Rust closures can&amp;rsquo;t: you can&amp;rsquo;t
create a &amp;ldquo;generic&amp;rdquo; closure in Rust. In particular, in C++ we can write this
code.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;template&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typename&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Fn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size_t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;CallMany&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;std&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;vector&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;})&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;std&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;foo&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;));&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;CallMany&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;([](&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;val&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;val&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;});&lt;/span&gt;

it. A very handy one is an &lt;em&gt;anonymous class&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s suppose I want to pass a callback into something. In Java 6, which I grew
up on, you did it like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-java highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;public&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kd&gt;interface&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Callback&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;run&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;arg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;public&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;runMyThing&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Callback&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;cb&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;cb&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;run&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;42&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=kd&gt;public&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;run&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;arg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;arg&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;arg&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;});&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Java&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;new Interface() {...}&lt;/code&gt; syntax mints a new class on the spot that implements
&lt;code&gt;Interface&lt;/code&gt;. You provide a standard class body between the braces, after the
name of the type. You can also do this with a class type too.&lt;p&gt;Now, this is a bit tedious: I need to re-type the signature of the one method.
This is fine if I need to implement a bunch of methods, but it&amp;rsquo;s a little
annoying in the one-method case.&lt;p&gt;In Java 8 we got lambdas (syntax: &lt;code&gt;x -&gt; expr&lt;/code&gt;). Java made the interesting choice
of not adding a &lt;code&gt;Function&lt;/code&gt; type to be &amp;ldquo;the type of lambdas&amp;rdquo;. For a long time I
thought this was a weird cop-out but I have since come to regard it as a
masterclass in language design.&lt;p&gt;Instead, Java&amp;rsquo;s lambdas are a sort of syntax sugar over this anonymous class
syntax.&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; Instead, you need to assign a lambda to an interface
type with a single abstract method, and it will use the body of the lambda to
implement that one method.&lt;p&gt;Interfaces compatible with lambdas are called single abstract method (SAM)
interfaces.&lt;p&gt;So, without needing to touch the existing library, I can turn the &lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt; syntax
into this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-java highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;runMyThing&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Java&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;chef&amp;rsquo;s kiss&lt;/em&gt;&lt;p&gt;Mind, Java &lt;em&gt;does&lt;/em&gt; provide a mess of &amp;ldquo;standard function interfaces&amp;rdquo; in the
&lt;code&gt;java.util.functional&lt;/code&gt; package, and quite a bit of the standard library uses
them, but they don&amp;rsquo;t need to express the totality of functions you might want to
capture as objects.&lt;p&gt;These &amp;ldquo;SAM closures&amp;rdquo; give closures a powerful &amp;ldquo;BYO interface&amp;rdquo; aspect. Lambdas in
Java are not &amp;ldquo;function objects&amp;rdquo;, they are extremely lightweight anonymous
classes the pertinent interface.&lt;p&gt;I think this can let us cut the gordian knot of generic closures in Rust.&lt;h2 id=sam-in-rust&gt;&lt;a href=#sam-in-rust&gt;SAM in Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;In what remains I will propose how we can extend the traits that closures
implement to be &lt;em&gt;any&lt;/em&gt; SAM trait, in addition to the traits they implement ipso
facto.&lt;p&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s a SAM trait in Rust? It&amp;rsquo;s any trait &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; with precisely ONE method that
does not have a default implementation, which must satisfy the following
constraints:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;It must have a &lt;code&gt;self&lt;/code&gt; parameter with type &lt;code&gt;Self&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;Self&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut Self&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;It does not mention &lt;code&gt;Self&lt;/code&gt; in any part of its argument types, its return
type, or its &lt;code&gt;where&lt;/code&gt; clauses, except for the aforementioned &lt;code&gt;self&lt;/code&gt; parameter.&lt;li&gt;Has no associated consts and no GATs.&lt;li&gt;All of its supertraits are &lt;code&gt;Copy&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;Send&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;Sync&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;These restrictions are chosen so that we have a shot at actually implementing
the entire trait.&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;In addition to the &lt;code&gt;Fn&lt;/code&gt; traits, ordinary closures automatically implement
&lt;code&gt;Clone&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;Copy&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;Send&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;Sync&lt;/code&gt; as appropriate.&lt;p&gt;None of these traits are SAM, so we can safely allow them to be automatically
derived for SAM closures to, under the same rules as for ordinary closures.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;To request a SAM closure, I will use the tentative syntax of
&lt;code&gt;impl Trait |args| expr&lt;/code&gt;. This syntax is unambiguously an expression rather than
an &lt;code&gt;impl&lt;/code&gt; item, because a &lt;code&gt;|&lt;/code&gt; cannot appear in a path-in-type, and &lt;code&gt;impl $path&lt;/code&gt;
must be followed by &lt;code&gt;{&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;for&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;where&lt;/code&gt;. The precise syntax is unimportant.&lt;p&gt;Applied to the &lt;code&gt;call_many&lt;/code&gt; example above, we get this.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;call_many&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;f&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Callback&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt;. We also need to verify that this trait&amp;rsquo;s captures are compatible with an
&lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;self&lt;/code&gt; receiver The same rules for when a trait implements &lt;code&gt;Fn&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;FnMut&lt;/code&gt;, and

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T2&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// What should this print?
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:23&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;If the type of &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; implements &lt;code&gt;T2&lt;/code&gt; directly, we print &lt;code&gt;&#34;hello&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, but if we
decide it implements &lt;code&gt;T1&lt;/code&gt; instead, it doesn&amp;rsquo;t, because we get the blanket impl.
If it decides it should implement both&amp;mldr; we get a coherence violation.&lt;p&gt;Currently, rustc does not have to produce impls &amp;ldquo;on demand&amp;rdquo;; the trait solver
has a finite set of impls to look at. What we are asking the trait solver to do
is to, for certain types, attempt to reify impls based on &lt;em&gt;usage&lt;/em&gt;. I.e., I have
my opaque closure type &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; and I the compiler decided it needed to prove a
&lt;code&gt;T: Foo&lt;/code&gt; bound so now it gets to perform type checking to validate whether it
has an &lt;code&gt;impl&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This seems unimplementable with how the solver currently works. It is not
insurmountable! But it would be very hard.&lt;p&gt;It is possible that there are relaxations of this that are not insane to
implement, e.g. the &lt;code&gt;impl ||&lt;/code&gt; expression is used to initialize an argument to a
function that happens to be generic, so we can steal the bounds off of that type
variable and hope it&amp;rsquo;s SAM. But realistically, this direction is more trouble
than its worth.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Generic lambdas are extremely powerful in C++, and allow for very slick API
designs; I often miss them in Rust. Although it feels like there is an
insurmountable obstruction, I hope that the SAM interface approach offers a
simpler, and possibly more pragmatic, approach to making them work in Rust.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Except for the part where they are extremely not. Where &lt;code&gt;new T() {}&lt;/code&gt; mints a
brand new class and accompanying &lt;code&gt;.class&lt;/code&gt; file, Java lambdas use this
complicated machinery from Java 7 to generate method handles on the fly, via
the &lt;code&gt;invokedynamic&lt;/code&gt; JVM instruction. This, I&amp;rsquo;m told, makes them much easier
to optimize.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
