  <entry>
    <title>The Alkyne GC</title>
    <link href="/2022/06/07/alkyne-gc"/>
    <updated>2022-06-07T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2022/06/07/alkyne-gc</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/alkyne&gt;Alkyne&lt;/a&gt; is a scripting language I built a couple
of years ago for generating configuration blobs. Its interpreter is a naive AST
walker&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; that uses ARC&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; for memory management, so it&amp;rsquo;s pretty
slow, and I&amp;rsquo;ve been gradually writing a
&lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/alkyne/tree/new-engine&gt;new evaluation engine&lt;/a&gt; for it.&lt;p&gt;This post isn&amp;rsquo;t about Alkyne itself, that&amp;rsquo;s for another day. For now, I&amp;rsquo;d like
to write down some notes for the GC I wrote&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; for it, and more generally
provide an introduction to memory allocators (especially those that would want
to collude with a GC).&lt;p&gt;This post is intended for people familiar with the basics of low-level
programming, such as pointers and syscalls. Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s GC is intended to be
simple while still having reasonable performance. This means that the design
contains all the allocator &amp;ldquo;tropes,&amp;rdquo; but none of the hairy stuff.&lt;p&gt;My hope is readers new to allocators or GCs will come away with an understanding
of these tropes and the roles they play in a modern allocator.&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Thank you to James Farrell, Manish Goregaokar, Matt Kulukundis, JeanHeyd
Meneide, Skye Thompson, and Paul Wankadia for providing feedback on various
drafts of this article. This was a tough one to get right. :)&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=trailhead&gt;&lt;a href=#trailhead&gt;Trailhead&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The Alkyne GC is solving a very specific problem, which allows us to limit what
it actually needs to do. Alkyne is an &amp;ldquo;embeddable&amp;rdquo; language like JavaScript, so
its heap is not intended to be big; in fact, for the benefit of memory usage
optimizations, it&amp;rsquo;s ideal to use 32-bit pointers (a 4 gigabyte address space).&lt;p&gt;The heap needs to be able to manage arbitrarily-large allocations (for lists),
and allocations as small as eight bytes (for floats&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;). Allocation
should be reasonably quick, but due to the size of the heap, walking the entire
heap is totally acceptable.&lt;p&gt;Because we&amp;rsquo;re managing a fixed-size heap, we can simply ask the
operating system for a contiguous block of that size up-front using the
&lt;code&gt;mmap()&lt;/code&gt; syscall. An Alkyne pointer is simply a 32-bit offset into this giant
allocation, which can be converted to and from a genuine CPU pointer by adding
or subtracting the base address of the heap.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-text highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 4GB Heap
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; +-------------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; |                x                                |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; +-------------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; ^                ^
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; base             base + ptr_to_x
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The OS won&amp;rsquo;t actually reserve 4GB of memory for us; it will
only allocate one system page (4KB) at a time. If we read or write to a
particular page in the heap for the first time, the OS will only then find
physical RAM to back it&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Throughout, we&amp;rsquo;ll be working with this fixed-size heap, and won&amp;rsquo;t think too
hard about where it came from. For our purposes, it is essentially a
&lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;[u8]&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, but we&amp;rsquo;ll call it a &lt;code&gt;Heap&amp;lt;[u8]&gt;&lt;/code&gt; to make it clear this memory we
got from the operating system (but, to be clear, the entire discussion applies
just as well to an ordinary gigantic &lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;[u8]&gt;&lt;/code&gt;)&lt;p&gt;The Alkyne language does not have threads, so we can eschew concurrency. This
significantly reduces the problems we will need to solve. Most modern allocators
and garbage collectors are violently concurrent by nature, and unfortunately,
much too advanced for one article. There are links below to fancier GCs you can
poke around in.&lt;h2 id=a-heap-of-trouble&gt;&lt;a href=#a-heap-of-trouble&gt;A Heap of Trouble&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;To build a garbage collector, we first need an allocator. We could &amp;ldquo;just&amp;rdquo;&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;
use the system heap as a source of pages, but most garbage collectors collude with
the allocator, since they will want to use similar data structures. Thus, if we
are building a garbage collector, we might as well build the allocator too.&lt;p&gt;An allocator, or &amp;ldquo;memory heap&amp;rdquo; (not to be confused with a min-heap, an unrelated
but &lt;em&gt;wicked&lt;/em&gt; data structure), services requests for &lt;em&gt;allocations&lt;/em&gt;:
unique leases of space in the managed heap of various sizes, which last for
lifetimes not known until runtime. These allocations may also be called
&lt;em&gt;objects&lt;/em&gt;, and a heap may be viewed as a general-purpose object pool.&lt;p&gt;The most common API for a heap is:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;trait&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Allocator&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Returns a *unique pointer* managed by this allocator
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// to memory as large as requested, and as aligned
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// as we&amp;#39;d like.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// 
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Returns null on failure.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;alloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;align&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Frees a pointer returned by `Alloc` may be called at
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// most once.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;free&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Originally the examples were in C++, which I feel is more accessible (lol)
but given that Alkyne itself is written in Rust I felt that would make the
story flow better.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is the &amp;ldquo;malloc&amp;rdquo; API, which is actually very deficient; ideally, we would
do something like Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/trait.Allocator.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;Allocator&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;,
which requires providing size &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; alignment to both the allocation &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt;
deallocation functions.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, this means I need to explain alignment.&lt;h3 id=good-pointers-evil-pointers-lawful-pointers-chaotic-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#good-pointers-evil-pointers-lawful-pointers-chaotic-pointers&gt;Good Pointers, Evil Pointers, Lawful Pointers, Chaotic Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Alignment&amp;rdquo; is a somewhat annoying property of a pointer. A pointer is aligned
to N bytes (always a power of 2) if its address is divisible by N. A pointer is
&amp;ldquo;well-aligned&amp;rdquo; (or just &amp;ldquo;aligned&amp;rdquo;) if its address is aligned to the natural
alignment of the thing it points to. For ints, this is &lt;em&gt;usually&lt;/em&gt; their size;
for structs, it is the maximum alignment among the alignments of the fields
of that struct.&lt;p&gt;Performing operations on a pointer requires that it be aligned&lt;sup id=fnref:8&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:8 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;8&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.
This is annoying because it requires some math. Specifically we need three
functions:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// Checks that `ptr` is aligned to an alignment.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;is_aligned&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;Int&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;align&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;align&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;==&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Arenas are very simple, but far from useless!
They&amp;rsquo;re great for holding onto data that exists for the context of a &amp;ldquo;session&amp;rdquo;,
such as for software that does lots of computations and then exits (a compiler)
or software that handles requests from clients, where lots of data lives for
the duration of the request and no longer (a webserver).&lt;p&gt;They are not, however, good for long-running systems. Eventually the heap will
be exhausted if objects are not recycled.&lt;p&gt;Making this work turns out to be hard&lt;sup&gt;[citation-needed]&lt;/sup&gt;.
This is the &amp;ldquo;fundamental theorem&amp;rdquo; of allocators:&lt;blockquote id=thm:1 class=thm thm math&gt;&lt;a href=#thm:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;theorem&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Handing out memory is easy. Handing it out &lt;strong&gt;repeatedly&lt;/strong&gt; is hard.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Thankfully, over the last fifty years we&amp;rsquo;ve mostly figured this out. Allocator
designs can get pretty gnarly.&lt;h2 id=four-tropes&gt;&lt;a href=#four-tropes&gt;Four Tropes&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;From here, we will gradually augment our allocator with more features to
allow it to service all kinds of requests. For this, we will implement four
common allocator features:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Blocks and a block cache.&lt;li&gt;Free lists.&lt;li&gt;Block merging and splitting.&lt;li&gt;Slab allocation.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;All four of these are present in some form in most modern allocators.&lt;h3 id=blocks&gt;&lt;a href=#blocks&gt;Blocks&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first thing we should do is to deal in fixed-size blocks of memory of some
minimum size. If you ask &lt;code&gt;malloc()&lt;/code&gt; for a single byte, it will probably give you
like 8 bytes on most systems. No one is asking &lt;code&gt;malloc()&lt;/code&gt; for single bytes, so
we can quietly round up and not have people care. (Also, Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s smallest
heap objects are eight bytes, anyways.)&lt;p&gt;Blocks are also convenient, because we can keep per-block metadata on each one,
as a header before the user&amp;rsquo;s data:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[repr(C)]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Block&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;BLOCK_SIZE&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

The easiest way to do this is with a stack. Note that the
heap is now made of &lt;code&gt;Block&lt;/code&gt;s, not plain bytes.&lt;p&gt;To allocate storage, first we check the stack. If the stack is empty, we
revert to being an arena and increment the cursor. To free, we push the block
onto the stack, so &lt;code&gt;alloc()&lt;/code&gt; can return it on the next call.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;BlockCache&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

directly from the OS, but &lt;code&gt;Vec&lt;/code&gt; talks to &lt;code&gt;malloc()&lt;/code&gt; (or something like it).
It also adds some pretty big overhead: the &lt;code&gt;Vec&lt;/code&gt; needs to be able to resize,
since it grows as more and more things are freed. This can lead to long pauses
during &lt;code&gt;free()&lt;/code&gt; as the vector resizes.&lt;p&gt;Cutting out the middleman gives us more control over this overhead.&lt;h3 id=free-lists&gt;&lt;a href=#free-lists&gt;Free Lists&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course, no one has ever heard of a &amp;ldquo;free stack&amp;rdquo;; everyone uses free lists!
A free list is the cache idea but implemented as an &lt;em&gt;intrusive linked list&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A linked list is this data structure:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;enum&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Node&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Using these abstractions we can upgrade &lt;code&gt;BlockCache&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;FreeList&lt;/code&gt;. to rename &lt;code&gt;free_stack&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;free_list&lt;/code&gt;, and make a one-line change:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Some&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;block&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;free_stack&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Some&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;block&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;free_list&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;first&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;   &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;block&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;unlink&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;block&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;as&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Hooray for encapsulation!&lt;p&gt;This is a very early &lt;code&gt;malloc()&lt;/code&gt; design, similar to the one described in the
K&amp;amp;R C book. It does have big blind spot: it can only serve up blocks up
to a fixed size! It&amp;rsquo;s also quite wasteful, because all allocations are served
the same size blocks: the bigger we make the maximum request, the more
wasteful &lt;code&gt;alloc(8)&lt;/code&gt; gets.&lt;h3 id=block-splitting-alkynes-way&gt;&lt;a href=#block-splitting-alkynes-way&gt;Block Splitting (Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s Way)&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The next step is to use a block splitting/merging scheme, such as the
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_memory_allocation&gt;&lt;em&gt;buddy system&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt;. Alkyne
does not precisely use a buddy system, but it does something similar.&lt;p&gt;Alkyne does not have fixed-size blocks. Like many allocators, it defines a &amp;ldquo;page&amp;rdquo;
of memory as the atom that it keeps its data structures. Alkyne defines a page
to be 4KB, but other choices are possible: TCMalloc uses 8KB pages.&lt;p&gt;In Alkyne, pages come together to form contiguous, variable-size &lt;em&gt;reams&lt;/em&gt; (get
it?). These take the place of blocks.&lt;h4 id=page-descriptors&gt;&lt;a href=#page-descriptors&gt;Page Descriptors&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Merging and splitting makes it hard to keep headers at the start of reams, so
Alkyne puts them all in a giant array somewhere else. Each page gets
its own &amp;ldquo;header&amp;rdquo; called a page descriptor, or &lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/alkyne/blob/a62ad3b7ee70268625da640c1edeea8ff7116512/src/eval2/gc.rs#L416&gt;&lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The array of page descriptors lives at the beginning of the heap, and the
actual pages follow after that. It turns out that this array has a maximum size,
which we can use to pre-compute where the array ends.&lt;p&gt;Currently, each &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; is 32 bytes, in addition to the 4KB it describes. If we
divide 4GB by 32 + 4K, it comes out to around four million pages (4067203 to
be precise). Rounded up to the next page boundary, this means that pages begin
at the 127102nd 4K boundary after the &lt;code&gt;Heap&amp;lt;[u8]&gt;&lt;/code&gt; base address, or an offset
of &lt;code&gt;0x7c1f400&lt;/code&gt; bytes.&lt;p&gt;Having them all in a giant array is also very useful, because it means the
GC can trivially find &lt;em&gt;every allocation&lt;/em&gt; in the whole heap: just iterate the
&lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; array!&lt;p&gt;So! This is our heap:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-text highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+  &amp;lt;-- mmap(2)&amp;#39;d region base
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;| Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | \
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+ |--- Page Descriptors
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;| Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | |    for every page we can
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+ |    ever allocate.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;: ...                                   : |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+ |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;| Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | Pd | /
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+  &amp;lt;-- Heap base address
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;| Page 0                                | \    = region + 0x7c1f400
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;|                                       | |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;|                                       | |--- 4K pages corresponding
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+ |    to the Pds above.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;| Page 1                                | |    (not to scale)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;|                                       | |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;|                                       | |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+ |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;: ...                                   | |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+ |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;| Page N                                | |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;|                                       | |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;|                                       | /
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;+---------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  (not to scale by a factor of about 4)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Each one of those little &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;s looks something like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[repr(C)]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;prev&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;next&lt;/code&gt; are the intrusive linked list pointers used for the free lists,
but now they are indices into the &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; array. The other fields will be used for
this and the trope that follows.&lt;p&gt;Given a pointer into a page, we can get the corresponding &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; by
&lt;code&gt;align_down()&lt;/code&gt;&amp;lsquo;ing to a page boundary, computing the index of the page (relative
to the heap base), and then index into the &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; array. This process can be
reversed to convert a pointer to a &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; into a pointer to a page, so going
between the two is very easy.&lt;blockquote id=note:2 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;I won&amp;rsquo;t cover this here, but Alkyne actually wraps &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; pointers in a special
&lt;code&gt;PdRef&lt;/code&gt; type that also carries a reference to the &lt;code&gt;Heap&lt;/code&gt;; this allows
implementing functions like &lt;code&gt;is_linked()&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;unlink()&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;data()&lt;/code&gt; directly.&lt;p&gt;I won&amp;rsquo;t show how this is implemented, since it&amp;rsquo;s mostly boilerplate.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h4 id=reams-of-pages&gt;&lt;a href=#reams-of-pages&gt;Reams of Pages&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h4&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is one giant free list that contains all of the reams. Reams use their
first page&amp;rsquo;s descriptor to track all of their metadata, including the list
pointers for the free list. The &lt;code&gt;len&lt;/code&gt; field additionally tracks how many
&lt;em&gt;additional&lt;/em&gt; pages are in the ream. &lt;code&gt;gc_bits&lt;/code&gt; is set to 1 if the page is in use
and 0 otherwise.&lt;p&gt;To allocate N continuous pages from the free ream list:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;We walk through the free ream list, and pick the first one with at least N
pages.&lt;li&gt;We &amp;ldquo;split&amp;rdquo; it: the first N pages are returned to fulfill the request.&lt;li&gt;The rest of the ream is put back into the free list.&lt;li&gt;If no such ream exists, we allocate a max-sized ream&lt;sup id=fnref:10&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:10 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;10&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (65536
pages), and split that as above.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;In a sense, each ream is an arena that we allocate smaller reams out of; those
reams cannot be &amp;ldquo;freed&amp;rdquo; back to the ream they came from.
Instead, to free a ream, we just stick it back on the main free list.&lt;p&gt;If we ever run out, we turn back into an arena and initialize the next
uninitialized &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; in the big ol&amp;rsquo; &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; array.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;ReamAlloc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;free&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Find the Pd corresponding to this page&amp;#39;s pointer. This
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// will always be a ream&amp;#39;s first Pd assuming the user
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// didn&amp;#39;t give us a bad pointer.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Pd&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;from_ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;free_list&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;push&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This presents a problem: over time, reams will shrink and never grow, and
eventually there will be nothing left but single pages.&lt;p&gt;Top fix this, we can merge reams (not yet implemented in Alkyne). Thus:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Find two adjacent, unallocated reams.&lt;li&gt;Unlink the second ream from the free list.&lt;li&gt;Increase the length of the first ream by the number of pages in the second.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// `reams()` returns an iterator that walks the `Pd` array using
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// the `len` fields to find the next ream each time.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;in&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;reams&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;gc_bits&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;continue&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;loop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;next&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;add&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;next&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;gc_bits&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;break&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;next&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;unlink&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;next&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;We don&amp;rsquo;t need to do anything to the second ream&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;; by becoming part of the
first ream, it is subsumed. Walking the heap requires using reams&amp;rsquo; lengths to
skip over currently-invalid &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;s, anyways.&lt;p&gt;We have two options for finding mergeable reams. Either we can walk the entire
heap, as above, or, when a ream is freed, we can check that the previous and
following reams are mergeable (finding the previous ream would require storing
the length of a ream at its first &lt;em&gt;and&lt;/em&gt; last &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;).&lt;p&gt;Which merging strategy we use depends on whether we&amp;rsquo;re implementing an ordinary
&lt;code&gt;malloc&lt;/code&gt;-like heap or a garbage collector; in the &lt;code&gt;malloc&lt;/code&gt; case, merging on free
makes more sense, but merging in one shot makes more sense for Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s GC
(we&amp;rsquo;ll see why in a bit).&lt;h3 id=slabs-and-size-classes&gt;&lt;a href=#slabs-and-size-classes&gt;Slabs and Size Classes&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;A &lt;em&gt;slab allocator&lt;/em&gt; is a specialized allocator that allocates a single type of
object; they are quite popular in kernels as pools of commonly-used object.
The crux of a slab allocator is that, because everything is the same size, we
&lt;em&gt;don&amp;rsquo;t&lt;/em&gt; need to implement splitting and merging. The &lt;code&gt;BlockCache&lt;/code&gt; above is
actually a very primitive slab allocator.&lt;p&gt;Our &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; array is also kind of like a slab allocator; instead of mixing them in
with the variably-sized blocks, they all live together with no gaps in between;
entire pages are dedicated just to &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;s.&lt;p&gt;The Alkyne page allocator cannot allocate pages smaller than 4K, and making them
any smaller increases the relative overhead of a &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;. To cut down on
book-keeping, we slab-allocate small objects by defining &lt;em&gt;size classes&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A size class is size of smaller-than-a-page object that Alkyne will allocate;
other sizes are rounded up to the next size class. Entire pages are dedicated to
holding just objects of the same size; these are called small object pages,
or simply &lt;em&gt;slabs&lt;/em&gt;. The size class is tracked with the &lt;code&gt;class&lt;/code&gt; field of the &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Each size class has its own free list of partially-filled slabs of
that size. For slabs, &lt;code&gt;gc_bits&lt;/code&gt; field becomes a bitset that tracks which slots
in the page are currently in-use, reducing the overhead for small objects to
only a little over a single bit each!&lt;p&gt;In the diagram below, bits set in the 32-bit, little-endian bitset indicate
which slots in the slab (no to scale!) are filled with three-letter words.
(The user likes cats.)&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-text highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  Pd--------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  | gc_bits: 0b01010011111010100110000010101011 |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  +---------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; Page--------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; | cat | ink |     | hat |     | jug |     | fig |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; +-----------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; |     |     |     |     |     | zip | net |     |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; +-----------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; |     | aid |     | yes |     | war | cat | van |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; +-----------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; | can | cat |     |     | rat |     | urn |     |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; +-----------------------------------------------+
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Allocating an object is a bit more complicated now, but now we have a really,
really short fast path for small objects:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Round up to the next highest size class, or else to the next page boundary.&lt;li&gt;If a slab size class&amp;mldr;
a. Check the pertinent slab list for a partially-filled slab.
i. If there isn&amp;rsquo;t one, allocate a page per the instructions below and
initialize it as a slab page.
b. Find the next available slot with &lt;code&gt;(!gc_bits).count_trailing_zeros()&lt;/code&gt;,
and set that bit.
c. Return &lt;code&gt;page_addr + slab_slot_size * slot&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Else, if a single page, allocate from the single-page list.
a. If there isn&amp;rsquo;t one, allocate from the ream list as usual.&lt;li&gt;Else, multiple pages, allocate a ream as usual.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Allocating small objects is very fast, since the slab free lists, if not
empty, will always have a spot to fill in &lt;code&gt;gc_bits&lt;/code&gt;. Finding the empty spot in
the bitset is a few instructions (a &lt;code&gt;not&lt;/code&gt; plust a &lt;code&gt;ctz&lt;/code&gt; or equivalent on most
hardware).&lt;p&gt;Alkyne maintains a separate free list for single free pages to speed up finding
such pages to turn into fresh slabs. This also minimizes the need to allocate
single pages off of large reams, which limits fragmentation.&lt;p&gt;Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s size classes are the powers of two from 8 (the smallest possible
object) to 2048. For the classes 8, 16, and 32, which would have more than 64
slots in the page, we use up to 56 bytes on the page itself to extend &lt;code&gt;gc_bits&lt;/code&gt;;
8-byte pages can only hold 505 objects, instead of the full 512, a 1% overhead.&lt;p&gt;Directly freeing an object via is now tricky, since we do not a priori
know the size.&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Round the pointer up to the next page boundary, and obtain that page&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;If this is a start-of-ream page, stick it into the appropriate free list
(single page or ream, depending on the size of the ream).&lt;li&gt;Else, we can look at &lt;code&gt;class&lt;/code&gt; to find the size class, and from that, and the
offset of the original pointer into the page, the index of the slot.&lt;li&gt;Clear the slot&amp;rsquo;s index in &lt;code&gt;gc_bits&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;If the page was full before, place it onto the correct slab free list; if
it becomes empty, place it into the page free list.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;At this point, we know whether the page just became partially full or empty,
and can move it to the correct free list.&lt;p&gt;Size classes are an important allocator optimization. TCMalloc takes this to
an .
These constants are generated by some crazy script based on profiling data.&lt;h2 id=intermission&gt;&lt;a href=#intermission&gt;Intermission&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Before continuing to the GC part of the article, it&amp;rsquo;s useful to go over what we
learned.&lt;p&gt;A neat thing about this is that most of these tricks are somewhat independent.
While giving feedback for an early draft, Matt Kulukundis shared
&lt;a href=&#34;https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LIb3L4vKZ7U&#34;&gt;this awesome talk&lt;/a&gt; that describes
how to build complex allocators out of simple ones, and covers many of the same
tropes as we did here. This perspective on allocators actually blew my mind.&lt;p&gt;Good allocators don&amp;rsquo;t just use one strategy; the use many and pick and chose the
best one for the job based on expected workloads. For example, Alkyne expects
to allocate many small objects; the slab pages were originally only for float
objects, but it turned out to simplify a lot of the code to make &lt;em&gt;all&lt;/em&gt; small
objects be slab-allocated.&lt;p&gt;Even size classes are a deep topic: TCMalloc uses &lt;a href=https://research.google/pubs/pub36575/&gt;GWP telemetry&lt;/a&gt;
from Google&amp;rsquo;s fleet to inform its &lt;em&gt;many&lt;/em&gt; tuning parameters, including its
&lt;a href=https://github.com/google/tcmalloc/blob/master/tcmalloc/size_classes.cc&gt;comically large&lt;/a&gt;
tables of size classes.&lt;p&gt;At this point, we have a pretty solid allocator. Now, let&amp;rsquo;s get rid of the
free function.&lt;h2 id=throwing-out-the-trash&gt;&lt;a href=#throwing-out-the-trash&gt;Throwing out the Trash&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Garbage collection is very different from manual memory management in that
frees are performed in &lt;em&gt;batches&lt;/em&gt; without cue from the user. There are no calls
to &lt;code&gt;free()&lt;/code&gt;; instead, we need to figure out which calls to &lt;code&gt;free()&lt;/code&gt; we &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt;
make on the user&amp;rsquo;s behalf that they won&amp;rsquo;t notice (i.e., without quietly freeing
pointers the user can still reach, resulting in a use-after-free bug). We need
to do this as fast as we can.&lt;p&gt;Alkyne is a &amp;ldquo;tracing GC&amp;rdquo;. Tracing GCs walk the &amp;ldquo;object graph&amp;rdquo; from a root set of
known-reachable objects. Given an object &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt;, it will &lt;em&gt;trace&lt;/em&gt; through any data
in the object that it knows is actually a GC pointer. In the object graph, &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;
is reachable from &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; if one can repeatedly trace through GC pointers to get
from &lt;code&gt;a&lt;/code&gt; to &lt;code&gt;b&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Alkyne uses tracing to implement garbage collection in a two-step process,
commonly called &amp;ldquo;mark-and-sweep&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Marking&lt;/em&gt; consists of traversing the entire graph from a collection of
reachable-by-definition values, such as things on the stack, and recording each
object that is visited. Every object &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; so marked must therefore be
definitely unreachable and can be reclaimed; this reclamation is called
&lt;em&gt;sweeping&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Alkyne reverses the order of operations somewhat: it &amp;ldquo;sweeps&amp;rdquo; first and then
marks, i.e., it marks every value as dead and then, as it walks the graph,
marks every block as alive. It then rebuilds the free lists to reflect the
new marks, allowing the blocks to be reallocated. This is sometimes called
&amp;ldquo;mark and don&amp;rsquo;t sweep&amp;rdquo;, but fixing up the free lists is effectively a sweeping
step.&lt;figure&gt;&lt;img src=https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4a/Animation_of_the_Naive_Mark_and_Sweep_Garbage_Collector_Algorithm.gif&gt;&lt;figcaption&gt;Marking and sweeping! (via Wikipedia, CC0)&lt;/figcaption&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;p&gt;Alkyne is a &amp;ldquo;stop-the-world&amp;rdquo; (STW) GC. It needs to pause all program execution
while cleaning out the heap. It is possible to build GCs that do not do this (I
believe modern HotSpot GCs very rarely stop the world), but also very difficult.
Most GCs are world-stopping to some degree.&lt;p&gt;One thing we do not touch on is &lt;em&gt;when&lt;/em&gt; to sweep. This is a more complicated and
somewhat hand-wavy tuning topic that I&amp;rsquo;m going to quietly sweep under the rug
by pointing you to &lt;a href=https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/runtime/mgcpacer.go&gt;how Go does it&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;h3 id=heap-armageddon-and-resurrection&gt;&lt;a href=#heap-armageddon-and-resurrection&gt;Heap Armageddon and Resurrection&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Delicate freeing of individual objects is quite difficult, but scorching the earth
is very easy. To do this, we walk the whole &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; array (see, I said this would be
useful!) and blow away every &lt;code&gt;gc_bits&lt;/code&gt;. This leaves the heap in a broken state
where every pointer appears to be dangling. This is &amp;ldquo;armageddon&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;To fix this up, we need to &amp;ldquo;resurrect&amp;rdquo; any objects we shouldn&amp;rsquo;t have killed
(oops). The roots are objects in the Alkyne interpreter stack&lt;sup id=fnref:11&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:11 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;11&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. To
mark an object, we convert a pointer to it into a &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; via the page-&lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;
correspondence, and mark it as alive by &amp;ldquo;allocating&amp;rdquo; it.&lt;p&gt;We then use our knowledge&lt;sup id=fnref:12&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:12 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;12&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; of Alkyne objects&amp;rsquo; heap layout
to find pointers to other objects in the heap (for example, the intepreter
&lt;em&gt;knows&lt;/em&gt; it&amp;rsquo;s looking at a list and can &lt;em&gt;just find&lt;/em&gt; the list elements within,
which are likely pointers themselves). If we trace into an
object and find it has been marked as allocated, we don&amp;rsquo;t recurse; this avoids
infinite recursion when encountering cycles.&lt;blockquote id=note:3 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:3&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s a big hard to give a code example for this, because the &amp;ldquo;mark&amp;rdquo; part
that&amp;rsquo;s part of the GC is mixed up with interpreter code, so there isn&amp;rsquo;t
much to show in this case. :(&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;At the end of this process, every reachable object will once again be alive, but
anything we couldn&amp;rsquo;t reach stays dead.&lt;h3 id=instant-apocalypse&gt;&lt;a href=#instant-apocalypse&gt;Instant Apocalypse&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;(Alkyne currently does not make this optimization, but really should.)&lt;p&gt;Rather than flipping every bit, we flip the
global &lt;em&gt;convention&lt;/em&gt; for whether 0 or 1 means &amp;ldquo;alive&amp;rdquo;, implemented by having
a global &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt; specifying which is which at any given time; this would
alternate from sweep to sweep. Thus, killing every living object is
now a single operation.&lt;p&gt;This works if the allocated bit of objects in the free lists is never read,
and only ever overwritten with the &amp;ldquo;alive&amp;rdquo; value when allocated, so that
all of the dead objects suddenly becoming alive isn&amp;rsquo;t noticed. This does not
work with slab-allocated small objects: pages may be in a mixed state where
they are partially allocated and partially freed.&lt;p&gt;We can still make this optimization by adding a second bit that tracks
whether the page contains &lt;em&gt;any&lt;/em&gt; living objects, using the same convention.
This allows delaying the clear of the allocated bits for small objects to
when the page is visited, which also marks the whole page as alive.&lt;p&gt;Pages that were never visited (i.e., still marked as dead) can be reclaimed
as usual, ignoring the allocated bits.&lt;h3 id=free-list-reconciliation&gt;&lt;a href=#free-list-reconciliation&gt;Free List Reconciliation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;At this point, no pointers are dangling, but newly emptied out pages are not in
the free lists they should be in. To fix this, we can walk over all
&lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt;s and put them where they need to go if they&amp;rsquo;re not full. This is the
kinda-but-not-really sweep phase.&lt;p&gt;The code for this is simpler to show than explaining it:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;in&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;reams&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
