&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;else&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;is_full&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// GC can&amp;#39;t make a not-full-list become full, so we don&amp;#39;t
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// need to move it.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;else&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Non-empty, non-full lists cannot be reams.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=fm&gt;debug_assert!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;class&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SizeClass&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;Ream&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;unlink&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;      &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;slab_free_lists&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;class&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;].&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;push&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;pd&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:19&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Of course, this will also shuffle around all pages that did not become
partially empty or empty while marking. If the &amp;ldquo;instant apocalypse&amp;rdquo; optimization
is used, this step must still inspect every &lt;code&gt;Pd&lt;/code&gt; and modify the free lists.&lt;p&gt;However, it is a completely separate phase: all it does is find pages that did
not survive the previous mark phase. This means that user code can run between
the phases, reducing latency. If it turns out to be very expensive to sweep
the whole heap, it can even be run less often than mark phases&lt;sup id=fnref:13&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:13 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;13&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This is also a great chance to merge reams, because we&amp;rsquo;re inspecting every
page anyways; this is why the merging strategy depends on wanting to be a GC&amp;rsquo;s
allocator rather than a normal &lt;code&gt;malloc()&lt;/code&gt;/&lt;code&gt;free()&lt;/code&gt; allocator.&lt;p&gt;&amp;mldr;and that&amp;rsquo;s it! That&amp;rsquo;s garbage collection. The setup of completely owning the
layout of blocks in the allocator allows us to cut down significantly on memory
needed to track objects in the heap, while keeping the mark and sweep steps
short and sweet. A garbage collector is like any other data structure: you
pack in a lot of complexity into the invariants to make the actual operations
very quick.&lt;h2 id=conclusion&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusion&gt;Conclusion&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s GC is intended to be super simple because I didn&amp;rsquo;t want to think too
hard about it (even though I clearly did lmao). The GC layouts are a whole
&amp;rsquo;nother story I have been swirling around in my head for months, which is
described &lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/alkyne/blob/a62ad3b7ee70268625da640c1edeea8ff7116512/src/eval2/value.rs#L78&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.
The choices made there influenced the design of the GC itself.&lt;p&gt;There are still many optimizations to make, but it&amp;rsquo;s a really simple but
realistic GC design, and I&amp;rsquo;m pretty happy with it!&lt;h3 id=a-note-on-finalizers-tools-of-the-devil&gt;&lt;a href=#a-note-on-finalizers-tools-of-the-devil&gt;A Note on Finalizers (Tools of the Devil!)&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Alkyne also does not provide finalizers. A finalizer is the GC equivalent of a
destructor: it gets run after the GC declares an object dead. Finalizers
complicate a GC significantly by their very nature; they are called in
unspecified orders and can witness broken GC state; they can stall the entire
program (if they are implemented to run during the GC pause in a multi-threaded
GC) or else need to be called with a zombie argument that either can&amp;rsquo;t escape
the finalizer or, worse, must be resurrected if it does!&lt;p&gt;If finalizers depend on each other, they can&amp;rsquo;t be run at all, for the same
reason an ARC cycle cannot be broken; this weakness of ARC is one of the major
benefits of an omniscient GC.&lt;p&gt;Java&amp;rsquo;s &lt;a href=https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html#finalize()&gt;documentation for &lt;code&gt;Object.finalize()&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
is a wall of text of lies, damned lies, and ghost stories.&lt;p&gt;I learned earlier (the week before I started writing this article) that Go ALSO
has finalizers and that they are &lt;a href=https://pkg.go.dev/runtime#SetFinalizer&gt;similarly cursed&lt;/a&gt;.
Go does behave somewhat more nicely than Java (finalizers are per-value and
avoid zombie problems by unconditionally resurrecting objects with a finalizer).&lt;h3 id=further-reading&gt;&lt;a href=#further-reading&gt;Further Reading&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Here are some other allocators that I find interesting and worth reading about,
some of which have inspired elements of Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s design.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://google.github.io/tcmalloc/design.html&gt;TCMalloc&lt;/a&gt; is Google&amp;rsquo;s crazy
thread-caching allocator. It&amp;rsquo;s really fast and really cool, but I work for
Google, so I&amp;rsquo;m biased. But it uses radix trees! Radix trees are cool!!!&lt;p&gt;Go &lt;a href=https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/master:src/runtime/mgc.go&gt;has a garbage collector&lt;/a&gt;
that has well-known performance properties but does not perform any wild
optimizations like moving, and is a world-stopping, incremental GC.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/master/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/heap/BlinkGCAPIReference.md&gt;Oilpan&lt;/a&gt;
is the Chronimum renderer&amp;rsquo;s GC (you know, for DOM elements). It&amp;rsquo;s actually
grafted onto C++ and has a very complex API reflective of the subtleties of
GCs as a result.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://www.hboehm.info/gc/&gt;libboehm&lt;/a&gt; is another C/C++ GC written by Hans
Boehm, one of the world&amp;rsquo;s top experts on concurrency.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://v8.dev/blog/trash-talk&gt;Orinoco&lt;/a&gt; is V8&amp;rsquo;s GC for the JavaScript heap
(i.e., Chronimum&amp;rsquo;s &lt;em&gt;other&lt;/em&gt; GC). It is a &lt;em&gt;generational&lt;/em&gt; or &lt;em&gt;moving GC&lt;/em&gt; that
can defragment the heap over time by moving things around (and updating
pointers). It also has a separate sub-GC just for short-lived objects.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04738&gt;Mesh&lt;/a&gt; is a non-GC allocator that can do
compacting via clever use of &lt;code&gt;mmap(2)&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/1cf8214e4daa1d0dd9777c987697e82c2a3c6584/upb/upb.c#L117&gt;&lt;code&gt;upb_Arena&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
is an arena allocator that uses free-lists to allows fusing arenas together.
This part of the μpb Protobuf runtime.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;In other words, it uses recursion along a syntax tree, instead of a more
efficient approach that compiles the program down to bytecode.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;A&lt;/em&gt;utomatic &lt;em&gt;R&lt;/em&gt;eference &lt;em&gt;C&lt;/em&gt;ounting is an automatic memory management
technique where every heap allocation contains a counter of how many
pointers currently point to it; once pointers go out of scope, they
decrement the counter; when the counter hits zero the memory is freed.&lt;p&gt;This is used by Python and Swift as the core memory management strategy, and
provided by C++ and Rust via the &lt;code&gt;std::shared_ptr&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;Arc&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; types,
respectively.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://github.com/mcy/alkyne/blob/a62ad3b7ee70268625da640c1edeea8ff7116512/src/eval2/gc.rs&gt;This is the file.&lt;/a&gt;
It&amp;rsquo;s got fairly complete comments, but they&amp;rsquo;re written for an audience
familiar with allocators and garbage collectors.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a tangent, but I should point out that Alkyne does not do &lt;a href=https://leonardschuetz.ch/blog/nan-boxing/&gt;&amp;ldquo;NaN
boxing&amp;rdquo;&lt;/a&gt;. This is a technique
used by some JavaScript runtimes, like Spidermonkey, which represent
dynamically typed values as either ordinary floats, or pointers hidden in
the mantissas of 64-bit IEEE 754 signaling NaNs.&lt;p&gt;Alkyne instead uses something like V8&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;a href=https://v8.dev/blog/pointer-compression&gt;Smi pointer compression&lt;/a&gt;, so our
heap values are four bytes, not eight. Non-Smi values that aren&amp;rsquo;t on the
stack (which uses a completely different representation) can only exist
as elements of lists or objects. Alkyne&amp;rsquo;s slab allocator design (described
below) is focused on trying to minimize the overhead of all floats being in
their own little allocations.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;The operating system&amp;rsquo;s own physical page allocator is actually solving the
same problem: given a vast range of memory (in this case, physical RAM),
allocate it. The algorithms in this article apply to those, too.&lt;p&gt;Operating system allocators can be slightly fussier because they need to
deal with virtual memory mappings, but that is a topic for another time.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;As you might expect, these scare-quotes are load-bearing.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;I tried leaving this out of the first draft, and failed. So many things
would be simpler without fussing around with alignment.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:8&gt;&lt;p&gt;Yes yes most architectures can cope with unaligned loads and stores but
compilers rather like to pretend that&amp;rsquo;s not true.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:8 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:9&gt;&lt;p&gt;Boutique means &lt;a href=https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#pointer-aliasing-rules&gt;provenance&lt;/a&gt;
in French.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:10&gt;&lt;p&gt;Currently Alkyne has a rather small max ream size. A better way to approach
this would be to treat the entire heap as one gigantic ream at the start,
which is always at the bottom of the free list.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:10 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:11&gt;&lt;p&gt;In GC terms, these are often called &amp;ldquo;stack roots&amp;rdquo;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:11 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:12&gt;&lt;p&gt;The interpreter simply &lt;em&gt;knows&lt;/em&gt; this and can instruct the GC appropriately.&lt;p&gt;In any tracing GC, the compiler or interpreter must be keenly aware of the
layouts of types so that it can generate the appropriate tracing code for
each.&lt;p&gt;This is why grafting GCs to non-GC&amp;rsquo;d languages is non-trivial, even though
people have totally done it: &lt;a href=https://www.hboehm.info/gc/&gt;libboehm&lt;/a&gt; and
&lt;a href=https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/master/third_party/blink/renderer/platform/heap/BlinkGCAPIReference.md&gt;Oilpan&lt;/a&gt;
are good (albeit sometimes controversial) examples of how this can be done.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:12 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:13&gt;&lt;p&gt;With &amp;ldquo;instant apocalypse&amp;rdquo;, this isn&amp;rsquo;t quite true; after two mark phases,
pages from the first mark phase will appear to be alive, since the global
&amp;ldquo;alive&amp;rdquo; convention has changed twice. Thus, only pages condemned in every
other mark phase will be swept; sweeping is most optimal after an odd number
of marks.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:13 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Move Constructors Revisited
</title>
    <link href="/2021/12/19/move-ctors-2"/>
    <updated>2021-12-19T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2021/12/19/move-ctors-2</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Almost a year ago I developed the &lt;a href=https://github.com/google/moveit&gt;&lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
Rust library, which provides primitives for expressing something like C++&amp;rsquo;s
&lt;code&gt;T&amp;&amp;&lt;/code&gt; and move constructors while retaining Rust&amp;rsquo;s so-called &amp;ldquo;destructive move
property&amp;rdquo;: moving a value transfers ownership, rather than doing a funny copy.&lt;p&gt;In an &lt;a href={{site.baseurl}}/2021/04/26/move-ctors&gt;earlier blogpost&lt;/a&gt; I described the
theory behind this library and some of the motivation, which I feel fairly
confident about, especially in how constructors (and their use of pinning) are
defined.&lt;p&gt;However, there is a problem.&lt;h2 id=a-not-so-quick-recap&gt;&lt;a href=#a-not-so-quick-recap&gt;A Not-so-Quick Recap&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The old post is somewhat outdated, since &lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt; uses different names for a lot
of things that are geared to fit in with the rest of Rust.&lt;p&gt;The core abstraction of &lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt; is the constructor, which are types that
implement the &lt;code&gt;New&lt;/code&gt; trait:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[must_use]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;trait&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;New&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nb&gt;Sized&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// The type to construct.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Output&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// Construct a new value in-place using the arguments stored
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;/// in `self`.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=sd&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;this&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;Pin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;Self&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;Output&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;New&lt;/code&gt; type is not what is being constructed; rather, it represents a &lt;em&gt;method&lt;/em&gt;
of construction, resembling a specialized &lt;code&gt;Fn&lt;/code&gt; trait. The constructed type is
given by the associated type &lt;code&gt;Output&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Types that can be constructed are constructed &lt;em&gt;in place&lt;/em&gt;, unlike most Rust
types. This is a property shared by constructors in C++, allowing values to
record their own address at the moment of creation. Explaining why this is
useful is a bit long-winded, but let&amp;rsquo;s assume this is a thing we want to be
able to do. Crucially, we need the output of a constructor to be pinned, which
is why the &lt;code&gt;this&lt;/code&gt; output parameter is pinned.&lt;p&gt;Calling a constructor requires creating the output location in advance so that
we can make it available to it in time:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Create storage for the new value.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;storage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Pin that storage on the stack; by calling this, we may never move
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// `storage` again, even after this goes out of scope.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Pin&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;new_unchecked&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;storage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Now we can call the constructor. It&amp;#39;s only unsafe because it assumes
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// the provided memory is uninitialized.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;as_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// This is now safe, since `my_new` initialized the value, so we can
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// do with it what we please.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;result&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;map_unchecked_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;assume_init_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;However, this is not quite right. &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;P&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s docs are quite clear that we must
ensure that, once we create an &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;&amp;amp;mut T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, we must call &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s destructor
before its memory is re-used; since reuse is unavoidable for stack data, and
&lt;code&gt;storage&lt;/code&gt; will not do it for us (it&amp;rsquo;s a &lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, after all), we must
somehow run the destructor separately.&lt;h3 id=an-easy-solution&gt;&lt;a href=#an-easy-solution&gt;An &amp;ldquo;Easy&amp;rdquo; Solution&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;One trick we could use is to replace &lt;code&gt;storage&lt;/code&gt; with some kind of wrapper over
a &lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; that calls the destructor for us:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;EventuallyInit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Drop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;EventuallyInit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;drop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;drop_in_place&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mf&gt;0.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;assume_init_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;())&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This &lt;em&gt;works&lt;/em&gt;, but isn&amp;rsquo;t ideal, because now we can&amp;rsquo;t write down something like a
C++ move constructor without running into the classic C++ problem: all objects
must be destroyed unconditionally, so now you can have moved-from state. Giving
up Rust&amp;rsquo;s moves-transfer-ownership (i.e. &lt;em&gt;affine&lt;/em&gt;) property is bad, but it turns
out to be avoidable!&lt;p&gt;There are also some scary details around panics here that I won&amp;rsquo;t get into.&lt;h3 id=t-mut-t--move-t&gt;&lt;a href=#t-mut-t--move-t&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt;, &amp;mldr; &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;move T&lt;/code&gt;?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt; instead provides a &lt;a href=https://docs.rs/moveit/latest/moveit/move_ref/struct.MoveRef.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;MoveRef&amp;lt;&#39;frame, T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
type that tries to capture the notion of what an &amp;ldquo;owning reference&amp;rdquo; &lt;em&gt;could&lt;/em&gt; mean
in Rust. An &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;move&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;own&lt;/code&gt; type has been discussed many times, but implementing
it in the full generality it would deserve as a language feature runs into some
interesting problems due to how &lt;code&gt;Box&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, the heap allocated equivalent,
&lt;a href=https://manishearth.github.io/blog/2017/01/10/rust-tidbits-box-is-special/&gt;currently behaves.&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;We can think of &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&amp;lt;&#39;frame, T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; as wrapping the &lt;em&gt;longest-lived&lt;/em&gt; &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt;
reference pointing to a particular location in memory. The longest-lived part
is crucial, since it means that &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; is entitled to run its pointee&amp;rsquo;s
destructor:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Notice parallels with EventuallyInit&amp;lt;T&amp;gt; above.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=o&gt;?&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Sized&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Drop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;drop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;drop_in_place&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;No reference to the pointee can ever outlive the &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; itself, by definition,
so this is safe. The owner of a value is that which is entitled to destroy it,
and therefore a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; &lt;em&gt;literally&lt;/em&gt; owns its pointee. Of course, this means
we can move out of it (which was the whole point of the original blogpost).&lt;p&gt;Because of this, we are further entitled to arbitrarily pin a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; with no
consequences: pinning it would consume the unpinned &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; (for obvious
reasons, &lt;code&gt;MoveRefs&lt;/code&gt; cannot be reborrowed) so no unpinned reference may outlive
the pinning operation.&lt;p&gt;This gives us a very natural solution to the problem above: &lt;code&gt;result&lt;/code&gt;
should not be a &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;&amp;amp;mut T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, but rather a &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;MoveRef&amp;lt;&#39;_, T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;storage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Pin&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;new_unchecked&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;storage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;as_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// do with it what we please.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;result&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;into_pinned&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;new_unchecked&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;map_unchecked_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;mp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;assume_init_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;())&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;));&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

library that ensures safe initialization and eventual destruction:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Allocate storage on the stack, emplace `my_new` onto it, and pin it
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// in an owning reference.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;moveit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;result&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;Pin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is also some reasonably complex machinery that allows us to do something
like an owning &lt;code&gt;Deref&lt;/code&gt;, which I&amp;rsquo;ll come back to in a bit.&lt;p&gt;However, there is a small wrinkle that I did not realize when I first designed
&lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;: what happens if I &lt;code&gt;mem::forget&lt;/code&gt; a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;?&lt;h2 id=undefined-behavior-obviously&gt;&lt;a href=#undefined-behavior-obviously&gt;Undefined Behavior, Obviously&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Quashing destruction isn&amp;rsquo;t new to Rust: we can &lt;code&gt;mem::forget&lt;/code&gt; just about
anything, leaking all kinds of resources. And that&amp;rsquo;s ok! Destructors alone
cannot be used in type design to advert &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; catastrophe, a well-understood
limitation of the language that we have experience designing libraries
around, such as &lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/leaking.html#drain&gt;&lt;code&gt;Vec::drain()&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s design creates a contradiction:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; is an owning smart pointer, and therefore can be safely pinned,
much like &lt;code&gt;Box::into_pinned()&lt;/code&gt; enables. Constructors, in particular,
are &lt;em&gt;designed&lt;/em&gt; to generate pinned &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;s!&lt;li&gt;Forgetting a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; will cause the pointee destructor to be suppressed,
but its storage will still be freed and eventually re-used, a violation of
the &lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt; drop guarantee.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;This would &lt;em&gt;appear&lt;/em&gt; to mean that a design like &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; is not viable at all,
and that this sort of &amp;ldquo;stack box&amp;rdquo; strategy is always unsound.&lt;blockquote id=aside:1 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;What about it? Even though we can trivially create a &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;Box&amp;lt;i32&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; via
&lt;code&gt;Box::pin()&lt;/code&gt;, this is a red herring. When we &lt;code&gt;mem::forget&lt;/code&gt; a &lt;code&gt;Box&lt;/code&gt;, we also
forget about its storage too. Because its storage has been leaked
unrecoverably, we are still, &lt;em&gt;technically&lt;/em&gt;, within the bounds of the &lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt;
contract. Only barely, but we&amp;rsquo;re inside the circle.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Interestingly, the Rust language has to deal with a similar problem; perhaps it
suggests a way out?&lt;h2 id=drop-flags-and-dynamic-ownership-transfer&gt;&lt;a href=#drop-flags-and-dynamic-ownership-transfer&gt;Drop Flags and Dynamic Ownership Transfer&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Carefully crafted Rust code emits some very interesting assembly. I&amp;rsquo;ve annotated

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Otherwise, make it someone else&amp;#39;s problem; they get to
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// free the memory for themselves. 
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;mov&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;rdi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rax&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;pop&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;rbx&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;jmp&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;example&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;someone_elses_problem&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;x86 Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The upshot is that &lt;code&gt;maybe_drop&lt;/code&gt; conditions the destructor of &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; on a &lt;em&gt;flag&lt;/em&gt;,
which is allocated next to it on the stack. Rust flips this flag when the value
is moved into another function, and only runs the destructor when the flag is
left alone. In this case, LLVM folded the flag into the &lt;code&gt;bool&lt;/code&gt; argument, so this
isn&amp;rsquo;t actually a meaningful perf hit.&lt;p&gt;These &amp;ldquo;drop flags&amp;rdquo; are key to Rust&amp;rsquo;s ownership model. Since ownership may be
transferred dynamically due to reasonably complex control flow, it needs to
leave breadcrumbs for itself to figure out whether the value wound up getting
moved away or not. This is unique to Rust: in C++, every object is always
destroyed, so no such faffing about is necessary.&lt;p&gt;Similarly, &lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt; can close this soundness hole by leaving itself breadcrumbs
to determine if safe code is trying to undermine its guarantees.&lt;p&gt;In other words: in Rust, it is not sufficient to manage a pointer to manage a
memory location; it is necessary to manage an explicit or implicit drop flag as
well.&lt;h2 id=a-flagged-moveref&gt;&lt;a href=#a-flagged-moveref&gt;A Flagged &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;We can extend &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; to track an explicit drop flag:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:9&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;frame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; can never be made &lt;code&gt;Send&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;Sync&lt;/code&gt; anyways. Inside of its destructor,

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Pin&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;into_inner_unchecked&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;).&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;assume_init_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;                &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// passing in a flag in addition to 
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;                &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// a reference to the owned value itself.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;));&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The trap is a deterrent against forgetting a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;: because the &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s
destructor flips the flag, the trap&amp;rsquo;s destructor will notice if this &lt;em&gt;doesn&amp;rsquo;t&lt;/em&gt;
happen, and take action accordingly.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;In &lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt;, this is actually implemented by having the &lt;code&gt;Slot&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; type
carry a reference to the trap, created in the &lt;code&gt;slot!()&lt;/code&gt; macro. However, this
is not a crucial detail for the design.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h3 id=an-earth-shattering-kaboom&gt;&lt;a href=#an-earth-shattering-kaboom&gt;An Earth-Shattering Kaboom&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The trap is another RAII type that basically looks like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;TrappedFlag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Cell&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;bool&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Drop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;TrappedFlag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;drop&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mf&gt;0.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;abort&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The trap is simple: if the contained drop flag is not flipped, it crashes the
program. Because &lt;code&gt;moveit!()&lt;/code&gt; allocates it on the stack where uses cannot
&lt;code&gt;mem::forget&lt;/code&gt; it, its destructor is guaranteed to run before &lt;code&gt;storage&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s
destructor runs (although Rust does not guarantee destructors run, it &lt;em&gt;does&lt;/em&gt;
guarantee their order).&lt;p&gt;If a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; is forgotten, it won&amp;rsquo;t have a chance to flip the flag, which the
trap will detect. Once the trap&amp;rsquo;s destructor notices this, it cannot return,
either normally or by panic, since this would cause &lt;code&gt;storage&lt;/code&gt; to be freed.
Crashing the program is the only&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; acceptable response.&lt;p&gt;Some of &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s functions need to be adapted to this new behavior:
for example, &lt;code&gt;MoveRef::into_inner()&lt;/code&gt; still needs to flip the flag, since moving
out of the &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; is equivalent to running the destructor for the purposes
of drop flags.&lt;h2 id=a-safer-derefmove&gt;&lt;a href=#a-safer-derefmove&gt;A Safer &lt;code&gt;DerefMove&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;In order for &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; to be a proper &amp;ldquo;new&amp;rdquo; reference type, and not just a
funny smart pointer, we also need a &lt;code&gt;Deref&lt;/code&gt; equivalent:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;pub&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;trait&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;DerefMove&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;DerefMut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Sized&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is the &lt;em&gt;original&lt;/em&gt; design for &lt;code&gt;DerefMove&lt;/code&gt;, which had a two-phase operation:
first &lt;code&gt;deinit()&lt;/code&gt; was used to create a destructor-suppressed version of the smart
pointer that would only run the destructor for the storage (e.g., for &lt;code&gt;Box&lt;/code&gt;,
only the call to &lt;code&gt;free()&lt;/code&gt;). Then, &lt;code&gt;deref_move()&lt;/code&gt; would extract the &amp;ldquo;inner
pointee&amp;rdquo; out of it as a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;. This had the effect of splitting the smart
pointer&amp;rsquo;s destructor, much like we did above on the stack.&lt;p&gt;This has a number of usability problems. Not only does it &lt;em&gt;need&lt;/em&gt; to be called
through a macro, but &lt;code&gt;deinit()&lt;/code&gt; isn&amp;rsquo;t actually safe: failing to call
&lt;code&gt;deref_move()&lt;/code&gt; is just as bad as calling &lt;code&gt;mem::forget&lt;/code&gt; on the result. Further,
it&amp;rsquo;s not clear where to plumb the drop flags through.&lt;p&gt;After &lt;a href=https://github.com/google/moveit/pull/23#issuecomment-963549869&gt;many attempts&lt;/a&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Construct a new MoveRef, converting `storage` from 
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// `&amp;amp;mut Box&amp;lt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&amp;gt;&amp;gt;` into `&amp;amp;mut T`.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;new_unchecked&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;storage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;assume_init_mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;drop_flag&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s own implementation illustrates the need for the explicit lifetime
bound:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=o&gt;?&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Sized&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;DerefMove&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;for&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;type&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Storage&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;deref_move&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;frame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;_&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;DroppingSlot&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;frame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;MoveRef&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;frame&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;where&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;Self&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;frame&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// We can just return directly; this is a mere lifetime narrowing.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Since this is fundamentally a lifetime narrowing, this can only compile if we
insist that &lt;code&gt;&#39;a: &#39;frame&lt;/code&gt;, which is implied by &lt;code&gt;Self: &#39;frame&lt;/code&gt;. Earlier iterations
of this design enforced it via a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&amp;lt;&#39;frame, Self&gt;&lt;/code&gt; receiver, which turned
out to be unnecessary.&lt;h2 id=conclusions&gt;&lt;a href=#conclusions&gt;Conclusions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;As of writing, I&amp;rsquo;m still in the process of self-reviewing
&lt;a href=https://github.com/google/moveit/pull/25&gt;this change&lt;/a&gt;, but at this point I
feel &lt;em&gt;reasonably&lt;/em&gt; confident that it&amp;rsquo;s correct; this article is, in part, written
to convince myself that I&amp;rsquo;ve done this correctly.&lt;p&gt;The new design will also enable me to finally complete my implementation of a
constructor and pinning-friendly vector type; this issue came up in part because
the vector type needs to manipulate drop flags in a complex way. For this
reason, the &lt;em&gt;actual&lt;/em&gt; implementation of drop flags actually uses a counter, not
a single boolean.&lt;p&gt;I doubt this is the last issue I&amp;rsquo;ll need to chase down in &lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt;, but for now,
we&amp;rsquo;re ever-closer to true owning references in Rust.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Arguably, running the skipped destructor is &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; a valid remediation
strategy. However, this is incompatible with what the user requested: they
asked for the destructor to be supressed, not for it to be run at a later
date. This would be somewhat surprising behavior, which we could warn about
for the benefit of &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; code, but ultimately the incorrect choice for
non-stack storage, such as a &lt;code&gt;MoveRef&lt;/code&gt; referring to the heap.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>

    <title>Understanding Assembly
Part I: RISC-V
</title>
    <link href="/2021/11/29/assembly-1"/>
    <updated>2021-11-29T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2021/11/29/assembly-1</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;A &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_tarpit&gt;Turing tarpit&lt;/a&gt; is a programming
language that is Turing-complete but very painful to accomplish anything in. One
particularly notable tarpit is
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brainfuck&gt;Brainfuck&lt;/a&gt;, which has a reputation
among beginner and intermediate programmers as being unapproachable and only
accessible to the most elite programmers hence the name, as Wikipedia puts it:&lt;blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;The language&amp;rsquo;s name is a reference to the slang term &lt;em&gt;brainfuck&lt;/em&gt;, which refers
to things so complicated or unusual that they exceed the limits of one&amp;rsquo;s
understanding.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Assembly language, the &amp;ldquo;lowest-level&amp;rdquo; programming language on any computer, has
a similar reputation: difficult, mysterious, and beyond understanding. A Turing
tarpit that no programmer would want to have anything to do with.&lt;p&gt;Although advanced programmers usually stop seeing assembly as mysterious and
inaccessible, I feel like it is a valuable topic even for intermediate
programmers, and one that can be made approachable and interesting.&lt;p&gt;This series seeks to be that: assuming you have already been using a compiled
language like Rust, C++, or Go, how &lt;em&gt;is&lt;/em&gt; assembly relevant to you?&lt;blockquote id=tip:1 class=tip tip&gt;&lt;a href=#tip:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;tip&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;If you&amp;rsquo;re here to just learn assembly and don&amp;rsquo;t really care for motivation,
you can just &lt;a href=#diving-in&gt;skip ahead&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This series is about learning to &lt;em&gt;understand&lt;/em&gt; assembly, not write it. I do
occasionally write assembly for a living, but I&amp;rsquo;m not an &lt;em&gt;expert&lt;/em&gt;, and I don&amp;rsquo;t
particularly relish it. I do read a ton of assembly, though.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=what-is-it-anyways&gt;&lt;a href=#what-is-it-anyways&gt;What Is It, Anyways?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;As every programmer knows, computers are very stupid. They are very good at
following instructions and little else. In fact, the computer is &lt;em&gt;so&lt;/em&gt; stupid, it
can only process basic instructions serially&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, one by one. The
instructions are very simple: &amp;ldquo;add these two values&amp;rdquo;, &amp;ldquo;copy this value from here
to there&amp;rdquo;, &amp;ldquo;go run these instructions over here&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;A computer processor implements these instructions as electronic circuits. At
its most basic level, every computer looks like the following program:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size_t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;program_counter&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;...;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Instruction&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;program&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;...;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;while&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;true&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;Instruction&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;next&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;program&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;program_counter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;switch&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;next&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;opcode&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Figure out what you&amp;#39;re supposed to be doing and do it.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;program_counter&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;++&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The array &lt;code&gt;program&lt;/code&gt; is a your program encoded as a sequence of these &amp;ldquo;machine
instructions&amp;rdquo; in some kind of binary format. For example, in RISC-V programs,
each instruction is a 32-bit integer. This binary format is called &lt;em&gt;machine
code&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;For example, when a RISC-V processor encounters the value &lt;code&gt;5407443&lt;/code&gt; decoding
circuitry decides that it means that it should take the value in the &amp;ldquo;register&amp;rdquo;
&lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt;, add &lt;code&gt;10&lt;/code&gt; to it, and place the result in the register &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=aside:1 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;5407443&lt;/code&gt; seems opaque, but when viewed as binary, we can see how the
processor decodes it:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-text highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;0b 000000000101 00101 000 00110 0010011
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;   \__________/ \___/ \_/ \___/ \_____/
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    |           |     |   |     |
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    imm         rs1   fn  rd    opcode
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;opcode&lt;/code&gt; describes what sort of instruction this is, and what format it&amp;rsquo;s in;
&lt;code&gt;0b0010011&lt;/code&gt; means it&amp;rsquo;s an &amp;ldquo;immediate arithmetic&amp;rdquo; instruction, which uses the
&amp;ldquo;I-type&amp;rdquo; format, given above. &lt;code&gt;fn&lt;/code&gt; further specifies what the operation does;
&lt;code&gt;0b000&lt;/code&gt;, combined with the value of &lt;code&gt;opcode&lt;/code&gt;, means this is an &lt;em&gt;addition&lt;/em&gt;
instruction.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;rs1&lt;/code&gt; is the source: it gives the name of the source register, &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt;, given by
it index, &lt;code&gt;0b00101&lt;/code&gt;, i.e., &lt;code&gt;10&lt;/code&gt;. Similarly, &lt;code&gt;rd&lt;/code&gt; specifies the destination
&lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt; by its index &lt;code&gt;11&lt;/code&gt;. Finally, &lt;code&gt;imm&lt;/code&gt; is the value to add, &lt;code&gt;0b000000000101&lt;/code&gt;,
or &lt;code&gt;10&lt;/code&gt;. The constant value appears immediately in the instruction itself, so
it&amp;rsquo;s called an &lt;em&gt;immediate&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;However, if you&amp;rsquo;re a human programming a computer, writing all of this by hand
is&amp;mldr; very 60s, and you might prefer to have a textual representation, so you
can write this more simply as &lt;code&gt;addi a1, a0, 10&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;addi a1, a0, 10&lt;/code&gt; is a single line of assembly: it describes a &lt;em&gt;single&lt;/em&gt;
instruction in text form. Assembly language is &amp;ldquo;just&amp;rdquo; a textual representation
of the program&amp;rsquo;s machine code. Your assembler can convert from text into machine
instructions, and a &lt;em&gt;dis&lt;/em&gt;assembler reverses the process.&lt;p&gt;The simple nature of these instructions is what makes assembly a sort of Turing
tarpit: you only get the most basic operations possible: you&amp;rsquo;re responsible for
building &lt;em&gt;everything&lt;/em&gt; else.&lt;h3 id=on-architectures&gt;&lt;a href=#on-architectures&gt;On Architectures&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;There isn&amp;rsquo;t &amp;ldquo;an&amp;rdquo; assembly language. Every computer has a different instruction
set architecture, or &amp;ldquo;ISA&amp;rdquo;; I use the terms &amp;ldquo;instruction set&amp;rdquo;, &amp;ldquo;architecture&amp;rdquo;,
and &amp;ldquo;ISA&amp;rdquo; interchangeably. Each ISA has a corresponding assembly language that
describes that ISA&amp;rsquo;s specific instructions, but they all generally have similar
overall structure.&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;m going to focus on three ISAs for ease of exposition, introduced in this
order:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;RISC-V, a modern and fairly simple instruction set (specifically, the rv32gc
variant). That&amp;rsquo;s Part I.&lt;li&gt;x86_64, the instruction set of the device you&amp;rsquo;re reading this on (unless it&amp;rsquo;s
a phone, an Apple M1 laptop, or something like a Nintendo Switch). That&amp;rsquo;s
Part II.&lt;li&gt;MOS 6502, a fairly ancient ISA still popular in very small microcontrollers.
That&amp;rsquo;s Part III.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;We&amp;rsquo;re starting with RISC-V because it&amp;rsquo;s a particularly elegant ISA (having been
developed for academic work originally), while still being representative of the
operations most ISAs offer.&lt;p&gt;In the future, I may dig into some other, more specialized ISAs.&lt;h2 id=but--why-&gt;&lt;a href=#but--why-&gt;But &lt;em&gt;Why&lt;/em&gt;?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s actually very rare to write actual assembly. Thanks to modern (relatively)
languages like Rust, C++, and Go, and even things like Haskell and JavaScript,
virtually no programmers need to write assembly anymore.&lt;p&gt;But that&amp;rsquo;s only because it&amp;rsquo;s the leading language written by &lt;em&gt;computers
themselves&lt;/em&gt;. A compiler&amp;rsquo;s job is, fundamentally, to write the the assembly you
would have had to write &lt;em&gt;for&lt;/em&gt; you. To better understand what a compiler is doing
for you, you need to be able to read its output.&lt;p&gt;At this point, it may be worth looking at my
&lt;a href=/2021/06/01/linker-script#seriously-whats-a-linker&gt;article on linkers&lt;/a&gt;
as a refresher on the C compilation model.&lt;p&gt;For example, let&amp;rsquo;s suppose we have the very simple C program below.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:square.c&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#include&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=cpf&gt;&amp;lt;stdio.h&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;

&lt;code&gt;clang -c square.c&lt;/code&gt;. &lt;code&gt;-c&lt;/code&gt; asks the compiler to stop before the link step,

But pay attention to the two lines with a &lt;code&gt;// !&lt;/code&gt;: the
first is &lt;code&gt;mul s0, a0, a0&lt;/code&gt;, which is the multiplication &lt;code&gt;x *= x;&lt;/code&gt;. The second is
&lt;code&gt;call printf&lt;/code&gt;, which is our function call to &lt;code&gt;printf()&lt;/code&gt;! I&amp;rsquo;ll explain what
everything else means in short order.&lt;p&gt;Writing assembly isn&amp;rsquo;t a crucial skill, but being able to read it is. It&amp;rsquo;s
actually so useful, that a website exists for quickly generating the assembly
output of a vast library of compilers: the
&lt;a href=https://godbolt.org/&gt;Compiler Explorer&lt;/a&gt;, frequently just called &amp;ldquo;godbolt&amp;rdquo;
after its creator, Matt Godbolt. Being able to compare the output of different
compilers can help understand what they do! Click on the &lt;code&gt;godbolt&lt;/code&gt; button in the
code fences to a godbolt for it.&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Low-level&amp;rdquo; languages like C aren&amp;rsquo;t the only ones where you can inspect assembly
output.
