&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;sw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// This is our `x *= x;` from before! Notice that the
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// compiler rewrote this to `temp = x * x;` at some
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// point, since the destination register is `s0`.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;mul&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// These two instructions load the address of a string
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// constant; this pattern is specific to RISC-V.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lui&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;hi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;L&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;lo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;L&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// This copies the multiplication result into `a1`.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;mv&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Call to printf!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;call&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;printf&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Move `s0` into `a0`, since it&amp;#39;s the return value.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;mv&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// This is the function epilogue, which restores state
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// saved in the prologue and de-allocates the stack
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// frame.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;ra&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;12&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// We&amp;#39;re done; return from the function!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// This tells the assembler to place what follows in
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// the `.rodata` section, for read-only constants like
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// strings.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;section&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rodata&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;L&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Give our string constant a private name. By convention,
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// .L labels are &amp;#34;private&amp;#34; names emitted by the compiler.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Emit an ASCII string into `.rodata` with an extra null
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// terminator at the end: that&amp;#39;s what the `z` stands for.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;asciz&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;%d&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=se&gt;\n&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:square.s&gt;square.s&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;{:id=&amp;ldquo;big-example&amp;rdquo;}&lt;h3 id=the-core-syntax&gt;&lt;a href=#the-core-syntax&gt;The Core Syntax&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;All assemblers are different, but the core syntax tends to be the same. There
are three main kinds of syntax productions:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Instructions, which consist of a &lt;em&gt;mnemonic&lt;/em&gt; followed by some number of
&lt;em&gt;operands&lt;/em&gt;, such as &lt;code&gt;addi sp, sp -16&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;call printf&lt;/code&gt; above. These are the
text encoding of machine code.&lt;li&gt;Labels, which consist of a symbol followed by a colon, like
&lt;code&gt;square_and_print:&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;.L.str:&lt;/code&gt;. These are used to let instruction operands
refer to locations in the program.&lt;li&gt;Directives, which vary wildly by assembler. GCC-style assembly like that above
uses a &lt;code&gt;.directive arg, arg&lt;/code&gt; syntax, as seen in &lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;.globl&lt;/code&gt;, and
&lt;code&gt;.asciz&lt;/code&gt;. They control the behavior of the assembler in various ways.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;An assembler&amp;rsquo;s purpose is to read the &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; file and serialize it as a binary
&lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; file. It&amp;rsquo;s kind of like a compiler, but it does virtually no interesting
work at all, beyond knowing how to encode instructions.&lt;p&gt;Directives control how this serialization occurs (such as moving around the
output cursor); instructions are emitted as-is, and labels refer to locations in
the object file. Simple enough, right?&lt;h3 id=anatomy-of-an-instruction&gt;&lt;a href=#anatomy-of-an-instruction&gt;Anatomy of an Instruction&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s look at the very first instruction in &lt;code&gt;square_and_print&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=o&gt;----&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;--&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=o&gt;--&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=o&gt;---&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;         &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;mnemonic&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=n&gt;immediate&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;operand&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;             &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;input&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;operand&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;             &lt;span class=o&gt;|&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            &lt;span class=n&gt;output&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;operand&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first token is called the &lt;em&gt;mnemonic&lt;/em&gt;, which is a painfully terse
abbreviation of what the instruction does. In this case, &lt;code&gt;addi&lt;/code&gt; means &amp;ldquo;add with
immediate&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;sp&lt;/code&gt; is a &lt;em&gt;register&lt;/em&gt;. Registers are special variables wired directly into the
processor that can be used as operands in instructions. The degree to which only
registers are permitted as operands varies by architecture; RISC-V only allows
registers, but x86, as we&amp;rsquo;ll see, does not. Registers come in many flavors, but
&lt;code&gt;sp&lt;/code&gt; is a GPR, or &amp;ldquo;general purpose register&amp;rdquo;; it holds a machine word-sized
integer, which in the case of 32-bit RISC-V is&amp;mldr; 32-bit&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=aside:2 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;One of my absolute favorite parts of RISC-V is how it names its registers. It
has 32 GPRs named &lt;code&gt;x0&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;x31&lt;/code&gt;. However, these registers have so-called
&amp;ldquo;ABI names&amp;rdquo; that specify the &lt;em&gt;role&lt;/em&gt; of each register in the ABI.&lt;p&gt;The usefulness of these names will be much more apparent when we discuss
&lt;a href=#the-calling-convention&gt;the calling convention&lt;/a&gt;, so feel free to come back
to this later.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;x0&lt;/code&gt; is called &lt;code&gt;zero&lt;/code&gt;, because of its special property: writes to it are
ignored, and reads always produce zero. This is handy for encoding certain
common operations: for example, it can be used to quickly get a constant
value= into a register: &lt;code&gt;addi rd, zero, 42&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;x1&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;x2&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;x3&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;x4&lt;/code&gt; have special roles and generally aren&amp;rsquo;t used for
general computation. The first two are the link register &lt;code&gt;ra&lt;/code&gt;, which holds the
&lt;u&gt;r&lt;/u&gt;eturn &lt;u&gt;a&lt;/u&gt;ddress, and &lt;code&gt;sp&lt;/code&gt;, the &lt;u&gt;s&lt;/u&gt;tack &lt;u&gt;p&lt;/u&gt;ointer.&lt;p&gt;The latter two are &lt;code&gt;gp&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;tp&lt;/code&gt;; the &lt;u&gt;g&lt;/u&gt;lobal &lt;u&gt;p&lt;/u&gt;pointer and the
&lt;u&gt;t&lt;/u&gt;hread &lt;u&gt;p&lt;/u&gt;pointer; their roles are somewhat complicated, so we
won&amp;rsquo;t discuss them in this post.&lt;p&gt;The remaining registers belong to one of three categories: &lt;em&gt;argument&lt;/em&gt;
registers, &lt;em&gt;saved&lt;/em&gt; registers, and &lt;em&gt;temporary&lt;/em&gt; registers, named so for their
role in calling a function (as described &lt;a href=#the-calling-convention&gt;below&lt;/a&gt;).&lt;p&gt;The argument registers are &lt;code&gt;x10&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;x17&lt;/code&gt;, and use the names &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt; through
&lt;code&gt;a7&lt;/code&gt;. The saved registers are &lt;code&gt;x8&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;x9&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;x18&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;x27&lt;/code&gt;, called
&lt;code&gt;s0&lt;/code&gt;, through &lt;code&gt;s11&lt;/code&gt;. The temporary registers are &lt;code&gt;x5&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;x7&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;x28&lt;/code&gt;
through &lt;code&gt;x31&lt;/code&gt;, called &lt;code&gt;t0&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;t6&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;As a matter of personal preference, you may notice me reaching for argument
registers for most examples.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;-16&lt;/code&gt; is an &lt;em&gt;immediate&lt;/em&gt;, which is a literal value that is encoded directly into
the instruction. The encoding of &lt;code&gt;addi sp, sp, -16&lt;/code&gt; will include the binary
representation of &lt;code&gt;-16&lt;/code&gt; (in the case of RISC-V, as a 12-bit integer). [The
decoding example above]{#decoding-instructions} shows how immediates are
literally encoded &lt;em&gt;immediately&lt;/em&gt; in the instruction.&lt;p&gt;Immediates allow for small but fixed integer arguments to be encoded with high
locality to the instruction, which is good for code size and performance.&lt;p&gt;The first operand in RISC-V is (almost) always the output. &lt;code&gt;addi, rd, rs, imm&lt;/code&gt;
should be read as &lt;code&gt;rd = rs + imm&lt;/code&gt;. Virtually all assembler syntax follows this
convention, which is called the
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-address_code&gt;three-address code&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Other kinds of operands exist: for example, &lt;code&gt;call printf&lt;/code&gt; refers to the &lt;em&gt;symbol&lt;/em&gt;
&lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt;. The assembler, which doesn&amp;rsquo;t actually know where &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt; is, will
emit a small note in the object file that tells the linker to find &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt; and
splat it into the assembly according to some instructions in the note. These
notes are called &lt;em&gt;relocations&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The instructions &lt;code&gt;lui a0, %hi(.L.str)&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;addi a0, a0, %lo(.L.str)&lt;/code&gt; use the
&lt;code&gt;%lo&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;%hi&lt;/code&gt; operand types, which are specific to RISC-V; they load the low
12 bits and high 20 bits of a symbol&amp;rsquo;s address into the immediate operand. This
is a RISC-V-specific pattern for loading an address into a register, which most
assemblers provide with the &lt;em&gt;pseudoinstruction&lt;/em&gt; &lt;code&gt;la a0, .L.str&lt;/code&gt; (where &lt;code&gt;la&lt;/code&gt;
stands for &amp;ldquo;load address&amp;rdquo;).&lt;p&gt;Most architectures have their own funny architecture-specific operand types to
deal with the architecture&amp;rsquo;s idiosyncrasy.&lt;h3 id=types-of-instructions&gt;&lt;a href=#types-of-instructions&gt;Types of Instructions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Available instructions tend to be motivated by providing one of three classes of
functionality:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;A Turing-complete
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_machine&gt;register machine&lt;/a&gt; execution
environment. This lends to the Turing tarpit nature of assembly: only the
absolute minimum in terms of control flow and memory access is provided.&lt;li&gt;Efficient silicon implementation of common operations on bit strings and
integers, ranging from arithmetic to cryptographic algorithms.&lt;li&gt;Building a secure operating system, hosting virtual machines, and actuating
hardware external to the processor, like a monitor, a keyboard, or speakers.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;Instructions can be broadly classified into four categories: arithmetic, memory,
control flow, and &amp;ldquo;everything else&amp;rdquo;. In the last thirty years, the bar for
general-purpose architectures is usually &amp;ldquo;this is enough to implement a C
runtime.&amp;rdquo;&lt;h4 id=arithmetic-instructions&gt;&lt;a href=#arithmetic-instructions&gt;Arithmetic Instructions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Arithmetic makes up the bulk of the instruction set. This always includes
addition, subtraction, and bitwise and, or, and xor, as well as unary not and
negation.&lt;p&gt;In RISC-V, these come in two variants: a three-register version and a
two-register, one immediate version. For example, &lt;code&gt;add a0, a1, a2&lt;/code&gt; is the
three-register version of addition, while &lt;code&gt;addi a0, a1, 42&lt;/code&gt; is the immediate
version. There isn&amp;rsquo;t a &lt;code&gt;subi&lt;/code&gt; though, since you can just use negative immediates
with &lt;code&gt;addi&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;not&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;neg&lt;/code&gt; are not actual instructions in RISC-V, but pseudoinstructions:
&lt;code&gt;not a0, a1&lt;/code&gt; encodes as &lt;code&gt;xori a0, a1, -1&lt;/code&gt;, while &lt;code&gt;neg a0, a1&lt;/code&gt; becomes
&lt;code&gt;sub a0, zero, a1&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Most instruction sets also have bit shifts, usually in three flavors: left
shifts, right shifts, and &lt;em&gt;arithmetic&lt;/em&gt; right shifts; arithmetic right shift is
defined such that it behaves like division by powers of two on signed integers.
RISC-V&amp;rsquo;s names for these instructions are &lt;code&gt;sll&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;srl&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;sra&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Multiplication and division are somewhat rarer, because they are expensive to
implement in silicon; smaller devices don&amp;rsquo;t have them&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. Division
in particular is very complex to implement in silicon. Instruction sets usually
have different behavior around division by zero: some architectures will fault,
similar to a memory error, while some, like RISC-V, produce a well-defined trap
value.&lt;p&gt;There is usually also a &amp;ldquo;copy&amp;rdquo; instruction that moves the value of one register
to another, which is kind of like a trivial arithmetic instruction. RISC-V calls
this &lt;code&gt;mv a0, a1&lt;/code&gt;, but it&amp;rsquo;s just a pseudoinstruction that expands to
&lt;code&gt;addi a0, a1, 0&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Some architectures also offer more exotic arithmetic. This is just a sampler of
what&amp;rsquo;s sometimes available:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Bit rotation, which is like a shift but bits that get shifted off end up at
the other end of the integer. This is useful for a vast array of numeric
algorithms, including ARX ciphers like
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salsa20#ChaCha_variant&gt;ChaCha20&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Byte reversal, which can be used for changing the endianness of an integer;
bit reversal is analogous.&lt;li&gt;Bit extraction, which can be used to form new integers out of bitfields of
another.&lt;li&gt;Carry-less multiplication, which is like long multiplication but you don&amp;rsquo;t
bother to carry anything when you add intermediates. This is used to implement
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois/Counter_Mode&gt;Galois/Counter mode encryption&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Fused instructions, like &lt;code&gt;xnor&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;nand&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Floating point instructions, usually implementing the
&lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754&gt;IEEE 754&lt;/a&gt; standard.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is also a special kind of arithmetic instruction called a &lt;em&gt;vector
instruction&lt;/em&gt;, but I&amp;rsquo;ll leave those for another time.&lt;h4 id=memory-instructions&gt;&lt;a href=#memory-instructions&gt;Memory Instructions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Load instructions fetch memory from RAM into registers, while store instructions
write it back. These instructions are what we use to implement pointers.&lt;p&gt;They come in all sorts of different sizes: RISC-V has &lt;code&gt;lw&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;lh&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;lb&lt;/code&gt; for
loading 32-, 16-, and 8-bit values from a location; &lt;code&gt;sw&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;sh&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;sb&lt;/code&gt; are
their store counterparts. 64-bit RISC-V also provides &lt;code&gt;ld&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;sd&lt;/code&gt; for 64-bit
loads and stores.&lt;p&gt;Load/store instructions frequently take an offset for indexing into memory.
&lt;code&gt;lw a1, 4(a0)&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; is effectively &lt;code&gt;a1 = a0[4]&lt;/code&gt;, treating &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt; like a
pointer.&lt;p&gt;These instructions frequently have an &lt;em&gt;alignment&lt;/em&gt; constraint: the pointer value
must (or, at least, should) be divisible by the number of bytes being loaded.
RISC-V, for example, mandates that &lt;code&gt;lw&lt;/code&gt; only be used on pointers divisible by 4.
This constraint simplifies the microarchitecture; even on architectures that
don&amp;rsquo;t mandate it, aligned loads and stores are typically far faster.&lt;p&gt;This category also includes instructions necessary for implementing atomics,
such as &lt;code&gt;lock cmpxchg&lt;/code&gt; on x86 and &lt;code&gt;lr&lt;/code&gt;/&lt;code&gt;sc&lt;/code&gt; on RISC-V. Atomics are fundamentally
about changing the semantics of reading and writing from RAM, and thus require
special processor support.&lt;p&gt;Some architectures, like x86, 65816, and very recently, ARM, provide
instructions that implement &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt; and its ilk in hardware: in x86, for
example, this is called &lt;code&gt;rep movsb&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h4 id=control-flow-instructions&gt;&lt;a href=#control-flow-instructions&gt;Control Flow Instructions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Control flow is the secret ingredient that turns our glorified calculator into a
Turing tarpit: they allow changing the flow of program execution based on its
current state.&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Unconditional jumps&lt;/em&gt; implement &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;: given some &lt;code&gt;label&lt;/code&gt;, the &lt;code&gt;j label&lt;/code&gt;
instruction jumps directly to it. &lt;code&gt;j&lt;/code&gt; can be thought of as writing to a special
&lt;code&gt;pc&lt;/code&gt; register that holds the program counter. RISC-V also provides a &lt;em&gt;dynamic&lt;/em&gt;
jump, &lt;code&gt;jr&lt;/code&gt;, which will jump to the address in a register. Function calls and
returns are a special kind of unconditional jump.&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Conditional jumps&lt;/em&gt;, often called &lt;em&gt;branches&lt;/em&gt;, implement &lt;code&gt;if&lt;/code&gt;.
&lt;code&gt;beq a0, a1, label&lt;/code&gt; will jump to &lt;code&gt;label&lt;/code&gt; if &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt; contain the same
value. RISC-V provides branch instructions for all kinds of comparisons, like
&lt;code&gt;bne&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;blt&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;bge&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Conditional and unconditional jumps can be used together to build loops, much
like we could in C using &lt;code&gt;if&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;goto&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;For example, to zero a region of memory:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Assume a0 is the start of the region, and a1 the
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// number of bytes to zero.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Set a1 to the end of the region.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;loop_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// If a0 == a1, we&amp;#39;re done!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;beq&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;loop_done&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Store a zero byte to `a0` and advance the pointer.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;sb&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;zero&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Take it from the top!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;j&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;loop_start&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;loop_done&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h4 id=miscellaneous-instructions&gt;&lt;a href=#miscellaneous-instructions&gt;Miscellaneous Instructions&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h4&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Everything else&amp;rdquo; is, well&amp;mldr; everything else.&lt;p&gt;No-op instructions do nothing: &lt;code&gt;nop&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s only purpose is to take up space in the
instruction stream. No-op instructions can be used to pad space in the
instruction stream, provide space for the linker to fix things up later, or
implement &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOP_slide&gt;&lt;code&gt;nop&lt;/code&gt; sleds&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Instructions for poking processor state, like &lt;code&gt;csrrw&lt;/code&gt; in RISC-V and &lt;code&gt;wrmsr&lt;/code&gt; in
&lt;code&gt;x86&lt;/code&gt; also belong in this category, as do &amp;ldquo;hinting&amp;rdquo; instructions like memory
prefetches.&lt;p&gt;There are also instructions for special control flow: &lt;code&gt;ecall&lt;/code&gt; is RISC-V&amp;rsquo;s
&amp;ldquo;syscall&amp;rdquo; instruction, which &amp;ldquo;traps&amp;rdquo; to the kernel for it to do something; other
architectures have similar instructions.&lt;p&gt;Breakpoint instructions and
&lt;a href=https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/lfence&gt;&amp;ldquo;fence&amp;rdquo; instructions&lt;/a&gt; belong here,
too.&lt;h2 id=the-calling-convention&gt;&lt;a href=#the-calling-convention&gt;The Calling Convention&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Functions are the core abstraction of all of programming. Assembly is no
different: we have functions there, too!&lt;p&gt;Like in any language, functions are &lt;em&gt;passed&lt;/em&gt; a list of arguments, perform some
work, and &lt;em&gt;return&lt;/em&gt; a value. For example, in C:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;identity&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;identity&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Returns 5.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, there isn&amp;rsquo;t anything like function call syntax in assembly. As
with everything else, we need do it instruction by instruction. All we &lt;em&gt;do&lt;/em&gt; get
in most architectures is a &lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt; instruction, which sets up a return address
somewhere, and a &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt; instruction, which uses the return address to jump to
where the function was called.&lt;p&gt;We need some way to pass arguments, return a computed value, and maintain a call
stack, so that each function&amp;rsquo;s return address is kept intact for its &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt;
instruction to consume. We also need this to be universal: if I pull in a
library, I should be able to call its functions.&lt;p&gt;This mechanism is called the &lt;em&gt;calling convention&lt;/em&gt; of the platform&amp;rsquo;s ABI. It&amp;rsquo;s a
convention, because all libraries must respect it in their exposed API for code
to work correctly at runtime.&lt;h3 id=a-function-call-in-slow-mo&gt;&lt;a href=#a-function-call-in-slow-mo&gt;A Function Call in Slow-Mo&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;At the instruction level, function calls look something like this:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Pre-call setup. The caller sets up the function call arguments by placing
them in the appointed locations for arguments. These are usually either
registers or locations on the stack. a. The caller also saves the
&lt;em&gt;caller-saved registers&lt;/em&gt; to the stack.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Jump to the function. The caller executes a &lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt; instruction (or whatever
the function call instruction might be called &amp;ndash; virtually all architectures
have one). This sets the program counter to the first instruction of the
callee.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Function prologue. The callee does some setup before executing its code. a.
The callee reserves space on the stack in an architecture-dependent manner.
b. The callee saves the &lt;em&gt;callee-saved registers&lt;/em&gt; to this stack space.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Function body. The actual code of the function runs now! This part of the
function needs to make sure the return value winds up wherever the &lt;em&gt;return
slot&lt;/em&gt; for the function is.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Function epilogue. The callee undoes whatever work it did in the prologue,
such as restoring saved registers, and executes a &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt; (or equivalent)
instruction to return.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Post-call cleanup. The caller is now executing again; it can unspill any
saved state that it needs immediately after the function call, and can
retrieve the return value from the return slot.&lt;p&gt;In some ABIs, such as C++&amp;rsquo;s on Linux, this is where the destructors of the
arguments get run. (Rust, and C++ on Windows, have &lt;em&gt;callee&lt;/em&gt;-destroyed
arguments instead.)&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;When people say that function calls have overhead, this is what they mean. Not
only does the &lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt; instruction cause the processor to slam the breaks on its
pipeline, causing all kinds of work to get thrown away, but state needs to be
delicately saved and restored across the function boundary to maintain the
illusion of a callstack.&lt;p&gt;Small functions which don&amp;rsquo;t need to use as many registers can avoid some of the
setup and cleanup, and &lt;em&gt;leaf functions&lt;/em&gt; which don&amp;rsquo;t call any other functions can
avoid basically all of it!&lt;p&gt;Almost all registers in RISC-V are caller-saved, except for &lt;code&gt;ra&lt;/code&gt; and the &amp;ldquo;saved&amp;rdquo;
registers &lt;code&gt;s0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;s11&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Callee-saved registers are convenient, because they won&amp;rsquo;t be wiped out by
function calls. We can actually see the call to &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt; use this: even though
the compiler could have emitted &lt;code&gt;mul a1, a0, a0&lt;/code&gt; and avoided the &lt;code&gt;mv&lt;/code&gt;, this is
actually less optimal. We need to keep the value around to return, and &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt; is
caller-saved, so we would have had to spill &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt; before calling &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt;,
regardless of whether &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt; overwrites &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt; or not. We would then have to
unspill it into &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt; before &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt;. This costs us a hit to RAM. However, by
emitting &lt;code&gt;mul s0, a0, a0; mv a1, s0&lt;/code&gt;, we speculatively avoid the spill: if
&lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt; is compiled such that it never touches &lt;code&gt;s0&lt;/code&gt;, the value never leaves
registers at all!&lt;h3 id=caller-side&gt;&lt;a href=#caller-side&gt;Caller-Side&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;We can see steps 1 and 2 in the call to &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lui&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;hi&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;L&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;%&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;lo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;L&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;str&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;mv&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;a1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;call&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;printf&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Arguments in the usual&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; RISC-V calling convention, word-sized
arguments are passed in the &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;a7&lt;/code&gt; registers, falling back to passing
on the stack if they run out of space. If the argument is too big to fit in a
register, it gets passed by reference instead. Arguments that fit into two
registers can be split across registers.&lt;p&gt;We can see this in action &lt;a href=#big-example&gt;above&lt;/a&gt;. The first argument, a string,
is passed by pointer in &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt;; &lt;code&gt;lui&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;addi&lt;/code&gt; do the work of actually putting
that pointer into &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt;. The second argument &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; is passed in &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt;, copied from
&lt;code&gt;s0&lt;/code&gt; where it landed from the earlier &lt;code&gt;mul&lt;/code&gt; instruction.&lt;p&gt;Complex function signatures require much more&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; work to set up.&lt;p&gt;Once we&amp;rsquo;re done getting arguments into place, we &lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt;, which switches
execution over to &lt;code&gt;printf&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s first instruction. In addition, it stores the
return address, specifically, the address of the instruction immediately after
the &lt;code&gt;call&lt;/code&gt;, into an architecture-specific location. On RISC-V, this is the
special register &lt;code&gt;ra&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h3 id=callee-side&gt;&lt;a href=#callee-side&gt;Callee-Side&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Meanwhile, steps 3 and 4 occur in &lt;code&gt;square_and_print&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s prologue/epilogue itself:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;square_and_print&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;sw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;ra&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;12&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;sw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=c1&gt;// ...
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;s0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;ra&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;12&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;addi sp, sp, -16&lt;/code&gt;, which we stared at so hard above, grows the stack by 16
bytes. &lt;code&gt;sp&lt;/code&gt; holds the &lt;em&gt;stack pointer&lt;/em&gt;, which points to the top of the stack at
all times. The stack grows downwards (as in most architectures!) and must be
aligned to 16-byte boundaries across function calls: even though
&lt;code&gt;square_and_print&lt;/code&gt; only uses eight of those bytes, the full 16 bytes must be
allocated.&lt;p&gt;The two &lt;code&gt;sw&lt;/code&gt; instructions that follow store (or &amp;ldquo;spill&amp;rdquo;) the callee-saved
registers &lt;code&gt;ra&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;s0&lt;/code&gt; to the stack. Note that &lt;code&gt;s1&lt;/code&gt; through &lt;code&gt;s11&lt;/code&gt; are &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt;
spilled, since &lt;code&gt;square_and_print&lt;/code&gt; doesn&amp;rsquo;t use them!&lt;p&gt;Th this point, the function does its thing, whatever that means. This includes
putting the return value in the return slot, which, for a function that returns
an &lt;code&gt;int&lt;/code&gt;, is in &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt;. In general, the return slot is passed back to the caller
much like arguments are: if it fits in registers, &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;a1&lt;/code&gt; are used;
otherwise, the caller allocates space for it and passes a pointer to the return
slot as a hidden argument (in e.g. &lt;code&gt;a0&lt;/code&gt;)&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The epilogue inverts all operations of the prologue in reverse, unspilling
registers and shrinking the stack, followed by &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt;. On RISC-V, all &lt;code&gt;ret&lt;/code&gt; does
is jump to the location referred to by the &lt;code&gt;ra&lt;/code&gt; register.&lt;p&gt;Of course, all this work is only necessary to maintain the illusion of a
callstack; if &lt;code&gt;square_and_print&lt;/code&gt; were a leaf function, it would not need to
spill anything at all! This results in an almost trivial function:&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:9&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button godbolt&#34; href=&#34;https://godbolt.org/clientstate/eyJzZXNzaW9ucyI6W3siY29tcGlsZXJzIjpbeyJpZCI6InJ2MzItY2NsYW5nIiwib3B0aW9ucyI6Ii1PeiJ9XSwiaWQiOjEsImxhbmd1YWdlIjoiYyIsInNvdXJjZSI6ImludCBzcXVhcmUoaW50IHgpIHtcbiAgcmV0dXJuIHggKiB4O1xufVxuIn1dfQ==&#34;&gt;godbolt&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:9&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:10&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// `x` is already in a0, and the
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// return value needs to wind up
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// in a0. EZ!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;square&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;mul&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;a0&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:10&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because leaf functions won&amp;rsquo;t call other functions, they won&amp;rsquo;t need to save the
caller-saved &lt;code&gt;tX&lt;/code&gt; registers, so they can freely use them instead of the &lt;code&gt;sX&lt;/code&gt;
registers.&lt;h2 id=the-end-for-now&gt;&lt;a href=#the-end-for-now&gt;The End, for Now&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Phew! We&amp;rsquo;re around six thousand words in, so let&amp;rsquo;s checkpoint what we&amp;rsquo;ve
learned:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Computers are stupid, but can at least follow &lt;em&gt;extremely&lt;/em&gt; basic
instructions, which are encoded as binary.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Assembly language is human-readable version of these basic instructions for
a particular computer.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Assembly language programs consist of &lt;em&gt;instructions&lt;/em&gt;, &lt;em&gt;labels&lt;/em&gt;, and
&lt;em&gt;directives&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Each instruction is a &lt;em&gt;mnemonic&lt;/em&gt; followed by zero or more &lt;em&gt;operands&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Registers&lt;/em&gt; hold values the machine is currently operating on.&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;Instructions can be broadly categorized as &lt;em&gt;arithmetic&lt;/em&gt;, &lt;em&gt;memory&lt;/em&gt;, &lt;em&gt;control
flow&lt;/em&gt;, and &amp;ldquo;miscellaneous&amp;rdquo; (plus &lt;em&gt;vector&lt;/em&gt; and &lt;em&gt;float&lt;/em&gt; instructions, for
another time).&lt;li&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;em&gt;calling convention&lt;/em&gt; describes the low-level interface of a general
function, consisting of some pre-call setup, and a prologue and epilogue in
each function.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;That&amp;rsquo;s all for now. RISC-V is a powerful but reasonably simple ISA. Next time,
we&amp;rsquo;ll dive into the much older, much larger, and much more complex Intel x86.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is a hilarious lie that is beyond the scope of this post. See, for
example, &lt;a href=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superscalar_processor&gt;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superscalar_processor&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;What&amp;rsquo;s a machine word, exactly? It really depends on context. Most popular
architectures has a straight-forward definition: the size of a GPR &lt;em&gt;or&lt;/em&gt; the
size of a pointer, which are the same.&lt;p&gt;This is not true of all architectures, so beware.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Thankfully, these can be polyfilled using the previous ubiquitous
instructions. Hacker&amp;rsquo;s Delight contains all of the relevant algorithms, so I
won&amp;rsquo;t reproduce them here. The division polyfills are particularly
interesting.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s a bit interesting that we don&amp;rsquo;t write &lt;code&gt;lw a1, a0[4]&lt;/code&gt; in imitation of
array syntax. This specific corner of the notation is shockingly diverse
across assemblers: in ARM, we write &lt;code&gt;ldr r0, [r1, #offset]&lt;/code&gt;; in x86,
&lt;code&gt;mov rax, [rdx + offset]&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;movq offset(%rdx), %rax&lt;/code&gt; for AT&amp;amp;T-flavored
assemblers (which is surprisingly similar to the RISC-V syntax!); in 6502,
&lt;code&gt;lda ($1234, X)&lt;/code&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;The calling convention isn&amp;rsquo;t actually determined by the architecture in most
cases; that&amp;rsquo;s why it&amp;rsquo;s called a &lt;em&gt;convention&lt;/em&gt;. The convention on x86 actually
differs on Windows and Linux, and is usually also language-dependent; C&amp;rsquo;s
calling convention is usually documented, but C++, Rust, and Go invent their
own to handle language-specific fussiness.&lt;p&gt;Of course, if you&amp;rsquo;re writing assembly, you can do whatever you want (though
the silicon may be optimized for a particular recommended calling
convention).&lt;p&gt;RISC-V defines a recommended calling convention for ELF-based targets:
&lt;a href=https://github.com/riscv-non-isa/riscv-elf-psabi-doc&gt;https://github.com/riscv-non-isa/riscv-elf-psabi-doc&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;The following listing shows how all kinds of different arguments are passed.

Given&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;typedef&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;100&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;];&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;X&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;lw&lt;/span&gt;      &lt;span class=n&gt;s1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;RISC-V Assembly&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Note that &lt;code&gt;sb s0, 0(s1)&lt;/code&gt; stores the input value &lt;code&gt;x&lt;/code&gt; into the first element
of the big array &lt;em&gt;after&lt;/em&gt; calling memset. If we move the store to before, we
can avoid much silliness, including some unnecessary spills:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-riscv highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;make_big&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;        &lt;span class=n&gt;addi&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;sp&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;
