  <entry>
    <title>Everything You Never Wanted To Know About Linker Script</title>
    <link href="/2021/06/01/linker-script"/>
    <updated>2021-06-01T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2021/06/01/linker-script</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Low level software usually has lots of &lt;code&gt;.cc&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;.rs&lt;/code&gt; files. Even lower-level
software, like your cryptography library, probably has &lt;code&gt;.S&lt;/code&gt; containing assembly,
my least favorite language for code review.&lt;p&gt;The lowest level software out there, firmware, kernels, and drivers, have one
third file type to feed into the toolchain: an &lt;code&gt;.ld&lt;/code&gt; file, a &amp;ldquo;linker script&amp;rdquo;.
The linker script, provided to Clang as &lt;code&gt;-Wl,-T,foo.ld&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, is like a
template for the final executable. It tells the linker how to organize code from
the input objects. This permits extremely precise control over the toolchain&amp;rsquo;s
output.&lt;p&gt;Very few people know how to write linker script; it&amp;rsquo;s a bit of an obscure skill.
Unfortunately, I&amp;rsquo;m one of them, so I get called to do it on occasion. Hopefully,
this post is a good enough summary of the linker script language that you, too,
can build your own binary!&lt;p&gt;Everything in this post can be found in excruciating detail in
&lt;a href=https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/index.html&gt;GNU &lt;code&gt;ld&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s documentation&lt;/a&gt;;
&lt;code&gt;lld&lt;/code&gt; accepts basically the same syntax. There&amp;rsquo;s no spec, just what your linker
happens to accept. I will, however, do my best to provide a more friendly
introduction.&lt;p&gt;No prior knowledge of how toolchains work is necessary! Where possible, I&amp;rsquo;ve
tried to provide historical context on the names of everything. Toolchains are,
unfortunately, bound by half a century of tradition. Better to at least know why
they&amp;rsquo;re called that.&lt;blockquote id=aside:1 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;On Windows, assembly files use the sensible &lt;code&gt;.asm&lt;/code&gt; extension. POSIX we use the
&lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; extension, or &lt;code&gt;.S&lt;/code&gt; when we&amp;rsquo;d like Clang to run the C preprocessor on them
(virtually all hand-written assembly is of the second kind).&lt;p&gt;I don&amp;rsquo;t actually have a historical citation&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; for &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt;, other
than that it came from the Unix tradition of obnoxiously terse names. If we
are to believe that &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; stands for &amp;ldquo;object&amp;rdquo;, and &lt;code&gt;.a&lt;/code&gt; stands for &amp;ldquo;archive&amp;rdquo;,
then &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; must stand for &amp;ldquo;source&amp;rdquo;, up until the B compiler replaced them with
&lt;code&gt;.b&lt;/code&gt; files! See &lt;a href=http://man.cat-v.org/unix-1st/1/b&gt;http://man.cat-v.org/unix-1st/1/b&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A final bit of trivia: &lt;code&gt;.C&lt;/code&gt; files are obviously different from &lt;code&gt;.c&lt;/code&gt; files&amp;mldr;
they&amp;rsquo;re C++ files! (Seriously, try it.)&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;This post is specifically about POSIX. I know basically nothing about
MSVC and &lt;code&gt;link.exe&lt;/code&gt; other than that they exist. The most I&amp;rsquo;ve done is helped
people debug trivial &lt;code&gt;__declspec&lt;/code&gt; issues.&lt;p&gt;I will also only be covering things specific to linking an executable; linking
other outputs, like shared libraries, is beyond this post.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=seriously-whats-a-linker&gt;&lt;a href=#seriously-whats-a-linker&gt;Seriously, What&amp;rsquo;s a linker?&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;A linker is but a small part of a &lt;em&gt;toolchain&lt;/em&gt;, the low-level programmer&amp;rsquo;s
toolbox: everything you need to go from source code to execution.&lt;p&gt;The crown jewel of any toolchain is the compiler. The LLVM toolchain, for
example, includes Clang, a C/C++&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; compiler. The compiler takes
source code, such as &lt;code&gt;.cc&lt;/code&gt;, and lowers it down to a &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; file, an &lt;em&gt;assembly
file&lt;/em&gt; which textually describes machine code for a specific architecture (you
can also write them yourself).&lt;p&gt;Another toolchain program, the assembler, &lt;em&gt;assembles&lt;/em&gt; each &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; into a &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt;
file, an &lt;em&gt;object file&lt;/em&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. An assembly file is merely a textual
representation of an object file; assemblers are not particularly interesting
programs.&lt;p&gt;A third program, the linker, &lt;em&gt;links&lt;/em&gt; all of your object files into a final
&lt;em&gt;executable&lt;/em&gt; or &lt;em&gt;binary&lt;/em&gt;, traditionally given the name &lt;code&gt;a.out&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This three (or two, if you do compile/assemble in one step) phase process is
sometimes called the &lt;em&gt;C compilation model&lt;/em&gt;. All modern software build
infrastructure is built around this model&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=aside:2 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:2&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Clang, being based on LLVM, actually exposes one stage in between the &lt;code&gt;.cc&lt;/code&gt;
file and the &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; file. You can ask it to skip doing codegen and emit a &lt;code&gt;.ll&lt;/code&gt;
file filled with LLVM IR, an intermediate between human-writable source code
and assembly. The magic words to get this file are &lt;code&gt;clang -S -emit-llvm&lt;/code&gt;. (The
Rust equivalent is &lt;code&gt;rustc --emit=llvm-ir&lt;/code&gt;.)&lt;p&gt;The LLVM toolchain provides &lt;code&gt;llc&lt;/code&gt;, the LLVM compiler, which performs the &lt;code&gt;.ll&lt;/code&gt;
-&gt; &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; step (optionally assembling it, too). &lt;code&gt;lli&lt;/code&gt; is an interpreter for the
IR. Studying IR is mostly useful for understanding optimization behavior;
topic for another day.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;The compiler, assembler, and linker are the central components of a toolchain.
Other languages, like Rust, usually provide their own toolchain, or just a
compiler, reusing the existing C/C++ toolchain. The assembler and linker are
language agnostic.&lt;p&gt;The toolchain also provides various debugging tools, including an interactive
debugger, and tools for manipulating object files, such as &lt;code&gt;nm&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;objdump&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;objcopy&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;ar&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;These days, most of this stuff is bundled into a single program, the compiler
frontend, which knows how to compiler, assemble, and link, in one invocation.
You can ask Clang to spit out &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; files with &lt;code&gt;clang -c&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; files with
&lt;code&gt;clang -S&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;blockquote id=aside:3 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:3&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;The UNIX crowd at Bell Labs was very excited about short, terse names. This
tradition survives in Go&amp;rsquo;s somewhat questionable practice of single-letter
variables.&lt;p&gt;Most toolchain program names are cute contractions. &lt;code&gt;cc&lt;/code&gt; is &amp;ldquo;C compiler&amp;rdquo;;
compilers for almost all other languages follow this convention, like &lt;code&gt;rustc&lt;/code&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;javac&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;protoc&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;scalac&lt;/code&gt;; Clang is just &lt;code&gt;clang&lt;/code&gt;, but is perfectly ok
being called as &lt;code&gt;cc&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;as&lt;/code&gt; is &amp;ldquo;assembler&amp;rdquo;; &lt;code&gt;ld&lt;/code&gt; is &amp;ldquo;loader&amp;rdquo; (you&amp;rsquo;ll learn why sooner). &lt;code&gt;ar&lt;/code&gt; is
&amp;ldquo;archiver&amp;rdquo;, &lt;code&gt;nm&lt;/code&gt; is &amp;ldquo;names&amp;rdquo;. Other names tend to be a bit more sensible.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h3 id=final-link&gt;&lt;a href=#final-link&gt;Final Link&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Some fifty years ago at Bell Labs, someone really wanted to write a program with
more than one &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; file. To solve this, a program that could &amp;ldquo;link&amp;rdquo; symbol
references across object files was written: the first linker.&lt;p&gt;You can take several &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; files and use &lt;code&gt;ar&lt;/code&gt; (an archaic &lt;code&gt;tar&lt;/code&gt;, basically) to
create a library, which always have names like &lt;code&gt;libfoo.a&lt;/code&gt; (the &lt;code&gt;lib&lt;/code&gt; is
mandatory). A static library is just a collection of objects, which can be
provided on an as-needed basis to the linker.&lt;p&gt;The &amp;ldquo;final link&amp;rdquo; incorporates several &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; files and &lt;code&gt;.a&lt;/code&gt; files to produce an
executable. It does roughly the following:&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;Parse all the objects and static libraries and put their &lt;em&gt;symbols&lt;/em&gt; into a
database. Symbols are named addresses of functions and global variables.&lt;li&gt;Search for all unresolved symbol references in the &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; files and match it up
with a symbol from the database, recursively doing this for any code in a
&lt;code&gt;.a&lt;/code&gt; referenced during this process. This forms a sort of dependency graph
between sections. This step is called &lt;em&gt;symbol resolution&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Throw out any code that isn&amp;rsquo;t referenced by the input files by tracing the
dependency graph from the entry-point symbol (e.g., &lt;code&gt;_start&lt;/code&gt; on Linux). This
step is called &lt;em&gt;garbage collection&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Execute the linker script to figure out how to stitch the final binary
together. This includes discovering the offsets at which everything will go.&lt;li&gt;Resolve &lt;em&gt;relocations&lt;/em&gt;, &amp;ldquo;holes&amp;rdquo; in the binary that require knowing the final
runtime address of the section. Relocations are instructions placed in the
object file for the linker to execute.&lt;li&gt;Write out the completed binary.&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;p&gt;This process is extremely memory-intensive; it is possible for colossal
binaries, especially ones with tons of debug information, to &amp;ldquo;fail to link&amp;rdquo;
because the linker exhausts the system&amp;rsquo;s memory.&lt;p&gt;We only care about step 4; whole books can be written about the previous steps.
Thankfully, Ian Lance Taylor, mad linker scientist and author of &lt;code&gt;gold&lt;/code&gt;, has
written several excellent words on this topic:
&lt;a href=https://lwn.net/Articles/276782/&gt;https://lwn.net/Articles/276782/&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;h2 id=object-files-and-sections&gt;&lt;a href=#object-files-and-sections&gt;Object Files and Sections&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Linkers, fundamentally, consume object files and produce object files; the
output is executable, meaning that all relocations have been resolved and an
entry-point address (where the OS/bootloader will jump to to start the binary).&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s useful to be able to peek into object files. The &lt;code&gt;objdump&lt;/code&gt; utility is best
for this. &lt;code&gt;objdump -x my_object.o&lt;/code&gt; will show &lt;em&gt;all&lt;/em&gt; headers, telling you what
exactly is in it.&lt;p&gt;At a high level, an object file describes how a program should be loaded into
memory. The object is divided into sections, which are named blocks of data.
Sections may have file-like permissions, such as allocatable, loadable,
readonly, and executable. &lt;code&gt;objdump -h&lt;/code&gt; can be used to show the list of sections.
Some selected lines of output from &lt;code&gt;objdump&lt;/code&gt; on my machine (I&amp;rsquo;m on a 64-bit
machine, but I&amp;rsquo;ve trimmed leading zeros to make it all fit):&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-terminal highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;$ objdump -h &amp;#34;$(which clang)&amp;#34;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;/usr/bin/clang:     file format elf64-x86-64
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;Sections:
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;Idx Name    Size      VMA       LMA       File off  Algn
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 11 .init   00000017  00691ab8  00691ab8  00291ab8  2**2
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY, CODE
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 12 .plt    00006bb0  00691ad0  00691ad0  00291ad0  2**4
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY, CODE
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 13 .text   0165e861  00698680  00698680  00298680  2**4
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY, CODE
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 14 .fini   00000009  01cf6ee4  01cf6ee4  018f6ee4  2**2
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY, CODE
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 15 .rodata 0018ec68  01cf6ef0  01cf6ef0  018f6ef0  2**4
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, READONLY, DATA
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 24 .data   000024e8  021cd5d0  021cd5d0  01dcc5d0  2**4
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            CONTENTS, ALLOC, LOAD, DATA
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 26 .bss    00009d21  021cfac0  021cfac0  01dceab8  2**4
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;            ALLOC
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;Terminal&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Allocateable (&lt;code&gt;ALLOC&lt;/code&gt;) sections must be &lt;em&gt;allocated&lt;/em&gt; space by the operating
system; if the section is loadable (&lt;code&gt;LOAD&lt;/code&gt;), then the operating system must
further fill that space with the contents of the section. This process is called
&lt;em&gt;loading&lt;/em&gt; and is performed by a &lt;em&gt;loader&lt;/em&gt; program&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. The
loader is sometimes called the &amp;ldquo;dynamic linker&amp;rdquo;, and is often the same program
as the &amp;ldquo;program linker&amp;rdquo;; this is why the linker is called &lt;code&gt;ld&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Loading can also be done beforehand using the &lt;code&gt;binary&lt;/code&gt; output format. This is
useful for tiny microcontrollers that are too primitive to perform any loading.
&lt;code&gt;objcopy&lt;/code&gt; is useful for this and many other tasks that involve transforming
object files.&lt;p&gt;Some common (POSIX) sections include:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt;, where your code lives&lt;sup id=fnref:8&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:8 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;8&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. It&amp;rsquo;s usually a loadable,
readonly, executable section.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;.data&lt;/code&gt; contains the initial values of global variables. It&amp;rsquo;s loadable.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;.rodata&lt;/code&gt; contains constants. It&amp;rsquo;s loadable and readonly.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;.bss&lt;/code&gt; is an empty allocatable section&lt;sup id=fnref:9&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:9 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;9&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. C specifies that
uninitialized globals default to zero; this is a convenient way for avoiding
storing a huge block of zeros in the executable!&lt;li&gt;Debug sections that are not loaded or allocated; these are usually removed for
release builds.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;After the linker decides which sections from the &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;.a&lt;/code&gt; inputs to keep
(based on which symbols it decided it needed), it looks to the linker script how
to arrange them in the output.&lt;p&gt;Let&amp;rsquo;s write our first linker script!&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* Define an output section &amp;#34;.text&amp;#34;. */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* Pull in all symbols in input sections named .text */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;text&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* Do the same for sections starting with .text.,
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;       such as .text.foo */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;text&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* Do the same for &amp;#34;.bss&amp;#34;, &amp;#34;.rodata&amp;#34;, and &amp;#34;.data&amp;#34;. */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;bss&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bss&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bss&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;data&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;rodata&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rodata&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rodata&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This tells the linker to create a &lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt; section in the output, which contains
all sections named &lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt; from all inputs, plus all sections with names like
&lt;code&gt;.text.foo&lt;/code&gt;. The content of the section is laid out in order: the contents of
all &lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt; sections will come before any &lt;code&gt;.text.*&lt;/code&gt; sections; I don&amp;rsquo;t think the
linker makes any promises about the ordering between different
objects&lt;sup id=fnref:10&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:10 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;10&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;As I mentioned before, parsers for linker script are fussy&lt;sup id=fnref:11&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:11 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;11&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;: the
space in &lt;code&gt;.text :&lt;/code&gt; is significant.&lt;p&gt;Note that the two &lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt; sections are different, and can have different names!
The linker generally doesn&amp;rsquo;t care what a section is named; just its attributes.
We could name it &lt;code&gt;code&lt;/code&gt; if we wanted to; even the leading period is mere
convention. Some object file formats don&amp;rsquo;t support arbitrary sections; all the
sane ones (ELF, COFF, Mach-O) don&amp;rsquo;t care, but they don&amp;rsquo;t all spell it the same
way; in Mach-O, you call it &lt;code&gt;__text&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Before continuing, I recommend looking at the &lt;a href=#appendix&gt;appendix&lt;/a&gt; so that you
have a clear path towards being able to run and test your linker scripts!&lt;blockquote id=aside:4 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:4&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;None of this syntax is used in practice but it&amp;rsquo;s useful to contextualize the
syntax for pulling in a section. The full form of the syntax is&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language- highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;archive:object(section1 section2 ...)
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Plaintext&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Naturally, all of this is optional, so you can write &lt;code&gt;foo.o&lt;/code&gt; or
&lt;code&gt;libbar.a:(.text)&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;:baz.o(.text .data)&lt;/code&gt;, where the last one means &amp;ldquo;not
part of a library&amp;rdquo;. There&amp;rsquo;s even an &lt;code&gt;EXCLUDE_FILE&lt;/code&gt; syntax for filtering by
source object, and a &lt;code&gt;INPUT_SECTION_FLAGS&lt;/code&gt; syntax for filtering by the
presence of format-specific flags.&lt;p&gt;Do not use any of this. Just write &lt;code&gt;*(.text)&lt;/code&gt; and don&amp;rsquo;t think about it too
hard. The &lt;code&gt;*&lt;/code&gt; is just a glob for all objects.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Each section has an &lt;em&gt;alignment&lt;/em&gt;, which is just the maximum of the alignments of
all input sections pulled into it. This is important for ensuring that code and
globals are aligned the way the architecture expects them to be. The alignment
of a section can be set explicitly with&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;super_aligned&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ALIGN&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;You can also instruct the linker to toss out sections using the special
&lt;code&gt;/DISCARD/&lt;/code&gt; output section, which overrides any decisions made at
garbage-collection time. I&amp;rsquo;ve only ever used this to discard debug information
that GCC was really excited about keeping around.&lt;p&gt;On the other hand, you can use &lt;code&gt;KEEP(*(.text.*))&lt;/code&gt; to ensure no &lt;code&gt;.text&lt;/code&gt; sections
are discarded by garbage-collection. Unfortunately, this doesn&amp;rsquo;t let you pull in
sections from static libraries that weren&amp;rsquo;t referenced in the input objects.&lt;h3 id=lma-and-vma&gt;&lt;a href=#lma-and-vma&gt;LMA and VMA&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Every section has three addresses associated with it. The simplest is the file
offset: how far from the start of the file to find the section.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;em&gt;virtual memory address&lt;/em&gt;, or VMA, is where the program expects to find the
section at runtime. This is the address that is used by pointers and the program
counter.&lt;p&gt;The &lt;em&gt;load memory address&lt;/em&gt;, or LMA, is where the loader (be it a runtime loader
or &lt;code&gt;objcpy&lt;/code&gt;) must place the code. This is almost always the same as the VMA.
Later on, in &lt;a href=#rom-ram-lma&gt;Using Symbols and LMAs&lt;/a&gt;, I&amp;rsquo;ll explain a place where
this is actually useful.&lt;p&gt;When declaring a new section, the VMA and LMA are both set to the
value&lt;sup id=fnref:12&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:12 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;12&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; of the &lt;em&gt;location counter&lt;/em&gt;, which has the &lt;em&gt;extremely&lt;/em&gt;
descriptive name &lt;code&gt;.&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:13&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:13 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;13&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. This counter is automatically incremented as
data is copied from the input&lt;p&gt;We can explicitly specify the VMA of a section by putting an expression before
the colon, and the LMA by putting an expression in the &lt;code&gt;AT(lma)&lt;/code&gt; specifier
&lt;em&gt;after&lt;/em&gt; the colon:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mh&gt;0x10008000&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;AT&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x40008000&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This will modify the location counter; you could also write it as&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mh&gt;0x10008000&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;AT&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x40008000&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Within &lt;code&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/code&gt;, the location counter can be set at any point, even while in
the middle of declaring a section (though the linker will probably complain if
you do something rude like move it backwards).&lt;p&gt;The location counter is incremented automatically as sections are added, so it&amp;rsquo;s
rarely necessary to fuss with it directly.&lt;h2 id=memory-regions-and-section-allocation&gt;&lt;a href=#memory-regions-and-section-allocation&gt;Memory Regions and Section Allocation&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;By default, the linker will simply allocate sections starting at address &lt;code&gt;0&lt;/code&gt;.
The &lt;code&gt;MEMORY&lt;/code&gt; statement can be used to define &lt;em&gt;memory regions&lt;/em&gt; for more finely
controlling how VMAs and LMAs are allocated without writing them down
explicitly.&lt;p&gt;A classic example of a &lt;code&gt;MEMORY&lt;/code&gt; block separates the address space into ROM and
RAM:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MEMORY&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;rom&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rx&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ORIGIN&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mh&gt;0x8000&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;     &lt;span class=n&gt;LENGTH&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;16&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;K&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;ram&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rw&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ORIGIN&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mh&gt;0x10000000&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;LENGTH&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;256&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;M&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;A region is a block of memory with a name and some attributes. The name is
irrelevant beyond the scope of the linker script. The attributes in parens are
used to specify what sections could conceivably go in that region. A section is
compatible if it has any of the attributes before the &lt;code&gt;!&lt;/code&gt;, and none which come
after the &lt;code&gt;!&lt;/code&gt;. (This filter mini-language isn&amp;rsquo;t very expressive.)&lt;p&gt;The attributes are the ones we mentioned earlier: &lt;code&gt;rwxal&lt;/code&gt; are readonly,
read/write, executable, allocated, and loadable&lt;sup id=fnref:14&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:14 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;14&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;When allocating a section a VMA, the linker will try to pick the best memory
region that matches the filter using a heuristic. I don&amp;rsquo;t really trust the
heuristic, but you can instead write &lt;code&gt;&gt; region&lt;/code&gt; to put something into a specific
region. Thus,&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTION&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ram&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;AT&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rom&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;AT&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is the &amp;ldquo;obvious&amp;rdquo; of &lt;code&gt;AT()&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, and sets which region to allocate the
LMA from.&lt;p&gt;The origin and length of a region can be obtained with the &lt;code&gt;ORIGIN(region)&lt;/code&gt; and
&lt;code&gt;LENGTH(region)&lt;/code&gt; functions.&lt;h2 id=other-stuff-to-put-in-sections&gt;&lt;a href=#other-stuff-to-put-in-sections&gt;Other Stuff to Put In Sections&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Output sections can hold more than just input sections. Arbitrary data can be
placed into sections using the &lt;code&gt;BYTE&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;SHORT&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;LONG&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;QUAD&lt;/code&gt; for placing
literal 8, 16, 32, and 64-bit unsigned integers into the section:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:9&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;screams_internally&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;LONG&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0xaaaaaaaa&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:9&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Numeric literals in linker script may, conveniently, be given the suffixes &lt;code&gt;K&lt;/code&gt;
or &lt;code&gt;M&lt;/code&gt; to specify a kilobyte or megabyte quantity. E.g., &lt;code&gt;4K&lt;/code&gt; is sugar for
&lt;code&gt;4096&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;h3 id=fill&gt;&lt;a href=#fill&gt;Fill&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;You can fill the unused portions of a section by using the &lt;code&gt;FILL&lt;/code&gt; command, which
sets the &amp;ldquo;fill pattern&amp;rdquo; from that point onward. For example, we can create four
kilobytes of &lt;code&gt;0xaa&lt;/code&gt; using &lt;code&gt;FILL&lt;/code&gt; and the location counter:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:10&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;scream_page&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;FILL&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0xaa&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;K&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:10&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &amp;ldquo;fill pattern&amp;rdquo; is used to fill any unspecified space, such as alignment
padding or jumping around with the location counter. We can use multiple FILLs
to vary the fill pattern, such as if we wanted half the page to be &lt;code&gt;0x0a&lt;/code&gt; and
half &lt;code&gt;0xa0&lt;/code&gt;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:11&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;scream_page&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;FILL&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x0a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;K&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;FILL&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0xa0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;K&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:11&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;When using one fill pattern for the whole section, you can just write &lt;code&gt;= fill;&lt;/code&gt;
at the end of the section. For example,&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:12&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;scream_page&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;4&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;K&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mh&gt;0xaa&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:12&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=linker-symbols&gt;&lt;a href=#linker-symbols&gt;Linker Symbols&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Although the linker needs to resolve all symbols using the input &lt;code&gt;.o&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;.a&lt;/code&gt;
files, you can also declare symbols directly in linker script; this is the
absolute latest that symbols can be provided. For example:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:13&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;my_cool_symbol&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;5&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This will define a new symbol with value &lt;code&gt;5&lt;/code&gt;. If we then wrote
&lt;code&gt;extern char my_cool_symbol;&lt;/code&gt;, we can access the value placed by the linker.
However, note that the value of a symbol is an &lt;em&gt;address&lt;/em&gt;! If you did&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;my_cool_symbol&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uintptr_t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;my_cool_symbol&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;the processor would be very confused about why you just dereferenced a pointer
with address &lt;code&gt;5&lt;/code&gt;. The &lt;em&gt;correct&lt;/em&gt; way to extract a linker symbol&amp;rsquo;s value is to
write&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;my_cool_symbol&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uintptr_t&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uintptr_t&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;my_cool_symbol&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;It seems a bit silly to take the address of the global and use that as some kind
of magic value, but that&amp;rsquo;s just how it works. The exact same mechanism works in
Rust, too:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:16&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;C&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[link_name = &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;my_cool_symbol&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:16&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The most common use of this mechanism is percolating information not known until
link time. For example, a common idiom is&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:17&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;__text_start&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;.;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* stuff */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;__text_end&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;.;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:17&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This allows initialization code to find the section&amp;rsquo;s address and length; in
this case, the pointer values are actually meaningful!&lt;blockquote id=aside:5 class=aside aside&gt;&lt;a href=#aside:5&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;aside&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;It&amp;rsquo;s common practice to lead linker symbols with two underscores, because C
declares a surprisingly large class of symbols reserved for the
implementation, so normal user code won&amp;rsquo;t call them. These include names like
&lt;code&gt;__text_start&lt;/code&gt;, which start with two underscores, and names starting with an
underscore and an uppercase letter, like &lt;code&gt;_Atomic&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;However, libc and STL headers will totally use the double underscore symbols
to make them resistant to tampering by users (which they are entitled to), so
beware!&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;Symbol assignments can even go inside of a section, to capture the location
counter&amp;rsquo;s value between input sections:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:18&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;text&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=n&gt;text_middle&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;.;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;text&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:18&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Symbol names are not limited to C identifiers, and may contain dashes, periods,
dollar signs, and other symbols. They may even be quoted, like
&lt;code&gt;&#34;this symbol has spaces&#34;&lt;/code&gt;, which C will never be able to access as an &lt;code&gt;extern&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;There is a mini-language of expressions that symbols can be assigned to. This
includes:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Numeric literals like &lt;code&gt;42&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;0xaa&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;4K&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;The location counter, &lt;code&gt;.&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Other symbols.&lt;li&gt;The usual set of C operators, such as arithmetic and bit operations. Xor is
curiously missing.&lt;li&gt;A handful of builtin functions, described below.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;There are some fairly complicated rules around how symbols may be given relative
addresses to the start of a section, which are only relevant when dealing with
position-independent code:
&lt;a href=https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Expression-Section.html&gt;https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Expression-Section.html&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Functions belong to one of two board categories: getters for properties of
sections, memory regions, and other linker structures; and arithmetic. Useful
functions include:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;ADDR&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;LOADADDR&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;SIZEOF&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;ALIGNOF&lt;/code&gt;, which produce the VMA, LMA, size,
and alignment of a previously defined section.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;ORIGIN&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;LENGTH&lt;/code&gt;, which produce the start address and length of a memory
region.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;MAX&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;MIN&lt;/code&gt; are obvious; &lt;code&gt;LOG2CEIL&lt;/code&gt; computes the base-2 log, rounded up.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;ALIGN(expr, align)&lt;/code&gt; rounds &lt;code&gt;expr&lt;/code&gt; to the next multiple of &lt;code&gt;align&lt;/code&gt;.
&lt;code&gt;ALIGN(align)&lt;/code&gt; is roughly equivalent to &lt;code&gt;ALIGN(., align)&lt;/code&gt; with some subtleties
around PIC. &lt;code&gt;. = ALIGN(align);&lt;/code&gt; will align the location counter to &lt;code&gt;align&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;Some other builtins can be found at
&lt;a href=https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Builtin-Functions.html&gt;https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Builtin-Functions.html&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;A symbol definition can be wrapped in the &lt;code&gt;PROVIDEO()&lt;/code&gt; function to make it
&amp;ldquo;weak&amp;rdquo;, analogous to the &amp;ldquo;weak symbol&amp;rdquo; feature found in Clang. This means that
the linker will not use the definition if any input object defines it.&lt;h3 id=using-symbols-and-lmas-rom-ram-lma&gt;&lt;a href=#using-symbols-and-lmas-rom-ram-lma&gt;Using Symbols and LMAs {#rom-ram-lma}&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;As mentioned before, it is extremely rare for the LMA and VMA to be different.
The most common situation where this occurs is when you&amp;rsquo;re running on a system,
like a microcontroller, where memory is partitioned into two pieces: ROM and
RAM. The ROM has the executable burned into it, and RAM starts out full of
random garbage.&lt;p&gt;Most of the contents of the linked executable are read-only, so their VMA can be
in ROM. However, the &lt;code&gt;.data&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;.bss&lt;/code&gt; sections need to lie in RAM, because
they&amp;rsquo;re writable. For &lt;code&gt;.bss&lt;/code&gt; this is easy, because it doesn&amp;rsquo;t have loadable
content. For &lt;code&gt;.data&lt;/code&gt;, though, we need to separate the VMA and LMA: the VMA must
go in RAM, and the LMA in ROM.&lt;p&gt;This distinction is important for the code that initializes the RAM: while for
&lt;code&gt;.bss&lt;/code&gt; all it has to do is zero it, for &lt;code&gt;.data&lt;/code&gt;, it has to copy from ROM to RAM!
The LMA lets us distinguish the copy source and the copy destination.&lt;p&gt;This has the important property that it tells the loader (usually &lt;code&gt;objcopy&lt;/code&gt; in
this case) to use the ROM addresses for actually loading the section to, but to
link the code as if it were at a RAM address (which is needed for things like
PC-relative loads to work correctly).&lt;p&gt;Here&amp;rsquo;s how we&amp;rsquo;d do it in linker script:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:19&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MEMORY&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nl&gt;rom&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=nl&gt;ram&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* .text and .rodata just go straight into the ROM. We don&amp;#39;t need
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;     to mutate them ever. */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;text&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;text&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rom&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;rodata&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;rodata&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rom&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* .bss doesn&amp;#39;t have any &amp;#34;loadable&amp;#34; content, so it goes straight
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;     into RAM. We could include `AT&amp;gt; rom`, but because the sections
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;     have no content, it doesn&amp;#39;t matter. */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;bss&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bss&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ram&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* As described above, we need to get a RAM VMA but a ROM LMA;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;     the &amp;gt; and AT&amp;gt; operators achieve this. */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nl&gt;data&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ram&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;AT&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rom&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;/* The initialization code will need some symbols to know how to
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;   zero the .bss and copy the initial .data values. We can use the
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=cm&gt;   functions from the previous section for this! */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bss_end&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;bss_start&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;SIZEOF&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bss&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data_end&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;data_start&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;+&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;SIZEOF&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rom_data_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[];&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;init_sections&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Zero the .bss.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;memset&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;bss_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;bss_end&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;bss_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Copy the .data values from ROM to RAM.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;memcpy&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;rom_data_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;data_end&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;-&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;data_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:20&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h2 id=misc-linker-script-features&gt;&lt;a href=#misc-linker-script-features&gt;Misc Linker Script Features&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Linker script includes a bunch of other commands that don&amp;rsquo;t fit into a specific
category:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;ENTRY()&lt;/code&gt; sets the program entry-point, either as a symbol or a raw address.
The &lt;code&gt;-e&lt;/code&gt; flag can be used to override it. The &lt;code&gt;ld&lt;/code&gt; docs assert that there are
fallbacks if an entry-point can&amp;rsquo;t be found, but in my experience you can
sometimes get errors here. &lt;code&gt;ENTRY(_start)&lt;/code&gt; would use the &lt;code&gt;_start&lt;/code&gt; symbol, for
example&lt;sup id=fnref:15&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:15 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;15&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;INCLUDE &#34;path/to/file.ld&#34;&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;code&gt;#include&lt;/code&gt; but for linker script.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;INPUT(foo.o)&lt;/code&gt; will add &lt;code&gt;foo.o&lt;/code&gt; as a linker input, as if it was passed at the
commandline. &lt;code&gt;GROUP&lt;/code&gt; is similar, but with the semantics of &lt;code&gt;--start-group&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;OUTPUT()&lt;/code&gt; overrides the usual &lt;code&gt;a.out&lt;/code&gt; default output name.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;ASSERT()&lt;/code&gt; provides static assertions.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;EXTERN(sym)&lt;/code&gt; causes the linker to behave as if an undefined reference to
&lt;code&gt;sym&lt;/code&gt; existed in an input object.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;(Other commands are documented, but I&amp;rsquo;ve never needed them in practice.)&lt;h2 id=real-linker-scripts&gt;&lt;a href=#real-linker-scripts&gt;Real Linker Scripts&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;It may be useful to look at some real-life linker scripts.&lt;p&gt;If you wanna see what Clang, Rust, and the like all ultimately use, run
&lt;code&gt;ld --verbose&lt;/code&gt;. This will print the default linker script for your machine; this
is a really intense script that uses basically every feature available in linker
script (and, since it&amp;rsquo;s GNU, is very poorly formatted).&lt;p&gt;The Linux kernel also has linker scripts, which are differently intense, because
they use the C preprocessor. For example, the one for amd64:
&lt;a href=https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/kernel/vmlinux.lds.S&gt;https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/kernel/vmlinux.lds.S&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Tock OS, a secure operating system written in Rust, has some pretty solid linker
scripts, with lots of comments:
&lt;a href=https://github.com/tock/tock/blob/master/boards/kernel_layout.ld&gt;https://github.com/tock/tock/blob/master/boards/kernel_layout.ld&lt;/a&gt;. I recommend
taking a look to see what a &amp;ldquo;real&amp;rdquo; but not too wild linker script looks like.
There&amp;rsquo;s a fair bit of toolchain-specific stuff in there, too, that should give
you an idea of what to expect.&lt;p&gt;Happy linking!&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Blame GCC for this. &lt;code&gt;-Wl&lt;/code&gt; feeds arguments through to the linker, and &lt;code&gt;-T&lt;/code&gt; is
&lt;code&gt;ld&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s linker script input flag. Thankfully, rustc is far more sensible
here: &lt;code&gt;-Clink-args=-Wl,-T,foo.ld&lt;/code&gt; (when GCC/Clang is your linker frontend).&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Correction, 2022-09-11. I have really been bothered by not knowing if this
is actually true, and have periodically asked around about it. I asked Russ
Cox, who was actually &lt;em&gt;at&lt;/em&gt; Bell Labs back in the day, and he asked Ken
Thompson, who confirms: it&amp;rsquo;s genuinely &lt;code&gt;.s&lt;/code&gt; for source, because it was the
only source they had back then.&lt;p&gt;I am glad I got this from the horse&amp;rsquo;s mouth. :)&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;And many other things, like Objective-C.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Completely and utterly unrelated to the objects of object-oriented
programming. Best I can tell, the etymology is lost to time.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;a.out&lt;/code&gt; is &lt;em&gt;also&lt;/em&gt; an object file format, like ELF, but toolchains live and
die by tradition, so that&amp;rsquo;s the name given to the linker&amp;rsquo;s output by
default.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;Rust does not compile each &lt;code&gt;.rs&lt;/code&gt; file into an object, and its &amp;ldquo;crates&amp;rdquo; are
much larger than the average C++ translation unit. However, the Rust
compiler will nonetheless produce many object files for a single crate,
precisely for the benefit of this compilation model.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;Operating systems are loaded by a bootloader. Bootloaders are themselves
loaded by other bootloaders, such as the BIOS. At the bottom of the turtles
is the mask ROM, which is a tiny bootloader permanently burned into the
device.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:8&gt;&lt;p&gt;No idea on the etymology. This isn&amp;rsquo;t ASCII text!&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:8 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:9&gt;&lt;p&gt;Back in the 50s, this stood for &amp;ldquo;block started by symbol&amp;rdquo;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:10&gt;&lt;p&gt;Yes, yes, you can write &lt;code&gt;SORT_BY_NAME(*)(.text)&lt;/code&gt; but that&amp;rsquo;s not really
something you ever wind up needing.&lt;p&gt;See &lt;a href=https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Input-Section-Wildcards.html&gt;https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Input-Section-Wildcards.html&lt;/a&gt;
for more information on this.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:10 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:11&gt;&lt;p&gt;You only get &lt;code&gt;/* */&lt;/code&gt; comment syntax because that&amp;rsquo;s the lowest common
denominator.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:11 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:12&gt;&lt;p&gt;Well, &lt;code&gt;.&lt;/code&gt; actually gets increased to the alignment of the section first. If
you insist on an unaligned section, the syntax is, obviously,&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:21&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-ld highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SECTIONS&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;unaligned&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=cm&gt;/* ... */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:21&gt;Linker Script&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;(That was sarcasm. It must be stressed that this is not a friendly
language.)&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:12 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:13&gt;&lt;p&gt;This symbol is also available in assembly files. &lt;code&gt;jmp .&lt;/code&gt; is an overly-cute
idiom for an infinity busy loop. It is even more terse in ARM and RISC-V,
where it&amp;rsquo;s written &lt;code&gt;b .&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;j .&lt;/code&gt;, respectively.&lt;p&gt;Personally, I prefer the obtuse clarity of &lt;code&gt;loop_forever: j loop_forever&lt;/code&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:13 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:14&gt;&lt;p&gt;These are the same characters used to declare a section in assembly. If I
wanted to place my code in a section named &lt;code&gt;.crt0&lt;/code&gt; but wanted it to be
placed into a readonly, executable memory block, use the the assembler
directive &lt;code&gt;.section .crt0, rxal&lt;/code&gt;&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:14 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:15&gt;&lt;p&gt;Note that the entry point is almost never a function called &lt;code&gt;main()&lt;/code&gt;. In the
default configuration of most toolchains, an object called &lt;code&gt;crt0.o&lt;/code&gt; is
provided as part of the libc, which provides a &lt;code&gt;_start()&lt;/code&gt; function that
itself calls &lt;code&gt;main()&lt;/code&gt;. CRT stands for &amp;ldquo;C runtime&amp;rdquo;; thus, &lt;code&gt;crt0.o&lt;/code&gt;
initializes the C runtime.&lt;p&gt;This file contains the moral equivalent of the following C code, which
varies according to target:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:22&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;argc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;char&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;**&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;argv&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;noreturn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;_start&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;init_libc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Initializes global libc state.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;run_ctors&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Runs all library constructors.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=kt&gt;int&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;main&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;get_argc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;get_argv&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;run_dtors&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;    &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Runs all library destructors.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;cleanup_libc&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Deinitializes the libc.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;exit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ret&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Asks the OS to gracefully destroy the process.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:22&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This behavior can be disabled with &lt;code&gt;-nostartfiles&lt;/code&gt; in Clang. The OSDev wiki
has some on this topic:
&lt;a href=https://wiki.osdev.org/Creating_a_C_Library#Program_Initialization&gt;https://wiki.osdev.org/Creating_a_C_Library#Program_Initialization&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:15 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
