  <entry>
    <title>The Taxonomy of Pointers</title>
    <link href="/2021/05/24/ptr-taxonomy"/>
    <updated>2021-05-24T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2021/05/24/ptr-taxonomy</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Writing &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; in Rust usually involves manual management of memory. Although,
ideally, we&amp;rsquo;d like to exclusively use references for this, sometimes the
constraints they apply are too strong. This post is a guide on those constraints
and how to weaken them for correctness.&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Unmanaged&amp;rdquo; languages, like C++ and Rust, provide &lt;em&gt;pointer&lt;/em&gt; types for
manipulating memory. These types serve different purposes and provide different
guarantees. These guarantees are useful for the optimizer but get in the way of
correctness of low-level code. This is especially true in Rust, where these
constraints are very tight.&lt;blockquote id=note:1 class=note note&gt;&lt;a href=#note:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;note&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;This post only surveys &lt;em&gt;data&lt;/em&gt; pointers. Function pointers are their own
beast, but generally are less fussy, since they all have static
lifetime&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;h2 id=basic-c-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#basic-c-pointers&gt;Basic C++ Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;First, let&amp;rsquo;s survey C++. We have three pointer types: the traditional C pointer
&lt;code&gt;T*&lt;/code&gt;, C++ references &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&lt;/code&gt;, and rvalue references &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&amp;&lt;/code&gt;. These generally have
pretty weak guarantees.&lt;p&gt;Pointers provide virtually no guarantees at all: they can be null, point to
uninitialized memory, or point to nothing at all! C++ Only requires that they
be aligned&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. They are little more than an address (until they are
dereferenced, of course).&lt;p&gt;References, on the other hand, are intended to be the &amp;ldquo;primary&amp;rdquo; pointer type. A
&lt;code&gt;T&amp;&lt;/code&gt; cannot be null, is well-aligned, and is intended to only refer to live
memory (although it&amp;rsquo;s not something C++ can really guarantee for lack of a
borrow-checker). References are short-lived.&lt;p&gt;C++ uses non-nullness to its advantage. For example, Clang will absolutely
delete code of the form&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;auto&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;if&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;==&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;nullptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;DoSomething&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because references cannot be null, and dereferencing the null pointer is always
UB, the compiler may make this fairly strong assumption.&lt;p&gt;Rvalue references, &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&amp;&lt;/code&gt;, are not meaningfully different from normal references,
beyond their role in overload resolution.&lt;p&gt;Choosing a C++ (primitive) pointer type is well-studied and not the primary
purpose of this blog. Rather, we&amp;rsquo;re interested in how these map to Rust, which
has significantly more complicated pointers.&lt;h2 id=basic-rust-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#basic-rust-pointers&gt;Basic Rust Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Like C++, Rust has two broad pointer types: &lt;code&gt;*const T&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;*mut T&lt;/code&gt;, the raw
pointers, and &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt;, the references.&lt;p&gt;Rust pointer have even fewer constraints than C++ pointers; they need not even
be aligned&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;! The &lt;code&gt;const&lt;/code&gt;/&lt;code&gt;mut&lt;/code&gt; specifier is basically
irrelevant, but is useful as programmer book-keeping tool. Rust also does not
enforce the dreaded strict-aliasing rule&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; on its pointers.&lt;p&gt;On the other hand, Rust references are among the most constrained objects in any
language that I know of. A shared reference &lt;code&gt;&amp;&#39;a T&lt;/code&gt;, lasting for the lifetime
&lt;code&gt;&#39;a&lt;/code&gt;, satisfies:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Non-null, and well-aligned (like in C++).&lt;li&gt;Points to a valid, initialized &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; for the duration of &lt;code&gt;&#39;a&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; is never ever mutated for the duration of the reference: the compiler may
fold separate reads into one at will. Stronger still, no &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt; is reachable
from any thread while the reference is reachable.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;Stronger still are &lt;code&gt;&amp;&#39;a mut T&lt;/code&gt; references, sometimes called &lt;em&gt;unique&lt;/em&gt; references,
because in addition to being well-aligned and pointing to a valid &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; at all
times, no other reachable reference ever aliases it in any thread; this is
equivalent to a C &lt;code&gt;T* restrict&lt;/code&gt; pointer.&lt;p&gt;Unlike C++, which has two almost-identical pointer types, Rust&amp;rsquo;s two pointer
types provide either no guarantees or &lt;em&gt;all&lt;/em&gt; of them. The following &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt;
operations are all UB:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;null&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;null&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// for a reference to u32.

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;as_ptr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// the same memory. This would also be fine in C++!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;p2&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;y&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;as&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=wide-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#wide-pointers&gt;Wide Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;Rust also provides the slice types &lt;code&gt;&amp;[T]&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; (of which you get
mutable/immutable reference and pointer varieties) and dynamic trait object
types &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;dyn Tr&lt;/code&gt; (again, all four basic pointer types are available).&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;[T]&lt;/code&gt; is a &lt;code&gt;usize&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:6&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:6 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;6&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; length plus a pointer to that many &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt;s. The pointer
type of the slice specifies the guarantees on the pointed-to buffer. &lt;code&gt;*mut [T]&lt;/code&gt;,
for example, has no meaningful guarantees, but still contains the length&lt;sup id=fnref:7&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:7 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;7&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.
Note that the length is part of the pointer value, &lt;em&gt;not&lt;/em&gt; the pointee.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;dyn Tr&lt;/code&gt; is a trait object. For our purposes, it consists of a pointer to some
data plus a pointer to a static vtable. &lt;code&gt;*mut dyn Tr&lt;/code&gt; is technically a valid
type&lt;sup id=fnref:8&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:8 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;8&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. Overall, trait objects aren&amp;rsquo;t really relevant to this
post; they are rarely used this way in &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; settings.&lt;h2 id=weakening-the-guarantees&gt;&lt;a href=#weakening-the-guarantees&gt;Weakening the Guarantees&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Suppose we&amp;rsquo;re building some kind of data structure; in Rust, data structures
will need some sprinkling of &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt;, since they will need to shovel around
memory directly. Typically this is done using raw pointers, but it is preferable
to use the &lt;em&gt;least weakened&lt;/em&gt; pointer type to allow the compiler to perform
whatever optimizations it can.&lt;p&gt;There are a number of orthogonal guarantees on &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt; we might want
to relax:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Non-nullness.&lt;li&gt;Well-aligned-ness.&lt;li&gt;Validity and initialized-ness of the pointee.&lt;li&gt;Allocated-ness of the pointee (implied by initialized-ness).&lt;li&gt;Global uniqueness of an &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;h3 id=pointer-to-zst&gt;&lt;a href=#pointer-to-zst&gt;Pointer to ZST&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The last three of these properties are irrelevant for a zero-sized type. For
example, we can generate infinite &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut ()&lt;/code&gt; with no consequences:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;unique_unit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;static&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mh&gt;0x1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;as&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;())&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; 
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;We materialize a non-null, well-aligned pointer and reborrow it into a static
reference; because there is no data to point to, none of the usual worries about
the pointee itself apply. However, the pointer itself must still be non-null and
well-aligned; &lt;code&gt;0x1&lt;/code&gt; is not a valid address for an &lt;code&gt;&amp;[u32; 0]&lt;/code&gt;, but &lt;code&gt;0x4&lt;/code&gt;
is&lt;sup id=fnref:9&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:9 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;9&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This also applies to empty slices; in fact, the compiler will happily promote
the expression &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut []&lt;/code&gt; to an arbitrary lifetime:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;unique_empty&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;static&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=null-references&gt;&lt;a href=#null-references&gt;Null References&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;The most well-known manner of weakening is &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;&amp;amp;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. Rust guarantees that
this is ABI-compatible with a C pointer &lt;code&gt;const T*&lt;/code&gt;, with &lt;code&gt;Option::&amp;lt;&amp;amp;T&gt;::None&lt;/code&gt;
being a null pointer on the C side. This &amp;ldquo;null pointer optimization&amp;rdquo; applies to
any type recursively containing at least one &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;C&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;DoSomething&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nb&gt;Option&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;do_something&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;DoSomething&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;None&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// C will see a `NULL` as the argument.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:5&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The same effect can be achieved for a pointer type using the
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ptr/struct.NonNull.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;NonNull&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; standard
library type: &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;NonNull&amp;lt;T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is identical to &lt;code&gt;*mut T&lt;/code&gt;. This is most
beneficial for types which would otherwise contain a raw pointer:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:6&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;ptr&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;NonNull&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;cap&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=fm&gt;assert_eq!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size_of&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(),&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;size_of&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Option&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nb&gt;Vec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;u8&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;())&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:6&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=uninitialized-pointee&gt;&lt;a href=#uninitialized-pointee&gt;Uninitialized Pointee&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;No matter what, a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; cannot point to uninitialized memory, since the compiler
is free to assume it may read such references at any time with no consequences.&lt;p&gt;The following classic C pattern is verboten:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:7&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;initialize_foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Rust doesn&amp;rsquo;t provide any particularly easy ways to allocate memory without
initializing it, too, so this usually isn&amp;rsquo;t a problem. The
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html#method.assume_init_ref&gt;&lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
type can be used for safely allocating memory without initializing it, via
&lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit::uninit()&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This type acts as a sort of &amp;ldquo;optimization barrier&amp;rdquo; that prevents the compiler
from assuming the pointee is initialized. &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is a pointer to
potentially uninitialized but definitely allocated memory. It has the
same layout as &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt;, and Rust provides functions like &lt;code&gt;assume_init_ref()&lt;/code&gt; for
asserting that a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is definitely initialized. This assertion is
similar in consequence to dereferencing a raw pointer.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; should almost be viewed as pointer
types in their own right, since they can be converted to/from &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt;
under certain circumstances.&lt;p&gt;Because &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; is almost a &amp;ldquo;subtype&amp;rdquo; of &lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, we are
entitled&lt;sup id=fnref:10&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:10 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;10&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; to &amp;ldquo;forget&amp;rdquo; that the referent of a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; is
initialized converting it to a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. This makes sense because &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt;
is covariant&lt;sup id=fnref:11&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:11 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;11&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; in &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt;. However, this is not true of &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt;, since
it&amp;rsquo;s not covariant:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=nc&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;transmute&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;uninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Oops, `x` is now uninit!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;These types are useful for talking to C++ without giving up too many guarantees.
&lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;&amp;amp;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is an almost perfect model of a &lt;code&gt;const T*&lt;/code&gt;, under the
assumption that most pointers in C++ are valid most of the time.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; also finds use in working with raw blocks of memory, such as in
a &lt;code&gt;Vec&lt;/code&gt;-style growable slice:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:9&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;struct&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;SliceVec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// Backing memory. The first `len` elements of it are
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// known to be initialized, but no more than that.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kp&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;],&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=kt&gt;usize&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;SliceVec&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;push&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;: &lt;span class=nc&gt;T&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=fm&gt;assert!&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;());&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;[&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MaybeUninit&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=n&gt;new&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;    &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=bp&gt;self&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;len&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;+=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;1&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:9&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;h3 id=aliased-pointee&gt;&lt;a href=#aliased-pointee&gt;Aliased Pointee&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt; can never alias any other pointer, but is also the mechanism by which
we perform mutation. It can&amp;rsquo;t even alias with pointers that Rust can&amp;rsquo;t see; Rust
assumes no one else can touch this memory. Thus, &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt; is not an appropriate
analogue for &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;p&gt;Like with uninitialized memory, Rust provides a &amp;ldquo;barrier&amp;rdquo; wrapper type,
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cell/struct.UnsafeCell.html&gt;&lt;code&gt;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;.
&lt;code&gt;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is the &amp;ldquo;interior mutability&amp;rdquo; primitive, which permits us to
mutate through an &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; so long as concurrent reads and writes do not
occur. We may even convert it to a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut T&lt;/code&gt; when we&amp;rsquo;re sure we&amp;rsquo;re holding the
only reference.&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; forms the basis of the &lt;code&gt;Cell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;RefCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;Mutex&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;
types, each of which performs a sort of &amp;ldquo;dynamic borrow-checking&amp;rdquo;:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;Cell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; only permits direct loads and stores.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;RefCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; maintains a counter of references into it, which it uses to
dynamically determine if a mutable reference would be unique.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;Mutex&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, which is like &lt;code&gt;RefCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; but using concurrency primitives to
maintain uniqueness.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;Because of this, Rust must treat &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; as always aliasing, but
because we can mutate through it, it is a much closer analogue to a C++ &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&lt;/code&gt;.
However, because &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;T&lt;/code&gt; assumes the pointee is never mutated, it cannot coexist
with a &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; to the same memory, if mutation is performed through it.
The following is explicitly UB:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:10&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;0&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// This is ok; creating the reference to UnsafeCell does not
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// immediately trigger UB.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kd&gt;let&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;q&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;transmute&lt;/span&gt;::&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;_&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;UnsafeCell&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;i32&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;x&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;// But writing to it does!
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;q&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;get&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;().&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;write&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=mi&gt;42&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:10&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;Cell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; type is useful for non-aliasing references to plain-old-data types,
which tend to be &lt;code&gt;Copy&lt;/code&gt;. It allows us to perform mutation without having to
utter &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt;. For example, the correct type for a shared mutable buffer in
Rust is &lt;code&gt;&amp;[Cell&amp;lt;u8&gt;]&lt;/code&gt;, which can be freely &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;d,
without worrying about aliasing&lt;sup id=fnref:12&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:12 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;12&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;p&gt;This is most useful for sharing memory with another language, like C++, which
cannot respect Rust&amp;rsquo;s aliasing rules.&lt;h3 id=combined-barriers&gt;&lt;a href=#combined-barriers&gt;Combined Barriers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;To recap:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;Non-nullness can be disabled with &lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;&amp;amp;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Initialized-ness can be disabled with &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;Uniqueness can be disabled with &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;blockquote id=warning:1 class=warning warning&gt;&lt;a href=#warning:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;warning&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;There is no way to disable alignment and validity restrictions: references
must always be aligned and have a valid lifetime attached. If these are
unachievable, raw pointers are your only option.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;We can combine these various &amp;ldquo;weakenings&amp;rdquo; to produce aligned, lifetime-bound
references to data with different properties. For example:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is as close as we can get to a C++ &lt;code&gt;T&amp;&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;&amp;amp;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is a like a raw pointer, but to initialized memory.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;Option&amp;lt;&amp;amp;mut MaybeUninit&amp;lt;T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is like a raw pointer, but with alignment,
aliasing, and lifetime requirements.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;&amp;[T]&gt;&lt;/code&gt; permits us to mutate the pointer to the buffer and its
length, but not the values it points to themselves.&lt;li&gt;&lt;code&gt;UnsafeCell&amp;lt;&amp;[UnsafeCell&amp;lt;T&gt;]&gt;&lt;/code&gt; lets us mutate both the buffer and its actual
pointer/length.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;Interestingly, there is no equivalent to a C++ raw pointer: there is no way
to create a guaranteed-aligned pointer without a designated lifetime&lt;sup id=fnref:13&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:13 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;13&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.&lt;h2 id=other-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#other-pointers&gt;Other Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Rust and C++ have many other pointer types, such as smart pointers. However, in
both languages, both are built in terms of these basic pointer types. Hopefully
this article is a useful reference for anyone writing &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; abstraction that
wishes to avoid using raw pointers when possible.&lt;div class=footnotes role=doc-endnotes&gt;&lt;hr&gt;&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li id=fn:1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Except in Go, which synthesizes vtables &lt;em&gt;on the fly&lt;/em&gt;. Story for another day.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:1 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:2&gt;&lt;p&gt;It is, apparently, a little-known fact that constructing unaligned pointers,
but then never dereferencing them, is still UB in C++. C++ could, for
example, store information in the lower bits of such a pointer. The
in-memory representation of a pointer is actually unspecified!&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:2 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:3&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is useful when paired with the Rust &lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;*const T&gt;::read_unaligned()&lt;/code&gt;
function, which can be compiled down to a normal load on architectures that
do not have alignment restrictions, like x86_64 and aarch64.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:3 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:4&gt;&lt;p&gt;Another story for another time.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:4 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:5&gt;&lt;p&gt;Comparable to the C++20 &lt;a href=https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/span&gt;&lt;code&gt;std::span&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
type.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:5 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:6&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;usize&lt;/code&gt; is Rust&amp;rsquo;s machine word type, compare &lt;code&gt;std::uintptr_t&lt;/code&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:6 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:7&gt;&lt;p&gt;The length of a &lt;code&gt;*mut [T]&lt;/code&gt; can be accessed via the unstable
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.pointer.html#method.len-1&gt;&lt;code&gt;&amp;lt;*mut [T]&gt;::len()&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
method.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:7 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:8&gt;&lt;p&gt;It is also not a type I have encountered enough to have much knowledge on.
For example, I don&amp;rsquo;t actually know if the vtable half of a &lt;code&gt;*mut dyn Tr&lt;/code&gt;
must always be valid or not; I suspect the answer is &amp;ldquo;no&amp;rdquo;, but I couldn&amp;rsquo;t
find a citation for this.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:8 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:9&gt;&lt;p&gt;Note that you &lt;em&gt;cannot&lt;/em&gt; continue to use a reference to freed, zero-sized
memory. This subtle distinction is called out in
&lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ptr/index.html#safety&gt;https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ptr/index.html#safety&lt;/a&gt;.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:9 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:10&gt;&lt;p&gt;Currently, a &lt;code&gt;transmute&lt;/code&gt; must be used to perform this operation, but I see
no reason way this would permit us to perform an illegal mutation without
uttering &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; a second time. In particular, &lt;code&gt;MaybeUninit::assume_init_read()&lt;/code&gt;,
which could be used to perform illegal copies, is an &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; function.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:10 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:11&gt;&lt;p&gt;A covariant type &lt;code&gt;Cov&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is once where, if &lt;code&gt;T&lt;/code&gt; is a subtype of &lt;code&gt;U&lt;/code&gt;, then
&lt;code&gt;Cov&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is a subtype of &lt;code&gt;Cov&amp;lt;U&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. This isn&amp;rsquo;t particularly noticeable in
Rust, where the only subtyping relationships are &lt;code&gt;&amp;&#39;a T&lt;/code&gt; subtypes &lt;code&gt;&amp;&#39;b T&lt;/code&gt;
when &lt;code&gt;&#39;a&lt;/code&gt; outlives &lt;code&gt;&#39;b&lt;/code&gt;, but is nonetheless important for advanced type
design.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:11 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:12&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;code&gt;Cell&amp;lt;T&gt;&lt;/code&gt; does not provide synchronization; you still need locks to share it
between threads.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:12 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;li id=fn:13&gt;&lt;p&gt;I have previously proposed a sort of &lt;code&gt;&#39;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; or &lt;code&gt;&#39;!&lt;/code&gt; &amp;ldquo;lifetime&amp;rdquo; that is
intended to be the lifetime of dangling references (a bit of an oxymoron).
This would allow us to express this concept, but I need to flesh out the
concept more.&amp;#160;&lt;a href=#fnref:13 class=footnote-backref role=doc-backlink&gt;&amp;#8617;&amp;#xfe0e;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;&lt;/div&gt;</content>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <title>Move Constructors in Rust:
Is it possible?
</title>
    <link href="/2021/04/26/move-ctors"/>
    <updated>2021-04-26T00:00:00+00:00</updated>
    <id>/2021/04/26/move-ctors</id>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I&amp;rsquo;ve been told I need to write this idea down &amp;ndash; I figure this one&amp;rsquo;s a good
enough excuse to start one of them programming blogs.&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;TL;DR&lt;/em&gt; You &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt; move-constructors the Rust! It requires a few macros but isn&amp;rsquo;t
much more outlandish than the &lt;code&gt;async&lt;/code&gt; pinning state of the art. A prototype of
this idea is implemented in my &lt;a href=https://crates.io/crates/moveit&gt;&lt;code&gt;moveit&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/a&gt; crate.&lt;h2 id=the-interop-problem&gt;&lt;a href=#the-interop-problem&gt;The Interop Problem&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Rust is the best contender for a C++ replacement; this is not even a question at
this point&lt;sup id=fnref:1&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:1 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. It&amp;rsquo;s a high-level language that provides users with
appropriate controls over memory, while also being memory safe. Rust
accomplishes by codifying C++ norms and customs around ownership and lifetimes
into its type system.&lt;p&gt;Rust has an ok&lt;sup id=fnref:2&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:2 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; FFI story for C:&lt;div markdown=1 class=code-multicol&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:1&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-c highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;into_rust&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;into_c&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;into_rust&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:1&gt;C&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:2&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;C&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;into_c&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;();&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=cp&gt;#[no_mangle]&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;extern&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;C&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;into_rust&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;unsafe&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;into_c&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:2&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Calling into either of these functions from the Rust or C side will recurse
infinitely across the FFI boundary. The &lt;code&gt;extern &#34;C&#34; {}&lt;/code&gt; item on the Rust side
declares C symbols, much like a function prototype in C would; the
&lt;code&gt;extern &#34;C&#34; fn&lt;/code&gt; is a Rust function with the C calling convention, and the
&lt;code&gt;#[no_mangle]&lt;/code&gt; annotation ensures that &lt;code&gt;recurse_into_rust&lt;/code&gt; is the name that the
linker sees for this function. The link works out, we run our program, and the
stack overflows. All is well.&lt;p&gt;But this is C. We want to rewrite all of the world&amp;rsquo;s C++ in Rust, but
unfortunately that&amp;rsquo;s going to take about a decade, so in the meantime new Rust
must be able to call existing C++, and vise-versa. C++ has a much crazier ABI,
and while Rust gives us the minimum of passing control to C, libraries like
[&lt;code&gt;cxx&lt;/code&gt;] need to provide a bridge on top of this for Rust and C++ to talk to each
other.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, the C++ and Rust object models are, a priori, incompatible.
In Rust, &lt;em&gt;every object&lt;/em&gt; may be &amp;ldquo;moved&amp;rdquo; via &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt;, whereas in C++ this only
holds for types satisfying &lt;code&gt;std::is_trivially_moveable&lt;/code&gt;&lt;sup id=fnref:3&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:3 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;.
Some types require calling a &lt;em&gt;move constructor&lt;/em&gt;, or may not be moveable at all!&lt;p&gt;Even more alarming, C++ types are permited to take the address of the location
where they are being constructed: the &lt;code&gt;this&lt;/code&gt; pointer is always accessible,
allowing easy creation of self-referential types:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:3&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;class&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Cyclic&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;public&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;Cyclic&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; 
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// Ensure that copy and move construction respect the self-pointer
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// invariant:
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;Cyclic&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;const&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Cyclic&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;amp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;    &lt;span class=k&gt;new&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;this&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;Cyclic&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=c1&gt;// snip: Analogous for other rule-of-five constructors.
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=c1&gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;private&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;Cyclic&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;ptr_&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=o&gt;=&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=k&gt;this&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;};&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:3&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The solution [&lt;code&gt;cxx&lt;/code&gt;] and other FFI strategies take is to box up complex C++
objects across the FFI boundary; a &lt;code&gt;std::unique_ptr&amp;lt;Cyclic&gt;&lt;/code&gt; (perhaps
reinterpreted as a &lt;code&gt;Box&lt;/code&gt; on the Rust side) can be passed around without needing
to call move constructors. The heap allocation is a performance
regression that scares off potential Rust users, so it&amp;rsquo;s not a viable solution.&lt;p&gt;We can do better.&lt;h3 id=notation-and-terminology&gt;&lt;a href=#notation-and-terminology&gt;Notation and Terminology&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo;Move&amp;rdquo; is a very, very overloaded concept across Rust and C++, and many people
have different names for what this means. So that we don&amp;rsquo;t get confused, we&amp;rsquo;ll
establish some terminology to use throughout the rest of the article.&lt;p&gt;A &lt;em&gt;destructive move&lt;/em&gt; is a Rust-style move, which has the following properties:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;It does not create a new object; from the programmer&amp;rsquo;s perspective, the object
has simply changed address.&lt;li&gt;The move is implemented by a call to &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt;; no user code is run.&lt;li&gt;The moved-from value becomes inaccessible and its destructor does not run.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;A destructive move, in effect, is completely invisible to the user&lt;sup id=fnref:4&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:4 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;, and
the Rust compiler can emit as many or as few of them as it likes. We will refer
to this as a &amp;ldquo;destructive move&amp;rdquo;, a &amp;ldquo;Rust move&amp;rdquo;, or a &amp;ldquo;blind, &lt;code&gt;memcpy&lt;/code&gt; move&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;A &lt;em&gt;copying move&lt;/em&gt; is a C++-style move, which has the following properties:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;It creates a new, distinct object at a new memory location.&lt;li&gt;The move is implemented by calling a user-provided function that initializes
the new object.&lt;li&gt;The moved-from value is still accessible but in an &amp;ldquo;unspecified but valid
state&amp;rdquo;. Its destructor is run once the current scope ends.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;A copying move is just a weird copy operation that mutates the copied-from
object. C++ compilers &lt;em&gt;may&lt;/em&gt; elide calls to the move constructor in certain
situations, but calling it usually requires the programmer to explicitly ask for
it. From a Rust perspective, this is as if &lt;code&gt;Clone::clone()&lt;/code&gt; took &lt;code&gt;&amp;amp;mut self&lt;/code&gt; as
an argument. We will refer to this as a &amp;ldquo;copying move&amp;rdquo;, a &amp;ldquo;nondestructive move&amp;rdquo;,
a &amp;ldquo;C++ move&amp;rdquo;, or, metonymically, as a &amp;ldquo;move constructor&amp;rdquo;.&lt;h2 id=pinned-pointers&gt;&lt;a href=#pinned-pointers&gt;Pinned Pointers&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;As part of introducing support for stackless coroutines&lt;sup id=fnref:5&gt;&lt;a href=#fn:5 class=footnote-ref role=doc-noteref&gt;5&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;
(aka &lt;code&gt;async&lt;/code&gt;/&lt;code&gt;await&lt;/code&gt;), Rust had to provide some kind of supported for immobile
types through &lt;em&gt;pinned pointers&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;p&gt;The [&lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt;] type is a wraper around a pointer type, such as &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;&amp;amp;mut i32&gt;&lt;/code&gt; or
&lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;Box&amp;lt;ComplexObject&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt;. &lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt; provides the following guarantee to unsafe
code:&lt;blockquote id=ref:1 class=ref ref math&gt;&lt;a href=#ref:1&gt;&lt;span class=chip&gt;reference&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;p&gt;Given &lt;code&gt;p: Pin&amp;lt;P&gt;&lt;/code&gt; for &lt;code&gt;P: Deref&lt;/code&gt;, and &lt;code&gt;P::Target: !Unpin&lt;/code&gt;, the pointee object
&lt;code&gt;*p&lt;/code&gt; will always be found at that address, and no other object will use that
address until &lt;code&gt;*p&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s destructor is called.&lt;/blockquote&gt;&lt;p&gt;In a way, &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;P&gt;&lt;/code&gt; is a witness to a sort of critical section: once constructed,
that memory is &lt;em&gt;pinned&lt;/em&gt; until the destructor runs. The &lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt; documentation goes
into deep detail about when and why this matters, and how unsafe code can
take advantage of this guarantee to provide a safe interface.&lt;p&gt;The key benefit is that unsafe code can create self-references behind the pinned
pointer, without worrying about them breaking when a destructive move occurs.
C++ deals with this kind of type by allowing move/copy constructors to observe
the new object&amp;rsquo;s address and fix up any self references as necessary.&lt;p&gt;Our progress so far: C++ types can be immoveable from Rust&amp;rsquo;s
perspective. They need to be pinned in some memory location: either on the heap
as a &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;Box&amp;lt;T&gt;&gt;&lt;/code&gt;, or on the stack (somehow; keep reading). Our program is now
to reconcile C++ move constructors with this standard library object that
explicitly prevents moves. Easy, right;&lt;h2 id=constructors&gt;&lt;a href=#constructors&gt;Constructors&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;C++ constructors are a peculiar thing. Unlike Rust&amp;rsquo;s &lt;code&gt;Foo::new()&lt;/code&gt;-style
factories, or even constructors in dynamic languages like Java, C++ constructors
are unique in that they construct a value in a &lt;em&gt;specific location&lt;/em&gt;. This concept
is best illustraced by the &lt;a href=https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/new#Placement_new&gt;&lt;em&gt;placement-&lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt; operation:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:4&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=kt&gt;void&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;MakeString&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;std&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;*&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;out&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;new&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;out&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;)&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;std&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;string&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=s&gt;&amp;#34;mwahahaha&amp;#34;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:4&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;Placement-&lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt; is one of those exotic C++ operations you only ever run into
deep inside fancy library code. Unlike &lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt;, which triggers a trip into the
allocator, placement-&lt;code&gt;new&lt;/code&gt; simply calls the constructor of your type with &lt;code&gt;this&lt;/code&gt;
set to the argument in parentheses. This is the &amp;ldquo;most raw&amp;rdquo; way you can call a
constructor: given a memory location and arguments, construct a new value.&lt;p&gt;In Rust, a method call &lt;code&gt;foo.bar()&lt;/code&gt; is really syntax sugar for &lt;code&gt;Foo::bar(foo)&lt;/code&gt;.
This is not the case in C++; a member function has an altogether different type,
but some simple template metaprogramming can flatten it back into a regular old
free function:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:5&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;class&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:7&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;Ctor&lt;/code&gt; is a &lt;em&gt;constructing closure&lt;/em&gt;. information for constructing a value of type &lt;code&gt;Output&lt;/code&gt; which will live at the
location &lt;code&gt;*dest&lt;/code&gt;. The &lt;code&gt;Ctor::ctor()&lt;/code&gt; function performs in-place construction,
making &lt;code&gt;*dest&lt;/code&gt; become initialized.&lt;p&gt;A &lt;code&gt;Ctor&lt;/code&gt; is not the constructor itself; rather, it is more like a &lt;code&gt;Future&lt;/code&gt; or
an &lt;code&gt;Iterator&lt;/code&gt; which contain the necessary captured values to perform the
operation. A Rust type that is constructed using a &lt;code&gt;Ctor&lt;/code&gt; would have functions
like this:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:8&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;impl&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;MyType&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:8&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;The &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt; markers serve distinct purposes:&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;It is an &lt;code&gt;unsafe trait&lt;/code&gt;, because &lt;code&gt;*dest&lt;/code&gt; must be initialized when &lt;code&gt;ctor()&lt;/code&gt;
returns.&lt;li&gt;It has an &lt;code&gt;unsafe fn&lt;/code&gt;, because, in order to respect the &lt;a href=https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/pin/index.html#drop-guarantee&gt;&lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt; drop guarantees&lt;/a&gt;,
&lt;code&gt;*dest&lt;/code&gt; must either be freshly allocated or have had its destructor run just
prior.&lt;/ul&gt;&lt;p&gt;Since we are constructing into &lt;code&gt;Pin&lt;/code&gt;ned memory, the &lt;code&gt;Ctor&lt;/code&gt; implementation can
use the address of &lt;code&gt;*dest&lt;/code&gt; as part of the construction procedure and assume that
that pointer will not suddenly dangle because of a move. This recovers our C++
behavior of &amp;ldquo;&lt;code&gt;this&lt;/code&gt;-stability&amp;rdquo;.&lt;p&gt;Unfortunately, &lt;code&gt;Ctor&lt;/code&gt; is covered in &lt;code&gt;unsafe&lt;/code&gt;, and doesn&amp;rsquo;t even allocate storage
for us. &lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:13&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;This is &lt;em&gt;truly&lt;/em&gt; analogous to C++ stack initialization, such as &lt;code&gt;Foo val(args);&lt;/code&gt;,

bee &lt;code&gt;Foo&amp;&lt;/code&gt;. This isn&amp;rsquo;t much of an obstacle, and just means that &lt;code&gt;Foo&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s API on
the Rust side needs to use &lt;code&gt;Pin&amp;lt;&amp;amp;mut Self&gt;&lt;/code&gt; for its methods.&lt;h2 id=the-return-value-optimization&gt;&lt;a href=#the-return-value-optimization&gt;The Return Value Optimization&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Now we go to build our Foo-returning function and are immediately hit with a
roadblock:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:14&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-rust highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;fn&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;make_foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;-&amp;gt; &lt;span class=nc&gt;Pin&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;lt;&amp;amp;&amp;#39;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=na&gt;wat&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=k&gt;mut&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=o&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;

&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;foo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=w&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:14&gt;Rust&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;What is the lifetime &lt;code&gt;&#39;wat&lt;/code&gt;? This is just returning a pointer to the current
stack frame, which is no good. In C++ (ignoring fussy defails about move
semantics), NRVO would kick in and &lt;code&gt;val&lt;/code&gt; would be constructed &amp;ldquo;in the return
slot&amp;rdquo;:&lt;div class=codeblock id=code:15&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;code class=&#34;language-cpp highlight&#34;&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=nf&gt;MakeFoo&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;()&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=p&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=n&gt;Foo&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;val&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=n&gt;args&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;  &lt;span class=k&gt;return&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class=n&gt;val&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class=line&gt;&lt;span class=cl&gt;&lt;span class=p&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/code&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;div class=codeblock-buttons&gt;&lt;a class=&#34;codeblock-button codeblock-anchor&#34; href=#code:15&gt;C++&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href=https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/copy_elision&gt;&lt;em&gt;Return value optimization&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/a&gt; (and the related &lt;em&gt;named return value
optimization&lt;/em&gt;) allow C++ to elide copies when constructing return values. Instead of
constructing &lt;code&gt;val&lt;/code&gt; on &lt;code&gt;MakeFoo&lt;/code&gt;&amp;rsquo;s stack and then copying it into the ABI&amp;rsquo;s
return location (be that a register like &lt;code&gt;rax&lt;/code&gt; or somewhere in the caller&amp;rsquo;s
stack frame), the value is constructed directly in that location, skipping the
copy. Rust itself performs some limited RVO, though its style of move
semantics makes this a bit less visible.&lt;p&gt;Rust does not give us a good way of accessing the return slot directly, for good
reason: it need not have an address! Rust returns all types that look roughly
like a single integer in a register (on modern ABIs), and registers don&amp;rsquo;t have
addresses. C++ ABIs typically solve this by making types which are
&amp;ldquo;sufficiently complicated&amp;rdquo; (usually when they are not trivially moveable) get
